Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil sites, strikes reported on Yemen's Aden
Unknown

Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil sites, strikes reported on Yemen's Aden
Oct 24 - Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks at Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war, Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the Houthi reports, and it was not immediately clear if the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif on Saturday.
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom. REUTERS

German man arrested for allegedly driving American teen girl to die by suicide, prosecutors say
German police, acting on an FBI tip-off, arrested an alleged online sadist accused of driving a 14-year-old U.S. girl to hang herself, prosecutors said Friday.
The 18-year-old German was arrested in Hamburg on Thursday, accused of being the indirect perpetrator of murder and grievous bodily harm.
FBI Indianapolis Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O'Malley said in a statement that their office worked with the Fort Wayne Police Department to provide information to the German police to help advance the arrest. The Fort Wayne Police Department said in a statement that its Homicide Unit identified a suspect who contributed to the juvenile's death.
"Anyone who targets or exploits a child should understand this: There is no safe haven from justice. It doesn't matter where you live or where you try to hide. The FBI will work with our partners around the world to find you and hold you accountable," O'Malley said.
The suspect was linked to an online group called "Nefarious Maniac Kult" or "NMK," part of a global network known by the labels "764" or "COM," the Hamburg public prosecutor's office said.
From September 2024 to September 2025, the FBI has seen a 300% increase in nihilistic violent extremism cases — many involving the 764 group, said FBI Director Kash Patel. The group 764 lacks a specific ideology, but members openly encourage self-harm and violence and encourage victims to produce videos documenting acts of self-harm or child sexual abuse material.
Between September and October, the suspect, then aged 17, allegedly "exerted influence" via the social network Discord over the girl from Indiana state whom prosecutors described as "psychologically fragile".
The suspect allegedly pressured the girl to cut herself and write the letters "NMK" on a wall in her own blood, and had her send him video recordings of these acts. A few days later, she hanged herself in her bedroom, prosecutors said.
The suspect allegedly sought a video recording of her death, hoping to gain status within the group or to secure entry into it.

Bardella wins 99% backing as Le Pen gears up for French presidential race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:19:15 UTC
02:19:15 KST

With the party leadership settled, all eyes are now on Marine Le Pen, who is preparing to lay out her vision for France at a major National Rally gathering in
Jordan Bardella has been overwhelmingly re-elected leader of France's National Rally (RN), securing 98.98% of the vote in an uncontested leadership election.
The result was announced on Saturday, the opening day of the party's two-day congress in Orléans, as the RN seeks to consolidate its position ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
Bardella received 75,497 votes, with 779 blank ballots cast, according to RN lawmaker Yoann Gillet, who oversaw the election. Turnout among party members reached nearly 68%, with electronic voting taking place between 21 September and 22 October.
Ahead of the official announcement, Bardella thanked party activists and urged them to rally behind Marine Le Pen's presidential ambitions.
"Once again, I am going to need you (...) to lead Marine Le Pen to the Élysée," he told supporters.
His re-election reinforces the division of roles between the RN's two leading figures, who have presented themselves as a "winning ticket" for the 2027 elections.
Under that strategy, Le Pen is expected to seek the presidency, while Bardella is positioning himself as a potential prime minister should the party secure a parliamentary majority.
Le Pen is due to address thousands of supporters on Sunday, when she is expected to set out the next phase of her presidential campaign.
Thousands protest against National Rally congress
The congress was accompanied by a large counter-demonstration, with thousands of protesters taking to the streets of Orléans on Saturday to voice their opposition to the RN.
Authorities estimated the turnout at around 11,000, while organisers put the figure at 26,000. The march, which began around midday, remained peaceful.
Officials had previously said they expected up to 30,000 demonstrators.
Several prominent left-wing politicians and trade union leaders joined the protest, including Bally Bagayoko, mayor of Saint-Denis and a leading figure in La France insoumise.
Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure accused the RN of contributing to what he described as a "poisonous, racist and xenophobic climate".
CGT trade union leader Sophie Binet also criticised the party, declaring that "there is no worse enemy of working men and women than the far right".
The demonstration comes amid heightened political and social tensions in France, following a renewed wave of protests and serious violence a week earlier.
Saturday's turnout was lower than the more than 50,000 people who demonstrated against a National Front congress in Strasbourg in March 1997, one of the largest protests against the party in its history.
Marine Le Pen prepares major presidential speech
Beyond Bardella's re-election, the Orléans congress is intended to showcase the RN's unity and political programme, six months before the presidential election.
Marine Le Pen is now preparing to lay out her vision for France at a major National Rally gathering in Orléans on Sunday ahead of the 2027 presidential election.
According to her entourage, the address will be a "high-calibre" speech centred on the theme of "rebirth".
The party has already begun presenting its economic and social priorities ahead of the election.
Earlier this month, the RN unveiled its alternative budget, challenging the government's fiscal proposals.
Le Pen also placed housing and the cost of living at the centre of her political agenda during a speech in Hénin-Beaumont on 14 September.
Sunday's address is expected to offer further details of the RN's strategy as it seeks to turn its electoral support into a victory in the 2027 presidential race.

Macklemore says ‘being human is not complicated’ as sold-out Gaza benefit tour opens
TEHRAN — American rapper Macklemore returned to the stage Thursday night at Colorado’s Red Rocks Amphitheatre with an explicit message of solidarity for Palestine.
Addressing a packed crowd in his first performance since being dropped from Ed Sheeran’s stadium tour, Macklemore condemned Israel’s ongoing genocidal campaign in Gaza, telling the audience, “I say, free Palestine! Being a human being in this moment is not complicated.”
During the set, the rapper broadened his remarks to address Western-backed oppression across Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Lebanon, and Haiti, alongside brutal ICE enforcement actions in the U.S.
The Red Rocks appearance served as a launchpad for his independent Free Palestine benefit tour, set to open in Dublin on October 26.
The momentum traces back to a September 4 concert at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium, where Macklemore declared “I say, free Palestine!” and performed “Hind’s Hall,” his protest anthem dedicated to Hind Rajab, the five-year-old girl brutally killed by Israeli forces in Gaza.
That performance sparked immediate retribution from pro-Israel networks, leading to his exclusion from Sheeran’s tour. Following intense pressure from Zionist advocacy groups such as the Israeli-American Council, New England Patriots owner and billionaire Robert Kraft led a campaign demanding his removal.
Venue owners issued an ultimatum to tour promoter Messina Touring Group: remove Macklemore or forfeit access to major American stadiums.
Rather than apologizing, Macklemore answered by announcing independent European arena dates. All three upcoming shows, in Dublin, Paris, and London, sold out within minutes.
Proceeds are slated for 12 humanitarian relief organizations operating in Gaza, including the Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, and UNRWA USA. He also committed his estimated $1 million in net earnings from Sheeran’s tour to Palestinian relief efforts.
The institutional purging of Macklemore triggered an immediate rift within the Western entertainment industry.
During a September 19 performance in Philadelphia, Sheeran read a scripted statement from a teleprompter, calling the situation in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable” while carefully avoiding any direct attribution of responsibility to Israel.
The highly stage-managed address drew swift ridicule and anger on social media, where critics blasted the pop star as spineless for delivering a carefully sanitized PR apology to protect his corporate tour revenues rather than taking a stand against genocidal violence.
Four supporting acts, including Irish singer Aaron Rowe, Beoga, Finneas, and Lukas Graham, resigned from Sheeran’s tour in direct protest of the corporate blacklist.
Condemning the corporate censorship, Rowe publicly called out the billionaire stadium owners for attempting to enforce political compliance, declaring that artists cannot stand by while powerful interests use their financial leverage to suppress voices speaking up against genocide.

Kazakhstan’s AI ambitions draw global media attention
CNBC covered Kazakhstan’s ambitions to become an AI computing hub serving Europe, drawing attention to its energy resources and plans to expand data center infrastructure, including the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz.
The South China Morning Post focused on Huang’s promotion of sovereign AI and his call for Kazakhstan to turn its “energy into intelligence” by developing domestic computing capabilities.
International coverage also extended to startups with Kazakh roots. Bloomberg, in an article republished by Yahoo Finance, reported that NVIDIA and investment firm TCV had invested in Higgsfield, an AI video generation company headquartered in San Francisco with most of its engineering talent based in Kazakhstan. Variety also covered the investment.
In an exclusive interview with 24KZ correspondent Adil Baltabayev, Huang estimated that a five-gigawatt computing hub could attract $250 billion in investment and generate $1 trillion in economic activity.
According to Huang, 300 megawatts of power capacity have already been allocated, while the long-term vision envisages expansion to five gigawatts.
“Each gigawatt is $50 billion, and Deputy Prime Minister Madiyev has declared that the data center valley will eventually have five gigawatts. Five gigawatts is $250 billion of investment, and it will generate a trillion dollars of economy,” Huang said.
Miras Zhiyenbayev, a foreign policy expert and adviser to the chairman of the board for international affairs at Maqsut Narikbayev University, said realizing this potential would require cleaner energy, faster infrastructure development, integration of NVIDIA technologies and investment in local talent.
“We need a new generation of local engineers and strategists to run these systems,” he said.
Zhiyenbayev emphasized that developing education alongside computing infrastructure would help Kazakhstan secure lasting economic benefits and strengthen its geopolitical influence.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev had praised the practical value of recommendations offered by NVIDIA co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang.

Three days before election, tens of thousands rally in Tel Aviv for October 7 state inquiry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:14:18 UTC
02:14:18 KST

Tens of thousands of Israelis gathered Saturday evening at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv, just three days before the October 27 election, demanding the establishment of an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre.
The rally, titled "For Them," was organized by the October Council, a group representing former hostages, bereaved families and survivors of the attack. Among those attending were Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot, Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman and Democrats head Yair Golan. 
The demonstration brought together families who lost loved ones in the massacre, relatives of hostages murdered in Gaza and survivors who returned from Hamas captivity. The organizers are demanding an official, independent investigation into the circumstances that allowed the October 7 attack to unfold and the failures surrounding Israel's response.
Participants included Elchanan Danino, father of Ori Danino, who was murdered in Hamas captivity; Zoli Gyongyoshi, the uncle who adopted former hostage Abigail Idan and her two siblings after their parents, Roy and Smadar Idan, were murdered on October 7; and former hostage Danielle Aloni.
Also attending were Maly Zander, whose daughter Noa was murdered at the Nova music festival; Sigal and Menashe Mansouri, whose daughters Norel and Roya were killed at the festival; Vicky Cohen, mother of former hostage Nimrod Cohen; and Yael Adar, whose son Tamir was abducted and murdered.
Other participants included Omer Ohana, whose partner Sagi Golan was killed fighting in Kibbutz Be'eri on October 7; Tomer Zisser, whose husband Ilay was killed that day; Tamar Edri, whose brother Ido was murdered at Nova; Noga Baram, whose brother Neta was killed at Nahal Oz; and Eyal Eshel, father of IDF surveillance soldier Roni Eshel, who was killed in the command center at the Nahal Oz military base.
Rafi Ben Shitrit, father of Elroi Ben Shitrit, who was killed in fighting at Nahal Oz and is ranked second on Yisrael Beytenu's Knesset list, also attended.
Ahead of the gathering, the October Council sent an urgent letter to Israel Police Commissioner Danny Levy, warning of alleged plans by individuals linked to coalition parties to disrupt the demonstration.
The families said they had received information from sources they considered credible, including leaders of parties contesting the election, suggesting that individuals connected directly or indirectly to coalition parties were preparing to provoke disturbances, introduce unauthorized signs and flags and undermine the rally's message. The allegations were not independently verified.
The organizers called for an increased police presence and preventive measures to stop any attempt to disrupt the gathering. They stressed that the rally's purpose was to demand accountability and an independent investigation into October 7, rather than allow provocations to overshadow the families' call for answers.

TIRANA - Albanian riot police used tear gas, water cannons and rubber bullets to disperse protesters who threw rocks at officers and started a fire at the door of the agriculture ministry in the capital, Tirana, on Oct 24.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities this month.

The protesters gathered on Oct 24 around 2pm in front of the education ministry, and threw stones and rocks at police.
The police pushed them away, and they dispersed to several locations in the city.
“Albanians have woken up,” said 28-year-old protester Daniel Tahiri, who described the government as a “dictatorship with the clothes of democracy”.

Around 410,000 people took part in demonstrations across France, according to the interior ministry, while the CGT trade union put the nationwide turnout at 800,000, as clashes with police, looting and vandalism were reported in several cities.
The Loire-Atlantique prefecture reported on Saturday that shops were being looted in Nantes, and said six people had been arrested.
In Grenoble, the Isere prefecture said around 400 masked individuals dressed in black bloc attire were causing damage and had attacked police with mortars and projectiles. Police were attempting to apprehend those involved and restore order.
The demonstration in Grenoble was organised by the CGT trade union and the Yellow Vest movement, according to the prefecture.
In Bordeaux, the Gironde prefecture said “hostile groups” were targeting security forces, throwing projectiles and setting up barricades at Place de la Bourse. It urged residents to avoid the area.
In Lille, projectiles were thrown at riot police as tensions escalated, according to journalists reporting from the scene. Police used water cannons against demonstrators.
The Nord prefecture estimated that 15,000 people had joined the demonstration in Lille and called on participants to leave the area peacefully.
Authorities reported 30 arrests in the Nord department by 1300 GMT, including 25 in Lille.
Police also seized numerous weapons, including hunting knives, butterfly knives and airsoft guns.
Curfews for unaccompanied minors in designated areas of Lille, Denain, Douai and Wattignies were extended until Monday morning and expanded to parts of Marly and Valenciennes.
The measures run from 1800 GMT to 0400 GMT and apply from Friday evening through Monday morning, according to a prefectural order published Friday.
In Nice, the Alpes-Maritimes prefecture said 40 people had been arrested by 1430 GMT.
In Paris, the police prefecture estimated that 110,000 people had joined the demonstration, matching the figure reported for the previous week.
Police later used water cannons against demonstrators in the capital. Individuals also vandalised the windows of a car dealership on Cours de Vincennes.
Authorities reported that more than 3,000 checks had been carried out in Paris and 65 people had been arrested. Trade union turnout figures for the demonstrations in Paris and Lille were not yet available.
In Marseille, tensions rose during a confrontation between police and demonstrators, with officers using tear gas. Firefighters also extinguished a fire near the march, according to local media.
Police used tear gas as a demonstration moved toward Place de la Republique in Rennes, while the Rhone prefecture estimated that 10,000 people had gathered in Lyon.
In Lyon, the prefecture reported 29 arrests by 1600 GMT, including people suspected of weapons and drug possession and participation in an unlawful gathering, according to local newspaper Le Progres.
No demonstrations had been authorised in the city.
In Chambery, clashes broke out between police and groups described by the Savoie prefecture as violent, as demonstrators blocked the city's urban motorway.
In Orleans, where the National Rally (RN) was holding its congress, the mayor announced 12 arrests following the day's demonstrations.
The city hall separately reported three arrests linked to the demonstration against the RN and 10 arrests outside the urban area.

She made aliyah at 16 - today, she's teaching the next generation about AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:10:15 UTC
02:10:15 KST

Using AI to solve real-world problems? That’s the aim of scientist Prof. Claudia V. Goldman.
Since July 2024, she has been an associate professor in the Data Science Department at the Hebrew University Business School in Jerusalem.
After making aliyah from Buenos Aires, Claudia graduated from Jerusalem’s Mae Boyer High School in 1986, followed by army service and three academic degrees from the Hebrew University: a BSc in Computer Science, Mathematics, and Electronics in 1991; an MSc in Computer Science in 1993; and a PhD in Computer Science in 1999, under the direction of Prof. Jeff Rosenschein, an award-winning scholar.
From 1999 to 2005, Goldman held research positions at Bar-Ilan University, the University of Massachusetts Amherst, and the University of Haifa.
She then transitioned into industry, spending three years as a team leader at Samsung Telecom Research in Herzliya, followed by 15 years as a research scientist in the Research and Development Organization of General Motors in Herzliya.
Claudia is a distinguished inventor with a remarkable track record of 24 patents. Over the years, she has published more than 50 academic papers.
She is married to a colleague, Prof. Roy Shenhar, a full professor at the Institute of Chemistry at the Hebrew University.
Claudia answers our most pressing questions
The Magazine recently sat down with Claudia in her Hebrew University office.
Note: Books could be written in response to some of the following questions. For this article, the focus is on brief answers.
Stanley Druckenmiller, a contributor to The Wall Street Journal, was challenged by readers for using AI in a recent article. He admitted to using the technology, responding, "I’m not embarrassed by it."
How do you deal with AI in your classroom?
I am clear when I want my students to use AI tools and for what purpose. When these tools are used, students are required to give credit and explain how it was used. I ask them not to provide full answers that were completely generated by AI. Students know that I can detect AI in their writing.
I ask them to brainstorm with AI tools and remain critical about the responses they receive. For example, they need to determine whether the information is biased and whether the source exists or was simply made up.
The evaluation of my students always combines work in class and presentations with discussions and activities that students organize for the whole class. This way, I can evaluate their understanding in person.
We discuss our responsibility as humans, our values, and what kind of researcher, professional, or person it is important to be.
At GatesNotes.com, Bill Gates recently wrote about the effects of AI and noted the many jobs that could disappear forever. He suggested that leadership consider a concept he calls ‘Human Reserved’ – setting aside some jobs for humans. Your thoughts?
It is not a simple binary question about which professions are going to remain human and which will be deferred to AI. It is a matter of understanding the benefits of AI playing different roles in different contexts and the need for critical skills to strengthen these benefits.
Much has been written about the damage that can be done to society by AI. I understand that, for you, the important issue is to study AI’s contribution to human value. With this goal in mind, what courses are offered at the Hebrew University Business School?
• AI for Social Good (#55982)
• Responsible AI (#55983)
• When AI Meets Humans and Society (#55022)
Note: Hebrew University offers a Free Listener Program that allows senior citizens to audit university courses. The fall semester is now beginning. For information, visit magid.huji.ac.il/course-19/
It’s been reported that more than 1 billion people worldwide use AI each month. Who coined the phrase ‘artificial intelligence’?
The term was coined by John McCarthy, a mathematics professor at Dartmouth College, together with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon, in a 1955 proposal submitted to the Rockefeller Foundation.
In 1950, the British mathematician Alan Turing had already posed the question of whether machines can think.
Note: Readers might be interested in the 2014 Hollywood movie The Imitation Game, which tells the story of Turing.
What was one issue you worked on during your tenure at General Motors?
Introducing learning agents to the vehicle user experience so that drivers could remain focused on the road and understand better autonomous driving functions.
What’s your family background?
My grandparents came to Argentina before many family members were murdered in the Holocaust. My parents were born in Argentina, and I was their only child. I went to a Jewish school in Buenos Aires through seventh grade, where we studied in Yiddish, Hebrew, and Spanish.
I then told my parents that I wanted to go to public school. For the next three years, I attended public secondary school in the mornings while continuing to study at the Jewish school in the afternoons.
What prompted your family to make aliyah when you were 16?
For many years, my father wanted to leave Argentina to search for a better future for the family. In 1983, in one of our conversations, I said: “The only place I can see myself growing up is Israel.” It then took six months until we made aliyah in January 1984.
When did you meet your husband?
When we were both studying on the Givat Ram campus of the Hebrew University. We met for the first time on the stairs of the Ross Building. When we met a third time, we remembered the Hebrew expression [“pa’am shlishit glida”] – when you unexpectedly run into the same person three times in a short period of time, one person owes the other person ice cream.
And so, he treated me to ice cream. The year was 1995, and we were married in 1999.■
Claudia V. Goldman
From Buenos Aires
to Jerusalem, 1984

Pentagon designates Chinese cultural centers national security threat
The Pentagon has designated cultural programs linked to China’s Confucius Institute as a national security threat, according to US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. He claims that the centers, which largely offer Chinese language courses on American college and university campuses, serve as a front for Beijing’s “propaganda” campaign – an allegation Chinese officials have previously denied.
In a video posted on Facebook on Friday, Hegseth said that while the US Congress had previously “banned” the Confucius Institutes from American educational institutions, they “came back disguised in new forms” and under new names.
Hegseth was apparently referring to several measures passed by Congress in recent years that stripped universities that hosted Confucius Institutes of federal funding. The pressure from the lawmakers has led to the closure of multiple centers on US soil.
According to Hegseth, over the past two months, the Department of War has “systematically dismantled” 80 new Chinese-backed cultural centers across 30 universities, adding “these sleeper organizations to our list of institutions that threaten our national security.”
The official alleged that the targeted entities had sought to “steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” but stopped short of providing any concrete evidence.
Back in 2020, the US Department of State designated Confucius Institutes as a “foreign mission of the People’s Republic of China,” requiring the institutions to regularly provide information regarding their Chinese personnel, recruitment, funding, and operations to the US government. The US Department of State characterized the China-funded cultural centers as “part of Beijing’s multifaceted propaganda efforts.”
Later that year, then-US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo alleged that the centers were working to recruit “spies and collaborators” at US colleges, and expressed hope that “we will get them all closed out.”
China’s Foreign Ministry at the time accused Pompeo of deliberately undermining cultural and educational exchanges “by discrediting Confucius Institutes… [out of] ideological bias and political expediency.”
Beijing urged Washington to “abandon the Cold War zero-sum mentality… [and to] stop interfering with normal people-to-people and cultural exchanges.”
Confucius Institutes have similarly come under government pressure in several other Western countries in recent years.
Last year, Australian media reported that six local universities had shut down Beijing-backed cultural centers amid government scrutiny, reducing the number of such entities in the country by half.
In 2020, several media outlets, including The Times, claimed that Sweden had become the first European nation to close all Confucius Institutes and related classrooms.

Suspect detained after fire wrecks Hitler’s mountain retreat

- Police detained a 33-year-old German man after seeing a rider on a red motorcycle with no number plate. Officials said the fire looks like arson, and a political motive is not ruled out.
- The historic site, built in 1937-38 and linked to Nazi rule, is a major visitor attraction and memorial. Bavarian officials said it will be restored and kept for remembrance.
AI generated
BERLIN - Firefighters battled on Oct 24 to put out flames that tore through Adolf Hitler’s “Eagle’s Nest” mountain retreat, as police detained a suspect who investigators said may have psychiatric problems.
The alarm was raised late on Oct 23 at the former guest house for top Nazi officials, a picturesque spot 1,834m up in the Bavarian Alps.
As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames at dawn on Oct 24.
By the afternoon, fire chief Michael Brandl told journalists the last elements of the inferno were being put out.
No-one has entered the building because of fears it could collapse, he added.
“We are very lucky that there are no injuries,” Brandl said.
Some 200 firefighters were mobilised for the operation at the Kehlsteinhaus residence on a summit above Obersalzberg in southern Germany. The site draws 350,000 visitors a year, according to Bavarian state authorities.
Authorities said access had been difficult after the fire alarm went off at 9.50pm.
Heavy rain was followed by a snow storm and then violent winds.
Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said the firefighters had needed breathing apparatus to get near.
Building ‘completely ablaze’ when firefighters arrived
Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.
Bavarian state interior minister Joachim Herrmann said the fire appeared to be “a malicious act” and police said that a suspect was detained at the scene.
Firefighters and police heading to the Eagle’s Nest saw “a rider on a red motorcycle with no licence plate” and stopped him, Robert Holzinger, a Bavarian police official, told journalists.
The suspect is a 33-year-old German with ties to the area but who does not live there, Rainer Vietze, of the public prosecutor’s office, told the local PNP newspaper.
“It looks likely to be a case of arson,” Vietze added – but given the historical context of the building said authorities were for the moment not ruling out a political motive.
The suspect underwent a psychiatric examination before being interned in a psychiatric establishment on a provisional basis, said Vietze.
Police blocked access to the retreat on Oct 24.
Toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich
Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews, as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists during the Holocaust.
It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator himself seldom visited the complex, which was heavily guarded. Hitler had another country residence nearby at Berghof.
Built of stone and granite, the Eagle’s Nest offers an exceptional view of the Alpine landscape and was designed to impress foreign diplomats. Hitler used it as a backdrop for his propaganda movies.
It survived World War II undamaged and later gained notoriety through post-war Hollywood films that recreated the residence.
Since 1952, it has hosted both an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.
The website says the Eagle’s Nest “stands for the insanity of the regime and the world on the Obersalzberg, where plans for war and mass murder were formed”.
The Bavarian interior minister said the retreat “will under no circumstances be left in a state of ruin”.
“This house – the entire site and its surroundings – is linked to a specific history. It is important that we continue our work of remembrance,” Herrmann said. AFP

alyona alyona underwent stomach-reduction surgery and explained why she decided to undergo the surgical procedure
Kyiv • UNN
The rapper underwent bariatric surgery after unsuccessful attempts to lose weight. She is currently recovering and aims to control her eating.
Ukrainian rapper alyona alyona underwent stomach-reduction surgery and spoke for the first time about how she is feeling after the procedure. The artist admitted that she is currently experiencing pain and is focused on recovery. She reported this on Instagram, UNN writes.
Details
According to the performer, after the surgery her main tasks are walking and lying down, as she is still going through the recovery period.
In a separate post, the rapper explained that she decided to undergo bariatric surgery after many years of trying to lose weight. Her decision was influenced by the experience of a childhood friend who, after undergoing the procedure, lost weight from 140 to 70 kilograms and has maintained the result for several years.
alyona alyona said that she had repeatedly tried to lose weight through exercise and other methods, including injections for weight loss. However, she was unable to achieve the desired result.
"I have shown my ways of losing weight with exercise and various things many times. I even shared how I injected myself and what those injections led to, and that they are not a panacea," the artist said.
The rapper admitted that she dreams of weighing 80 kilograms, but realizes that surgery will not automatically solve all her problems. She explained that because of her work schedule, acquired habits, and ADHD, it is difficult for her to devote her entire life to losing weight.
"In order for me to lose all the weight, I would have to give up my career and work and devote my entire life to losing weight," the performer explained.
According to alyona alyona, she views the surgery as a way to control her eating and avoid overeating. The artist also emphasized that this is her personal choice and that she is ready for possible criticism.
"For me, it is very important to work on myself, develop, change, and be an example. I am choosing this path. I do not care whether someone condemns me, devalues me, or refutes me — this is my path," the rapper concluded, thanking everyone who supports her during her recovery.

American are done paying for Trump’s family business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:03:17 UTC
02:03:17 KST

American are done paying for Trump’s family business
TEHRAN — Donald Trump won the White House promising to “Make America Great Again,” then promised Americans a short, cheap war on Iran. They got a closed Strait of Hormuz, Brent crude above $116 a barrel, and gasoline past $5 a gallon in several states. He and his family got a windfall.
Nine days before the November 3 midterms, the distance between those two experiences has become the central fact of American politics.
In CNBC’s final pre-election survey, 36 percent of registered voters named government corruption among their top issues, ahead of food prices at 34 percent and gasoline at 23 percent.
Fox News found 60 percent of voters extremely concerned. People are reading their grocery receipts and the headlines as one story.
A war with a customer list
The campaign of aggression against Iran has already cost tens of billions of dollars, paid from the public purse. Some of it is landing with companies the president’s sons own or advise.
Powerus, which Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are backing toward a stock listing, holds an Air Force contract worth up to $90 million for interceptors meant to counter Iranian drones.
Skeptics doubt the systems can stop Iran’s one-way attack drones, which have proved themselves in large numbers. Powerus is pitching them to Arab governments in the Persian Gulf anyway, the same clients Washington claims to be defending.
Trump Jr. also holds roughly $4 million in Unusual Machines, where he serves as an adviser. The “War” Department bought 3,500 drone motors and related parts from the company, and the Army has floated a follow-on order of 20,000.
Its shares jumped when his link became public. Rep. Jason Crow says firms tied to the sons have drawn about $3.7 billion in federal money this term.
The youngest Trump son, Barron, joined 1789 Capital days after the 2024 election. Among its holdings is Anduril, approved for a possible $2 billion interceptor sale to Kuwait.
Trump’s own portfolio includes Palantir, Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics and Northrop Grumman, whose revenues have swelled with U.S. military warmongering.
Richard Painter, who served as ethics lawyer in George W. Bush’s White House, told the Wall Street Journal that he sees no modern precedent. That is a notable benchmark, given the Bush administration’s own notorious record of foreign aggression and corporate enrichment.
Persian Gulf states, he says, are “under immense pressure to buy from Trump’s sons,” so the president will deliver what they want. It may be the first time, he adds, that a president’s family has made vast sums from a war launched without congressional authorization.
Arab monarchy money and a crypto pipeline
The Persian Gulf runs through the family’s earlier business too. In his upcoming book Princes and Thieves, Matthew Cole reports that Jared Kushner had access to at least two accounts tied to the UAE and Israel, together receiving about $2 billion, part of it Saudi-backed and moved through banks in Baku.
Dutch intelligence, which had penetrated his phone, helped trace the transfers. A third account, the report says, paid for an Israeli pledge to defend the Emirates against Iranian strikes.
Then came crypto. Days before the 2025 inauguration, an entity backed by Tahnoon bin Zayed, the UAE’s national security adviser, agreed to buy 49 percent of World Liberty Financial for $500 million.
An Abu Dhabi fund he chairs later bought $2 billion of the firm’s USD1 stablecoin. Months on, the administration eased AI chip exports to Emirati firms, including G42, which Tahnoon controls.
Trump also pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, whose company had paid $4.3 billion in fines, and accepted a $400 million jet from Qatar.
On October 22, a Circle shareholder sued in federal court, alleging violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause.
Trump’s disclosures show $2.2 billion in earnings for his first year back, $1.4 billion of it from crypto, including about $636 million from a memecoin whose promoters advertised a dinner with him for its 185 biggest holders.
‘Slime, not crime’
Smaller scandals keep piling up. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned after the Wall Street Journal reported she asked a donor to cover a $100,000 credit card bill.
Adviser Corey Lewandowski faces a Justice Department inquiry. The New York Times says Alina Habba, Trump’s former lawyer, agreed to a $50 million deal with the family of a Venezuelan billionaire who later received a pardon.
Trump’s answer was to warn that dishonest allies “have to be prosecuted,” while his Justice Department charged a Virginia Democrat, state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Expect few convictions. Experts point to the Supreme Court: McDonnell in 2016 narrowed “official acts,” Snyder in 2024 excused gratuities paid after the fact, and Trump v. United States granted presidents sweeping immunity.
The Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section was effectively shut down in February 2025. What remains, some prosecutors say, is “slime, not crime,” despite overwhelming evidence of corruption that Americans across party lines can no longer ignore.
Nine days to judgment
Voters have noticed anyway. A Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll found nearly two in three Americans think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, with most of the rise coming from Republicans and their leaners.
His approval sits at a record low of 33 percent, and Democrats have spent $182 million on corruption ads, more than the last four cycles combined, according to data from the firm AdImpact.
Vice President JD Vance calls the charge “laughable.” Trump’s pollster argues undecided voters will still choose on pocketbook issues. Perhaps. But $5 gasoline and a president’s sons selling drones are hard to pull apart.
The deeper question is what the money buys. In Matthew Cole’s account, Kushner held signing rights on an Emirati account while Abu Dhabi wanted the 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) dead.
Trump quit the agreement in May 2018. Months after he left office, Saudi Arabia’s sovereign fund gave his firm $2 billion, despite a screening panel finding its due diligence “unsatisfactory in all aspects.”
Today, at least some of the transactions happen in plain sight: Emirati stablecoin purchases, chip exports, drone contracts, and more.

Trump says he may move White House press corps to new location
Trump’s remarks come amid a fractious moment between the US president and the journalists who cover him.
United States President Donald Trump has confirmed he could move the White House press corps to a different location, possibly away from the executive residence.
In a social media post on Friday, Trump described reports that he planned to remove the White House press briefing room in favour of restoring a historic swimming pool located underneath as “Fake News”.
“I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing!” he wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump, however, indicated he may relocate dozens of reporters who cover the White House “to a less obnoxious location”.
The New York Times on Tuesday reported that Trump had pitched his former press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, on an idea to move journalists out of the White House’s storied James S. Brady Press Briefing Room. That proposal did not move forward during Leavitt’s tenure, which ended on August 27.
Trump’s remarks come amid a fractious moment between him and the journalists who cover him.
Last month, Trump banned journalists from three US-based media outlets – CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO – from the White House, a move that proponents of free speech said violated First Amendment protections.
A US federal judge ruled that the order was likely unconstitutional, forcing the White House to restore the journalists’ access. The Trump administration continues to fight the ruling.
Trump has also regularly chided and denigrated members of the media he claims cover him unfairly.
The latest incident was during an Oval Office event on Tuesday when Trump attacked The Independent’s White House Correspondent Andrew Feinberg.
“What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person? I actually think there’s something wrong with you”, Trump said as Feinberg tried to ask a question. The moment was amplified by the White House on social media.
If Trump opts to proceed with changes to the White House press briefing room, it would be the latest in a long list of controversial projects he has ordered that would transform the property.
Since returning to power last year, the US president has demolished the White House East Wing to construct a new ballroom, installed concrete pavers over the lawn centred in the White House Rose Garden and built a helipad on the South Lawn.
The Times reported Trump told aides he wanted to bring back a West Wing indoor pool constructed in 1933 for use by President Franklin D Roosevelt, who suffered from polio and often swam, according to his presidential library, to ease soreness.
In the 1970s, former President Richard Nixon had a floor constructed above the pool to accommodate a briefing room for the growing White House press corps. The pool remains beneath the floor of the briefing room.
Leavitt confirmed during a Friday interview that Trump was “flirting” with the idea of restoring the pool.
“He just, maybe, wants to restore it to all of its glory”, Leavitt said during an appearance on HBO’s “Real Time with Bill Maher”. “I don’t know if he’ll do it.”
The White House did not immediately return Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Ste Marie imbues Monos Vancouver office with “residential quality”
Canadian interiors studio Ste Marie has designed the Vancouver headquarters of luggage brand Monos to emphasise simplicity and shift mood throughout the day.
Located in the city’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, the Monos office was created to reflect the brand’s development to date and provide space for continued growth.
Ste Marie was presented with an open-ended brief, allowing the studio to develop a “flexible framework” for a company that is “still exploring what it could become” and would allow its team to collaborate, experiment and host.
“Monos is a brand grounded in design, mindfulness, human connection, and we understood this as an opportunity to create a place where those values could be put into practice,” said Ste Marie.
“A place where their people could come together to work, create, exchange ideas, test new things, host events and gather as an extended community.”
The studio, which previously designed the interiors for a Monos store in Toronto, approached the workplace like a residential project and organised the spaces into three overlapping areas.
“Like an apartment, it accommodates everyday activity as naturally as moments of hosting,” said the studio. “The residential quality also supports Monos’ culture of openness.”
The first area features low, soft modular sofas for lounging and conversation, and enclosed banquettes below conical pendant lights that facilitate personal exchanges, small meetings or shared meals.
An elongated communal table at the centre of the open plan provides a flexible surface for meetings, product development, testing, dining and gathering.
Here, the custom millwork is arranged in perpendicular planes that form vertical supports and horizontal overhead light boxes.
At the back is a kitchen and tea room with solid-surface counters and handleless cabinets, continuing the minimalist schema that runs throughout.
“These areas can expand and contract as needed: a meeting can become a meal, a work surface can become a display, and a lounge can transform into an event space,” Ste Marie said.
The hardness of the polished concrete flooring and rift-cut timber millwork is offset by soft furnishings, natural-fibre rugs and sheer curtains.
Dimmable lighting enables the mood to shift from early morning focused work to more casual afternoon meetings and then evening events.
“The result is a workplace that feels considered but not overly designed, with the warmth and informality of a personal space and the flexibility of a creative studio,” said Ste Marie.
Ste Marie was founded by Craig Stanghetta and has developed a reputation for its cinematic hospitality spaces across North America.
Other recent projects by the studio include a trio of venues in Edmonton, a series of amenity spaces within a renovated 1960s tower in Chicago and a Vancouver restaurant influenced by Hong Kong’s “love motels”.

Operation al-Khalil exposes limits of Israeli aggression
TEHRAN – The resistance operation in al-Khalil (Hebron), which took place just days before the Israeli elections, was far more than an isolated security incident.
It raises fundamental questions about the limits of power within the Israeli regime’s security establishment and its ability to prevent armed resistance operations in the occupied West Bank.
Despite continued raids, tighter military restrictions, an expanding campaign of searches, arrests, detentions, and home demolitions, armed resistance remains ongoing. This exposes the gap between the ability to establish control on the ground and the ability to achieve lasting security.
The operation is significant because of its timing and the context in which it occurred. Raids by Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) alongside settler terrorism on Palestinians, their land, and their property in the West Bank have been escalating, alongside threats to expand the aggression.
The question is not only what security consequences the resistance operation has produced, but what it reveals about the shortcomings of the regime’s approach in the West Bank. The IOF continues to pursue policies aimed at imposing new realities through aggression and the complete control daily life in the occupied territories.

On October 17, settlers attacked the village of Ma’in near al-Khalil, injuring three Palestinians, one of whom was shot with live ammunition. They also stole 380 sheep. On October 19, farmers were attacked while harvesting olives.
These incidents are also inseparable from the IOF restrictions imposed on Palestinians at the Ibrahimi Mosque in al-Khalil and the continued measures enforcing its division by time and space.
Palestinians face conditions in which Israel’s pressure extends beyond military operations into the details of everyday life and their ability to remain on their land, amid the ongoing threat of ethnic cleansing.
The al-Khalil operation raises questions about the occupation regime’s ability to prevent armed resistance, even under heightened alert and strict security measures. Military superiority, a heavy military occupation, and the capacity to carry out raids and arrests do not necessarily mean an ability to anticipate every operation or prevent it from taking place.
This is where the central contradiction emerges. The IOF can expand its raids and impose sweeping restrictions on Palestinians in the West Bank, but it cannot automatically turn this into lasting, guaranteed security. Controlling territory is not the same as being able to control every security or political development that occurs within it.
The fact that an armed resistance operation took place in al-Khalil at this particular moment exposes the IOF’s security failure to anticipate the operation, issue an early warning, and prevent it from happening. It also puts claims of comprehensive security control to a serious test and serves as a reminder that the regime’s security policy in the West Bank, however extensive, prolonged, or intensified, cannot eliminate the underlying factors sustaining the aggression against Palestinians.
This becomes even more significant given the Netanyahu government’s reliance on military force as its primary tool for establishing deterrence and reshaping the situation in the West Bank. As arrests and terror expand, the possibility of renewed confrontation remains strong. This is a natural consequence of any occupation.
The al-Khalil operation comes at a sensitive electoral moment for the Netanyahu coalition, which seeks to present its strategy of maintaining security control over the West Bank as proof of the success of its policies. An armed resistance operation occurring amid this rhetoric and strategy raises questions within the regime itself about the effectiveness of the approach and the Netanyahu government’s ability to deliver on its security promises.

The rhetoric is reminiscent of similar aggression used during the Second Intifada in 2002 under Ariel Sharon.
The regime’s continued reliance on military force raises a fundamental question about the limits of this approach, which has failed to deliver security. Establishing security control does not guarantee safety or eliminate the causes of the conflict with the Palestinian people.
Nor can expanding the aggression guarantee complete security as long as the occupation, its policies, and its violations of Palestinian rights remain. The regime refuses to acknowledge these underlying factors and openly declares its intention to settle the conflict by force, presenting this outcome as inevitable.
Looking back, the occupation regime’s past experiences with the use of excessive force have failed to deliver the strategic outcomes.
In other words, force cannot settle a struggle over land. The strategic significance of the al-Khalil operation lies not simply in its immediate security impact, but also in what it reveals about the difficulty of turning IOF superiority into a definitive resolution amid the West Bank aggression.
The regime possesses overwhelming military power and an extensive, integrated security and military apparatus. It can impose realities on the ground and carry out its plans against Palestinians, but it cannot guarantee lasting security and stability.
From this perspective, many believe that the return of armed resistance operations amid the choices of occupation, settlement expansion, and ongoing aggression against Palestinians reinforces a crucial point: the issue goes beyond an isolated intelligence failure. The more pressure Palestinians face, the more likely such operations are to recur as a consequence of IOF policies and settler terrorism.
Armed resistance operations do not emerge in a vacuum. They arise in response to the occupation regime’s policies imposed on a people whose entire existence is under threat, even on their own land. Palestinian land is being seized and subjected to Judaization, while Palestinians face growing threats to their rights, presence, future, land, and holy sites.
With a large-scale IOF assault and forced displacement underway in al-Khalil, the West Bank faces the possibility of an escalation that could spiral out of control.
The regime’s real dilemma is not simply how to tighten its control over the West Bank, but its belief that control through force can bring the resistance to an end. Every military operation carried out by the IOF may alter certain realities on the ground, but it cannot erase Palestinians’ rights to their land or their other rights, nor can it extinguish their aspirations for freedom.
The regime’s military superiority does not, by any means, guarantee that the armed struggle can be brought to a definitive end as long as its political roots remain unresolved and resistance can rise again from the ashes.

‘PMLA case not examined’: ED moves Supreme Court against HC order quashing proceedings against NewsClick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:49:01 UTC
01:49:01 KST

NEW DELHI: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has moved the Supreme Court challenging the Delhi high court’s order quashing a money laundering case against news portal NewsClick and its editor-in-chief, Prabir Purkayastha, over alleged violations of foreign direct investment (FDI) rules.The ED argued that the high court quashed its Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR) without examining the merits of the case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). It also flagged a five-month delay in the pronouncement of the judgment.The matter is yet to be listed for hearing.
Why Delhi HC quashed ED's case against NewsClick
In a judgment dated May 29, Justice Neena Bansal Krishna of the Delhi high court described the continuation of an FIR registered by the Delhi Police’s Economic Offences Wing (EOW) as “nothing but a gross abuse of the process of law”. The judge held that quashing the FIR for the predicate offence also warranted the closure of the ED’s ECIR.Also Read | ‘Gross abuse of law’: Delhi HC quashes FIR, ED case against Newsclick, founderThe court ruled that the investment was an "economic decision that did not spell out any criminal offence”. Citing the Union ministry of information and broadcasting’s reply to NewsClick, Justice Krishna noted there was no cap or restriction on FDI in digital media at the time.The single-judge bench ruled that the investment followed acceptable practices and that the allegations, even if accepted, did not establish cheating or criminal breach of trust.
The alleged victim in the cheating case should have been M/s Worldwide Media Holdings LLC, but the company had filed no complaint. Instead, the complaint came from “merely an informant”.Justice Krishna also rejected the fund-siphoning allegation, noting that a digital media company would naturally incur expenses on salaries, consultation fees and rent.The high court further dismissed the ED’s attempt to sustain the money laundering case on the basis of criminal conspiracy under the IPC, holding that the agency must establish the “illegal objective” or “means” allegedly adopted by NewsClick and others.“Pertinently, extensive investigations were carried out by the ED for about a year and a half, and the petitioners as well as their employees have been summoned and examined many a times, but nothing incriminating till date has been found or placed on record," the order said.
“Aside from bald assertions of a criminal conspiracy, there is not a whisper of any incriminating allegation, which would even remotely suggest the commission of the offence punishable under Section 4 of the PMLA,” it added.The bench further stated that the request for a copy of the ECIR had become "infructuous" after the report was quashed.
The case
The EOW’s 2020 FIR alleged that PPK Newsclick Studio Pvt Ltd, NewsClick’s parent company, received Rs 9.59 crore in FDI from US-based Worldwide Media Holdings LLC in 2018-19 in violation of foreign investment rules, causing a loss to the government exchequer.It alleged that the company’s shares were grossly overvalued to circumvent the 26% FDI cap for digital news websites, and that over 45% of the investment was siphoned off through salaries, consultation fees and rent for ulterior motives.The ED subsequently registered a money laundering case against NewsClick, Purkayastha and others.PPK Newsclick Studio sought quashing of the FIR, arguing that it contained "vague" allegations.(With PTI inputs)

About 25,000 rally in Madrid in support of Spain’s state pension scheme
Demonstrators want pensions to remain indexed to inflation and the gender pension gap to be eliminated.
Approximately 25,000 people have gathered in the Spanish capital in support of the state pension scheme, as protests continue across Europe, prompted by a range of issues, including the cost of living, school conditions and alleged corruption.
Protesters from across the country marched through Madrid on Saturday before next month’s general election.
The pressure on Spain’s state pension scheme is being driven by several factors, including an ageing population, a low birth rate and wage stagnation, as well as a declining ratio of workers to pensioners.
Demonstrators are concerned that the state pension scheme could be significantly weakened depending on who wins next month’s election. The country’s monthly pension bill hit a record high this year of almost 14.5 billion euros ($16.2bn).
Protesters marched from Atocha train station to the Gran Via, Madrid’s busiest and most famous street.
Several of the demonstrators carried banners reading “protect and guarantee our pensions”.
Emilio Delgado serves as the deputy spokesperson of the left-wing party Mas Madrid in the Assembly of Madrid. Posting on X, he said that “no pension should be below the minimum wage. A lifetime of work deserves a dignified retirement.”
Protesters want pensions to remain indexed to inflation and are calling for the gender pension gap to be eliminated.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has accused the right-wing Popular Party (PP) of planning to weaken inflation-linked pension increases if it wins next month’s election.
However, leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo said on Monday that he would continue to raise pensions in line with inflation if his party wins the vote.
Sanchez has pledged to protect pensions if he remains in office and says the current pension system is affordable.
The system has gradually become more reliant on state funding because of a growing number of pensioners and increases in monthly payments.

Reports could not be immediately verified by the Kyiv Independent.
Ozon and its competitor Wildberries have been targeted by Ukrainian forces in recent months. The two are a major part of Russia's economy, with their broader ecosystems accounting for about 8.5% of Russia's GDP.
Ukraine has targeted facilities that often serve as storage sites for dual-use goods used in weapons production and other military purposes.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Omsk Oblast was also under fire in an attack on Oct. 8. Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck the Omsk oil refinery.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," Ukraine's General Staff said.
More recently, on Oct. 24, the General Staff said that Ukrainian forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, Samara Oblast, as well as an aircraft at the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai.
The synthetic rubbers are used to make solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles, according to the General Staff.

Silence about attacks on nuclear facilities is unforgivable
Jam-e-Jam criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its response to attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities. The article argued that military strikes carried out by the United States and Israel against Iran’s nuclear sites in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious violations of international law and the prohibition on aggression.
According to the paper, both the governing bodies and the Secretariat of the IAEA failed to issue even a statement condemning these actions, a situation unprecedented in the agency’s history. The newspaper claimed this failure exposed a major institutional weakness and raised concerns about the consistent application of principles that the agency is supposed to uphold. It argued that the IAEA cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks on safeguarded facilities as a secondary concern. Therefore, the agency should clearly reaffirm that attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities are unlawful, unacceptable, and should never be tolerated under any circumstances.
Donya-e-Eqtesad: Decoding an Emirati flight to Tehran
Donya-e-Eqtesad examined the repeated landing of an Emirati aircraft in Tehran. These flights sparked speculation about possible contacts between the UAE and Iran ahead of a potential new phase of regional tensions. The visits occurred at a time of intensified diplomatic activity across the region. The newspaper also noted that Trump’s support for Netanyahu before Israel’s national elections increased concerns about possible new attacks against Iran. Since the UAE aligned itself with the United States and Israel after the outbreak of conflict and was reportedly targeted by Iranian retaliatory actions, the return of a government-linked Emirati aircraft to Tehran attracted attention. Combined with earlier reports regarding possible arrangements related to frozen Iranian assets, the flights fueled speculation about behind-the-scenes communication between the two countries. Nevertheless, the true purpose of the flights remains unclear, leaving open the question of whether they were intended to ease tensions or serve another mission.
Ettelaat: E3’s proposal for mediation amid tensions
Ettelaat discussed the announcement by Germany, France, and the United Kingdom (known as European trio) that they are prepared to act as mediators between Tehran and Washington over the Iran nuclear issue. According to the newspaper, these three countries possess extensive experience in talks concerning Iran’s nuclear program and have long participated in diplomatic efforts aimed at ensuring its peaceful nature. The European initiative remains focused on preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, a goal that Berlin, Paris, and London continue to regard as essential for reducing regional tensions. European governments are therefore seeking to keep the door open for negotiations while responding to the rapidly evolving security situation in the Middle East. At the same time, Iran’s response to the proposal remains uncertain. Since the European troika has largely been sidelined in recent phases of the nuclear dispute, it remains to be seen whether Iran and the United States will once again bring these countries back into the negotiating process.
Etemad: Washington’s messages not genuine diplomatic initiatives
Etemad interviewed former Iranian parliamentarian Heshmatollah 
 
Falahatpisheh about the likelihood of war versus successful negotiations. While diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions continue, assessments of potential Iran-US talks remain cautious. Falahatpisheh argued that Washington’s recent messages are not genuine diplomatic initiatives but rather ultimatums containing strict demands. He believes the United States seeks to restrict significant parts of Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities, and that its proposals appear closer to demands for surrender than a basis for agreement. At the same time, he noted that Iran is trying to highlight the costs and vulnerabilities of any military confrontation, taking into account both US electoral considerations and Iran’s military posture. In his view, this strategy can strengthen deterrence while keeping diplomatic channels open.
Javan: No violations in the Strait of Hormuz
In an article, Javan addressed developments in the Strait of Hormuz. Contrary to misleading narratives from Trump and CENTCOM, field reports indicate that vessels involved in oil smuggling or other violations have reduced or halted their activities. The newspaper suggested that military measures and restrictions may be influencing maritime calculations in this strategic waterway. Meanwhile, rising oil prices, with crude exceeding $117 per barrel, demonstrated that developments in the Strait of Hormuz are not merely military issues but also have immediate consequences for global energy markets and the international economy. In this context, warnings from the IRGC Navy about expanding responses to US actions, alongside statements from the speaker of Parliament regarding the costs of conflict with Iran, reflected two complementary messages: Iran’s ability to affect one of the world’s most important energy corridors and a warning about the broader economic and strategic consequences of escalating tensions.

Venezuela will restore the operation of an important power plant with China&apos;s help
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
19:45:40 EEST
01:45:40 KST

Venezuela will restore the operation of an important power plant with China's help
Kyiv • UNN
A Chinese company plans to restore the 600 MW Planta Centro power unit next month. This should reduce power outages.
The Chinese company China Machinery Engineering Corp. plans to commission a 600 MW power unit at Venezuela’s Planta Centro power plant next month. The facility has been largely out of operation since 2021. Restoring the site’s operations is expected to help address the country’s prolonged power outages. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to the publication’s sources, the company plans to commission the plant’s sixth power unit, which runs on fuel oil. This will restore about 25% of the complex’s former capacity. Fuel for the generator will be supplied by the state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela SA.
The Planta Centro power plant is located approximately 135 km west of Caracas, in the state of Carabobo. Construction of the complex began about 50 years ago, and at one time it supplied electricity to Venezuela’s capital. If fully commissioned, all six power units will be able to generate more than 2,500 MW of electricity.
The plant has been largely out of operation since 2021 due to equipment failures, wear and tear, fuel shortages, and other problems. The Chinese company is working to restore it under a contract concluded around 2010, during the presidency of Hugo Chávez.
Venezuela’s energy crisis
Venezuela’s power system is suffering from years of underfunding and inadequate maintenance. The situation is being compounded by economic problems and U.S. sanctions. According to the Venezuelan Observatory of Social Conflict, 531 protests over power outages were recorded in the country in September—more than 20 times as many as during the same period last year.
According to BloombergNEF estimates, Venezuela theoretically has generating capacity to produce about 37,000 MW of electricity, approximately half of which comes from hydropower plants. At the same time, many facilities are in a dilapidated condition, and equipment from some power units is being used to repair others.
Other international companies are also working to restore the energy infrastructure. In particular, GE Vernova signed a preliminary agreement with Venezuela in June to repair the power system, but the work has slowed due to negotiations and delays in equipment deliveries. The Argentine company Impsa is repairing the Tocoma hydroelectric plant on the Caroní River.
Restoring electricity supplies is particularly important for the oil industry, which is the backbone of Venezuela’s economy and depends heavily on the stable operation of the power system.
At the same time, the Chinese company’s involvement in restoring Planta Centro indicates that China’s economic presence in Venezuela is being maintained despite statements by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump about its intention to reduce Beijing’s influence in the country.

“Unfortunately the speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there,” Zelensky told the Hudson Institute think tank.
He said Kyiv was also waiting for US interceptor missiles to protect it from Russian strikes.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham separately “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink” in a call with Donald Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.
However, Donald Trump told reporters he would speak to Musk if there was still an issue.
“If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out,” he said.
The US leader has pivoted back toward Moscow over the past two weeks, announcing a diesel deal that he hopes would bring down oil prices sent soaring by the Iran war and postponing sanctions on Russia.
Moscow has in exchange freed a US detainee — and apparently given Donald Trump’s wife a gift.
Melania Trump said she had worked with the Russian and Ukrainian leaderships on the Oleshky plan.
Civilian leaders from both countries would visit the devastated city to assess aid needs, she said.

Richard Metson (麥人杰) was among the artists honored at the 17th Golden Comic Awards ceremony on Thursday, with awards presented in seven categories and prizes totaling NT$2.75 million (US$84,595).
Metson was presented with the Special Contribution Award, while five artists were honored in the Comic of the Year category.
The other awards were for Best Cross-media Application, Best Editor, Best New Talent and Online Popularity, as well as the Golden Comic Grand Prize.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Culture
Twenty-four works from 185 submissions were shortlisted for this year’s awards.
Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) presented the Special Contribution Award to Metson, recognizing his more than 40 years of “dedication to comic creation.”
It was Metson’s second award following his first win in the China Times National Comics Contest in 1984 with Heavenly Questions (天問).
He is a pioneering Taiwanese comic artist whose work spans comics, animation, film, video games and illustration, the organizers said.
Metson has created a wide range of works, from sci-fi classics Birdman (鳥人) and Zero Legend (零代傳說), and comedy series Brain Twisters (腦筋急轉彎) to alternative graphic novels Deadline (期限) and Black Book (黑色大書).
He collaborated on the graphic novel anthology Sept Reves du Louvre (Seven Dreams of the Louvre), directed animation for the landmark Taiwanese film Grandma and Her Ghosts (魔法阿媽) and developed major animation series, including Happy Star Cat (快樂星貓).
Metson said he had initially thought the phone call informing him of the award was a scam because he had not submitted an application.
He wondered why a scam ring would target a comic artist, he said.
When he won his first award in 1984 with Heavenly Questions, people had disliked him because he did not treat them to a meal to celebrate, he said.
“This time, I will buy dinner,” he said.
Metson’s Twin Crowns: Little Prince and Princess Saga (雙寶記:星星穿越宇宙而來) won the Golden Comic Grand Prize.
Five works received Comic of the Year awards: Plant Collectors’ Notebooks Vol. 5 (採集人的野帳5), The Banana Sprout Vol. 3 (芭蕉的芽Vol.3), Wonder Land (良田:柚子異色精選集), To Be the One You Love (喜歡你喜歡的樣子) and Adeus Adeus (再見了再見).
Three Unmarried Women Musical (三個不結婚的女人) claimed the Best Cross-media Application Award.
Lai Hsuan-pei (賴萱珮) won the Best Editor Award with Our Messy Love (難搞的戀愛體質).
Wu Kuan-xiong (吳冠熊) won the Best New Talent Award with Blue Whale, Wandering Boy (藍鯨與龍少年).
The Online Popularity Award was won by Yuzu (柚子) for Wonder Land.

Storm leaves after killing one and injuring 616
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:44:02 UTC
01:44:02 KST

Tropical Storm Champi left one person dead, injured 616 and caused some damage to infrastructure before moving away from Taiwan yesterday afternoon, the Central Emergency Operations Center said.
With the storm on a course toward southern Japan, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) lifted its sea warning last night at 8:30pm. It lifted its land warning at 2:30pm.
As of 5pm yesterday, Champi had led to the death of one person and injured 616 since beginning to affect Taiwan on Thursday as a typhoon, the center said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
The death was reported in Pingtung County’s Liouciou Township (琉球), where a man was on Thursday swept away by storm-driven waves on a beach, the center said.
Most injuries were minor scrapes and bruises, with no one reported missing, it said.
Of the 9,027 reports of damage received, 3,287 involved fallen trees, including 1,282 in Taipei, the most of any administrative region, followed by 646 in Taichung. Another 3,033 involved essential infrastructure, while 1,014 involved billboards and signs, the center said.
Photo courtesy of the Taiwan Power Co
It said more than 340,000 households lost power during the storm, and about 22,000 were still without electricity as of yesterday evening, but were expected to have service restored by 11pm.
Yilan County recorded 650mm of accumulated rainfall from Thursday through 4pm yesterday, the highest in the nation, while Taoyuan and Hsinchu County each received more than 500mm. Taipei recorded 469.5mm, the center said.
Yesterday alone through 4pm, Miaoli County had recorded 302mm of rainfall, Hsinchu County and Taipei had recorded about 250mm, Chiayi and Nantou counties had recorded 170mm, and Yunlin County had recorded 150mm.
Photo: I-hwa Cheng, AFP
A total of 4,960 people had been evacuated by 4pm yesterday as a precaution against landslides, including residents in New Taipei City, Taoyuan, Keelung and Tainan, and Yilan, Hualien, Nantou, Yunlin, Pingtung, Hsinchu, Chiayi and Taitung counties, the center said.
As of 5pm yesterday, Champi was centered about 320km northeast of Taipei, moving north-northeast to northeast at 14kph to 21kph. It had maximum sustained winds of 101kph, with gusts of up to 126kph, the CWA said.
CWA forecaster Lin Ping-yu (林秉煜) said Champi’s outer circulation would bring intermittent rain north of Miaoli County last night and early today.
Showers would gradually ease and become limited to areas north of Taoyuan and the mountainous areas of Taipei and New Taipei City before tapering off early today, Lin said.
Most areas in Taiwan would be partly cloudy to sunny today and tomorrow, with some rain in the east, Lin said, adding that Hualien and Taitung could see heavier rain, while mountainous areas of central and southern Taiwan could get scattered afternoon showers.
Champi also disrupted air and sea transport to Taiwan’s outlying islands, as well as international flights.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
At Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, 563 flights were canceled on Friday, while another 261 had been canceled as of 10:15am yesterday, the airport operator said.
Flights to and from Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) were also disrupted yesterday, with several flights canceled and others diverted.
The airports expected flight operations to gradually recover while urging travelers to check their flight’s status with their airlines before heading to the airport, as schedules remained subject to change.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Agriculture yesterday said Champi had caused an estimated NT$133.36 million (US$4.1 million) in agricultural losses across Taiwan as of yesterday afternoon.
The brunt of the losses reported to date have occurred in Yunlin County, accounting for more than 80 percent of the total, with garlic crops sustaining the heaviest losses, it said.
