====================================================================================================

Bipartisan US Lawmakers Push Back On Trump's Russia Policy, Vow Support For Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:51:22 UTC
23:51:22 KST

WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is stepping up efforts to defend Ukraine, challenging President Donald Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian energy imports and demanding guarantees that Kyiv will retain access to critical American military and intelligence support.
In a series of legislative initiatives, congressional inquiries, and appeals to the administration, Republicans and Democrats have warned that decisions benefiting Moscow or disrupting Ukraine’s battlefield capabilities could undermine US national security, weaken congressional authority, and prolong Russia’s war.
The pushback comes after the administration authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, amid reports that Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink and military-grade Starshield satellite communications systems had been restricted.
Ukrainian officials say the disruptions have affected military operations, although they reported on October 24 that satellite connection speeds had been restored. Questions remain about who imposed the restrictions.
A Ukrainian official familiar with the matter told RFE/RL that SpaceX had not responded to Kyiv about the previous restrictions. The official added that although Kyiv had been in touch with the US government, "no one has explained what happened or what will happen next."
The developments have exposed growing divisions over the administration’s Russia policy, with some Republicans joining Democrats in demanding accountability and stronger safeguards for Ukraine.
Bill Targets Russian Oil Waiver
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican and co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, has introduced the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, alongside Republican Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska and Democratic Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.
The bill would nullify a Treasury Department waiver issued on October 9 that authorized transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, including imports into the United States. The temporary authorization is due to expire on April 7, 2027.
Trump has defended the agreement with Russia as a way to increase global diesel supplies and bring down fuel prices. Announcing the deal on October 9 following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, he said Russia had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, with further shipments to follow. Diesel prices have risen sharply amid disruptions to global energy supplies linked to the war in Iran.
The proposed bill would also prohibit future waivers allowing Russian energy imports and require intelligence agencies to provide support for Ukraine’s defense, notifying congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.
The legislation seeks to reinforce a 2022 federal law prohibiting Russian oil imports, which the sponsors say the administration has undermined through its latest decision.
“Congress must be a check to the president’s egregious appeasement to Putin,” Bacon told RFE/RL.
In a statement announcing the bill, Fitzpatrick argued that Washington could not credibly demand accountability from Russian President Vladimir Putin while allowing American markets to support the energy revenues sustaining his war.
“We must not import a single drop of Russian oil,” Fitzpatrick said, adding that Congress had approved the prohibition with overwhelming bipartisan support in 2022.
He invoked the late President Reagan’s foreign policy doctrine, arguing that strength was necessary to secure peace and that aggression must carry a cost greater than its rewards.
Bacon accused Trump of reversing his own criticism of European countries for purchasing Russian energy.
“For years, President Trump criticized Europe for buying Russian energy and propping up Putin’s war economy,” Bacon said. “Now, Trump wants to make it easier for Putin to sell diesel fuel. He is wrong.”
Gluesenkamp Perez also condemned the waiver, saying it ran roughshod over American national interests and the bipartisan will of Congress. She argued that if Trump wanted to reduce gasoline prices, he should pursue policies that end the war in Iran rather than direct American money toward Russia.
The bill has been referred to three House committees for consideration. Its introduction marks one of the first legislative responses to the administration’s recent Russia-related decisions.
Lawmakers Press Pentagon Over Ukraine Satellite Access
Concern over Ukraine’s military capabilities has also brought together lawmakers from both parties in the House and Senate.
Eight lawmakers -- Representatives Marcy Kaptur (Dem.-Ohio), Brian Fitzpatrick (Rep.-Pennsylvania), Mike Quigley (Dem.-Illinois), Jim Costa (Dem.-California), and Jimmy Panetta (Dem.-California), along with Senators Mark Kelly (Dem.-Arizona), Thom Tillis (Rep.-North Carolina), and Elissa Slotkin (Dem.-Michigan) -- have urged Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to expand the Pentagon’s Starshield contract and ensure uninterrupted access to Starlink and Starshield services.
The lawmakers called for the restoration of unrestricted service speeds, sufficient geographic coverage for Ukraine’s lawful military operations, including over Russian territory, and a seamless transition from commercial Starlink to government-contracted Starshield.
“Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine’s military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm’s way,” they wrote.
They also urged the Defense Department to consider using its authority under the Defense Production Act to ensure reliable access to the satellite communications on which Ukrainian forces depend for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications and drone operations.
“Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine’s ability to defend itself,” the lawmakers said.
The appeal followed Ukrainian reports that restrictions introduced on October 13 disrupted communications for drones and other military platforms moving faster than 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), affecting Ukraine’s ability to guide defensive drones and conduct operations against Russian positions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the restrictions remained in place despite Trump’s assertion that the service had been restored.
Musk Faces Questions Over Ukraine Satellite Restrictions
The satellite dispute has prompted additional congressional investigations into who ordered the restrictions and whether the US government has sufficient oversight of the communications systems it relies on.
New York Representative Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Democratic Senator Peter Welch of Vermont have led a group of six Democratic lawmakers demanding answers from SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
Their letter questions Musk’s public assertion that restrictions were determined by the US military and ultimately the president, citing reports that Musk himself proposed limiting Ukrainian communications.
The lawmakers have asked whether Musk or SpaceX officials discussed restricting access with Trump, Putin, or their representatives; who ordered any limitations; what conditions Ukraine must meet to regain full access; and who will control future operational decisions.
They also raised concerns about corporate governance and the implications of a private company exercising decisive influence over a foreign military’s communications.
Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has separately opened a congressional inquiry, demanding written answers from Musk by November 5 and a briefing from SpaceX officials by November 12.
Blumenthal is seeking details about who authorized the restrictions, whether Ukraine received advance notice, and whether SpaceX can degrade Starshield service for US or allied forces without Pentagon authorization. He has also requested information on the value of SpaceX’s government contracts since 2020.
Separately, Democratic Representatives Sam Liccardo and Ro Khanna of California, along with Panetta, have called on White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to initiate a government-wide investigation and provide a briefing within two weeks.
“Either a private contractor independently made life-and-death national security decisions, or President Trump directed the restriction of critical military communications supporting a US ally,” they wrote.
The demands for answers come amid conflicting accounts of who authorized the restrictions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has denied that Trump or other administration officials ordered them or knew about them in advance. Musk, meanwhile, has said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that decisions on restrictions ultimately rest with the military and the president.
Trump has said service was restored following contact with Musk, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has disputed that account, saying restrictions remain in place.
The uncertainty has also drawn criticism from Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who wrote on X: “Whoever is handing Putin the gift of a more vulnerable Ukraine should at least have the guts to put their name on it.”

Gwadar in the Regional Energy Equation: Strategic Opportunity or Costly Promise for Pakistan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:42:01 UTC
23:42:01 KST

Marine bunkering services have begun at Gwadar. Meanwhile, according to reporting in June 2026, the proposed $10 billion Saudi refinery announced for the port in 2019 had yet to attract the promised investment. These contrasting experiences raise a fundamental question: where should Pakistan begin with Gwadar’s development? The strongest starting point is commercial activity with existing customers and measurable revenue. That can provide a foundation for larger investments.
Pakistani fuel, a new market
According to a July 2026 announcement by Pakistan’s Port Community System, Gwadar’s inaugural commercial bunkering operation delivered 2,500 tonnes of very low sulphur fuel oil produced by Cnergyico. Vitol conducted the operation with Pakistan’s National Logistics Corporation (NLC). Cnergyico’s coastal refining complex is located in Hub, Balochistan. Gwadar therefore offers an outlet for domestically refined fuel to international shipping.
The immediate challenge is securing repeat business. A vessel will choose Gwadar if fuel prices and the total cost of the call are competitive, and supply is reliable. Can the initial service become a sustained commercial operation?
Publishing sales volumes and net revenue would help answer that question. Investors would gain evidence of an established market rather than projections of potential demand.
Fujairah and Duqm: competition beyond geography
Gwadar faces competitors that have spent years building their commercial networks. The Port of Fujairah describes itself as one of the world’s three largest bunkering hubs. Storage and blending facilities, supported by established suppliers, give customers operational advantages. Fujairah also lies outside the Strait of Hormuz. That geographical position is no exclusive advantage for Gwadar.
In Oman, Duqm’s refinery provides an industrial foundation for the port. The Omani-Kuwaiti joint venture OQ8 announced in February 2025 that refinery throughput had reached 255,000 barrels per day, exceeding its nameplate capacity of 230,000. Duqm illustrates how sustained production and sales give economic substance to a coastal location.
Gwadar’s geographical advantages also have limits. Oil loaded at terminals inside the Gulf must still pass through Hormuz to reach Gwadar, unless pipelines first carry it to export terminals outside the strait.
Gwadar can offer another location for services and distribution. Becoming an alternative energy export route requires connections extending beyond the port itself.
From TAPI to CASA-1000: How can Afghanistan benefit from energy corridors?
The Saudi refinery: a shifting location
Reuters reported in January 2019 that Saudi Arabia planned a $10 billion refinery at Gwadar. In June 2021, the Financial Times reported that the proposed location had shifted towards Karachi. Yet the Express Tribune’s June 2026 report again described Pakistan seeking Saudi investment in a Gwadar refinery. This history makes clarification of the project’s final location and structure essential.
For Pakistan, the distinction between proposed and committed investment has practical consequences. Building associated infrastructure around funding that remains unsecured increases the cost of waiting. Publishing the project’s implementation stage and conditions for a final investment decision would help prevent premature commitments.
Gulf investors have multiple options. Reuters reported in March 2025 that Aramco was discussing investments in two proposed Indian refineries. Saudi Arabia and the UAE also signed the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor memorandum. Pakistan is negotiating for capital within this competitive environment. Predictable access to foreign exchange and profit repatriation will form part of investors’ calculations alongside project economics.
The China route: strategic value, financial responsibility
Transporting oil from Gwadar to Xinjiang has geopolitical appeal. The engineering difficulties remain substantial. Research by Andrew Erickson and Gabriel Collins in the Naval War College Review examined the challenges of crossing the approximately 4,700-metre Khunjerab Pass and the associated pumping requirements. Severe cold and landslide risks also affect maintenance costs.
An independent assessment of transport costs and guaranteed demand should precede public financial commitments. The route’s strategic value to China should be reflected in its financial contribution. Any future transport agreement should specify ship-or-pay obligations and establish who bears the cost of unused capacity if throughput falls. That allocation will determine Pakistan’s exposure to commercial risk.
From underground wealth to diplomatic power: Azerbaijan’s energy strategy
Balochistan: protection and local participation
The March 2024 attack on an administrative complex near the port demonstrated its vulnerability. Reuters reported that two soldiers and eight attackers were killed, with the Baloch Liberation Army claiming responsibility. Across the wider corridor, the 2017 announcement establishing a dedicated protection force put its strength at 15,000 personnel. That figure was not specific to Gwadar, but indicates the scale of the protection mission.
Security expenditure belongs in the project’s economic accounts. Local support also affects investment durability. A 2023 field study of Gwadar’s fishing communities examined their exclusion from aspects of development decision-making. Participation and continued access to livelihoods would strengthen residents’ stake in the port’s future. Their civilian demands must be considered separately from armed violence.
Pakistan’s priority: building Gwadar’s market
At this stage, expanding maritime services with identifiable customers offers a credible foundation. Evidence of sustained trade would strengthen the case for further investment, while tangible benefits for Balochistan’s residents would give development a firmer local footing.
Pakistan’s strongest negotiating position will come from a port that earns revenue today. Larger projects should build on that record, with partners sharing the financial risks of the strategic benefits they seek.

How French presidential hopefuls turn unrest into campaign ammo – RT reports
France’s presidential hopefuls are turning burning streets, smashed storefronts, and accusations of police brutality into campaign ammunition, RT’s Oumaima Ichchar has reported.
While right-wing firebrand and potential front runner Marine Le Pen blames collapsing state authority, her left-wing rival, Jean-Luc Melenchon, accuses the government of failing to hear the voice of the people.
Nationwide protests began in September over underfunded schools and rising living costs, and escalated into widespread violence last week. Rioters have torched cars, looted or damaged thousands of businesses, and set fire to Limoges’ 143-year-old city hall. The clashes have also left hundreds of protesters and law enforcement officers injured and led to thousands of arrests.
In some of the most brazen incidents, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand to a police grenade, while a 17-year-old girl permanently lost sight in one eye after being struck by a projectile in Mulhouse. Macron, meanwhile, blamed radical-left militants and criminals for much of the destruction, and on Thursday ordered the local authorities to ban protests and restrict officially organized marches.
The unrest came ahead of the French presidential election scheduled for the spring of 2027, in which Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. His potential successors, however, have scrambled to use the protests to score votes.
Le Pen has urged a tougher crackdown on rioters to restore order. “Our country is caught in a vice, if not held hostage, between violence and powerlessness,” Le Pen said, pledging support for police and demanding tougher penalties for rioters. National Rally president Jordan Bardella blamed far-left militants and criminals from the suburbs for the unrest, proposing to suspend family benefits for repeat offenders and make vandals pay for damage.
On the left, Melenchon backed the protests while pointing to a growing disconnect between the public and the institutions. “French democracy is in a very bad way,” the ‘France Unbowed’ leader said, calling for greater public participation and constitutional change.
Meanwhile, Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, two former prime ministers under Macron, sought to distance themselves from their ex-boss, whose approval rating has sunk to a record low of 15%, according to an October Ipsos survey. While Attal insisted that the priority should be the defense of people and property, Philippe called for the “reestablishment of the authority of the state, the punishment of looters and vandals, as well as a detailed method for restoring discussion with high school students and trade union organizations.”
Recent polls show Le Pen – who has long ridden a wave of public discontent over immigration, crime, and the rising cost of living – holding a commanding lead over her rivals ahead of the 2027 election. An OpinionWay survey published on Thursday put her at 36% in the first round, compared to 16% for Melenchon, and 12% for Philippe. A separate Ifop-Fiducial poll conducted after the October 17 unrest also placed Le Pen ahead in every hypothetical second-round matchup, including 56% against Philippe and 68% against Melenchon.

Fire destroys Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat

Fire destroys Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat
The Eagle’s Nest mountainous retreat built for Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler in the Bavarian Alps has been devastated by a blaze, the German police have said.
The former tea house for the leader of the Third Reich, which was constructed on the peak of the Obersalzberg in southern Germany in 1938, sits at an altitude of 1,834 meters (6,000 feet).
A fire alarm at the Eagle’s Nest went off on Friday evening, and it was completely engulfed in flames by the time emergency services arrived, the police said.
The high elevation complicated the work of some 200 fire fighters, who were only able to extinguish the blaze on Saturday morning, they added.
“It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved,” a police spokesperson told Bild tabloid.
The police said that a suspect had been arrested in connection with the fire, but revealed no further details.
According to Bild, the detained person was a motorcyclist whom the officers encountered on their way to the burning retreat, but his involvement in the case currently remains unclear. Investigators believe arson caused the fire, the paper’s sources claimed.
Following reports of the blaze, the Bavarian authorities announced plans to rebuild the structure, Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said.
“We will not allow ruins to remain there,” DPA quoted him as saying.
The Eagle’s Nest was one of the few historic building from Hitler’s era to avoid damage by bombing during the World War II. The retreat hosted a museum and a restaurant since the 1950s, becoming a popular tourist destination. It was preserved as “a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship,” according to its website.

Founded by Sapir Academic College’s School of Audio and Visual Arts, the festival will highlight filmmakers from Sderot and the western Negev, including works exploring life in the three years since the October 7 Hamas-led massacres in Israel.

Closing film to pay tribute to two-time Ophir Award winner Nili Feller

Israeli films, TV series that got our vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:37:13 UTC
23:37:13 KST

Given how central politics is to Israeli life and how passionate most Israelis are about it, you might think it would be a mainstay of Israeli entertainment, but except for a few feature films and series, it hasn’t been. Perhaps that is because when people go to the movies, they want to escape from the political discussions that roil everyday life here.
When it comes to the documentary realm, there are enough political films to fill an encyclopedia, and they vastly outnumber feature films and television shows that dramatize or poke fun at the political realm.
But as we head into what is arguably the most contentious election in Israeli history, here is a selective list of feature films and television series that show what Israelis have thought and felt about their political system at different points in the country’s history. Most are available on various streaming platforms, including the Israeli Film Archive (https://jfc.org.il/en).
Twelve movies to enjoy this week
1. Sallah Shabati (1964) – Legendary writer/director Ephraim Kishon dominated the early years of Israeli cinema, and his films always included some kind of dig at the political system, but his criticism was as funny as it was insightful. Sallah Shabati is a classic comedy about a new Mizrahi immigrant (Chaim Topol) navigating Israeli bureaucracy, and it includes the very funny election plotline in which rival parties try to secure his vote. He is in a quandary until he learns about the secret ballot, and then he promises each party representative his vote, in exchange for perks.
I first saw this movie in ulpan, and my teacher promised that if we learned enough to understand every reference in the movie, we would understand just about everything going on in Israel. This turned out to be true, and it’s remarkable how little has changed. It was also the first Israeli movie to be nominated for a Best Foreign Language Film Oscar. Arik Einstein appears in one of his early roles as a kibbutznik who falls in love with Sallah’s daughter.
2. The Big Dig/Blaumilch Canal (1969) – Another Kishon classic, this spoofs how an escaped psychiatric patient’s unauthorized digging upends Tel Aviv as politicians vying for votes in an upcoming municipal election try to take credit for this supposed urban improvement project.
3. The Fox in the Chicken Coop (1978) – A third Kishon film, this stars Shaike Ophir (after whom the Ophir Awards are named) as an aging political wheeler-dealer who visits a peaceful village and introduces political organizations, rivalries, and power struggles into the lives of its residents.
4. The Battle for the Committee (1986) – The battle for power in a tenants’ committee is the subject of this satire by Avi Cohen, starring the comedy trio HaGashash HaHiver.
5. Streets of Yesterday (1989) – Judd Ne’eman’s political thriller about the assassination of Israel’s foreign minister just as he is announcing peace negotiations with the Palestinians turned out to be sadly prescient after prime minister Yitzhak Rabin’s murder a few years later.
6. Time of Favor (2000) – Joseph Cedar’s debut feature is a thriller infused with political themes, as it tells the story of a love triangle set in the milieu of a yeshiva led by a radical West Bank rabbi, played by Assi Dayan, who tries to mobilize an army unit to carry out terrorist acts against Palestinians.
7. Rabin, the Last Day (2015) – Amos Gitai’s docudrama about Rabin’s assassination explores its theme through archival material and dramatized scenes surrounding the Shamgar Commission’s investigation.
8. The 90 Minute War (2016) – Eyal Halfon made a mockumentary proposing that the Israeli-Palestinian conflict be settled by a soccer match, which, in the film’s telling, looks like a pretty good idea.
9. Norman: The Moderate Rise and Tragic Fall of a New York Fixer (2016) – Another film by Cedar, this one told the story of a failed American-Jewish businessman (Richard Gere), who finds himself in a position to influence the Israeli prime minister (Lior Ashkenazi).
10. The Unorthodox (2018) – Eliran Malka’s dramedy is about the birth of the Shas party and portrays its founders as rather lovable.
11. Silent (2022) – Shemi Zarhin directed this movie about a television interviewer who confronts the rise of a candidate for prime minister who refuses to speak or reveal his positions.
12. Yes (2025) – A provocative political satire by Nadav Lapid, set after October 7, following a musician and his dancer wife who entertain Israel’s elite after the musician is assigned to create a new national anthem.
Television series to enjoy this week
On the small screen, most political satire has been confined to sketch comedy shows, such as Zehu Ze and Eretz Nehederet. But a few others exist, and most can be streamed as well.
1. "War Room" (2005) – Written and created by Yair Lapid, currently one of Israel’s leading politicians, about a fictional unit in the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) coordinating national-security decisions, which many felt was inspired by "The West Wing."
2. "Polishuk" (2009-2014) – Sasson Gabai plays an unlikely government minister navigating advisers, rival politicians, scandals, and his own limitations in this political satire, created by Shmuel Hasfari.
3. "The Prime Minister’s Children" (2011-2012) – Created by Shahar Magen and Noa Rothman, the series features Rami Heuberger as the prime minister and follows how his family adjusts to power, public scrutiny, and life inside the official residence.
4. "Shadow Government" (aka "State Rules") (2018) – A political thriller about parliamentary aides whose relationships, ambitions, and intrigues shape what happens in the Knesset.
5. "Autonomies" (2018) – A dystopian drama that portrays an Israel divided between a secular state centered in Tel Aviv and an ultra-Orthodox autonomy centered in Jerusalem, that was created by Ori Elon and Yehonatan Indursky.
6. "Sweetie’s Party" (aka "Motek Bool Ba’emtza") (2021-2025) – Shmuel Hasfari returned to political comedy with this series about a broke former reality-show contestant and social media influencer who enters the Knesset and discovers the world of lobbying, political deals, manipulation, parliamentary power, and mostly, the money and perks that come with the job.

Mona Lisa off limits as Paris shuts museums over protest fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:37:07 UTC
23:37:07 KST

Demonstrators took to the streets of France on Saturday under the watch of 70,000 police officers, with unrest appearing markedly less severe than a week earlier despite scattered confrontations in several cities.
Tens of thousands of people marched peacefully through the French capital, according to police numbers, denouncing the high cost of living and accusing President Emmanuel Macron of cutting public services while failing to tackle rising inequality.
"Down with the state, the police and the fascists," some of the flag-waving crowds chanted.
Elsewhere, police fired tear gas at people in Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice, where a water cannon was deployed after protesters refused orders to pull back.
In France's second and third cities, Marseille and Lyon, clashes broke out between hooded youths and police.
The government deployed 10,000 more police and gendarmes than on October 17, when nationwide protests descended into some of the worst unrest in France in years.
"We have to be ultra, ultra responsive," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who has accused far-left groups and criminal gangs of fomenting violence.
Nunez told reporters that police had arrested 135 people nationwide by early afternoon, many following pre-emptive searches that he said had uncovered fireworks, ball bearings and other items that could be used as weapons.
Top tourist destinations shuttered
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
"There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
"Everything's boarded up, and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
The route for Paris' main demonstration was settled only after a legal battle triggered by a last-minute police order moving organizers away from the city center towards the southeastern fringes of the capital.
Police said the original route passed through areas with a high concentration of businesses similar to those targeted last weekend. Leftist politicians said the late change was aimed at causing confusion and keeping people away.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a "magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint."
He said the protests would continue unless Macron addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world's richest nations but with a growing debt that has alarmed investors.
"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.
Islamophobic shooting carried out in Paris
Many demonstrators have accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Élysées, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.
"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.
The first authorized march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.
A shooting west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

Thousands protest in Turkey over journalists’ arrests, media shutdowns
ISTANBUL – Thousands rallied in Istanbul and Ankara on Oct 24 against what they described as growing pressure on journalists in Turkey, including arrests, media shutdowns and the appointment of state administrators.
“Enough. We can no longer breathe,” shouted marchers in the crowds, which were composed mainly of journalists, rights groups and opposition party representatives.
Press freedom has been increasingly constrained in Turkey since a failed coup attempt in 2016, with sweeping prosecutions and digital censorship.
But recent weeks have seen what rights advocates say is mounting pressure on independent journalism.
Eleven journalists have been jailed in the past two months and several media outlets shut down, according to the Turkish Journalists’ Union.
At least 3,000 people gathered on the Asian side of Istanbul, according to police.
They held up photos of jailed journalists, chanting: “We will not be silenced. Enough is enough!” and “We will not bow to pressure”.
Earlier in October, police raided Turkey’s most-watched news channel, Halk TV, halting broadcasts and installing a government-appointed administrator.
The move was the latest against media outlets seen as critical of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his government.
It followed the closure of the website and social media accounts belonging to leading digital news outlet T24 over what authorities described as “LGBT propaganda”.
“This gathering is not simply about standing up for journalists,” veteran journalist Zafer Arapkirli told AFP after the Istanbul protest.
“It is also about defending respect for society’s right to access information and news through journalists and independent media,” said the columnist for the BirGun daily.
Intimidation
For Arapkirli – who himself faces lawsuits – the more intense the pressure becomes, the stronger the response and the determination to stand against it must be.
“What the regime wants is to intimidate, silence and frighten society through such pressure – by arresting individual journalists, seizing media outlets, banning news coverage and blocking access to social media,” he said.
“We must show that we will not allow this to happen.
“We have done so up to now. I believe we are now moving towards demonstrating this determination on a much larger scale.”
In Ankara, at least 3,000 protesters gathered, according to a police count.
They shouted: “No to censorship” and “Freedom for jailed journalists”.
“Today’s protest was important both because it brought journalists together to make their voices heard and because it defended citizens’ right to access information,” Gokcer Tahincioglu, coordinator for the shutdown T24, told AFP in Ankara.
“Journalists are determined to get one message across: we want to practise journalism, and we want to be able to do so freely,” he said.
Praising the solidarity after the now shut T24, Tahincioglu said: “We want to regain the conditions necessary to report freely as soon as possible.” AFP

2026-10-24

Days before tight elections are due to be held in Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has announced a massive operation on the West Bank after two Israeli soldiers were killed by militants at a checkpoint.
Israeli forces carried out a major security operation in the West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday, a day after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others at a military checkpoint near the city.
The Israeli military said the operation was aimed at locating militants and weapons in the area where the attackers had operated. Both gunmen were killed during Friday's exchange of fire.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a large-scale military response following the attack, saying Israeli forces would conduct an extensive operation in Hebron.
The military said its forces were conducting "precise, targeted and thorough searches" and that the operation was expected to continue for several days.
According to the Israeli military, the operation is focused on the area from which the attackers came. Residents leaving the affected neighbourhoods are being directed through designated exit points, where security checks are being conducted.
Hundreds of Palestinian residents displaced
The military operation has also resulted in the displacement of hundreds of Palestinian residents.
Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari and local activist Issa Amro estimated that approximately 250 families had been forced to leave their homes, while Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin put the figure at 150 families.
In the Ein Dir Baha neighbourhood, Israeli troops marked buildings with X symbols after clearing them of residents. Streets were largely deserted, with military vehicles patrolling the area.
Local Palestinian officials said the operation had affected approximately one-third of the city, although the Israeli military described its actions as focused on the neighbourhoods linked to Friday's attack.
Governor Dudin criticised the scale of the operation, arguing that civilians who had no involvement in the shooting were being affected.
"This amounts to collective punishment being imposed on civilians who have nothing at all to do with this," he told AFP.
The mayor said local authorities were working to provide assistance and temporary accommodation to displaced residents.
"We will find them shelter and provide these people with all the help they need," he said.
Israeli forces also restricted vehicle access to Hebron, with gates at entrances to the city closed to traffic. Palestinians were seen crossing checkpoints on foot.
Netanyahu promises further security measures
The operation comes just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday, with Netanyahu facing a closely contested race against an opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu has pledged a strong response to the killing of the soldiers, signalling that additional military measures could follow.
Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has called for the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority, which administers parts of the West Bank under agreements reached with Israel in the 1990s.
Netanyahu has also reiterated his opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, saying he had resisted pressure from successive US administrations on the issue.
The Israeli government's security policies in the West Bank remain a major issue in the election campaign, alongside concerns over attacks against Israeli civilians and military personnel.
Meanwhile, tensions across the occupied West Bank remain high amid continuing Israeli military operations and reports of violence involving Israeli settlers and Palestinian residents.
Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din reported 672 incidents of settler violence over a 26-day period, nearly half of them linked to the olive harvest.
The latest operation in Hebron is expected to continue for several days, with Israeli authorities maintaining that their immediate objective is to address security threats following Friday's deadly attack.

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Commentary: Marking Taiwan Recovery Day with shared resolve to advance China's reunification
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
22:25:02 CST
23:25:02 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- As China prepares to mark the 81st anniversary of its recovery of Taiwan and observe the Taiwan Recovery Day on Oct. 25, the occasion offers an opportunity to revisit a glorious chapter of history, in which people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait jointly resisted foreign aggression, and to draw strength from the past to advance reunification.
China's recovery of Taiwan in 1945 was a hard-won victory in the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression during World War II, and a defining moment in the nation's struggle to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Starting in 1840, China endured a period of immense suffering amid foreign aggression and the decay of feudal rule. Japan's aggression marked some of the darkest chapters in modern Chinese history. Following its war against China in 1894, Japan seized Taiwan and the Penghu Islands in 1895, subjecting Taiwan to five decades of colonial rule.
Faced with both internal turmoil and foreign invasion, the Chinese people valiantly fought against the invaders, ultimately defeating Japanese aggression to safeguard the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
On Oct. 25, 1945, after China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the broader World Anti-Fascist War, Taiwan was recovered. This historic day, forever etched in the history of the Chinese nation, deserves to be remembered by people on both sides of the Strait.
Throughout the struggles against foreign aggression and for national liberation, Taiwan shared the fate of its motherland China. Patriots in Taiwan resisted Japanese colonial rule through political, military and cultural struggles, with more than 650,000 giving their lives during the five decades of Japanese occupation.
Driven by the conviction that "to save Taiwan, one must first save the motherland," over 50,000 people in Taiwan went across the Strait to join the fight against Japanese aggression, risking their lives to defend the dignity and honor of the Chinese nation.
Historical archives and photographs capture the island's jubilant celebrations when China recovered Taiwan in 1945. Families decorated their homes with lanterns, brought out ancestral tablets, and burned incense to share the good news with their forebears. Residents poured spontaneously into streets to cheer, while the sound of firecrackers rang out into the night.
These memories, forged through bloodshed and sacrifice, testify to the deep-rooted bonds between people in Taiwan and their fellow Chinese on the mainland, as well as the shared destiny of people on both sides of the Strait.
China's recovery of Taiwan was an important outcome of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, and provides compelling evidence that the Chinese government resumed the exercise of sovereignty over Taiwan.
The Cairo Declaration, issued in 1943, stipulates that all territories Japan had stolen from China, including Taiwan and the Penghu Islands, shall be restored to China. The Potsdam Proclamation of 1945 reiterates that "the terms of the Cairo Declaration shall be carried out."
In September 1945, Japan signed the instrument of surrender, pledging to fulfill the obligations set out in the Potsdam Proclamation. On Oct. 25 that year, the Chinese government announced that it was resuming its exercise of sovereignty over Taiwan. A ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in Taipei.
From that point forward, China had recovered Taiwan de jure and de facto through a host of documents with international legal effect. Taiwan's status as an inalienable part of the Chinese territory was thereby reaffirmed, and the question of Taiwan's status was resolved.
However, an unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation.
The fact that the two sides of the Taiwan Strait have yet to be fully reunified is a scar left by history on the Chinese nation, but the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
Driven by their political interests and secessionist agenda, Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and other secessionist forces have repeatedly claimed that Taiwan's status remains undetermined, distorted historical accounts in textbooks, pursued educational policies that remove Chinese cultural elements, and propagated a separatist narrative in an attempt to sever historical ties across the Strait and mislead younger generations in Taiwan.
Since Lai Ching-te took office in 2024, the DPP authorities have conspicuously avoided mentioning China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and China's recovery of Taiwan. The DPP authorities have also repeatedly downplayed or whitewashed Japan's colonial rule over Taiwan. Such actions betray the fundamental interests of the Chinese nation.
Achieving national reunification is a responsibility shared by all Chinese people, including people in Taiwan. The establishment of the Taiwan Recovery Day enables people on both sides of the Strait to commemorate this historic moment together.
The Taiwan question originated in a weak and ravaged China, and will be resolved as China achieves national rejuvenation. Commemorating Taiwan's recovery today is an opportunity to draw strength and resolve from the sacrifices of the war and the recovery of lost territory, while reaffirming the determination and confidence to advance national reunification. ■

Ukraine says Starlink restored as attacks continue in Russia and Ukraine
Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi next month.
Ukraine says restrictions on its military’s Starlink satellite connections have been lifted after more than a week of disruption that hampered drone operations against Russian forces.
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield connections were stable on equipment travelling above 400 kilometres per hour (250 miles per hour). He credited talks with Washington and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s diplomacy.
Ukraine relies heavily on Elon Musk’s SpaceX satellite services for communications and drone missions. However, who ordered the restrictions remains unclear, with US President Donald Trump denying responsibility while defending Elon Musk.
The disruption further strained relations between Kyiv and Washington, already under pressure over Trump’s agreement to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel and allow US imports.
Trump also called earlier this month for Ukraine to have a new president, then suggested on Monday that someone other than Zelenskyy should negotiate for Kyiv. The exchanges follow their public confrontation at the White House in February 2025.
Talks planned in Abu Dhabi
The lifting of the Starlink restrictions comes as the United States seeks to revive peace negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv. Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the planned negotiations on Friday, while Zelenskyy also announced agreement on technical-level meetings.
It comes as Trump credited his wife, Melania Trump, with securing a local ceasefire in Oleshky, in southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, which Russian forces have occupied since 2022.
Subsequent Ukrainian and Russian statements putting the ceasefire’s start on October 27, with the humanitarian operation planned for October 29.
Deadly attacks continue
A Russian missile strike on Lozova, in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region, killed a man and wounded two others on Saturday, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said, while in northern Ukraine, a Russian attack on Chernihiv on Friday killed a man and wounded at least 25 people, local authorities said.
Shelling in Kramatorsk killed one person and wounded six, including three children, according to Donetsk officials. In nearby Sloviansk, attacks on Friday killed a 62-year-old woman and wounded four people, Mayor Vadym Lyakh said.
Ukraine reported strikes inside Russia on Friday and overnight into Saturday, including on Togliatti’s Togliattikauchuk petrochemical plant, a major synthetic rubber producer. Mayor Ilya Sukhikh confirmed industrial damage but reported no casualties.
Ukraine also said it struck Oryol’s Proton electronics plant, which it says makes missile components. Regional Governor Andrei Klychkov reported three deaths in an attack on an unidentified facility.
Authorities in Russian-occupied Crimea reported power cuts after overnight Ukrainian attacks.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said air defences intercepted a SCALP cruise missile, four Neptune missiles and 1,297 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over 24 hours, TASS reported. The figures could not be independently verified.

Protecting minorities: A test for Syria's new political order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:22:24 UTC
23:22:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Protecting minorities: A test for Syria's new political order
Damascus - Almost two years on from the fall of Assad’s regime in 2024, continued violence targeting Syria’s ethnic minorities is placing the country’s post-war recovery under strain as the government struggles to manage persistent sectarian tensions.
Earlier this month, pro-government demonstrators gathered in Kurdish areas of Hasakeh and Raqqa, vandalising Kurdish symbols and calling for the government to take full control of the region.
This comes amid the ongoing integration of the Kurdish-led SDF into the Syrian state.
The unrest followed a series of mob attacks and acts of vandalism targeting Christian homes, vehicles and shops in Al-Suqaylabiyah, a predominantly Greek Orthodox town in Hama province.
These are not isolated incidents. Post-Assad Syria has seen “several minority communities that have feared systemic discrimination and unfair treatment - particularly the Kurdish, Druze and Alawite communities,” Caroline Rose, a senior director at the Soufan Center, tells The New Arab.
Al-Suqaylabiyah has already experienced a previous spate of mob violence over the past year, while Syria continues to witness sectarian killings on an almost daily basis.
The country’s post-war recovery was also blighted by a series of massacres targeting Syria’s Alawite and Druze minorities in 2025.
Syria’s decade-long civil war deepened sectarian hostility. Assad sought to frame the conflict as a sectarian war between Syria’s minority communities and Sunni “Islamists” and “terrorists”.
As the revolution progressed, opposition to Assad became increasingly Islamist and sectarian in nature. During the conflict, communities on all sides were targeted, with many villages and neighbourhoods suffering killings and displacement.
The collapse of the regime saw many displaced communities return to their destroyed homes, in many cases living alongside those they believed had destroyed them in the first place.
While the government has repeatedly moved to clamp down on outbreaks of violence, two years into Syria’s “transitional period”, it has struggled to address many of the underlying grievances that allow disputes to escalate into communal violence.
Rebuilding trust in the security services
It is this legacy of civil war grievances that allows disputes, often rooted in personal conflicts or criminal activity, to escalate into communal violence. The recent violence in Al-Suqaylabiyah began with a fight between two men, one of whom returned to his village to rally a mob.
Although Damascus has made efforts to deploy its security services to quell unrest, in many parts of Syria this does not necessarily create a greater sense of security among local communities.
“Local officials and security chiefs come mainly from the networks that toppled Assad, often recruited for their loyalty. Minority recruitment into the security forces remains limited,” explains Dr Nanar Hawach, an independent expert specialising in Syria, to The New Arab.
“The already few minority recruits mostly hold desk or traffic jobs, and the armed patrols in their areas are often drawn from elsewhere,” he adds.
“As a result, many ethnic minority residents hesitate to report threats to the officers who patrol their streets, who they may not trust.”
Over the past two years, although the government has made significant strides in filling the security vacuum that emerged after the collapse of the regime, the Interior Ministry remains understaffed according to analysts.
One way to address this, alongside the communal sense of distrust, would be to encourage the recruitment and active deployment of security personnel from minority backgrounds, particularly in areas where minorities make up a substantial proportion of the local population.
However, Gregory Waters, an independent researcher and senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, cautions against establishing a system of local communal policing on ethnic or religious lines which he believes in the long run may serve to “solidify sectarian divisions” by clearly demarcating that “this is a Christian town with Christian police, and that is a Sunni town with Sunni police”.
He argues that alongside more personnel, the local security services need to improve their coordination with local communities, in order to be quickly made aware of and pre-emptively halt sectarian mobilisations before they become violent.
However, analysts agree that establishing civil peace requires more than simply securitising the issue.
Achieving a sense of justice
Local disputes have long been common in many of these communities, although they have taken on a more sectarian character in post-Assad Syria because of grievances that emerged during the civil war.
“For many of those people returning home, seeing their hometowns destroyed has a very visceral impact,” says Waters.
He suggests that this sense of grievance manifests as anger stemming from the perception that “the people responsible were let off the hook”. Those affected perceive a lack of genuine transitional justice.
The Syrian government has begun the long and complicated process of trying those responsible for crimes committed during the civil war. In August, Bashar Al-Assad and several senior regime figures were sentenced to death in absentia.
Despite this, many lower-level figures have not yet been arrested. According to Waters, this gives aggrieved communities “an excuse to cause problems”, even when those targeted by retaliatory violence were not actually responsible for the original crimes.
However, many within minority communities are sensitive to perceived state overreach. Genuine arrests linked to transitional justice can also be misrepresented, with such actions “often get[ting] blown up and distorted through misinformation and fake news”, explains Waters.
The arrests “become construed as the government targeting ethnic minorities – which can aggravate these communities further”.
Waters suggests that building genuine civil peace requires more than simply imposing justice. Instead, he argues, there needs to be “a systemic whole-of-sector approach, that brings together local leadership, revolutionary figures, security chiefs, and most importantly, those who are causing the civil disturbances”.
Local governance and the economy
Governance disputes appear to be a driving force behind much of the recent violence in northeast Syria.
The integration of the SDF into the government is “sparking fears amongst Kurdish communities about the loss of Kurdish political autonomy, Kurdish language rights and security control in the region,” says Rose.
“These fears have been exacerbated by increasing fuel prices and the general cost of living, which have also contributed to public demonstrations.”
Meanwhile, Arab communities in the northeast are frustrated by the slow pace of integration. Reflecting long-standing grievances over what they perceive as corruption and discrimination under SDF rule, some want Damascus to take a more direct role in governing the region.
There is an economic dimension to this issue. The risk of violence erupting is heightened by the lack of real livelihoods for young men, and the sense that material support remains scant.
“You have unemployed young men, angry that their homes and workplaces are destroyed with nowhere else to channel their frustration,” says Waters. “These are the types that are sparking incidents.”
Alongside economics, part of the frustration is rooted in the sense that “communities have limited influence over how their areas are governed,” Hawach explains to The New Arab.
“Alongside security officials, local civilian leaders are often recruited from opposition networks. Minority candidates may be viewed with a degree of distrust, particularly Alawites, given their association with the former regime.”
Hawach suggests that the authorities could address these concerns by giving local communities more meaningful decision-making powers. He points to the Ismaili Council in the town of Salamiyah as a key example.
The Ismaili Council, which represents Syria’s Ismaili community, established contact with HTS before the fall of the regime and helped facilitate the city’s handover to advancing opposition forces.
Since then, the council has worked closely with local security chiefs and community leaders to ensure that occasional incidents of violence do not spiral into broader communal conflict.
“Syria could develop these local bodies with genuine authority over local services, public employment and disputes,” suggests Hawach.
Ultimately, ensuring civil peace in Syria will require the Syrian government to not only develop its security architecture but also address the grievances that cause local disputes to escalate.
Without meaningful accountability, economic development and greater local representation, efforts to restore stability risk leaving the underlying causes of communal tension unresolved.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues

Thai authorities are continuing to step up enforcement against Israeli tourists, with a special committee on the island of Koh Phangan recommending the revocation of an Israeli woman's visa following complaints about her conduct toward hotel staff and tourists.
The "Special Committee for Reviewing the Behavior of Foreign Nationals on Koh Phangan" announced on Thursday that it had recommended revoking the visa of Einav Ashuel, a 33-year-old Israeli woman, after local police received complaints alleging "threatening and abusive behavior toward employees and tourists."
According to an official statement from the Koh Phangan district administration, two police complaints were filed against Ashuel.
Authorities allege that while visiting Than Sadet National Park and a hotel, she "used services without paying for them, shouted, cursed, insulted employees, and even threatened to physically harm staff members and tourists."
The recommendation followed a Thursday meeting chaired by Koh Phangan District Chief Paisit Thongcharoen, with local police commanders, immigration and tourist police representatives, and senior local officials in attendance.
Thai authorities have taken a strict approach to such incidents. Following the meeting, the committee recommended revoking Ashuel's visa and referred the case to immigration police for further action.
However, authorities have not confirmed whether her visa has been revoked or whether she has been deported.
Three Israelis previously deported from Thailand
Ashuel is not the first Israeli to face immigration enforcement measures on Thailand's popular tourist islands.
In late March, the same committee recommended revoking the visas of three Israelis who had displayed Chabad "Messiah" flags, distributed leaflets, and used WhatsApp groups to invite people to Passover activities on the nearby island of Koh Tao.
Thai authorities said at the time that the activities had raised concerns among residents, business owners, and tourists, and warned that they could disrupt public order.
The three Israelis were subsequently deported, according to a report published on a Chabad website.
In a separate case in September, Thai Prime Minister and Interior Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a deportation order against Israeli citizen Yaakov Ohayon after he was convicted of making threats during a dispute involving a zoo on the island of Koh Samui.
A court sentenced Ohayon to a suspended 15-day prison term and fined him 5,000 baht. A deportation order was later issued against the zoo's owner, a French citizen, over his conduct in the same dispute.
Thailand increases scrutiny of foreign tourists
Although Israeli nationals have repeatedly appeared in reports issued by Thai authorities, the stricter enforcement measures are not limited to Israelis.
In early April, the Koh Phangan district chief announced that authorities had revoked the visas of 13 foreign tourists in the preceding period due to inappropriate behavior.
He said inspections and monitoring would continue as part of efforts to protect the safety of residents and tourists.
The Israeli Embassy in Bangkok also issued a special warning to Israeli travelers in May after authorities in Phuket province stepped up enforcement of local laws.
In its advisory, the embassy said local officials had been instructed to impose stricter penalties on those who violate the law, including revoking visas in serious cases.
The embassy urged Israelis traveling to Thailand to comply with local laws and regulations to avoid legal or immigration consequences.
Responses from Ashuel and the Foreign Ministry regarding the allegations in the current case have not yet been received.

'We will get them': Haredi Public Party leader vows to help fill IDF manpower shortage

Haredi Public Party chairman Moti Leitner insisted that his party would cross the electoral threshold in the upcoming Knesset election despite pressure from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and established haredi parties to withdraw from the race, telling 103FM on Friday morning that internal polling showed growing support.
Speaking to Ron Kofman and Prof. Aryeh Eldad, Leitner discussed his party's chances of entering the Knesset and explained why he believes a segment of the haredi community is seeking an alternative political home.
"We are setting out to win. We will cross the electoral threshold with full force. Our polls show us winning between two and three seats, and we are on an upward trajectory," Leitner said.
"I can see the momentum. It started at fractions of a percentage point, and we have already crossed 2%. We will see what the polls we conduct in the coming days show. We are here for those who have no political home."
Leitner also described his party's preparations for election day.
"Of course, we have invested significant resources and established a large, highly calibrated operation. We are fully focused on election day," he said.
Haredi voters reluctant to publicly support the party
Leitner acknowledged that his party's polls have struggled to accurately measure support among haredi voters, partly because some are reluctant to publicly identify with the party.
"Our pollsters are having difficulty sampling our voters. We are also seeing considerable growth outside the haredi community, particularly among the traditional public. But some voters are afraid to express their identification with the party and openly acknowledge it. Anyone who publicly identifies with it faces threats and violence and could pay a very heavy price."
"People are sending anonymous links, and it is hard to believe who is behind them," he added.
According to Leitner, the haredi community is not a monolithic bloc, and attitudes toward his party vary among its communities and rabbis.
"There is no chief of staff here," he said. "Haredi society is divided into many streams and diverse communities. Tens of thousands of haredim ask their rabbis a great many questions. Alongside the rabbis who support us, we see many rabbis who have not publicly announced their support for us but express that support to their students."
Leitner believes support for his party is much broader than its public visibility suggests.
"We feel that there are tens of thousands of haredim who are going to vote for us, who want to take responsibility for our future and the future of the country."
Haredi enlistment and responsibility for Israel's future
The issue of haredi enlistment in the IDF is central to the party's platform. Leitner seeks to distinguish between haredi men who are not studying Torah and yeshiva students, whom he believes should continue to receive exemptions from military service.
"Anyone who does not study Torah must take responsibility and enlist. We will encourage them and respect them."
At the same time, he argued that yeshiva students should remain exempt from military service.
"We believe that the Torah is the foundation of our existence and that it is what has protected us to this day. This is a debate we will not resolve," he said.
He emphasized the need to pursue practical solutions.
"In politics, the goal is to solve problems and move us forward. The IDF says it is short 12,000 combat soldiers? We will get them."
Leitner argued that greater haredi participation in civic and national security responsibilities serves the interests of both the haredi community and the country as a whole.
"The fundamental problem is one of values. We, as haredim, need to take responsibility for our lives, understand that the State of Israel is also ours, take responsibility for the country, participate in the economy and in security service, and be part of the Jewish story," Leitner declared.
"If we do not do this, we are putting both haredi society and the State of Israel at risk."

As the National Football League expands its international ambitions to Paris, FRANCE, Kamara offers a unique perspective that reaches well beyond the spectacle of American football's arrival in the French capital. Just days before the Saints' anticipated encounter with the Pittsburgh Steelers, Kamara describes the occasion as "an opportunity unlike any other," while reflecting on his remarkable career, his interest in representing his country in flag football at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, and his ambitions to develop sporting opportunities in Liberia, his parents' country of birth.
At the heart of the conversation lies a broader question: how can the globalisation of professional sport translate into meaningful opportunities for communities beyond its traditional centres of influence? Kamara identifies flag football's accessibility as a potential catalyst for wider participation, arguing that the simplified format gives newcomers an opportunity to discover the sport "on a smaller scale."
His ambitions extend to Liberia, where he hopes to support youth engagement, entrepreneurship and development. "I go to Liberia as frequently as I can, not only to be an ambassador for sport, but also for economic growth and development," he explains.
This Spotlight segment offers a revealing portrait of an athlete whose vision connects elite sporting performance with international representation, cultural exchange and grassroots development. From the historic stage of Paris to the prospect of Olympic competition and the future of American football in Africa, Kamara's reflections illustrate both the opportunities and the challenges of a sport seeking a genuinely global identity.

flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:15:07 UTC
23:15:07 KST

flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
biodegradable capsules packed with native seeds and beneficial fungi help restore wildfire-damaged landscapes across northern quebec.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
flash forest plants for life after wildfires
Across the blackened forests of northern Quebec, drones fly above the remains of burned trees, launching small, seed-filled capsules into the earth. Each carries the beginnings of a new tree, packed with ingredients intended to help it grow in damaged soil. The system is developed by Canadian company Flash Forest, which is using aerial technology to replant landscapes devastated by wildfire, including remote areas that are difficult to reach on foot.
The work follows Quebec’s devastating 2023 wildfire season, when around 4.5 million hectares of forest burned across the province. Flash Forest has since expanded its planting operations across Canada. According to its latest impact report, the company planted 686,147 trees across five sites in 2025, covering 429 hectares of burned forest. The technology allows large areas to be seeded quickly while keeping heavy planting equipment off the forest floor.
tiny engineered pods give seeds a place to grow
At the center of Flash Forest’s operation is a biodegradable seed pod designed to support a young tree through its earliest stages of growth. Each capsule contains nutrients, moisture-retaining additives and mycorrhizal fungi, which can help developing roots absorb nutrients from the soil. Customized drones propel the pods directly into the ground, where the seeds can germinate without first spending years growing in a nursery.
The capsules are manufactured to consistent dimensions so they can pass through the drones’ automated feeding mechanisms. Their composition is developed around the needs of the seeds, with materials intended to retain moisture and support early growth. By sowing seeds directly into the landscape, the company also avoids the transplant shock that can affect nursery-grown saplings. Yet even with this engineered starting point, germination remains dependent on the conditions of each planting site.
collecting millions of seeds in northern quebec
Behind the automated planting process is a remarkable effort to gather seeds from the forests themselves. Flash Forest has been working with the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation to restore areas damaged by the 2023 wildfires, which destroyed wildlife habitats and affected traditional hunting grounds. When northern Quebec faced a shortage of native seeds, the team worked with local partners to collect jack pine cones directly from trees, traveling by snowmobile and climbing through forests in temperatures as low as -30°C.
The winter operation yielded approximately 8.5 million jack pine seeds, which were incorporated into planting pods within five months of collection. For Benny Blacksmith of the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation, the aerial process offers a way to restore habitats while avoiding further disturbance to the land. He describes the impact of the fires on wildlife, recalling how even small animals disappeared from affected areas, disrupting the food sources of larger species. The community hopes to see native trees such as white birch and black spruce return to the damaged landscape.
the longer process of rebuilding a forest
Flash Forest’s work continues after the drones have finished planting. The company surveys each site to assess existing vegetation before returning to monitor seedling growth. Experimental plots compare the performance of its engineered pods against untreated seeds and areas left to regenerate naturally. Some sites in Quebec have already experienced delayed germination following warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall, with further monitoring planned for fall 2026.
Wildfire is itself part of the natural cycle of boreal forests. Jack pine cones can open in response to heat, releasing seeds onto the exposed ground, although increasingly severe fires and changing climate conditions can interrupt this process. Flash Forest’s technology offers a way to introduce new seeds where that recovery is struggling. The drones can put them into the ground in a matter of seconds. Whether they establish themselves, and what kind of forest eventually grows around them, will become apparent over the years ahead.
project info:
project: Flash Forest automated reforestation
company: Flash Forest | @flashforest.ca
founders: Bryce Jones, Cameron Jones, Angelique Ahlstrom
location: Canada
founded: 2019
project partners: Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation

NEW DELHI: The National Medical Commission (NMC) is considering a revised proposal to rotate heads of departments (HoDs) in medical colleges every five years, instead of the three-year tenure proposed earlier, following feedback from stakeholders.Under the revised proposal, rotation would be restricted to professors, rather than including both professors and eligible associate professors as envisaged in the draft amendment published in May 2025, M K Ramesh, president of the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), told TOI.Ramesh said the commission had received substantial feedback on the earlier proposal and that valid points raised by stakeholders would be considered. Suggestions included rotation periods of five or 10 years, as well as doing away with mandatory rotation altogether.The original draft amendment to the Postgraduate Medical Education Regulations, 2023, proposed rotating the HoD post every three years among eligible professors and associate professors, based on seniority. Nearly a year and a half after the draft was published, the proposal remains unresolved.
Ramesh said the proposal would need to be taken up afresh and that the revised draft would be moved shortly. Once initiated, the process would be completed within six weeks, he said.He did not confirm whether the NMC would invite stakeholders to comment again on the revised proposal or take a decision based on the feedback already received.The delay had also prompted an RTI application by Dr A N Dattatri, professor and head of the department of pharmacology at Karnataka Medical College and Research Institute, Hubballi, seeking the PGMEB’s detailed note on stakeholder feedback and its views on the proposal. In a reply dated September 16, 2026, the board said the matter was under consideration and declined to disclose the information, citing Section 8(1)(i) of the RTI Act.The proposed change could affect how leadership positions are assigned in medical college departments. The five-year rotation plan remains a proposal and has not yet been formally notified.
