Turkey's new deal on Mediterranean maritime boundaries with Libya is exacerbating issues with Greece and the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

Greece protests Turkey-Libya deal on Mediterranean maritime corridor
October 24, 2026
On Tuesday, the parliament of Libya unanimously approved a maritime agreement with Turkey to establish a direct maritime economic corridor between the countries.
Turkey had agreed on the corridor with the UN-recognized Government of National Accord in western Libya in 2019. However, the agreement faced opposition from the rival Libyan government in the country's east. Now, though, the eastern parliament has reversed its previous opposition.
The decision, which was welcomed by Turkey's Foreign Ministry, is likely to contribute to tensions with other countries in the eastern Mediterranean — especially Greece .
'Null and void'
The agreement establishes a direct maritime corridor between the southern coast of Turkey and the northern coast of Libya. Large oil and gas deposits have recently been discovered in the region in question — estimates suggest that natural gas reserves worth several hundred billion US dollars may lie beneath the seabed. Turkey and Libya aim to secure their economic rights to these raw materials and are seeking to jointly exploit the resources.
The planned corridor disregards Greek islands such as Crete, Karpathos and Rhodes. Greece's government insists that it possesses a comprehensive exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, around these islands and has already announced its opposition to the accord.
In a post on X, the Foreign Ministry announced that Greece firmly rejects the agreement and has the support of the European Union in doing so. "The European Union has described the Turkish-Libyan memorandum as null and void, stressing that it violates the sovereign rights of third states and is not consistent with the Law of the Sea," the ministry posted.
Similar wording came straight from Brussels. "I raised yesterday's Libyan vote on a maritime MoU with Türkiye and stressed that it infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states," Kaja Kallas, the European Union high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, posted on X.
International maritime law
Whose claims are legitimate in the eastern Mediterranean is the central point of contention. Greece primarily cites the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS. According to Article 121 of the convention, inhabited islands that "support an economic life of their own” have the same rights to an EEZ as the mainland. This applies to Crete, Rhodes and Lesbos.
Athens cites precedents such as a 2022 ruling by the International Court of Justicethat found that Colombia had violated the sovereign rights of Nicaragua by authorizing fishing activities in the Central American country's EEZ. The ICJ found that when interests overlap a fair demarcation must be reached that takes coastlines, geographical conditions and the implications of a potential boundary into account.
Turkey's government argues that the geography of the Mediterranean plays a special role: If every small Greek island off the coast of Turkey and Cyprus were granted a full EEZ, Turkey would be largely cut off from access to the open sea. This, the government argues, must be given greater consideration when demarcating the boundary.
Unlike Greece, Turkey has never signed UNCLOS. Therefore, it does not agree to have the dispute heard by a UN arbitration tribunal. Moreover, even international experts on the law of the sea disagree on what a "fair division” might look like in this specific case.
Turkey and Libya
When Turkey pushed for the agreement in 2019, a brutal civil war was still raging in Libya. At that time, Turkey intervened militarily in the west to support the government in Tripoli, thereby repelling the offensive by eastern Libyan General Khalifa Hifter.
Since then, the relationship has changed fundamentally: A successful charm offensive by Turkey's government appears to have led to a political rapprochement with Hifter and his camp. Turkey's government now maintains mutually advantageous relations with both parts of Libya. In addition to the countries' plan to develop energy resources in the Mediterranean together, Turkish construction companies have secured contracts worth billions in recent years for Libya's reconstruction. Furthermore, the Turkish state-owned oil company TPAO and the Libyan National Oil Corporation are already working on joint plans for seismic surveys off of Libya's coast.
Turkey's government has established itself as a new military partner for Hifter's forces, supplying weapons and offering training programs. In doing so, Turkey is pushing back against the influence of Egypt and Russia in eastern Libya and strengthening its role as a geopolitical player in the region.
With the agreement now approved in the regional parliament, eastern Libya also aims to secure its share of the lucrative natural resources. This could give Hifter greater international influence in the future. Disputes in the eastern Mediterranean are likely to escalate further as a result of the agreement — particularly once Turkey and Libya begin extracting oil and gas from the disputed maritime area.
The agreement also jeopardizes a major project that is still in the planning stages: the EastMed pipeline, which is intended to transport natural gas from Israel and Cyprus via Greece, thereby making an important contribution to energy security in the European Union. However, the corridor established by Turkey and Libya cuts across the planned route of the pipeline. Turkey has also argued that projects involving cables or pipelines on its claimed continental shelf require its consent.
In the long term, this could lead to a division of the eastern Mediterranean region into two competing energy and defense blocs: The Turkey-Libya axis might be countered by an EU-supported alliance of Greece, Cyprus, Egypt and Israel.

US President Donald Trump announced the deal earlier this month, as US diesel prices hit a record $6.50+ per gallon in September and prices in parts of California topped $8. Under the waiver, struck just weeks ahead of the impending November midterm elections, Moscow agreed to immediately put 300,000 tons of diesel into the market, and commit to further releases.
The disruption of global energy markets, caused by the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict, has resulted in rising gas prices in the US, further denting the positions of Republicans ahead of the vote. Diesel is the key fuel type extensively used in agriculture and freight; its price affects the cost of virtually all goods, resulting in further cost-of-living issues. Rural communities, smalltime farmers, and truckers are particularly vulnerable to diesel prices spikes.
Senate Democrats are now seeking to investigate the diesel deal, the Washington Post reported on Thursday, citing an unnamed Senate Democratic aide. According to the aide, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee has requested companies involved in the scheme to preserve documents ahead of a possible probe by the panel.
“[The companies] should have liability concerns as well as investigative concerns,” the aide told WaPo.
Further action against the diesel deal has been taken by Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (PA-1), an outspoken hawk, Ukraine backer, and proponent of sanctions against Russia. The proposed legislation, titled the Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act of 2026, would effectively block Russian oil imports for good.
The bill would nullify the standing Russian oil waiver, “immediately rendering General License 135 ineffective and prohibiting future waivers or general licenses authorizing the importation of Russian energy products,” as well as strip the Treasury from the ability to expend funds “on agreements that violate the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022,” the legislation that sanctioned Russian energy products, including diesel, in the first place.
Apart from the energy part, the bill also would “reinforce critical intelligence support for Ukraine,” obliging spy agencies to cooperate with Kiev and to “notify congressional intelligence committees within 24 hours of any interruption.”

Ukraine Is Winning Time on the Battlefield, But Can It Win the Battle for Its Future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:07:00 UTC
23:07:00 KST

Having lived and invested in Ukraine for more than three decades, I have witnessed this country’s remarkable transformation, its revolutions, economic crises, political disappointments and, above all, the extraordinary courage of its people. But I have also learned that patriotism should never prevent us from facing uncomfortable realities.
Recent analytical reports, economic assessments, military evaluations and public opinion surveys paint a picture that is both encouraging and deeply troubling. While interpretations and forecasts differ, a recurring concern emerges: Ukraine is demonstrating remarkable resilience on the battlefield while facing mounting economic, political, demographic and social pressures.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
This contradiction deserves serious attention, particularly from those responsible for shaping Ukraine’s future. The question is no longer simply how long Ukraine can continue fighting, but what kind of country will emerge when the fighting eventually stops.
Military success does not necessarily mean strategic victory
There is no denying the extraordinary resilience of Ukraine’s armed forces. Against a much larger adversary, Ukrainian soldiers have repeatedly demonstrated ingenuity, determination and technological innovation.
Russian advances have slowed, and in certain areas Ukrainian forces have successfully counterattacked. The increasing use of drones, improved command structures and precision strikes has helped compensate for Russia’s numerical superiority.
Moscow Eyes European Security Overhaul in Talks With US Envoys
But military achievements come at a price.
Every successful counterattack requires soldiers, equipment, ammunition and money. Russia, despite its own enormous losses, possesses a larger population, substantial industrial capacity and the ability to sustain a prolonged war of attrition.
Meanwhile, Russia has increasingly shifted its attention towards destroying the economic foundations that allow Ukraine to continue fighting.
Power stations, ports, railways, industrial enterprises and logistics centers are no longer simply collateral victims of the war. They have become central targets.
I know from personal experience how difficult it is to operate businesses in a country where electricity supplies, transport connections and the security of industrial facilities can no longer be taken for granted.
A country may successfully defend its territory while gradually losing the economic capacity to sustain that defense.
That is the danger Ukraine must confront.
Ukrainians want peace, but not capitulation
Perhaps one of the most revealing developments concerns the changing attitudes of ordinary Ukrainians.
According to a Rating Group survey conducted in early October, 57% of respondents favor ending hostilities through negotiations and compromise, compared with only 12% in February 2023.
Even more significantly, 56% would consider territorial concessions in exchange for a lasting peace backed by credible American and European security guarantees.
Another 68% believe that any territorial settlement should be approved through a nationwide referendum.
These figures should not be interpreted as surrender.
Ukrainians have demonstrated beyond any doubt that they are prepared to defend their country. But after years of destruction, displacement, casualties and uncertainty, many understandably want to know what realistic political outcome their sacrifices are intended to achieve.
There is a difference between refusing to surrender and refusing to negotiate.
Unfortunately, discussing possible compromises remains politically dangerous in Ukraine. Anyone suggesting negotiations risks being accused of undermining national interests.
Yet negotiations do not automatically mean accepting Russian demands. They mean recognizing that wars ultimately require political solutions, even when those solutions are imperfect.
Recent political assessments suggest that Ukrainian society may be moving towards this recognition faster than its political leadership.
That gap deserves attention.
Washington is pursuing its own interests
Another uncomfortable reality is that Ukraine cannot assume its international partners will always place Ukrainian interests above their own.
Recent diplomatic assessments point to a potentially significant shift in Washington’s approach towards Moscow, particularly through reported US-Russian energy arrangements and discussions about easing certain economic sanctions.
There are indications that Washington is increasingly willing to explore commercial agreements with Russia without necessarily obtaining corresponding concessions over Ukraine.
Whether every detail of these reported negotiations proves accurate remains to be seen. But the underlying lesson is clear.
America has its own elections, economic priorities, energy concerns and strategic interests. Europe has its own financial limitations, political divisions and growing public fatigue.
Ukraine’s survival depends heavily on these partners, but their interests will not always coincide with Kyiv’s.
It would be dangerous to build a national strategy on the assumption that external assistance will remain unlimited or unconditional.
Ukraine needs strong allies. But it also needs sufficient diplomatic flexibility to protect its interests when those allies change direction.
Europe’s support is essential, but is it sustainable?
Europe has become Ukraine’s indispensable financial and political supporter.
Yet European governments face increasingly difficult choices.
Their economies are under pressure, defense expenditure is rising, and the financial requirements of supporting Ukraine extend well beyond current budget cycles.
Economic projections cited in recent assessments put Ukraine’s external financing requirements for 2027 at approximately $91 billion, with a substantial portion still unidentified.
Public debt is projected to reach approximately 114% of GDP.
These are alarming figures.
Of course, wartime economies cannot be judged by ordinary peacetime standards. But eventually, emergency financing must give way to productive economic activity.
Loans, grants and military assistance can keep a government functioning. They cannot indefinitely substitute for factories producing goods, businesses generating profits, workers paying taxes and investors creating employment.
Even if the guns fell silent tomorrow, Ukraine would still face an enormous reconstruction challenge.
And reconstruction requires much more than international conferences and impressive financial pledges.
It requires confidence.
Corruption and governance cannot wait until the war ends
For decades, Ukraine has struggled with corruption, weak institutions, inconsistent enforcement of laws and uncertainty surrounding property rights.
The war has understandably pushed many domestic reforms into the background. But it has not made these problems disappear.
On the contrary, the enormous sums required for reconstruction make institutional credibility more important than ever.
Foreign investors will not commit billions simply because Ukraine needs rebuilding.
They will ask whether their investments are protected, whether courts are independent, whether contracts are enforceable and whether government institutions respect legitimate ownership rights.
These are not theoretical questions.
I have invested hundreds of millions of dollars in Ukraine over the years, and I know how much potential this country possesses. I also know how damaging arbitrary administrative decisions, corruption and legal uncertainty can be to investor confidence.
If Ukraine wants private capital to finance its recovery, it must demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone, including the state itself.
International sympathy may attract financial assistance. Only trust, predictable laws and credible institutions will attract sustainable investment.
The demographic crisis may prove even more dangerous
There is another problem that receives far less attention than battlefield developments.
People.
Millions of Ukrainians have left the country. Many are building new lives abroad, educating their children, establishing businesses and finding employment.
Some will return after the war. Others may not.
Demographic estimates indicate that Ukraine’s working-age population in government-controlled territory has declined substantially since 2022.
This creates a fundamental question: who will rebuild Ukraine?
Reconstruction requires engineers, technicians, construction workers, doctors, teachers, entrepreneurs and skilled industrial workers.
Money alone cannot replace an entire generation of lost human capital.
Ukraine must therefore create conditions that encourage its citizens to return.
That means security, certainly. But it also means decent salaries, functioning schools, healthcare, reliable infrastructure and genuine economic opportunity.
A rebuilt country without enough people to inhabit and develop it would be a tragic outcome.
Peace must be more than the absence of war
Several geopolitical assessments suggest that a comprehensive ceasefire remains unlikely in the immediate future, with some forecasts extending into spring 2027, although limited arrangements involving energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping may be possible sooner.
Predictions about the timing of peace should always be treated cautiously. Too many forecasts during this war have proved wrong.
Nevertheless, one conclusion deserves emphasis: A ceasefire alone will not solve Ukraine’s problems. It will not automatically restore destroyed factories, bring back millions of refugees, repair damaged infrastructure or persuade investors to risk their capital. Nor will it eliminate the threat of renewed Russian aggression.
A sustainable peace must therefore combine credible security guarantees with economic recovery, institutional reform and a realistic strategy for national development.
Ukraine needs not merely a plan for ending the war, but a serious plan for what comes afterwards.
Ukraine must begin thinking beyond the battlefield
I have never doubted the courage of the Ukrainian people. Their resistance has astonished the world. But courage, however extraordinary, cannot replace economic planning, sound governance and effective diplomacy.
The real question is no longer simply whether Ukraine can prevent Russia from achieving its military objectives. It is whether Ukraine can emerge from this war as a secure, economically viable, democratic and prosperous country.
That requires difficult conversations, including conversations about negotiations, territorial realities, reconstruction financing, corruption and the limits of international assistance.
These subjects should not be treated as taboo.
Patriotism is not measured by how loudly we reject uncomfortable questions. Sometimes it is measured by our willingness to ask them.
Ukraine has already demonstrated that it knows how to fight for its survival. Now it must demonstrate that it knows how to secure its future.
Because ultimately, the greatest victory would not simply be preventing Russia from winning the war. It would be ensuring that Ukraine does not lose its future in the process of fighting it.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has signed decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC) to impose sanctions on Russian entities and individuals. These parties are involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles or supply equipment and components to Russian defense industry enterprises for use in military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, and drones.
Relevant decrees, Nos. 1058/2024 and 1059/2024, are dated October 24 and have been published on the head of state’s official website.
The first sanction list includes 51 individuals and 44 legal entities involved in the manufacture of ballistic missiles—weapons that the Russian Federation uses to attack critical and civilian infrastructure, as well as to shell Ukrainian cities and communities. These entities produce and supply raw materials, equipment, and tools used to create long-range strike systems, including the Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101, and Kinzhal.
The sanction package specifically targets Russian enterprises that manufacture weaponry, components, and related software, as well as the executives of these companies.
All individuals subject to these sanctions are citizens of the Russian Federation. Of the 44 entities on the first list, 42 are registered in the Russian Federation, while two are registered in the People's Republic of China.
Additionally, sanctions have been imposed on 32 Russian citizens and 35 Russian companies that are part of the production and supply chains for high-precision industrial equipment, tools, components, electronics, and raw materials intended for entities that serve Russia’s defense-industrial complex.
Sanctions have also been imposed on enterprises belonging to the Russian industrial group Rusal—entities that are significant to the aggressor state and involved in the production of military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile systems, drones, and other military hardware.
"We are systematically identifying enterprises involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles and other weaponry, and applying sanctions against them. We are also working to extend these sanctions to other jurisdictions. Taken together, these measures should significantly weaken the capacity of the Russian military-industrial complex to manufacture weapons," noted Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Advisor and Presidential Commissioner for Sanction Policy.

The psychology behind Taylor Swift’s billion-dollar media empire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:00:46 UTC
23:00:46 KST

The intense, one-sided connections fans feel toward pop star Taylor Swift and their fear of missing out on shared cultural moments strongly predict whether they will attend her concerts and watch her films. These predictive links highlight how the psychological need for social belonging drives large-scale consumer behavior, according to a recent study published in Psychology of Popular Media.
A parasocial relationship occurs when an audience member develops a one-sided bond with a media figure, such as a musician, actor, or internet personality. While the celebrity is unaware of the individual fan, the fan experiences genuine emotions and reactions that mimic real-life friendships.
Taylor Swift has cultivated an exceptionally robust parasocial dynamic with her audience over her career. By interacting with followers online and weaving personal details into her music, she has built an environment where fans feel they truly know her. When her Eras Tour launched, it shattered records, selling over two million tickets in a single day. The researchers noted that Swift used the resulting ticketing challenges to align herself with her fans, strengthening their perceived bond.
Such pervasive cultural conversation often triggers a phenomenon known as the fear of missing out, commonly referred to as FoMO. Researchers divide this concept into two distinct categories. Trait fear of missing out is a long-standing personality characteristic where a person generally worries that others are having rewarding experiences without them. State fear of missing out is a temporary, situation-specific anxiety in response to a particular event.
The researchers anchored their investigation in Self-Determination Theory. This psychological framework suggests that human beings are motivated by a fundamental need for relatedness, or the desire to feel connected to others. In the context of entertainment, people might consume specific media to satisfy this need, either by bonding with a celebrity or by joining a community of fellow fans.
Lindsey Conlin Maxwell and Caroline Neese of the University of Southern Mississippi, along with Alec C. Tefertiller of Baylor University, designed the study to see how these psychological elements influenced audience behavior. They used Swift and her wildly popular Eras Tour as an ideal testing ground. The team aimed to determine if long-term personality traits could predict parasocial bonds and if those bonds predicted purchasing tickets for concerts and movies.
To capture these emotions at their peak, the researchers conducted a national survey during the opening weekend of the concert film, “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour,” in October 2023. They recruited 303 adults in the United States using an online task platform. The respondents answered questions designed to measure their baseline personality traits, their current feelings about the movie release, and their perceived relationship with the pop star.
The survey asked participants to rate their agreement with statements about missing out on rewarding experiences in general, capturing their trait-level anxieties. It also asked specific questions about whether they feared others would enjoy watching the concert film more than them, measuring their temporary state of anxiety. Additionally, the questionnaire evaluated the depth of their parasocial relationship with Swift and recorded their actual behaviors regarding concert and movie attendance.
The data revealed that an individual’s general fear of missing out was a strong predictor of their parasocial relationship with Swift. The researchers noted that this long-standing personality trait explained roughly one-third of the variations in how strongly people felt connected to the singer. People who routinely worry about being left out of social experiences appear highly motivated to build imaginary bonds with media figures to alleviate that apprehension.
Both the personality trait and the parasocial relationship predicted concert-related behaviors. As scores on the parasocial relationship scale increased, respondents were nearly twice as likely to have attempted to buy Eras Tour tickets. They were also substantially more likely to have actually attended one of the live stadium shows.
Similar patterns emerged for the concert film. High levels of baseline anxiety about missing out, as well as a strong perceived relationship with Swift, predicted whether someone had already seen the movie during its opening weekend. These factors also predicted whether a person intended to see the film in theaters later or watch it once it became available on streaming platforms.
One of the most notable results involved temporary, event-specific anxiety. The researchers tested whether attending the live concert satisfied fans to the point of reducing their anxiety about the movie release. The data showed the exact opposite pattern.
People who had already attended the live Eras Tour experienced higher levels of temporary anxiety about missing out on the movie than those who had not attended the concert. Attending the concert did not quench the desire to engage with the media event. Going to the live show actually increased the likelihood that someone wanted to see the theatrical release.
The researchers suggest that a parasocial relationship can become so potent that individuals seek repeated positive experiences with the celebrity to maintain the bond. Because fans experience a strong sense of relatedness when participating in these events, the desire to rejoin the community and relive the excitement remains high. The shared euphoria among thousands of fans, known as collective effervescence, likely fuels this ongoing demand.
The attempt to replicate the concert experience inside movie theaters capitalized on this collective effervescence. By trading friendship bracelets and singing together in theaters, fans who could not attend the live shows found a way to participate in the cultural phenomenon. This shared environment allowed audiences to maintain their parasocial relationship with the singer while simultaneously relieving their anxieties about missing out.
While the study provides a detailed look at consumer motivations, it carries a few limitations. The participants were drawn from a convenience sample, and they were allowed to self-select into a survey they knew was about Taylor Swift. As a result, roughly two-thirds of the respondents identified as fans, and the demographic makeup was predominantly female and white, which could affect how well the results apply to the broader population.
The research relied on self-reported survey data, which is useful for identifying predictive links but cannot definitively prove cause and effect. It remains possible that other unmeasured variables influence both the psychological traits and the purchasing habits of the respondents.
Future investigations could explore how fans develop interpersonal relationships with one another based on their mutual parasocial connections to a single celebrity. The researchers also recommend looking closer at how social media amplifies the fear of missing out during major entertainment events. Measuring the direct impact of shared euphoric experiences could further explain why people are so driven to participate in massive cultural moments.
The study, ““It’s You and Me, There’s Nothing Like This”: Parasocial Relationships, Fear of Missing Out, and How Fans Consume the Products in Taylor Swift’s Media Empire,” was authored by Lindsey Conlin Maxwell, Alec C. Tefertiller, and Caroline Neese.

All six hundred and twenty three Mechanised Infantry Vehicle Boxers are being delivered to a common build standard, which has made variant and build configuration effectively the same thing.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for an updated breakdown of the 623 vehicles by variant, build configuration and role, referring back to an answer given in June 2021.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave on 18 December 2025 to Question 100025, which set out the number of Mechanised Infantry Vehicle (MIV) Boxers contracted for by variant. This information remains extant. “The Department keeps under review its approach to the disclosure of information, taking account of a range of factors. An updated breakdown by role could pose a risk to operational security and, therefore, I am unable to provide this information.”
A common build standard means the hulls and drive modules come off the line identically whatever mission module they eventually carry, which is the design logic of the vehicle: the mission module can be lifted off and another fitted. Ministers confirmed earlier this month that Boxers will be able to recover one another in the field and that the vehicle has been built with the electrical and physical margin to take a remote weapon station later.
Boxer is being built in Britain by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford and Stockton-on-Tees, with WFEL at Stockport, under contracts covering the 623 vehicles for the British Army.

NEW DELHI: The long-awaited 666-bed super speciality block at Dr Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital has secured fire safety clearance, bringing the Rs 482-crore facility a step closer to becoming operational and expanding access to specialised treatment at the Central government-run hospital.The 11-storey block will add 666 beds to the hospital’s existing capacity of 1,538, taking the total to 2,204. The timeline for making the block operational, however, has not been specified.The development comes as Union health minister JP Nadda reviewed healthcare services and infrastructure development at RML Hospital on Friday, emphasising patient-centric care and wider access to advanced medical facilities.Once operational, the new block is expected to significantly expand RML Hospital’s tertiary care capacity, catering to patients from Delhi and neighbouring states.

Do abstaining voters hold the key to Brazil’s 2026 presidential election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:58:14 UTC
22:58:14 KST

Sao Paulo, Brazil – The first time she voted in a Brazilian presidential election, in 2014, Larissa Campelo voted for centre-right Senator Aecio Neves. Four years later, in the next presidential race, she supported a centre-left candidate, former Sao Paulo Mayor Fernando Haddad.
But ahead of what is expected to be one of Brazil’s tightest presidential run-offs ever, the 30-year-old mother of one has decided she has had enough with politics.
She is abstaining from the vote on Sunday, just as she did during the first round of the election on October 4.
Voting is compulsory for most Brazilian adults. But Campelo is part of a historically large chunk of the electorate sitting out this year's presidential race.
Some 33.4 million Brazilian adults did not show up to vote in the first round, resulting in a 21 percent abstention rate, the highest for a general election since 1998.
“It’s my form of protest. I don’t want to dirty my hands with these candidates,” said Campelo, who lives in the Sao Paulo city of Araraquara.
“This isn’t apathy. It’s because I don’t feel there’s anyone qualified enough to earn my vote.”
But appealing to abstaining voters like Campelo may prove to be a path to victory in Sunday's run-off.
A dead heat
The final vote features two presidential candidates well known in Brazil's political establishment.
The left-wing contender, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is the incumbent president, seeking an unprecedented fourth, non-consecutive term in office.
His rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, is a member of a far-right political dynasty, hoping to follow in the footsteps of his father, imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro.
In the first round of voting, Bolsonaro won 47 percent of votes cast, surpassing Lula’s 45 percent. Just 2.2 million ballots separated them, out of more than 158.7 million registered voters.
The final round is set to be even tighter. The research firm Quaest published a poll on Wednesday that showed the two candidates in a statistical deadlock.
Bolsonaro earned 50.5 percent of respondents' support, well within the margin of error for Lula's 49.5 percent.
But experts say polarisation within Brazilian politics has created a population of voters unwilling to cast a ballot for either Lula or Bolsonaro.
In the Quaest poll, 52 percent of respondents said they would never vote for Bolsonaro.
Some 47 percent said the same for Lula, although the pollster noted that the president’s rejection rate had fallen six points in a week, in a promising sign for the incumbent.
A polarised political climate
Joao Guilherme Bastos dos Santos, a director at the Democracy in Check Institute, an independent research nonprofit, explained that polarisation reinforces the public's disengagement with politics.
In a deeply divided political landscape, dos Santos pointed out that voter behaviour often changes.
Voters can become motivated by fear. In turn, they are more likely to vote in opposition to a candidate than in support of one.
"That creates profound exhaustion," dos Santos said. "The fighting seems to go nowhere."
Campelo, the mother in Sao Paulo, echoed that sense of exhaustion. Her decision to stay home during Sunday's election was motivated in part by her rejection of Brazil's deeply antagonistic political culture.
"Politics in Brazil has become like supporting a football team," she said. "Politicians do things wrong, and people keep defending them. It makes no sense."
The morning of her interview with Al Jazeera, Campelo said her husband's family broke into an argument over Lula on their WhatsApp group.
"People are adopting their own pet politicians," she quipped.
Who are the abstainers?
Abstaining voters like Campelo are a diverse group, according to experts. Their reasons for dodging the ballot box can vary dramatically.
Mayra Goulart, a political scientist at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said that those who actively reject Lula and Bolsonaro may only be a minority of Brazil’s abstainers.
Many could be merely uninterested in politics. "Life is difficult enough that they don't have the headspace, time or resources to devote to politics," she explained.
Luciana Veiga, a political science professor at the Federal University of the State of Rio de Janeiro, also pointed out that Brazil’s abstainers are not merely a bloc of disillusioned voters waiting to be won over.
They may have practical considerations that prevent them from casting a ballot. “We cannot say that abstention is simply a political 'no' to voting," Veiga said.
Abstention, she noted, often occurs among people who move cities without transferring their voter registration, as well as those who have work or family care duties on election day.
There are also some voters in isolated areas who struggle to reach distant polling stations.
In addition, voting is optional for 16- and 17-year-olds, people aged 70 or older, and those who cannot read or write.
"Of Brazil's electorate of [158.7] million people, around 21 million are not legally required to vote," Veiga explained.
The penalty for failing to vote is often minor. Without justification for their absence, voters face a fine of up to 3.51 Brazilian reals — less than a dollar — and can have their registrations cancelled after three missed elections in a row.
Until these fines are paid, citizens are unable to obtain or renew passports and other ID documents, nor can they take part in the selection process for civil service jobs.
A final push for victory
With such a slim margin between the candidates, both campaigns are hoping to court the first-round abstainers ahead of Sunday’s showdown.
In the weeks since the first vote, Bolsonaro has promised new tax breaks to help boost the economy.
A central part of his platform is a pledge to address his father's legal predicament: Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence following his conviction over a coup plot.
Lula, meanwhile, has made reducing abstention a central part of his second-round push.
After round one, his campaign has highlighted Lula's work to end Brazil’s six-day workweek and unveiled proposals for free public transport on weekends and debt relief for small-scale entrepreneurs.
Goulart said that these measures "have much more of an effect on those who are uninterested in politics than on those who reject the candidates".
The first round, however, seemed to hand Bolsonaro an advantage. Not only did he secure the largest number of votes, but many of the candidates who were eliminated were his right-wing competitors.
Some experts predict that the nearly 8 percent who voted for those candidates will migrate to Bolsonaro's camp in the final round.
Bolsonaro also has historical precedent on his side. Brazil began holding direct elections for president in 1989, after its return to democracy.
Since that time, no candidate who trailed in the first round of voting has ever won in the second round.
But Goulart warns against treating precedent as destiny. “A historical observation is not a causal relationship," she said.
She also pointed out that voters may act in unpredictable ways. Wednesday's Quaest poll suggests those who backed eliminated candidates in the first round have not uniformly flocked to Bolsonaro.
While the senator has attracted 43 percent of that support, Quaest found that 37 percent were leaning towards Lula — a more balanced redistribution than initially expected.
Quaest's results also indicate Lula may have an advantage among voters who abstained in the first round or left their ballot blank.
Forty percent of those respondents supported Lula in the poll, compared with 36 percent for Bolsonaro.
While poll numbers do not guarantee results, even modest fluctuations in voter participation could be decisive in such a narrow race, according to experts.
Veiga, the political science professor, believes some of the most crucial statistics will be voter participation rates in regions where each candidate has a strong base.
Lula has a left-wing stronghold in the northeast, while Bolsonaro boasts strong backing in the south and southeast.
"Look at whether turnout falls in either candidate's bases," Veiga said. "Any small movement makes a difference."

Starlink Is Back at 400+ Km/h as Ukraine Breaks Through Speed Restrictions After High-Level Talks
After days of restrictions that disrupted Ukrainian drone operations, Starlink and Starshield are back at high speeds following direct talks at the highest political level, Ukraine’s defense minister says.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has confirmed that Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems are once again operating at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour, restoring connectivity critical to Ukrainian military operations, including drones, logistics, and battlefield communications.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Responding to journalists’ questions on October 24, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said the ministry’s monitoring systems had recorded the restoration of high-speed connectivity.
“The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems are recording the restoration of Starlink and Starshield connectivity at high speeds. We are registering speeds exceeding 400 km/h, with stable connections,” Khmara said.
The minister attributed the development to direct negotiations and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s efforts at the highest political level.
“This is another example of how direct dialogue and the President of Ukraine’s persistent position at the highest level deliver results. Above all, this result is important for our front line, our military personnel, drone operations, logistics, and communications,” Khmara said.
He added that the Ministry of Defense would continue monitoring and documenting the performance of Starlink and Starshield systems.The announcement marks a significant change from the situation reported just a day earlier.
On October 23, Zelenskyy said Starlink and Starshield speed restrictions remained in place, despite earlier claims that connectivity had been restored.
The restrictions were first reported overnight on October 14, when SpaceX introduced a speed limit of approximately 160 km/h for Starshield terminals operating in motion, without advance warning to Ukrainian forces.
In some cases, Ukrainian units reported losing connectivity at even lower speeds. The disruptions affected interceptor drones, medium-range strike missions, reconnaissance, and frontline logistics.
On October 16, Zelenskyy said the restrictions had prevented Ukrainian forces from intercepting some Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which can travel at speeds exceeding 400 km/h.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,980 Troops, 413 Vehicles, and 64 Artillery Systems in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,980 troops and hundreds of pieces of military equipment over the past 24 hours, bringing its total personnel losses since the start of the full-scale invasion to approximately 1,576,600, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 24.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost five tanks and three armored combat vehicles, bringing cumulative losses in those categories to 12,444 and 25,600, respectively.
Another 64 artillery systems were added to the tally, raising the total to 51,565, while two multiple-launch rocket systems and two air defense systems brought those figures to 2,232 and 1,722, respectively.
Ukraine also reported eight ground robotic systems lost, bringing the cumulative total to 3,011. Another 1,855 operational-tactical UAVs were recorded, pushing estimated losses in that category to 579,064.
Russia’s aviation losses remained unchanged at 449 aircraft and 356 helicopters, while cruise missile losses stayed at 5,138. Naval losses remained at 35 ships and boats and two submarines.
Another 413 vehicles and fuel tankers were recorded as lost over the past day, bringing cumulative losses to 166,501. One additional piece of special equipment raised that total to 4,852.
Ukrainian and Russian forces clashed 181 times across the front during the latest reporting period, with particularly intense fighting in the Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk sectors, where Ukrainian forces recorded 23 and 19 Russian attacks, respectively.
Earlier, on October 23, a missile strike reportedly hit Russia’s Proton defense electronics plant in Orel, which manufactures components used in Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.

US warns Houthi attacks could spread, updates travel advisories for Israel and Gulf states

2026-10-24
13:53:59 UTC
22:53:59 KST

The United States updated travel advisories across the Middle East on Friday, warning of the growing threat of attacks by Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis against countries across the region. The warnings cover Israel, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Lebanon, amid concerns that the escalation could spread beyond Saudi territory.
The State Department cited the "threat of increased Iranian-supported Houthi regional aggression" following a series of missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi airports, energy facilities and other infrastructure. Recent strikes have killed civilians and disrupted air travel, raising concerns about the safety of international travelers and American personnel.
The updated advisories did not change the countries' formal travel-risk levels. Israel, Qatar and the UAE remain at Level 3, advising Americans to reconsider travel, while Iraq and Lebanon remain at Level 4, the highest warning, advising against all travel. The revisions instead emphasize the heightened regional threat and the possibility of sudden disruptions to commercial flights.
In Israel, American authorities warned that regional tensions could escalate without warning, potentially affecting transportation and security conditions. Similar warnings were issued for Gulf states, where travelers were advised to remain vigilant, monitor local security announcements and prepare contingency plans.
The heightened alert comes as Washington reduces its diplomatic presence in parts of the region. On October 21, the State Department ordered nonemergency U.S. government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, while staffing adjustments have also been reported at American diplomatic missions in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE.
The developments follow an intensifying Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia and mounting tensions between Washington and Tehran, raising fears that further attacks could trigger a broader regional confrontation.

Ukraine begins process of joining OECD Nuclear Energy Agency – Shmyhal
According to Ukrinform, First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal reported this on Telegram.
He said that "the next step will be an agency assessment mission to analyze Ukraine's nuclear sector, our technical capabilities, as well as our institutional and legal framework. Based on the mission's findings and subsequent decisions by member states, Ukraine may become the next NEA member."
"I had the honor of addressing the meeting's participants and presenting Ukraine's vision for further cooperation with the agency. I am grateful to OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann and NEA Director-General William Magwood for their support for Ukraine and assistance in advancing our path toward membership," Shmyhal said.
He stressed that "joining the NEA is an important step toward full OECD membership, European integration and the implementation of the highest nuclear safety standards. Future membership will enable Ukraine to participate more actively in the work of expert committees and working groups, deepen scientific and technical cooperation, and develop research and professional training."
"At the same time, Ukraine is ready to make its own contribution to the agency's work. We have a strong nuclear energy sector, developed infrastructure, experienced engineers and scientists, and extensive expertise in the operation and modernization of nuclear power plants, nuclear safety, radioactive waste management and the development of advanced technologies. We also have unique experience in operating a nuclear energy system during a full-scale war. This experience could benefit the international community in matters of emergency preparedness and risk management. Ukraine is ready to undergo the necessary assessment process, fulfill its obligations, and become an active and responsible member of the NEA community," Shmyhal said.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukraine is applying for membership in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development's Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA).
The Nuclear Energy Agency is an intergovernmental agency established within the framework of the OECD.
The NEA's mission is to assist its member countries in maintaining and further developing, through international cooperation, the scientific, technological and legal bases required for the safe, environmentally sound and economical use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes.

Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:51:08 UTC
22:51:08 KST

Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers
Sudan is suffering from a cost-of-living crisis affecting millions across the country.
Azhari Mohamed drives his minibus and eight passengers seven times a day from the Shagar neighbourhood in the Port of Sudan to the city centre and back again.
But despite the long hours – working from 6am to 9pm – fuel shortages in the city have made it difficult for the 60-year-old to make a living.
Azhari’s minibus uses three gallons (11 litres) of petrol a day, costing him about 105,000 Sudanese pounds ($11.30 a day, according to Sudan’s parallel-market exchange rate). With fuel increasingly difficult to obtain, he now spends two days on the road and a third day queuing for fuel.
He can spend more than five hours waiting in line when he needs to fill the tank of his minibus and often finds petrol has run out before his turn comes. When that happens, he goes to the back of the queue at another petrol station hoping to fill up there.
The shortages have led to price rises with a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol now costing 40,000 Sudanese pounds ($4.30) in Gazira State, south of Khartoum, while in Port Sudan it is 35,000 pounds ($3.80) a gallon.
“We can no longer work because of the fuel shortages. The transport fares are no longer enough to cover the cost of running the vehicle and our household expenses,” Azhari told Al Jazeera.
He says the long hours spent queueing for petrol is time he could spend earning money to support his family.
“I spend long hours of the day waiting to refuel, so I have to work extra hours at night to make up for the time I lose during the day,” he said. “My livelihood depends on what I earn each day.”
After subtracting his vehicle’s operating costs, Azhari has just 50,000 Sudanese pounds ($5.40) left a day, barely enough to cover the needs of his family, which includes his wife and daughter who is at university and needs support for her tuition fees and daily expenses.
“We just need fuel to be available so we can work,” he said. “If fuel is available, we will not face this obstacle.”
Due to the crisis, Sudan’s Transport Chambers Union, which regulates public and private transport services, this month raised intercity bus fares by 40% and minibus fares by 30%.
Aziza Ibrahim from the Umm al-Qura neighbourhood of Port Sudan, works as a cleaner to support her four children. Just getting to work by bus has become a huge financial burden for the 38-year-old, who has cut back her work days to three times a week due to the high travel costs.
Before the war, a journey from her home to the main transport station in the city centre cost 700 Sudanese pounds ($0.08) per passenger. Fares have since risen to 2,500 pounds ($0.27) on some routes, while others charge 2,000 pounds ($0.22).
“I go to work three days a week to reduce transport costs. I need 11,000 pounds ($1.18) a day for the round trip between my home and workplace,” she told Al Jazeera.
Transport costs now consume nearly half of Aziza’s monthly salary of 400,000 pounds ($43), while costly treatment for her diabetes is another financial burden.
“Sometimes I have to borrow money just to be able to go to work. I repay it at the beginning of the month when I receive my salary, which is barely enough to cover my family’s needs,” she told Al Jazeera.
According to the United Nations Development Programme, the war has pushed average incomes in Sudan back to levels last seen in the 1990s.
That is partly due to the effects of the civil war on Sudan’s oil sector. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) began on April 15, 2023.
Last year, the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum estimated war-related losses at $20 billion. The World Bank has reported that attacks on the Balila oil field disrupted supplies to the Khartoum refinery, which previously met about 60% of the country’s demand for petrol and liquefied petroleum gas.
War damage has seen a sharp decrease in oil production, leaving Sudan reliant on imports amid the global fuel crisis that has pushed up prices of gas, petrol and diesel, among other commodities.
Economic analyst Sidi Ohaj said that the government requirements for petroleum importers have also contributed to the shortages. They include a stipulation that importers must deposit 200kg of gold in the Central Bank and own fuel storage facilities in order to operate in Sudan. Some importers have been unable to meet those requirements, forcing them out of the market which reduces supply.
“One of the causes of the current crisis is the government’s decision to regulate the operations of petroleum import companies,” Sidi told Al Jazeera. “Some companies did not meet the requirements, which led to their exit from the market. This reduced supply relative to demand.”
The government needs to urgently ease import procedures to increase domestic supplies, he said, with shortages affecting the wider economy.
But as the war between the United States and Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets, there is little hope the situation will improve any time soon.
“The continuation of the war [in Sudan], particularly drone attacks that threaten infrastructure across Sudan, is one of the main challenges facing the oil sector,” Sidi told Al Jazeera.
Prices have also risen due to the energy crisis, impacting the purchasing power of citizens and profits of businesses.
Ahmed al-Haj is a local trader in Omdurman market who sells skincare products, such as petroleum jelly, which he packages himself . He said high energy prices are costing almost all areas of his business.
“The raw materials for the products I sell are imported. Higher diesel and petrol prices have increased the cost of transporting a tonne of goods by 30 to 50 percent,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera.
“That increase is then reflected in the price of the products.”
When electricity cuts force him to use a fuel-powered generator for heating or packaging, the additional fuel costs add to his daily bills.
Deliveries within Omdurman, which previously cost 5,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.70) now cost between 10,000 and 12,000 pounds ($1.07 and $1.29). Reaching customers in other states has become impossible due to the high transport costs.
“Transport and distribution workers have also reduced the number of trips they make, leading to goods piling up at traders’ premises,” he added.

====================================================================================================

Israeli-born oligarch behind Russia's $14 billion sanctions-evading cash network linked to Iran, Hamas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:41:54 UTC
22:41:54 KST

As Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu calls for Israel to prepare an economy capable of operating around international sanctions, one Israeli citizen has already become a central figure in Russia's efforts to circumvent Western financial restrictions. Ilan Shor, a Moldovan oligarch born in Israel who holds Israeli citizenship, is behind a vast Russian payment network that has processed billions of dollars since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. American authorities now accuse that network of serving not only Russia but also Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Hamas. 
Four and a half years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin has developed an array of mechanisms to keep international trade and financial transactions moving despite Western sanctions. One of the most significant is A7, an international payments company established in 2024 by Shor, 39. He holds a 51% stake in the company, while the remaining 49% belongs to Promsvyazbank, or PSB, a Russian state-owned bank itself subject to extensive international sanctions.
An investigation published this week by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), working with independent Russian media outlet Proekt, revealed the extraordinary scale of A7's operations. Between November 2024 and July 2025, the company processed at least 283 tons of Russian banknotes, worth more than $14 billion. Internal documents showed how the company used cash brokers, financial intermediaries and companies registered outside Russia to help businesses complete payments that conventional banking channels had made increasingly difficult. 
How billions in Russian cash reach foreign suppliers
At the heart of the operation is Moscow's Sadovod Market, a sprawling wholesale and retail complex in the southeastern part of the Russian capital. According to the investigation, brokers operating there receive payment instructions from Russian businesses seeking to purchase goods overseas, particularly from Chinese suppliers. Rather than transferring money directly through Russian banks, clients hand over large quantities of rubles in cash.
The brokers place the banknotes in numbered bags, which are transported to an A7 cash-processing center. There, teams of cashiers count the money and record the amounts, bag numbers and payment instructions. The cash is then delivered to PSB, which deposits the funds into A7 accounts. Companies registered outside Russia subsequently arrange payments to foreign recipients, often through intermediaries in Kyrgyzstan, Hong Kong and other jurisdictions. The result, investigators found, is that the Chinese banks receiving the transfers may have no visibility into the original Russian source of the money.
The scale of the transactions is substantial. A payment register from late 2024 contained approximately 2,300 proposed or documented transfers linked to brokers at Sadovod, most intended for recipients in mainland China or Hong Kong. Many were routed through accounts belonging to a Kyrgyz state-owned trading company. A7 has also promoted the speed of its system, announcing in December 2025 that it had completed a transfer to China in just one hour and 40 minutes. 
The Kremlin has taken a direct interest in the project. During a video conference with President Vladimir Putin in September 2025, Shor presented A7's achievements and plans for expansion. He reported that the platform was processing approximately 1,500 to 2,000 transactions daily and described payment volumes running into trillions of rubles. The company also outlined plans to expand its operations in Asia, where it said more than half of its payments were being directed. These figures were company claims and have not all been independently verified.
US sanctions and alleged connections to Iran and Hamas
On October 1, the U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions on the A7 network, designating it a significant transnational criminal organization. The department described A7 as a shadow banking operation that uses money-laundering techniques to disguise illicit payments as legitimate commercial transactions and move enormous sums across borders in violation of sanctions and other laws.
The American allegations extend far beyond Russian trade. According to the Treasury Department, A7 has provided financial support to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Iranian-backed organizations, including Hamas. U.S. authorities also linked the network to Nobitex, Iran's largest digital asset exchange, sanctioned by Washington in June 2026, and to transactions associated with North Korean cryptocurrency exchange hacks and other illicit activity.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the action was intended to dismantle financial infrastructure that enables Iran and other U.S. adversaries to evade sanctions and move illicit funds. A7 has rejected the American allegations of wrongdoing, saying it operates compliance procedures and was established to facilitate payments for Russian businesses facing what it considers illegitimate restrictions. The company's denials include the allegations concerning Iran and terrorist organizations. 
From Israel to the Kremlin's protection
Shor's personal history is as unusual as the financial operation he now oversees. Born in Tel Aviv in 1987 to a family originally from Moldova, he moved with his parents to Chisinau during the 1990s. His father, Miron Shor, established a successful duty-free retail business, which Ilan joined as a young man. After his father's death, he took control of the family enterprise and expanded into other sectors, building a business empire before entering Moldovan politics.
His political career was overshadowed by one of Moldova's largest financial scandals. In 2017, Shor was convicted in connection with the theft of approximately $1 billion from the country's banking system, a case widely known in Moldova as the "theft of the century." Initially sentenced to seven and a half years in prison, he remained free during his appeal and fled to Israel in 2019. In April 2023, a Moldovan appeals court increased his prison sentence to 15 years for fraud and money laundering. His political party was subsequently banned. Shor has maintained that he was the victim of political persecution by Moldova's pro-Western authorities. 
After spending several years in Israel, Shor relocated to Russia, where he emerged as an outspoken supporter of Putin and increasingly appeared in Kremlin-aligned media. Despite remaining wanted by Moldova, he has continued to conduct major business operations from Russia under the protection of the country's political establishment. His role in A7 has made him a prominent figure in Moscow's efforts to maintain international financial connections despite Western restrictions.
The revelations come as Netanyahu warns that Israel could eventually face economic and banking sanctions of its own and has instructed advisers to examine alternative financial arrangements, including blockchain technology and cryptocurrencies. Netanyahu has not proposed adopting A7's methods, and his comments concerned preparations for possible future restrictions, rather than sanctions already imposed on Israel's banking system. Nevertheless, Shor's story illustrates both the scale that sanctions-resistant payment networks can reach and the serious legal and security consequences they can face when their activities attract international scrutiny.

NEW DELHI: With US sanctions squeezing Indian firms trading in Iranian petroleum and petrochemicals, Tehran has a message for Indian businesses: "Both sides are determined to strengthen economic relations and to find practical ways to ensure the continuation of bilateral trade."Iran's ambassador to India, Mohammad Fathali, told TOI that sanctions and payment disruptions had dented trade and "the prices of some goods in Iran have increased for common people," but ruled out "essential shortages,” including Indian basmati rice, a major Indian export to Iran, saying Tehran had prepared for disruptions and had multiple import channels. “We do not expect these challenges to lead to shortages of essential goods, including Indian basmati rice,” Fathalisaid, adding that price rises reflected wider economic pressures rather than supply shortages.Amid US sanctions on Indian firms over Iranian petroleum trade,Iran’s ambassador to India urged Indian businesses to continue and expand trade with Tehran, acknowledging that sanctions and payment disruptions had reduced bilateral trade “to some extent”.Iran’s ambassador also pitched the country’s energy market to Indian firms, saying Tehran was ready to engage companies interested in the sector. “Any company that wishes to operate and trade in Iran’s energy market can benefit from the opportunities available in this market,” Fathali said.

Iran seeks negotiations to achieve a genuine result, not to provide another opportunity for pressure to be imposed on the country."

Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:39:26 UTC
22:39:26 KST

Who was behind the deadly church shooting in Jordan?
Authorities are investigating the rare attack on a Christian church; the assailants remain unidentified and at large.
Security forces in Jordan are searching for three gunmen who opened fire at a church in Karak governorate on Friday, killing eight people and injuring dozens more, according to Jordan’s Ministry of Health.
King Abdullah II said those behind the attack would face the “harshest penalties”, as he offered his condolences to the victims’ families. He has ordered a review of the country’s security procedures for responding to terrorist attacks.
Authorities are calling this rare attack on a Christian place of worship an act of terror, with the perpetrators yet to be identified.
Here’s what we know about how the attack unfolded, and what was behind it.
What happened during the church shooting in Karak?
On Friday afternoon, three masked gunmen opened fire during a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud.
Survivors said they heard an explosion just after the start of the service. Two attackers who arrived in a vehicle were joined by a third carrying a semi-automatic rifle. They entered the church and opened fire for several minutes.
One survivor, Nasser al-Burqan, a lawyer, told the Reuters news agency that one of the attackers, standing about two metres (6.5 feet) away, pointed a handgun at him and opened fire.
“When everything finally quietened down, I looked out the window behind me, and I saw two [assailants] – one was masked, the other was not; he was carrying a handgun,” said al-Burqan, a lawyer.
Later, his son, who had also been present, called him to say he had been shot in the leg and was being treated in hospital.
Tarek Ammarin, who was visiting a relative injured in the attack, now in hospital, said: “A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word.”
Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a list of officials condemning what he called a “wicked” attack.
“God willing, this country will remain safe,” he said.
State news channel Al-Mamlaka reported that security forces were deployed to the church and were in pursuit of the two suspects who had arrived in a vehicle.
How many people were killed or injured?
Eight people were killed in the shooting, including seven who died at the scene and one who succumbed to her injuries hours after the attack, Jordan’s Petra news agency reported on Saturday.
Of the 40 people injured, 27 are still in hospital. The Director of Prince Ali Military Hospital in Karak said one person is in critical condition, after undergoing surgery.
Who carried out the attack?
The identity of the three attackers has not been confirmed, with government statements referring to them as “unknown assailants”.
Security camera footage of the attack has been circulating online, however. Video broadcast by Al-Mamlaka shows three people shooting outside the church and running towards its entrance.
Other footage also shows the attackers opening fire on a group of men outside the building trying to flee.
Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin Al-Farrayeh said a group of “extremists” that have “no relationship to humanity” were responsible for the attack, though no specific groups were mentioned.
Why was the church targeted?
Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said on Friday that the attack was a by-product of terrorist ideology and “blind extremism”, but did not give specifics about the attackers.
The motive remains unclear since the attackers’ identities have yet to be revealed.
Where is Karak, and what do we know about its Christian community?
Karak governorate is about 120km (75 miles) south of Amman and is home to many from Jordan’s Christian minority, which makes up about 300,000 of the country’s population of 11.5 million people.
Taylor Luck, senior Middle East correspondent at the Christian Science Monitor, told Al Jazeera that Jordan’s Christians “pride themselves on [their] interfaith solidarity and coexistence”.
He said that Christians and Muslims have lived side-by-side in Karak for generations and that if the attack had been carried out in an attempt to divide the community, it is more likely that the “community come[s] back even stronger”.
Jordan is also home to many biblical sites that draw visitors from around the world.
What has the response been to this shooting?
Several countries, including Azerbaijan, Iraq, Poland, Palestine and Qatar, have issued statements condemning the attack and expressing their solidarity with Jordan.
Ahmed al-Tayeb, the grand imam of Al-Azhar in Cairo, a leading Sunni religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of the victims, calling the shooting a “heinous terrorist attack”.
“This crime contradicts the teachings of the Abrahamic religions and reveals that its perpetrators are devoid of all compassion, humanity and morality,” he wrote in a social media post.
The United States embassy in Jordan also released a statement on X offering condolences to victims and survivors of the attack.
“On behalf of the American people, we offer our most heartfelt condolences to the victims and survivors of the terror attack today at a church in Karak, Jordan,” it said.
The Jordanian Prime Minister declared three days of mourning following the attack, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public buildings.
Has Jordan experienced similar attacks before?
Yes, although they are rare.
In 2016, the ISIL (ISIS) group carried out a series of attacks across Karak, including a deadly siege on a Crusader-era castle in which 10 people were killed, including a Canadian tourist and seven police officers. Dozens of others were injured.
Four attackers were later killed by Jordanian security forces following a long standoff.

More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:38:05 UTC
22:38:05 KST

More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Everyone is due an extra hour’s sleep on Sunday as the clocks will roll back an hour at 3am to 2am.
Daylight saving time in the Netherlands has been in place since 1977, following the oil crisis of the 70s, when saving energy on lighting became a priority.
The clocks go forward in spring, on the last Sunday of March, to give lighter evenings. Staying on summer time into the winter would mean very dark mornings, so in October the clocks return to standard time.
The EU has debated ending daylight saving time altogether and the European Parliament voted to stop it in 1996 but member states have not yet committed to it.
So tomorrow you can lie in a little longer.

UAE's Ras Al Khaimah shuts all beaches as neighbours grapple with oil spill
Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after an offshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighbouring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah.
The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given.
The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment.
All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said.
The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions.
Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE's northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict's environmental fallout.
Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts' planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island.
The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE's first commercial gaming licence in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027.
Wynn said in March it had resumed construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East.
Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday.
UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.

How Operation Santa Claus grew from Christmas donations to ‘engine’ of change
Fundraising drive has evolved over its nearly 40 years from simply disbursing funds to building sustained relationships with NGOs
Over nearly four decades, Operation Santa Claus (OSC) has grown from a quirky holiday fundraiser into an “engine” for community change in Hong Kong.
For some beneficiaries, the journey was a full circle. Rachel Chow Chiu-yan learned about the fundraising drive in Young Post when she was a student, later pitched for funds on behalf of a group helping teenage girls and later joined the charity.
“Ten to 20 years ago, Operation Santa Claus disbursed some funding to charities that saw it as seed money. Now, after successful pilot schemes, the initiatives have been replicated,” Chow, former senior manager of the programme, said.
The drive was established by the South China Morning Post and public broadcaster RTHK in 1988.

Merve Berker

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Saturday called for reforms to make the UN Security Council more just and inclusive, stressing the need to strengthen the organization's ability to address global crises.
In a message marking UN Day and the 81st anniversary of the organization's founding, shared by Türkiye's Communications Directorate on the Turkish social media platform NSosyal, Erdogan said the UN's founding mission remains increasingly important amid global challenges.
"It has become particularly important to establish a more just and inclusive structure for the UN Security Council that can meet the expectations of the international community," he said.
Erdogan cited ongoing wars, humanitarian disasters, climate change, hunger, poverty, racism, xenophobia and Islamophobia as challenges demonstrating the continued importance of the UN.
He said the organization, established after two world wars to "save succeeding generations from the scourge of war," has assumed significant responsibilities in maintaining international peace and security and promoting development and prosperity.
Referring to Gaza, Erdogan said the deaths of more than 74,000 people in the "genocide," along with conflicts elsewhere, demonstrate the urgency of reform.
He called on countries to uphold the UN Charter more strongly and support reforms aimed at improving the effectiveness of the organization's principal bodies.
Erdogan also reaffirmed Türkiye's support for the UN80 Initiative launched by Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
"We are working in close cooperation with the organization toward our goal of making Istanbul a UN hub," he said.
Congratulating UN personnel worldwide, Erdogan reiterated Türkiye's determination to support efforts toward a more effective and inclusive international system.

Under the scheme, passengers can opt for insurance by paying a premium of 45 paise per passenger, offering coverage of up to ₹10 lakh in case of death or permanent total disability arising from a railway accident or untoward incident.
LUCKNOW: Indian Railways has decided to extend its Optional Travel Insurance Scheme (OTIS) to passengers booking reserved tickets through Passenger Reservation System (PRS) counters from October 27, in compliance with Supreme Court directions.In an order issued on Saturday, the Railway Board directed all zonal railways to make necessary arrangements for implementing the scheme at reservation counters.The decision follows the Supreme Court's October 6 order in the Union of India versus Radha Yadav case.Under the scheme, passengers can opt for insurance by paying a premium of 45 paise per passenger, offering coverage of up to Rs 10 lakh in case of death or permanent total disability arising from a railway accident or untoward incident.The policy also provides Rs 7.5 lakh for permanent partial disability, up to Rs 2 lakh towards hospitalisation expenses and Rs 10,000 for transportation of mortal remains.According to the Railway Board, insurance will remain optional, and reservation staff must inform passengers about its availability before booking.
Passengers opting for insurance must provide a mobile number and pay the premium through digital payment modes only.
The premium will be collected along with the ticket fare.Insurance policy details will be communicated to passengers through their registered mobile numbers.The Board clarified that the existing terms and conditions applicable to IRCTC e-ticket insurance will also apply to tickets purchased at reservation counters.Divisional railway managers and commercial officers have been directed to monitor implementation, while zonal railways must submit compliance reports confirming operational readiness.
