Harmonized regulatory frameworks urged in Africa to advance pharmaceutical self-reliance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
21:32:57 CST
22:32:57 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Industry experts and stakeholders on Friday called for concerted action to establish a robust ecosystem for bioequivalence testing to ensure locally manufactured generic medicines across Eastern and Southern Africa are safe, accessible, and scientifically proven.
The call was made during a regional workshop focused on developing a White Paper on bioequivalence testing and regulatory harmonization in Eastern and Southern Africa, held in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia. The five-day event, which ran from Oct. 19 to 23, highlighted the critical need for harmonized regulatory frameworks and expanded domestic testing capacity to eliminate costly reliance on overseas facilities.
Jointly organized by the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the Ethiopian government and the World Bank, the workshop brought together national regulators, pharmaceutical manufacturers, experts and researchers, as well as development partners to establish a comprehensive regional framework for bioequivalence testing.
Experts and policymakers at the gathering emphasized that relying on external testing facilities imposes significant economic burdens and causes regulatory approval delays for locally manufactured generic drugs. They stressed the urgent need to expand domestic testing capacity to support sustainable pharmaceutical growth across the region.
Addressing the workshop, Girum Hailu, a senior policy and partnership specialist at IGAD, highlighted several critical gaps affecting the sector, including limited regional bioequivalence testing facilities, heavy dependence on overseas testing, high study costs, and inconsistent regulatory requirements across borders.
To overcome these challenges, experts advocated for advancing regulatory harmonization aligned with international standards, implementing phased, risk-based compliance pathways for legacy products, and establishing shared regional testing capacity backed by strong oversight mechanisms to support local manufacturers.
Stakeholders also underscored the vital importance of making bioequivalence services more affordable and accessible to local pharmaceutical manufacturers, outlining priority investments and capacity-building measures for accredited centers across the region. ■

Hu Jieguo, secretary-general of the China Council for the Promotion of Peaceful National Reunification in Western Africa, said Taiwan was liberated from Japanese colonial rule and returned to China 81 years ago.

"The African people, including the people of Nigeria, endured the suffering brought by colonialism, just as China did, and went through the same historical process of striving for national independence, state sovereignty and national dignity," Gui said.

"There is a certain similarity between China's efforts to maintain national unity and Nigeria's own experience in maintaining its territorial integrity," Ibrahim said, expressing confidence that China would eventually achieve peaceful reunification with Taiwan.

Justice chancellor: Wild boar cannot be made to suffer when training hunting dogs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Justice chancellor: Wild boar cannot be made to suffer when training hunting dogs
The Ministry of Regional Affairs and the Ministry of Climate should establish clear legal rules for training hunting dogs using live wild boars to ensure animal welfare and legal clarity, the Chancellor of Justice's Office says.
Four years ago in May, the regional affairs minister issued a regulation on measures to prevent and control African swine fever, introducing an exemption under which the ban on keeping pigs outdoors does not apply to wild boars kept for training hunting dogs.
The Estonian Union for the Protection of Animals asked the chancellor of justice to examine whether the regulation complies with the Animal Protection Act. The organization also pointed out that the law provides no legal basis for using wild boars kept in artificial environments to train hunting dogs and that no detailed requirements have been established for such training.
Deputy Chancellor of Justice-Adviser Olari Koppel said the ban on keeping pigs outdoors is a biosecurity measure and that the minister has the authority to introduce exemptions, provided they comply with EU law and do not undermine animal disease prevention. Koppel therefore sees no reason to believe that the exemption for training hunting dogs violates these conditions.
However, he noted that the regulation only provides an exemption from the ban on keeping pigs outdoors. It does not provide a legal basis for using wild boars to train hunting dogs or authorize activities prohibited under the Animal Protection Act.
"The absence of a specific legal provision does not, however, mean that such an activity is prohibited, provided other applicable rules are followed," Koppel said, adding that it must be possible to conduct training without endangering the animal's welfare.
The law does not establish a specific legal basis or detailed requirements for training hunting dogs using live wild boars. The activity is primarily governed by the Nature Conservation Act and the general animal welfare requirements arising from it.
Under the Animal Protection Act, animals must not be subjected to suffering or pain. According to Koppel, if hunting dog training cannot be conducted without causing such harm, the executive branch cannot make the activity permissible through regulations, guidelines or administrative practices.
"In that case, only the Riigikogu can decide through legislation whether the objective of the training and the benefits it provides justify making an exception to the prohibition established by law," Koppel said.
Koppel said the lack of clarity in the regulations is a problem. To address it, the Ministry of Regional Affairs and the Ministry of Climate should establish the conditions for training hunting dogs in legislation rather than merely in guidelines or explanatory memorandums. This would ensure compliance with animal welfare requirements and provide legal clarity.

Molodist Film Festival Marks 55 Years, Bringing International Cinema to Kyiv Oct. 24-Nov. 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The 55th Molodist International Film Festival will take place in Kyiv from Oct. 24 to Nov. 1, 2026.
One of Eastern Europe’s leading film events marks its anniversary with a new visual identity while maintaining its mission of discovering emerging talent and helping debut filmmakers find their place in world cinema.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Founded in 1970 as a student film showcase, Molodist has evolved over more than five decades into an international platform for emerging filmmakers. Its program features feature-length debuts and short films – fiction, documentary and animation – by filmmakers from Ukraine and around the world.
From student films to an international festival
The first festival lasted just two days and featured 33 short films made by students of the Kyiv State Institute of Theatrical Arts named after Ivan Karpenko-Kary. The event was founded by film directors Vadym Chubasov and Viktor Ivchenko.
Since then, Molodist has become a platform for discovering new talent and introducing Ukrainian audiences to international cinema. The festival is accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (FIAPF), which recognizes its standing on the international film circuit.
The competition program includes student films, short films and feature-length debuts, with a dedicated competition for documentaries. The non-competition program features sections such as Festival of Festivals, Forma, The Century of the Greats and Midnight Screening, among others.
Russia Hits Central Kyiv With Cluster Missile
The festival’s top award is the Scythian Deer statuette, presented to winners of its competition programs.
Oleh Sentsov to head the international jury
The international jury of the 55th Molodist Film Festival will be chaired by Oleh Sentsov, a Ukrainian film director, screenwriter and writer, former Kremlin political prisoner and serviceman in the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU).
Sentsov directed the feature films “Gamer” (2011) and “Numbers” (2019), as well as the documentary “Real” (2024). His honors include the European Parliament’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought in 2018, Ukraine’s Taras Shevchenko National Prize in 2016 and France’s Legion of Honour.
The international jury also includes Matthijs Wouter Knol of the Netherlands, CEO and executive director of the European Film Academy, Iranian filmmaker and human rights advocate Mahnaz Mohammadi, Ukrainian theater director Yevhen Lavrenchuk, and Latvian film scholar and critic Anita Uzulniece.
The jury will assess student films, shorts and feature-length debuts from around the world and select the recipient of the festival’s Grand Prix.
A separate jury for the National Competition will include Ukrainian director Viacheslav Turyanytsia, Polish film programmer Radek Lipka and French-British film programmer and Film Republic founder Xavier Henry-Rashid.
How to attend the festival
Screenings will take place at the Zhovten Cinema and the House of Cinema in Kyiv. Festival passes are already on sale. Students can purchase passes at a discounted rate, while Ukrainian military personnel are eligible for free passes upon verification of their service status.
Over 55 years, Molodist has grown from a student film showcase into an international cinema forum while retaining its core mission: supporting a new generation of filmmakers and introducing audiences to films that will help shape the future of cinema.

CIA contractor accused of leaking US reports on Israel to journalist girlfriend who published them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:29:57 UTC
22:29:57 KST

A classified U.S. intelligence assessment warning that Israel could descend into civil conflict, claims that Israeli officials pressed the Trump administration to assassinate a senior Iranian leader, and a secret report detailing efforts to secure American military support beyond Donald Trump's presidency are among the revelations at the center of a major intelligence leak scandal in Washington. 
On Friday, the FBI arrested a CIA contractor suspected of passing classified information to his journalist girlfriend, whose reporting included five stories based on sensitive intelligence, three of them directly concerning Israel.
The suspect, Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of Washington, D.C., held a Top Secret security clearance with access to highly sensitive intelligence. Prosecutors allege that for months he exploited his access to U.S. intelligence systems to examine classified reports unrelated to his duties and pass information to his romantic partner, who operated an independent news publication on Substack. Investigators linked his access to sensitive documents with telephone conversations between the couple and the publication dates of articles allegedly containing information from those reports.
American authorities have not publicly identified the journalist, referred to in the FBI affidavit as "Individual 1," or disclosed the subjects of the classified reports. However, documents obtained by ynet indicate that she is American journalist Aída Chávez, founder of the independent investigative publication Capital & Empire. Chávez previously worked for The Hill, contributed to The Washington Post and served as a congressional correspondent for The Intercept and Washington correspondent for The Nation. Five articles published on her website match the dates identified in the FBI affidavit, while a passage from a September fundraising appeal appears almost word for word in the document. Chávez has not been charged with any offense in connection with the investigation.
Israel's alleged assassination request and fears of civil war
One of the most significant articles appeared on May 28, under the headline "EXCLUSIVE: Israel Privately Pressing U.S. to Kill Iran's Lead Negotiator and Launch New Strikes." Chávez reported that Israeli officials had urged the Trump administration to assassinate Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament and a central figure in negotiations between Tehran and Washington. According to the report, Israel sought to persuade the Americans to abandon negotiations and resume attacks on Iran's oil infrastructure, believing further economic damage could trigger widespread protests and potentially bring down the Iranian regime.
Chávez said her reporting drew on a classified intelligence assessment circulated within the U.S. intelligence community and conversations with officials familiar with its contents. The FBI affidavit states that Brinksman accessed a classified report on May 26 and called his girlfriend three times that day. Two days later, she published an article that investigators say contained information from the same report.
Another article, published on July 29, described a U.S. intelligence assessment concerning Israel's efforts to preserve its strategic relationship with Washington as American public support for Israel weakened. According to Chávez, Israeli officials were seeking to embed their country more deeply within the American military, intelligence and defense industries, making it more difficult for future administrations to reduce cooperation. The reported strategy included discussions about a possible permanent U.S. military base in Israel, expanded joint weapons development and stronger ties with influential American technology executives. Investigators said Brinksman accessed a Top Secret document on July 28, spoke with his girlfriend several times that day and that an article containing information from the document appeared the following day.
The third Israel-related article, published on October 5 in cooperation with Drop Site News, concerned a reported CIA assessment titled "Fracture From Within." According to two American sources cited in the article, the assessment was prepared in August by the CIA's Red Cell, a unit tasked with challenging conventional intelligence assumptions and examining alternative scenarios. It warned that Israel's political crisis, disputes over military conscription for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, economic pressure, social divisions and the psychological consequences of prolonged warfare could combine to produce severe internal conflict or even institutional breakdown ahead of the October 27 election.
The reported assessment raised concerns about armed military veterans returning from combat with psychological trauma, worsening political polarization and mounting resentment over exemptions from military service. It also examined the possibility of foreign technology companies withdrawing from Israel, deteriorating regional relationships and Hamas or Hezbollah exploiting domestic instability. Crucially, the report did not constitute an official U.S. intelligence prediction that civil war would occur. It was an assessment of potential risks and scenarios, as described by the journalist's sources.
The FBI affidavit details another striking sequence of events. Brinksman allegedly accessed a classified document several times in August and again on October 1. Telephone records show that he spoke with his girlfriend for 47 minutes that day, followed by another conversation lasting 37 minutes. Four days later, the article on Israel's potential internal collapse appeared.
The two remaining articles concerned other Middle Eastern developments. On March 11, Chávez reported that Bahrain had brought in forces from Jordan to help suppress protests over its involvement in the war with Iran. On May 13, she reported on a classified CIA assessment describing divisions among Washington's Gulf allies, with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain favoring continued strikes against Iran while Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait preferred renewed negotiations. Investigators allege that classified information accessed by Brinksman also appeared in these reports.
More than 800 calls and a trail of classified documents
The evidence that led investigators to Brinksman is detailed in a 13-page FBI affidavit. He began working for a U.S. government agency in 2020 before moving to a contractor serving the same agency. In 2022, he took a position involving computer systems integration, including work transferring data between classified and unclassified systems. CIA Director John Ratcliffe confirmed that Brinksman had provided services to the agency.
His position required him to work inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF, a secure area where personal phones and electronic devices are prohibited. Employees must use identification cards to enter and leave, creating records that became central to the investigation. According to the FBI, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified reports, left the secure area and contacted his girlfriend, sometimes within minutes. Investigators believe these intervals allowed him to retrieve his personal phone, possibly from his vehicle, and communicate sensitive information.
In one example, the journalist called Brinksman at 8:41 a.m. on March 11. Less than half an hour later, he accessed a classified intelligence report at 9:09 a.m. and again at 10:01 a.m. He subsequently left the secure facility and received another call from her that evening, lasting about 14 minutes. An article published that day allegedly contained Top Secret information from the document he had examined.
Investigators found records of more than 800 telephone calls or attempted calls between the couple during 2026. They also examined computers at Brinksman's workplace and discovered that he was among no more than six people who had accessed the journalist's Substack publication from that facility during the period under investigation. According to the affidavit, no other individual combined access to all five classified reports with visits to all five articles that authorities believe contained information from those documents.
A notebook discovered on Brinksman's desk on October 10 also attracted investigators' attention because corners had been torn from several pages. An FBI agent noted that individuals who transmit sensitive information sometimes write notes to reproduce accurate or near-verbatim quotations. However, the affidavit did not establish that the notebook contained leaked secrets or provide direct evidence that its missing pages had been used to transmit information.
‘I'm helping her build her publication’
One of the most personal details in the investigation emerged from an email Brinksman sent to a friend in November 2025. He described his new relationship with a journalist who had recently become independent and explained that he was helping her establish a publication focused on foreign policy. He added that the project had proved surprisingly fulfilling. Other emails examined by investigators supported the conclusion that the two were romantically involved.
According to the affidavit, their collaboration extended beyond conversations about published stories. On March 13, Brinksman received permission to edit a Google Docs document concerning a Middle Eastern country. Minutes later, he suggested a wording change, which his girlfriend marked as resolved. The article published that day matches a Chávez report concerning Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer, a prominent supporter of Israel, and congressional votes related to the war with Iran. Investigators did not identify classified information in that particular article. Brinksman had also sought advance publication clearance, as required of security clearance holders, for articles he co-authored with the journalist.
Brinksman's background adds an unusual dimension to the allegations. A graduate of Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service, he co-authored a study published in May 2019 titled "Millennial Considerations on Insider Threat: Are We A Threat Or An Opportunity?" The research examined the risks posed by employees with access to sensitive information and proposed measures to prevent security breaches, including employee training, monitoring potential warning signs and addressing vulnerabilities associated with social media and mobile technology. Seven years later, Brinksman faces allegations involving precisely the kind of insider threat his research sought to help organizations prevent.
Chávez describes Capital & Empire as an independent publication investigating the interests driving American military and economic policy. In a September fundraising appeal, she said she had published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that she believed the public deserved to know about. She also encouraged readers with inside information to provide leaks.
Brinksman has been charged with unlawfully transmitting national defense information, an offense carrying a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg accused him of going far beyond his duties to obtain closely guarded American intelligence and passing it to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish it. Eisenberg described the alleged conduct as a betrayal of the trust placed in someone holding a security clearance. FBI Director Kash Patel pledged to pursue anyone who abuses access to government secrets, while Ratcliffe said the arrest followed a referral from the CIA and warned that unauthorized disclosures could endanger intelligence sources, ongoing operations and agency personnel. Brinksman remains presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

22:25:46 KST

Cornell University’s Jane Doe told faculty members that she felt  “unsupported and disbelieved” by the Ivy League university’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, NBC reported on Wednesday.
In a letter to Cornell’s faculty senate, Doe provided what she called a secondhand account of a meeting between Kotlikoff and the then-president of her sorority, Tri Delta.
“After the conversation she shared with me, with concern, that President Kotlikoff’s initial response was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’” Doe wrote in the letter. “She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story.”
The meeting was held months after October 19-20, 2024, when Doe was allegedly raped by seven members of the now-defunct Chi Phi fraternity.
She alerted campus police to the incident on November 8, 2024.
Cornell claims comments were taken out of context
The meeting that Jane Doe is claiming to provide a secondhand account of occurred in January 2025.
In the letter, Doe wrote that her sorority president told her that at least one other faculty member “appeared distressed” at Kotlikoff’s line of questioning, and said that the person believed that “the President’s response was inappropriate.”
Cornell said in a statement that while Kotlikoff did make a similar comment at the meeting, the secondhand account was taken out of context.
“The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account,” the statement added. “The question ‘why did it take so long for the assault to be reported’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024. He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.”
Cornell's Jane Doe felt the administration didn't believe her
But Jane Doe said in her letter that the comment left her feeling unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff.
“It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school.”
This comes ahead of a vote of no confidence in Kotlikoff’s administration.
Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told NBC that the letter she wrote to the faculty senate was for “informational purposes only.”
“Jane Doe thought it important that the faculty senate have this information as it deliberates and considers the resolutions or motions before it,” Giuffra said. “Jane Doe would ask the faculty senate to give her letter whatever weight or credibility it deems appropriate.”

Amnesty Indonesia is right, the Foreign Ministry is wrong: Quit Trump&#8217;s Board of Peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:25:22 UTC
22:25:22 KST

On Thursday, Indonesia’s Foreign Ministry defended the country’s seat on the Board of Peace. Ministry spokesperson Vahd Nabyl Mulachela said joining the Board is part of Indonesia’s effort to support Palestine and help rebuild Gaza. He hoped the Board could lead to an independent Palestine living next to Israel.
He was answering Amnesty International Indonesia. A day earlier, its director, Usman Hamid, said the Board was a mistake from the very beginning and that Indonesia still has time to leave. He spoke in Jakarta after an event with Francesca Albanese, the United Nations expert on the occupied Palestinian territories. Usman said the Board is controlled by the United States, a country that fully supports Israel and its military campaign that has killed so many Palestinian civilians.
The real question is whether the Board of Peace is the right tool. Amnesty says it is not, and Amnesty is right.
The ministry’s hope is understandable. But hope is not a plan. The way the Board actually works tells a different story.
Neil Quilliam, a researcher at Chatham House, a respected think tank in London, studied the Board’s design in February. He explained that real power sits with the Board and its chairman, Trump. Daily decisions go to a Gaza Executive Board, which has no Palestinian members. A foreign military force keeps security.
There is a Palestinian committee of 15 people, but Israel checked and approved its members under American supervision. In simple words, outsiders choose who speaks for Palestinians, and those Palestinians get very little power.
Quilliam also pointed out that the UN Security Council decision backing the plan does not promise a Palestinian state. It only says statehood might become possible after many conditions are met, such as Gaza giving up all its weapons and the Palestinian Authority carrying out reforms. Until then, Gaza and the West Bank stay separated, at least until the end of 2027, when the Board’s mandate ends. By that time, he warns, it may be too late.
The rebuilding plan is no better. Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, has presented a New Gaza with new districts designed to look like Dubai. Quilliam argues the plan treats Gaza like empty beach property, not as part of a Palestinian homeland, and that Palestinians were barely consulted. Building will start in New Rafah, an area under Israeli army control, and Israel and its partners may decide which Palestinians can live there. The likely result, in his view, is two Gazas: one clean, disarmed and closely watched, and another left in ruins, where most Palestinians live.
READ: Why Indonesia joined the Badr pact, and what it must do next
Then there is the West Bank. In February, Israel’s security cabinet approved new rules that widen Israeli control there and make it easier to take Palestinian land. As Quilliam notes, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said Israel would “continue to bury the idea of a Palestinian state.” The Board of Peace has no power over any of this. It only looks at Gaza.
Most painful of all, the killing has not stopped. In September, Hamas urged the Board to stop Israeli attacks on Gaza. This week, UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that attacks by Israeli settlers are meant to push Palestinians off their land.
A body that cannot stop bombs in Gaza or land grabs in the West Bank is not bringing peace. It is only managing the damage on terms that suit Israel.
The ministry says Indonesia can steer the Board from the inside. Yet the same spokesperson admitted that Indonesia has put all its discussions in the Board on hold while it watches events in the Middle East. If Indonesia has already stepped back, what influence is it really using?
Staying also has a price. Indonesia has a proud history of standing with Palestine at the United Nations. Indonesia’s name on the Board makes a process built without Palestinians look more acceptable to the world. That works against the very cause Indonesia says it defends.
There is a better road. Amnesty has called on Indonesia to make full use of its place at the UN. Indonesia can work with Arab, Asian and European countries to protect the goal of a Palestinian state, push for sanctions when international law is broken, and help Palestinian groups unite. Even Quilliam says governments must move beyond statements and apply real pressure, or the chance of a Palestinian state will disappear.
Indonesia says it wants to help Palestine. Leaving the Board of Peace would show the world that it means it.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Isamaa party promises to close the climate ministry and create scandals committee

"Those same three parties that, under SALK's leadership, have established a politics of lies under both Kaja Kallas' and Kristen Michal's governments are now maneuvering to escape political punishment and put up camouflage nets," Reinsalu said, referring to the coalition Reform Party and Eesti 200, as well as the opposition Social Democrats.
According to the Isamaa chairman, Eesti 200 is being pressured to withdraw from the elections so that its remaining voters will instead bolster the Reform Party and the Social Democrats.
"So much for political accountability," Reinsalu said. "With the prime minister's speech to the party council, the Reform Party has launched a new wave of fearmongering and lies. This is being dressed up in a marketing campaign whose underlying message is that, yes, we have failed, but we will do better in the future."
"The Reform Party is featuring a beloved actor in its campaign, while the Social Democrats have adopted a different tactic, attempting to conceal their complicity in the Kallas-Michal government by maneuvering to put forward the secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as their candidate for prime minister. This maneuver will not succeed!" the Isamaa chairman said.
Reinsalu summed up Isamaa's political plans following the 2027 Riigikogu elections with the words "Let the citizens decide."
The party plans to give citizens the right to initiate early elections, following the Latvian model, and to establish a commission of inquiry into scandals after the elections. Lying before the commission would be a criminal offense.
In the area of defense, the party plans to close the border with Russia.
Isamaa also pledged to introduce a supplementary budget that would cut spending.
"Cost-cutting starts at the top: parliamentary and ministerial salaries, closing the Ministry of Climate and a critical review of foundations and subsidies," the party pledged.

The party also promised to end what it described as the harassment of businesses. "The Climate Act will be thrown in the trash. Investment certainty and a stable operating environment will be restored for the resource-based economy."

Isamaa promised to protect fundamental freedoms and repeal unnecessary restrictions.
The party also pledged to ease the burden of raising children on families and protect teachers' incomes.
In the energy sector, the party will emphasize oil shale. "The energy sector will be provided with dispatchable generation capacity, domestic resources (including oil shale) and affordable prices. Efforts to render oil shale-based energy production unviable will be halted."
The party also promised stricter requirements for the use of Estonian in public spaces, a conservative immigration policy and the restoration of regional balance.
Parliamentary elections will take place in March 2027.

British jets escort French jets on ‘nuclear strike’
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:18:23 BST
22:18:23 KST

RAF Typhoons have escorted French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike mission over the Mediterranean, the first time British aircraft have taken part in a French nuclear exercise, according to the government.
Exercise Rummy ran on 20 and 21 October, with the Rafales launching from Saint-Dizier air base in eastern France, the home of the French air force’s airborne nuclear component. No nuclear weapons were involved, and the Ministry of Defence said the exercise was conducted under robust safety and security arrangements and focused on how the two air forces work together.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “This exercise marks a new chapter in the defence nuclear relationship between the United Kingdom and France.
“As Europe’s nuclear powers, we have a shared responsibility to contribute to the security and stability of the Euro-Atlantic region. This exercise demonstrates the depth of our partnership, the credibility of our deterrents and our determination to stand together in the face of emerging threats.
“In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt: the UK and France remain united in our commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations.”
Catherine Vautrin, the French Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans, said: “Having independent nuclear forces does not exclude coordination. Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom keeps deepening: on Tuesday night, UK Typhoons participated for the very first time to a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafales.
“Through coordination, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the Alliance and to the peace and stability of the Euro Atlantic area.”
The exercise falls under the Northwood Declaration, the agreement signed last year under which the two countries said that no extreme threat to Europe could arise which would not prompt a response by both, while each retains sovereign and independent nuclear forces and national decision making. Britain and France are the only nuclear armed states in Europe, and the declaration established a joint nuclear steering group to coordinate their policy, capabilities and operations.
Saint-Dizier is the base of the 4th Fighter Wing, which operates Rafales carrying the ASMP-A supersonic stand-off missile that forms the airborne half of the French deterrent. The French maintain both an airborne component and ballistic missile submarines, while Britain has relied on submarines alone since the WE.177 bomb was withdrawn in 1998.
That changes with the purchase of twelve F-35A aircraft and British entry into NATO’s nuclear mission, which will return a nuclear role to the Royal Air Force after more than a quarter of a century. Air Marshal Johnny Beck told a committee this year that the aircraft were not bought for the nuclear role, while the government has presented the purchase as the means of joining the mission.
The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise, funding the Dreadnought ballistic missile submarines, SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, a new sovereign warhead and the supporting infrastructure. The refreshed Lancaster House agreement between Britain and France covers an expanded joint deployable force, deeper nuclear cooperation and work on the next generation of weapons.

Investment security key to global gas market stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:15:57 UTC
22:15:57 KST

According to Iranian oil ministry's news service-SHANA, in an interview, Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, deputy oil minister for international affairs and trade and Iran’s representative at international energy forums, discussed the Moscow summit’s objectives, Iran’s agenda, the GECF’s role in global energy governance and opportunities for advancing Iran’s gas diplomacy.
Q: What are the circumstances surrounding the eighth GECF summit, and how do you assess its significance?
Mousavi: The eighth GECF summit is taking place at a critical juncture in the evolution of the international energy system and coincides with the forum’s 25th anniversary. In recent years, the global natural gas market has undergone significant changes driven by geopolitical, economic, technological and environmental factors.
Changes in international gas trade patterns, the expansion of liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure, growing concerns over supply and demand security, intensifying competition for investment and rising energy needs in emerging economies have underscored the importance of dialogue and coordination among gas-producing and exporting countries.
Against this backdrop, the summit provides an opportunity for leaders to exchange views at the highest political level, assess long-term market trends and strengthen common approaches to strategic issues facing the natural gas industry.
The significance of the summit extends beyond reviewing market developments. It can also help reinforce the GECF’s position as an influential platform for international energy dialogue and for safeguarding the legitimate interests of gas-producing and exporting countries.
Q: What level of participation will Iran have at the Moscow summit, and what is planned for the Iranian delegation?
Mousavi: Iran was the principal proponent of establishing the GECF and is one of its founding members. As a country with some of the world’s largest proven natural gas reserves, Iran has consistently played an active and influential role in the forum’s activities.
At the eighth summit, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will lead a high-level delegation accompanied by Hamid Bovard, caretaker oil minister.
The president’s address to the summit, outlining Iran’s principled positions on international developments and the global energy market, as well as the country’s views on the future of gas cooperation, will be among the main events of the visit.
Before the leaders’ summit, the forum’s 28th ministerial meeting will bring together ministers and senior representatives of member countries. The meeting will review and approve the secretariat’s programs and finalize the documents to be presented to the summit.
The Iranian delegation also plans to hold bilateral meetings with senior officials from member and observer countries, particularly on energy cooperation. Discussions will explore opportunities to expand bilateral and multilateral ties in natural gas trade, investment, infrastructure development, technology transfer, technological cooperation and the use of shared capacities among member countries.
Q: What are Iran’s main priorities and positions at the eighth summit?
Mousavi: Iran’s positions can be outlined along two principal dimensions: political issues and strategic energy priorities.
On the political front, one of the Iranian delegation’s priorities will be to explain the dimensions of the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran and condemn actions targeting the country’s national sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.
In this context, the martyrdom of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, military commanders and civilians, as well as events related to Minab and Lamerd, will be addressed in line with Iran’s official positions.
In the energy sector, our key priorities include protecting the collective interests of forum members, strengthening the role of natural gas in energy security, ensuring continued investment across the gas value chain, countering unilateral restrictive measures against producers, and expanding technical, commercial and investment cooperation.
We believe energy security is a balanced, multidimensional concept. Achieving it requires simultaneous attention to security of supply for consumers, security of demand for producers, investment security and the sustainability of energy trade flows.
Q: Given recent geopolitical developments, how do you view the relationship between political stability and security in the global gas market?
Mousavi: Because the natural gas industry is capital-intensive, involves long investment recovery periods and depends on extensive production, transmission, processing and export infrastructure, it requires political stability, investment security and predictable market conditions more than many other economic activities.
Any escalation in geopolitical tensions, threats to energy infrastructure, disruption of transportation routes or imposition of unilateral restrictions can affect project financing costs, investment risks and energy prices, ultimately undermining supply security in regional and global markets.
For this reason, we emphasize the need to prevent the politicization of energy trade and its use as an instrument in international relations. I believe the global gas market should develop on the basis of cooperation, mutual benefit, respect for contractual obligations and nondiscriminatory access to technology, equipment and financial resources.
Energy security is a shared responsibility among producers, consumers and countries through which energy is transported. None of these stakeholders can guarantee lasting energy security without taking the interests and concerns of the others into account.
Q: How do you assess the role of natural gas in the global energy mix in the years ahead?
Mousavi: Given its technical, economic and environmental characteristics, natural gas will remain an important pillar of global energy supply in the coming decades.
Compared with coal, natural gas emits less carbon dioxide when burned to produce the same amount of energy. If methane emissions across the supply chain are effectively managed, it can also help reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
In addition, the flexibility of gas-fired power plants allows them to support the integration of intermittent renewable energy sources, including solar and wind power.
Population growth, industrial development, urbanization and rising electricity demand in developing countries also provide considerable scope for natural gas to maintain its role in the global energy mix.
However, energy transition pathways differ from one country to another. Energy policies must reflect each country’s economic conditions, level of development, resource base and national priorities.
At the Oil Ministry, we believe the energy transition should be realistic, equitable and based on diversifying energy sources. It should not lead to unreasonable restrictions on investment in the natural gas industry.
Q: The GECF has emphasized the need for investment in the gas industry. Why is this important?
Mousavi: The sustainable development of the natural gas industry requires continuous, long-term investment across the entire value chain, from exploration and field development to processing, transmission, storage, exports and LNG infrastructure.
Because major gas projects generally require substantial financial resources and long periods for design, construction and operation, a stable and predictable investment environment is particularly important.
Reduced or delayed upstream investment can constrain supply capacity over the medium and long term, intensify price volatility and increase the vulnerability of the global gas market. Such an outcome would benefit neither producers nor consumers.
Accordingly, one of Iran’s key messages at the Moscow summit will be the need to strike a balance among energy security objectives, economic development and environmental considerations.
Producer countries must have fair access to financial resources, advanced technologies and consumer markets. Political barriers and unilateral restrictions should not obstruct the development of natural gas production and export capacity.
Q: What role does the GECF play in developments in the global gas market, and can it be considered an organization similar to OPEC?
Mousavi: The GECF is an intergovernmental organization with a consultative, analytical and cooperative mandate. It was established to strengthen engagement among natural gas-producing and exporting countries.
Unlike OPEC, the GECF does not have a mechanism for setting production quotas or directly managing natural gas supply volumes in the global market.
Structural differences between oil and gas markets, including the significant role of long-term contracts in gas trade, dedicated transmission infrastructure and the regional characteristics of gas markets, mean that cooperation within the forum operates differently.
Nevertheless, the GECF can play an effective role in strengthening natural gas’s position and defending producers’ shared interests by facilitating the exchange of views, experience and information; conducting specialized studies; providing long-term market outlooks; promoting technical cooperation; and coordinating members’ positions in international forums.
Strengthening the secretariat’s technical and research capabilities, expanding technological cooperation and increasing the forum’s participation in global energy discussions can further enhance its role in international energy governance.
Q: What capacity does Iran have to expand gas cooperation with other GECF members?
Mousavi: Thanks to its vast natural gas reserves, strategic geographical position, extensive gas transmission network, long experience in developing and operating gas fields, and technical and engineering capabilities, Iran has considerable potential to expand regional and international cooperation.
Iran’s geographical position, connecting energy-rich regions with consumer markets, offers opportunities to develop regional gas trade and transit cooperation.
Potential areas of cooperation with GECF members include expanding gas exports through pipelines and LNG, establishing swap and transit arrangements, cooperating in field development, participating in processing and infrastructure projects, and exchanging technical expertise.
Cooperation in reservoir management, improving recovery rates, reducing gas flaring, optimizing energy consumption, cutting methane emissions and developing technologies across the gas value chain could also become part of specialized engagement among member countries.
Realizing this potential will require political will among member countries, favorable economic, technical, contractual and investment conditions, and arrangements that ensure mutual benefits for all parties involved.

Brussels boutiques board up storefronts ahead of potential rioting

BRUSSELS, October 24. /TASS/. Shops in Brussels have taken extensive precautions ahead of a potential new wave of rioting this Saturday, boarding up their storefronts with wooden panels, a TASS correspondent reported.
Several major retailers and shopping arcades, including the flagship Apple store and numerous jewelry boutiques, have opted to suspend operations entirely.
In the capital’s luxury shopping districts along Avenue Louise, Boulevard de Waterloo, and in the Rue Neuve and Sablon areas, more than half of the storefronts have been covered with particleboard panels.
"Naturally, we hope that the police will be able to contain the unrest this time. But we have a grim history. Hopes aren't always realized," Antoine, the owner of a city center electronics store, told TASS.
According to him, the emergency installation of panels on a small shop featuring two glass display windows and a door costs owners between 1,500 and 2,000 euros. Although the panels are firmly screwed into the structural framework, such defensive measures "will only deter opportunistic rioters who aren't specifically targeting a particular store."
Last weekend, street unrest that began as student protests devolved into the looting of city center shops. This week, calls to "take to the streets for social justice on October 24" have once again circulated widely across Belgian social media. Shop owners are discussing online the possibility of legally using civilian or non-lethal weapons to defend against rioters. However, Belgian self-defense law justifies the use of force only to protect life and physical well-being, not property.
Brussels authorities have also undertaken extensive preparations. Reinforced police units are stationed at major intersections in the city center, and the number of patrols circulating throughout the city significantly exceeds that of an ordinary day.
By midday, the situation in the city remained calm. The areas around Brussels’ three main railway stations - North, South, and Central - where groups of protesters typically gather, are under heightened police surveillance, though the situation there remains peaceful for now.

Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:15:00 UTC
22:15:00 KST

Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- Queen Mary University of London
- Summary:
- A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.
- Share:
A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.
Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.
The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.
How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure
The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.
By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.
The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.
Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients
The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.
Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.
Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.
The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.
However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.
Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension
Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.
A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.
This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.
Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:
"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.
"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."
A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure
High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.
Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.
This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.
Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.
For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Queen Mary University of London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ajay Gupta, David Collier, James Steckelmacher, Jane Field, George Collett, Olivier Zongo, Mital Patel, Manish Saxena, Annastazia Learoyd, Amrita Ahluwalia, and Peter Sever on behalf of SCRATCH Trial Investigators . Safety, Acceptability and Efficacy of Noninvasive Transcutaneous-Autonomic Neuromodulation in Uncontrolled Hypertension. Hypertension, DOI: 10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.126.27847

Germany is negotiating a deal with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones, a German official with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24.
Berlin is discussing the deal with Kyiv as Germany plans to buy thousands of deep-strike weapons from European arms companies, as initially reported by Bloomberg on Oct. 23.
According to officials Bloomberg spoke with, Germany’s future strategic thinking involves using masses of cheap missiles to overwhelm enemy air defenses. Currently, Germany’s army only operates midrange Taurus cruise missiles, while the U.S. warned its allies to expect years-long delays for missile deliveries.
The Bars jet powered drone has a range of 1,000 kilometers and can reach speeds of up to 700 kilometers per hour. The manufacturer of the drones is not publicly known for security reasons.
The Ukrainian army launches around 2,000 of these drones per month, targeting Russian oil refineries, power plants, and substations, a representative of the company told Ukrainian media outlet NV in September.
Germany and Ukraine signed a deal to jointly produce Bars in July 2026 as part of the Build with Ukraine initiative. Under the first stage of the deal, Germany would finance the production of the drones, while all manufactured equipment would be sent to Ukraine’s Armed Forces.
Recently, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Bars have proven to be one of the most effective interceptors against Russian jet-powered drones, as Moscow escalates attacks on Ukrainian cities, Ukrinform reported on Oct. 10.
Germany has emerged as the biggest foreign partner in Ukraine’s burgeoning defense tech sector. A September report from the Kyiv School of Economics Institute found that there were 36 joint ventures between Ukrainian and German firms, as Berlin prioritizes deep-strike technology and intelligence.

Dominican Republic becomes latest Latin American country to adopt IHRA antisemitism definition amid regional shift to the right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

On August 24, the Dominican government adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, infamous for equating opposition to Israeli apartheid and Zionist colonialism with antisemitism. President Luis Abinader made the announcement in Santo Domingo, while speaking at an event organized by the U.S. Zionist organization Combat Antisemitism Movement. Subsequently, a statement from the Dominican Foreign Ministry justified the decision by invoking a supposed official policy against hate and discrimination dating back to 1938 when, according to the text, “the Dominican State was the only one to offer asylum in Sosúa to a significant number of Jewish refugees fleeing the war crimes perpetrated by the Nazi regime”.
In 1938, the racist and genocidal Trujillo dictatorship was in power. Just as the Israeli regime pushes for the redefinition of antisemitism to shield itself, in Orwellian fashion, Abinader is rewriting the past to accommodate the neo-Trujilloist present.
It is not surprising that the Dominican government, led by Abinader, would uphold the Trujilloist legacy. This is a government that has denied the significance of slavery during the Spanish colonial period that preceded the formation of the Dominican state, that does not officially commemorate the genocide against Haitians in 1937, known as the Parsley Massacre, and that denies the existence of widespread racism in the Dominican Republic while keeping more than 200,000 Dominicans of Haitian descent stateless. President Abinader boasts of following the ideas of dictator Joaquín Balaguer, one of the Trujillo era’s main ideologues. Abinader follows in Trujillo’s footsteps regarding what Dominican racists dub “the Haitian problem,” as shown by his policy of mass deportations and the construction of a border wall—an aggiornamento of the Trujillo-era political program known as the “Dominicanization of the border.”
Today’s neo-Trujilloist regime, with its apartheid policies of racial mass deportations, denationalization and statelessness, is coherent in its support of the genocidal Israeli regime and in claiming the legacy of the dictatorship. This is the true significance of the Dominican endorsement of the IHRA definition through a statement that upholds the legacy of a totalitarian regime that extorted and killed Jewish refugees.
In the context of the ongoing genocide in Gaza, the Dominican government has signed agreements with Israel on issues such as water management and has acquired Israeli weapons. By adopting the IHRA’s working definition of antisemitism, Abinader now threatens to further erode the weak democratic rights that still exist in this Caribbean country by moving in the direction of weaponizing accusations of antisemitism to criminalize solidarity with Palestine.
Abinader’s total subordination to Trump is another key driver of his support for Israel. The Dominican government has aligned itself with the pro-Trump “Shield of the Americas” regional coalition and has made its airports available for U.S. military operations in the Caribbean and against Venezuela; it has even agreed to accept deportees from third countries arriving from the U.S.
The Dominican government’s alliance with Israel is part of this broader trend, and one of the clearest indicators of the region’s shift to the right is the intensification of ties with Israeli apartheid.
The IHRA definition and the regional shift to the right
Due to a combination of strong U.S. interference and the decline of center-left parties, elections over the past year have brought right-wing governments to power in Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, and Colombia. In the cases of Bolivia and Colombia, which had no diplomatic relations with Israel, these were immediately reestablished. In Chile and Honduras, where relations had been degraded by the withdrawal of ambassadors, there was a full diplomatic normalization.
The Venezuelan government’s capitulation to Trumpism, following the U.S. military attack on January 3, 2026, and the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro, is also part of this regional shift to the right. Interim president Delcy Rodríguez reestablished diplomatic relations with Israel in August, following a campaign of “disaster diplomacy” by Netanyahu, who took advantage of the twin earthquakes in northern Venezuela that left more than 6,500 dead and tens of thousands injured. Relations had been broken since 2009.
In turn, the adoption of the IHRA’s definition of antisemitism has become an indicator of how closely Latin American regimes align with the objectives of Israeli foreign policy and their willingness to criminalize solidarity with Palestine. The definition in question was drafted in 2004 and adopted by the IHRA in 2016, after which it was promoted by Israeli foreign policy as part of its “new antisemitism” doctrine, which views opposition to Israel as the most significant form of antisemitism. Its text includes questioning the democratic character of the State of Israel among its examples of antisemitism. The definition was referenced in a Trump executive order in 2019 and in Latin America it has been adopted by right-wing governments in Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama, Guatemala, and Uruguay before being adopted by the Dominican Republic.
Over the past two years in Argentina, legal proceedings have been initiated, using the IHRA definition, against Alejandro Bodart, Vanina Biasi, and Mariano Soria, leaders of the Left and Workers’ Front-Unity, a Trotskyist coalition that holds four seats in the National Congress. In Brazil, socialist leader Zé María of the PSTU and the Jewish journalist Breno Altman have been criminalized for criticizing the Israeli state and calling for Palestinian freedom “from the river to the sea.” Zé María was sentenced to two years in prison, Altman was fined, Bodart won an appeal that overturned his conviction, and the cases against Biasi and Soria remain open.
Kenneth Stern, the main drafter of the IHRA definition, who describes himself as a liberal Zionist, has criticized its use by right-wing Jewish sectors to limit freedom of expression and foster a McCarthyist environment, citing the case of Germany, where authorities have used it to label Jewish people as “anti-Semites” for opposing Israeli crimes in Gaza. Stern recommended the U.S. Senate in 2025 to not adopt the IHRA definition.
Dominican legal scholar Jaime Rodríguez has pointed out that, within the Dominican legislative framework, the Abinader administration’s endorsement of the IHRA definition is not yet legally binding, though he has warned of the risks of censorship and persecution that would result from moving forward with enshrining it into law. Democratic guarantees and freedoms in the country are already fragile, and the alliance with Israel has contributed to their weakening, as evidenced by the Dominican government’s use of the Israeli spyware Pegasus against journalists.
But the peril is an even greater one. There is a clear affinity between the Neo-Trujillista regime led by Abinader and the Zionist project, as Israel is viewed by the Dominican right as a blueprint for Dominican apartheid. Neonazi organizations regularly wield Israeli flags at racist marches against Haitians. Much like Trujillo in 1938, Abinader is unconcerned about antisemitism or discrimination more broadly, as the regime he leads is carrying out a brutal crackdown on Haitian migrants and Dominicans of Haitian descent, conducting a campaign of more than one million deportations over the past six years during which dozens of people have been killed and many more subjected to horrific violence. Normalizing genocide abroad is a way of normalizing apartheid and ethnic cleansing it at home.
