KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Many tourists visiting Malaysia recently have shared photos of haze-shrouded Kuala Lumpur on social media, lamenting that the city's famous skyline seems to have "disappeared." Local residents have also complained of throat irritation, allergies and other health problems caused by the haze.
"I don't think the haze has ever been this bad since I was in primary school," said Azariah, a Malaysian girl born in the 1990s.
Haze has continued to plague Malaysia since August. According to real-time rankings of the world's most polluted major cities published by Swiss air quality tracker IQAir, Kuala Lumpur's air quality index (AQI) surged to 244 on the afternoon of Oct. 15, making it the most polluted major city in the world at the time. As of the morning of Oct. 23, the index remained at 172, a level classified as "unhealthy."
The haze has significantly disrupted daily life. Schools in some areas have been forced to close due to deteriorating air quality. The combination of persistent high temperatures and haze has also left some poultry farmers facing slower poultry growth and declining output, forcing them to invest more in ventilation and cooling facilities.
Malaysia's environmental authorities said the current haze episode has multiple causes, including open burning, the El Nino phenomenon and prevailing weather conditions, as well as transboundary haze from ongoing forest fires in various parts of Indonesia.
According to data from Nusantara Atlas, a deforestation monitoring platform, more than 1.9 million hectares of land in Indonesia had been burned by fires as of the end of September this year. Large amounts of smoke generated by forest and peatland fires have been carried across national borders by monsoon winds and atmospheric circulation, drifting into Malaysia and other neighboring countries.
Malaysia's meteorological authorities have forecast that a shift in wind direction next week could gradually ease the haze, while the northeast monsoon, expected to arrive in November, may also help improve air quality. However, persistent hot and dry conditions could keep the risks of forest fires and transboundary haze elevated across the region.
Against the backdrop of global warming, which is contributing to more frequent periods of extreme heat and drought, reducing the risk of forest and land fires, strengthening cross-border pollution monitoring and tackling pollution at its source have become shared challenges for countries in the region.
Malaysia's Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup said the transboundary haze problem must be addressed through collective action and closer regional cooperation. He called on ASEAN member states to fulfill their respective responsibilities, strengthen data sharing, law enforcement cooperation and fire prevention efforts, and translate regional commitments into concrete action.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto recently approved the acceptance of firefighting assistance offered by Singapore and Malaysia. Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said Malaysia has offered firefighting aircraft, helicopters and personnel to assist Indonesia in combating forest fires. ■

China's Long March legacy through Turkish eyes

BEIJING/ISTANBUL, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March and the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Türkiye. Turkish scholars, students and political figures say the military odyssey offers insights into China's revolutionary history and development path, while calling for deeper cultural and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.
The Red Army, led by the Communist Party of China (CPC), was mainly made up of soldiers from peasants' and workers' families during the Chinese revolution. Between 1934 and 1936, the army trekked roughly 12,500 kilometers to break through the encirclement of the Kuomintang forces, a journey later known as the Long March.
Murat Tamer, a Turkish scholar specializing in cultural exchanges between China and Türkiye, said the Long March deserved greater recognition in Türkiye. More than a historic march, it demonstrated the CPC's determination, organizational strength and strategic thinking in the face of formidable challenges, he said.
The great spirit of the Long March, Tamer added, could help Turkish people better understand how China overcame difficulties and forged its own path of development.
For Turkish students in China, the Long March also offers lessons that resonate with their own experiences.
Berfin Adiyaman, a master's student in applied economics at Northwestern Polytechnical University, said learning about the Long March had deepened her understanding of the importance of perseverance.
While studying in China, she has faced challenges including language barriers and homesickness. Her involvement in exchanges between Chinese and Turkish businesses, as well as her work at a logistics company in Xi'an, northwest China, enabled her to gain a closer look at Chinese society, she said.
"Whether it is a country or an individual, courage and perseverance are essential in the face of adversity," Adiyaman said, adding that she hoped to contribute to China-Türkiye economic cooperation and youth exchanges.
Yuksel Mansur Kilinc, a member of the Türkiye-China Interparliamentary Friendship Group of the Grand National Assembly of Türkiye, said China's development path has attracted attention in Türkiye, particularly its focus on common prosperity, harmony between humanity and nature, and the coordinated development of material and spiritual civilization.
Kilinc said China and Türkiye have new opportunities to deepen bilateral ties. Events marking the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations have been held across Türkiye this year, reflecting interest in expanding exchanges between the two countries.
Describing cultural exchanges as an important foundation for bilateral relations, he called for closer cooperation in the media and cultural sectors alongside economic and technological collaboration, saying such efforts could promote mutual understanding and support the long-term development of China-Türkiye relations. ■

Scientists propose a way to detect dangerous “mirror life” before it exists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:39:16 UTC
21:39:16 KST

Scientists propose a way to detect dangerous “mirror life” before it exists
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- https://www.strath.ac.uk/
- Summary:
- Scientists have proposed a way to detect “mirror life,” a hypothetical form of life that could pose serious risks to humans, animals, and ecosystems if artificially created. Using special fluorescent molecules and a type of polarized light also used in 3D movie technology, researchers believe they could distinguish ordinary organisms from their mirror-image counterparts.
- Share:
Scientists have proposed what they believe is the first way to detect "mirror life," a hypothetical form of life built from molecules that are reversed versions of those found in living organisms on Earth.
Researchers from the University of Strathclyde and Durham University have developed a proposed detection technique that uses molecules capable of emitting light with distinct left and right-handed properties. By analyzing these light signals, scientists may eventually be able to distinguish conventional organisms from their mirror-image counterparts.
Although mirror life does not currently exist, some experts consider its potential creation a serious biological safety concern. These artificial organisms could behave in unpredictable ways when interacting with Earth's ecosystems and might evade certain natural defenses that protect people, animals, and plants.
The likelihood of mirror life emerging is considered low, but its possible consequences could be severe enough to justify developing detection methods in advance.
Why Mirror Life Could Pose a Biological Threat
Concerns about mirror life have prompted scientists to recommend restrictions on research intended to produce organisms capable of reproducing using mirror-image biological molecules.
The potential dangers have also attracted attention from governments and international organizations, including the UK Government Office for Science and the United Nations Secretary General's Scientific Advisory Board.
The underlying science involves a property of molecules known as chirality, often described as molecular "handedness." Just as a person's left and right hands are mirror images that cannot be perfectly aligned, some molecules can exist in two forms that have identical chemical components but different three-dimensional arrangements.
These subtle structural differences can have major biological consequences. Two mirror-image versions of a molecule contain the same atoms connected in the same order, yet the human body may respond to them very differently. For example, one form of a medication could successfully treat a disease, while its mirror-image counterpart might be ineffective or even harmful.
Scientists are concerned that organisms assembled from reversed biological building blocks could interact with existing life in unexpected ways.
Importantly, the researchers emphasize that mirror life remains entirely hypothetical. Their proposed detection method is intended as a precaution, not a response to an existing biological threat.
How Light Could Reveal Mirror-Image Life
The proposed approach relies on a phenomenon called circularly polarized luminescence (CPL), which can reveal the molecular handedness, or chirality, of certain substances and biological structures.
Light can exhibit different polarization patterns, including forms that rotate in opposite directions. By studying these patterns, researchers can obtain information about the three-dimensional arrangement of molecules.
The underlying concept has a surprisingly familiar application: the polarized light technology used in modern 3D movie glasses to create the illusion of depth.
The research, published in Royal Society Open Science under the title 'Circularly Polarized Luminescence (CPL) as a Contingency Assay for "Mirror Life" Bio-Hazards', was led by Dr. Lewis MacKenzie of the University of Strathclyde's Department of Pure and Applied Chemistry, working with Professor Robert Pal of Durham University.
Dr. MacKenzie said: "We don't expect mirror life to appear tomorrow, but if it did arise, the consequences could be severe, and it makes sense to develop detection methods before they are needed. Professor Pal and I had been working on CPL technologies before recent concerns became prominent, and guarding against mirror life was a clear fit for our research."
A Molecular Fingerprint for Detecting Mirror Life
To identify a possible mirror organism, the researchers suggest using specialized fluorescent probes that attach to particular structures inside cells.
Once bound to their targets, these probes would generate characteristic CPL signals. Scientists could analyze the resulting patterns to determine whether a biological sample contains the molecular handedness associated with ordinary terrestrial life or its reversed equivalent.
In effect, the light signals could serve as a molecular fingerprint, revealing differences that might otherwise be difficult to identify.
However, relying on a single fluorescent probe could produce misleading results. To improve reliability and reduce the risk of false readings, the team proposes combining several probes designed to recognize different cellular structures.
By examining multiple signals together, researchers hope to develop a more dependable way to distinguish conventional organisms from hypothetical mirror life.
Testing the Technology Without Creating Mirror Organisms
One important advantage of the proposed technique is that scientists could begin investigating and refining it using ordinary biological samples. There would be no need to manufacture mirror organisms simply to explore whether the underlying detection principles work.
The researchers also believe the method could eventually be incorporated into several types of scientific equipment, potentially allowing mirror-life screening in different environments.
Professor Pal has already demonstrated laboratory-scale CPL detection technologies involving microscopes, cameras, and biological cell plate readers, which are instruments commonly used to examine large numbers of cell samples.
However, the complete detection method specifically designed to identify mirror life has not yet been experimentally demonstrated. Further research will be necessary to determine whether the proposed approach can reliably distinguish between different forms of molecular handedness in biological samples.
Professor Pal added: "CPL detection relies on the same fundamental concept that allows modern 3D cinema glasses to create a stereoscopic image.
"This CPL detection approach can be adapted to many types of systems for analysis of cells, including biological plate readers, microscopes, and cameras. This means our mirror life assay approach could be generalized to many environments depending on end user needs."
Story Source:
Materials provided by https://www.strath.ac.uk/. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lewis E. MacKenzie, Dominic J. Black, Robert Pal. Circularly polarized luminescence as a contingency assay for ‘mirror life’ bio-hazards. Royal Society Open Science, 2026; 13 (10) DOI: 10.1098/rsos.260921

“The enemy struck a civilian cattle-breeding enterprise in Konotop district,” Hryhorov stated.
“Russia continues to strike civilian enterprises, destroy farms, and take the lives of people who were simply carrying out their work.”
Four wounded, including child, in Dnipropetrovsk drone strike
Concurrently on Saturday, Russian forces launched an aerial drone attack against the Pokrovske community in the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk region, injuring four civilians, regional officials confirmed.
Head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration Oleksandr Hanzha reported that the wounded included a 14-year-old boy. Emergency medical teams stabilized the boy at the scene before transferring him in critical condition to a regional pediatric hospital in Dnipro.

A 46-year-old man was also hospitalized in serious condition, while medical personnel treated two other wounded adults. Emergency response detachments initiated structural inspections across surrounding residential neighborhoods to assess blast impacts and repair severed local utilities.

“This is why we are seeing these catastrophes ... There is no accountability,” she added.
A report by Kenya’s National Building Inspectorate found that 87% of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked the required approvals.
“Our concern is to save lives,” Nairobi Gov. Johnson Sakaja told reporters, adding, “This building has no occupation certificate ... this has potentially cost lives.”
An occupation certificate is formal approval from the relevant authorities confirming that a building is safe and legally fit for occupancy.

“People here are saying distresses were observed, like cracks,” he told reporters.

The number of buildings completed annually in Nairobi rose from 20,025 in 2022 to 25,090 last year, according to the country’s statistics bureau, as East Africa’s leading business hub attracts people from rural areas and neighboring countries.

AFP journalists saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.
A report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis documented 86 building collapses in Nairobi between 2009 and 2019, resulting in an estimated 200 deaths.
Corruption has allowed contractors to cut corners and bypass building regulations.

Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, had asked whether the case had been completed.

A Strategic Outline Case is the first of the Treasury’s five case stages and sets out the need and the range of options before any procurement decision is taken. Ministers confirmed earlier this month that all four Point class roll-on roll-off sealift ships will receive extensive refits, work that keeps the existing capability available while the replacement programme is developed.

The ships were built in Germany and South Korea and entered service from 2002 under a private finance arrangement, with the Ministry of Defence later buying the hulls outright.

Over 100 groups call for release of Mada Masr editor-in-chief

Breadcrumb
Over 100 civil society organisations, media outlets call for Egypt to release Mada Masr editor-in-chief
At least 119 civil society organisations and media outlets issued a statement on Friday calling on Egypt to urgently release the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr and shedding light on what they describe as an unprecedented attack on press freedom in the country.
“Lina Attalah’s referral to trial constitutes an unprecedented escalation that threatens the future of the entire independent media, knowledge production, and civil society space in Egypt,” the statement reads.
It is signed by various organisations and rights groups, including Access Now, Al Manasa, Arab Reform Initiative, Daraj Media, Drop Site News, Egyptian Front for Human Rights, among others.
The move follows the editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, being summoned to appear for questioning before the Supreme State Security Prosecution earlier this week.
The targeting of Attalah took place in the wake of Mada Masr and seven other independent organisations from around the Middle East setting up a flash investigations newsroom to fill the gap left by the Matsadaash newsroom after they were detained.
Attalah was interrogated for six hours on 21 October and was questioned about Mada Masr’s coverage following the arrest of the Matsadaash newsroom.
She was also questioned about the legal status of Mada Masr’s licence, before facing charges of running an outlet without a licence and publishing fake news with the aim of disrupting public peace.
On Thursday, she was informed that she would be referred to trial on charges of establishing, managing, and operating a website without a licence, with the first session set to begin on 27 October.
The civil society organisations and media outlets have raised serious alarm over the charges, noting that Mada Masr has previously made every effort to register for a licence and operate lawfully in accordance with the country’s laws.
In 2018, Mada Masr applied for a license but received no response, and applied again in 2020 with the same result.
During an interrogation in 2022, Mada Masr found out that their licensing application had been rejected without them receiving proper notice or disclosure. Despite filing a lawsuit that same year, their latest application for a licence has been pending since 2023.
The joint statement from the rights group states that for the charges against Attalah, there could be a potential penalty of between LE 1 million ($18,000) and 3 million ( $54,000), subject to a doubling of the fine for recurrence.
The statement also says that one of the biggest concerns is that the court could also order for Mada Masr to be closed, adding that this would be a major hit to one of the remaining independent media outlets in the country.
“For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations, and chill freedom of expression,” the statement says.
“To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space and to permanently close what remains,” it continued.
This marks the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in the space of six years.
The outlets and rights groups have demanded that Egyptian authorities immediately drop the prosecution of Attalah and grant Mada Masr a licence to operate.
It issued a stark warning that if such repression continued, the consequences could be much worse for civil society and the press.

Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:23:38 UTC
21:23:38 KST

Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- National Institutes of Natural Sciences
- Summary:
- The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a surprisingly complex network of magnetic structures hidden above regions of the Sun that appear relatively calm. Using the Sunrise-III solar observatory, which traveled high into Earth's stratosphere aboard a balloon in 2024, an international research team led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (NAOJ) discovered intricate, thread-like magnetic features that had previously been difficult to observe.
The findings reveal that even the Sun's seemingly quiet regions contain elaborate magnetic structures. They also offer new clues to how energy travels upward through the solar atmosphere and contributes to its heating.
A Hidden Web of Magnetic Threads Above the Sun
Sunrise-III detected numerous thin, elongated magnetic structures woven into a larger network of magnetic fields above a quiet region of the Sun. This network, known as the magnetic canopy, extends through the chromosphere, a layer of the solar atmosphere located above the Sun's visible surface.
The canopy develops as magnetic fields concentrated at the solar surface (photosphere) spread outward and arch upward into the chromosphere (chromosphere). Rather than forming a relatively smooth, uniformly expanding structure, however, the new observations reveal that the canopy contains many narrow, thread-like features.
To investigate how these structures form, researchers used computer simulations that successfully reproduced the patterns recorded by Sunrise-III. The results suggest that movements on the solar surface twist magnetic field lines, creating the intricate structures observed higher in the atmosphere.
The observatory also examined another quiet region near the solar limb (visible edge of the Sun). There, it measured magnetic fields within spicules, narrow jets of solar material that extend upward from the surface. These observations revealed how the distribution of magnetic fields changes with increasing height above the Sun's visible edge.
Why the Sun's Quiet Regions Are Difficult to Study
Although the Sun is constantly active, much of its surface lacks prominent features such as sunspots. Scientists describe these comparatively inactive areas as "quiet." They cover most of the Sun, making them especially important for understanding how our star behaves.
However, quiet does not mean magnetically inactive. These regions contain magnetic fields that are generally weaker than those found in more active areas of the Sun. Their subtle structures are difficult to measure, especially with telescopes on the ground, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere can blur fine details.
Sunrise-III was designed to overcome this obstacle by carrying a powerful solar telescope far above most of the atmosphere.
A Balloon-Borne Telescope Reveals New Solar Details
Sunrise-III is an international research project built around a 1-meter telescope carried by a high-altitude balloon. During its 2024 mission, the observatory floated approximately 35 kilometers (about 22 miles) above Earth in the stratosphere, where atmospheric interference is greatly reduced.
This elevated vantage point allowed the telescope to capture exceptionally detailed measurements of the Sun's magnetic fields.
The balloon's gondola carried three scientific instruments developed through contributions from different countries. One of these was SCIP (Sunrise Chromospheric Infrared spectroPolarimeter), a near-infrared instrument developed under NAOJ's leadership.
SCIP is designed to measure magnetic fields continuously across different layers of the solar atmosphere, from the photosphere to the chromosphere. This capability allowed researchers to examine how magnetic structures extend and change with altitude rather than studying only a single layer.
New Clues to How the Sun's Atmosphere Is Heated
By observing from the stratosphere, Sunrise-III provided researchers with an unusually detailed picture of magnetic fields above the Sun's quiet regions. Its measurements revealed that the chromosphere contains far more intricate magnetic structures than a simple expanding canopy would suggest.
Understanding these structures could help scientists investigate how energy generated by motions near the solar surface is transferred into higher layers of the atmosphere.
The discovery offers an important step toward explaining how magnetic activity contributes to heating the Sun's atmosphere, including in regions that appear calm when viewed from afar.
Story Source:
Materials provided by National Institutes of Natural Sciences. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

BERLIN – Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for unity in his struggling coalition on Oct 24, saying Germany faced growing threats from political extremists and what he described as daily Russian efforts to destabilise the country.
Speaking at a conference of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of his conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), Merz said Germany faced “extraordinarily serious challenges”.
“How do we safeguard our freedom and our security in Europe, in the face of growing threats from extremists within and foreign powers from without?” he said, adding that Russia was seeking “to destabilise Germany on a daily basis”.
Relations between Berlin and Moscow have fallen to their lowest level since the Cold War following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine but Russia rejects accusations that it is conducting a hybrid campaign against Germany and other European countries.
Merz’s comments follow weeks of tension with the ruling coalition after heavy regional election defeats in eastern Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came first in two states and the far-left Left Party (Die Linke) topped the poll in Berlin.
Merz’s approval ratings have fallen to record lows, while tensions have surfaced both between the coalition partners and between the CDU and CSU.
The two conservative sister parties have a long history of disagreements but have generally managed to overcome them.
On Oct 24, delegates broke into loud applause when Merz mentioned Ilse Aigner, the CSU politician the party has proposed as successor to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who is due to step down in 2027.
The CDU has so far stopped short of endorsing Aigner, and party sources say it has not abandoned hopes of putting forward its own candidate for the largely ceremonial post of head of state.
Merz, who entered the conference hall to a Bavarian brass band playing The Eye Of The Tiger, praised CSU ministers in the government and paid tribute to CSU leader Markus Soeder.
But he repeated his rejection of calls from some conservatives to seek ways of cooperating with the AfD, which leads national opinion polls, saying any politician who voted with the party “has no place in our Union”.
He also urged the Social Democrats and Greens not to form a coalition in Berlin with the Left Party, which he accused of tolerating anti-Semitism within its ranks. The Left Party denies any systemic anti-Semitism in the party.
Merz said rapid reforms to Germany’s pension, tax and welfare systems were essential to revive the economy and restore confidence in public institutions. REUTERS

As expected, talks on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine have shifted to talks on a new division of Europe.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Europeans are not yet being invited to the conversation about European security. Peskov specified that representatives of Ukraine, Russia and the US will meet in Abu Dhabi. He acknowledged that European countries cannot be left out going forward, but tied their participation to the position they take (whether they behave themselves).
Revival of December 2021 ultimatum and territorial claims
Some Russian experts have a quite concrete picture of what the coming talks should cover. Valdai Club expert Stanislav Tkachenko speaks openly of a return to the demands of December 2021: limiting NATO’s military presence to pre-enlargement levels, removing new bases and military facilities from the Baltic states and Eastern Europe, and halting further enlargement. To this he adds recognition of territorial seizures, the lifting of sanctions and the return of frozen assets. His reasoning is that Moscow regards the European Union as a losing party as well, and therefore expects concessions from it too. Tkachenko even suggests new claims on Odesa, Mykolaiv and Kharkiv, arguing that Putin’s references to “historical territories” leave room for them.

At the same time, it is possible to negotiate and continue the war.
Frontline combat alongside protracted diplomacy
Dmitri Trenin, president of the Russian International Affairs Council, believes that freezing hostilities along the current front line does not suit Russia. Talking to the US is nevertheless worthwhile, since it is already producing some results. He notes that Moscow has agreed to discuss, first and foremost, the future post-war security system. The fighting itself, he predicts, may continue into 2027. He links the concrete terms of any agreement to the situation on the battlefield: talks can happen now, while decisions will depend on military outcomes.
Explanations for the case that negotiations once again lead nowhere are also already being prepared. Fyodor Lukyanov interprets the new Ukrainian proposals as Zelensky’s attempt to ease pressure from Trump. He suggests that Kyiv may walk away from agreements already reached, with the Europeans backing it. For that reason, in his view, Witkoff’s arrival with new ideas does not yet mean anything.
Political messaging ahead of US midterms
Meanwhile, Moscow is finding reasons to celebrate even before any deal. A concrete outcome of the meeting is not even necessary for this assessment. He takes the comparison of a possible Putin–Trump–Xi meeting with “Yalta-2” as recognition of Russia’s special status: it is once again among the states that shape the future order.
Practical gains are added to the symbolic success. Duma deputy Leonid Slutsky calls the meeting with Witkoff a diplomatic “master class” by Putin and points to sanctions relief and the diesel deal with the US. For him, this is already evidence of a successful restoration of relations with Washington. He envisions further negotiations taking Russia’s interests fully into account.
Trump is also seen as a partner for exerting influence on Ukraine and Europe. Political commentator Gevorg Mirzayan suggests that Moscow and Washington are discussing a coordinated policy towards them. In his view, Trump wants to show voters a foreign-policy success, bring the Europeans back into greater obedience, and establish energy cooperation with Russia.
The rush ahead of the US elections is also viewed as an opportunity for Russia. Boris Mezhuev openly calls Trump an ally on the question of a settlement. He believes the US president needs a peace plan he can present to voters, even if it has not yet been signed. Russia can help him secure such a political result while advancing its own demands.
And yet there are still some in Moscow who remain dissatisfied, such as Dugin, Malofeev and Karaganov, united by a shared mental disorder: a passion for using nuclear weapons. In their latest interviews and publications, they openly call on Putin to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine and Europe.

21:16:00 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) to impose sanctions on Russian entities and individuals involved in manufacturing ballistic missiles and supplying critical components to Moscow’s military-industrial complex, the Office of the President of Ukraine announced.
The statutory measures target Russian enterprises and executive leadership providing raw materials, specialized machine tools, precision optics, and electronic modules required to produce standoff strike systems – such as Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101, and Kinzhal missiles – alongside military aviation, armored vehicles, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are systematically identifying and imposing sanctions on enterprises involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles and other strike weapons,” said Presidential Advisor and Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
“We are working to coordinate these sanctions with other international jurisdictions. Cumulatively, this should significantly degrade the Russian defense sector’s capacity to manufacture weapons.”
Ballistic missile supply chains and research institutes
The primary sanctions list targets 51 individuals and 44 corporate entities directly linked to the development and serial production of Russian ballistic and cruise missiles deployed against Ukrainian civilian settlements and municipal life-support systems.
Russian Border Strikes and EU EES Challenge Checkpoints
Key institutions designated under the presidential decrees include the Petrov Plastics Institute, identified as the sole manufacturer in Russia of specialized composite polymer components supplied to defense, aerospace, aviation, and naval shipyards.
The measures also target the Komet Corporation of Special Purpose Space Systems, the lead enterprise of a scientific and production consortium manufacturing surface-to-air missile systems, radar equipment, and airborne avionics suites, alongside VitaReaktiv, an industrial enterprise specializing in chemical raw materials integrated into ballistic missile propulsion systems and warheads.
Additional designations focus on research bodies and high-technology developers.
Among them are Promenergo, a defense contractor that develops optical, laser, and optoelectronic targeting systems alongside avionics testing facilities; the Kirov Biochemical Plant, engaged in the chemical synthesis and technical modernization of military armaments; and the Mendeleev All-Russian Research Institute of Metrology, a national scientific body that provides metrological research, precision measurement systems, and software architectures for military equipment.
Industrial tooling, electronics, and RUSAL aluminum imports
A second decree enacts sanctions against an additional 32 Russian citizens and 35 commercial entities embedded in supply chains for precision machine tools, microelectronics, and tactical communication components.
The measures target Gagaring, a commercial enterprise specializing in communications hardware and flight controllers for first-person view (FPV) strike drones; Virgin-EK, which procures foreign electronic components for the Russian armed forces; and the Pressmash Machine Tool Association, a wholesale distributor of metalworking machinery that supplies factories producing Kh-101 and Kh-59 cruise missiles alongside Orion medium-altitude UAVs.
The sanctions package also designates corporate entities belonging to the Russian metals group RUSAL. According to Ukrainian government data, between April 2024 and March 2025, United Company RUSAL Trading House and the RUSAL Taishet Aluminum Smelter imported aluminum oxide valued at nearly 150 million rubles ($1.6 million) into Russia.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed that these raw materials were diverted into manufacturing pipelines for military aircraft, armored combat vehicles, missile systems, and loitering munitions.
Air defense strains and transatlantic divergence
The enactment of domestic sanctions follows recurring Russian ballistic missile barrages against Ukrainian regional infrastructure ahead of the winter season.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Russian forces launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and surrounding districts without advance radar notification, damaging over 10 energy facilities and cutting electricity to at least 550,000 households. The strike underscored operational risks amid conflicting accounts between Washington and Kyiv over early-warning missile tracking feeds.
President Zelensky previously stated that Ukraine receives roughly 12 Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors per month – approximately one-quarter of the volume delivered under the Biden administration – despite paid commitments through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) and calculated domestic operational requirements of 350 interceptors monthly.
The Ukrainian sanctions push also unfolds amid transatlantic friction over economic deterrence. On Oct. 16, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to waive mandatory statutory penalties, including 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties on third-party petroleum purchasers.
EU leaders expressed regret over the suspension of US energy penalties during their Brussels summit, pledging to maintain European sanctions and expand coordination with Kyiv to close secondary procurement loopholes underwriting Moscow’s defense manufacturing base.

Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:12:40 BST
21:12:40 KST

Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
- Published
Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.
Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.
This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.
"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.
Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea.
Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.
They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

Russia and China step up spy flights near Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

- China and Russia flew five military intelligence missions near Japan from Oct. 20 to 23, and Japanese fighters scrambled each day.
- Chinese Y-9s crossed the Okinawa-Miyako gap on Oct. 20 and 21, and Russian IL-20s flew off Shimane on Oct. 22 and 23.
China and Russia sent military intelligence aircraft toward Japan on four consecutive days this week, prompting the Japan Air Self-Defense Force to scramble fighters each day, as two Chinese Y-9 aircraft crossed the gap between Okinawa and Miyako-jima into the Pacific on Oct. 20 and 21 and Russian IL-20 aircraft flew over the Sea of Japan to waters off Shimane Prefecture on Oct. 22 and 23, Japan’s Joint Staff said.
In all, Japan tracked five flights over the four days: three by Chinese Y-9s and two by Russian IL-20s. No violations of Japanese airspace were reported.
The Y-9 is a Chinese four-engine turboprop built in several military versions, including maritime patrol and electronic intelligence variants.
The IL-20 is a Russian turboprop modified to collect electronic and signals intelligence.
On the morning of Oct. 20, a Chinese Y-9 patrol aircraft flew in from the East China Sea, passed between Okinawa’s main island and Miyako-jima into the Pacific and continued to waters off Amami Oshima before turning back and returning the same way toward mainland China. That afternoon, a second Y-9, an intelligence-gathering aircraft, flew a round trip over the East China Sea between waters south of the Danjo Islands in Nagasaki Prefecture and an area northwest of Okinawa’s main island. The Air Self-Defense Force’s Southwestern Air Defense Force scrambled fighters in response.
A Chinese Y-9 intelligence-gathering aircraft flew the same route on Oct. 21, crossing between Okinawa and Miyako-jima, flying to waters off Amami Oshima and returning through the gap toward the mainland, and Southwestern Air Defense Force fighters again scrambled.
Russia then flew the same mission on back-to-back days. On both Oct. 22 and Oct. 23, a Russian IL-20 flew in from the direction of the mainland, crossed the Sea of Japan to waters off Shimane Prefecture on Honshu’s western coast, then turned around and headed back. Each time, the Air Self-Defense Force’s Northern Air Defense Force and other units scrambled fighters.
The flights came as the United States and Japan hold Keen Sword, a large-scale joint exercise running from Oct. 19 to 29 for which Japan planned to commit about 45,000 personnel, 260 aircraft and 40 vessels. They also followed operations by China’s Liaoning carrier group, which passed between Okinawa and Miyako-jima on Oct. 14 and conducted fighter takeoffs and landings about 250 km (155 miles) south of Ishigaki-jima, prompting another Air Self-Defense Force scramble.
The waters between Okinawa and Miyako-jima form one of the main routes Chinese military ships and aircraft use to move between the East China Sea and the Pacific.
Japan’s Joint Staff publishes reports on foreign military aircraft that approach Japan and draw a fighter scramble, and its releases for Oct. 20 through 23 do not say whether the Chinese and Russian flights are connected.

The administrations of current U.S. President Donald Trump and his predecessor, Joseph Biden, on several occasions requested that Elon Musk’s company, SpaceX, enable or disable the Starlink satellite communication service in various countries—long before access was restricted for the Ukrainian military in October of this year. This is reported by Reuters, citing sources among former high-ranking U.S. officials who requested anonymity.
“During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials. Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters,” the message reads.
According to the publication’s sources, the Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy: Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability. In their turn, they several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries. The administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of the terminals were deactivated.
Shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, officials in the Biden administration urged SpaceX to expand the Ukrainian armed forces' use of Starlink. At the same time, however, as noted in the report, Musk was already taking steps to limit Ukraine’s access to the Starlink network. Specifically, in 2022, he ordered SpaceX employees to restrict Starlink coverage in areas that Ukraine was attempting to liberate from Russian occupation—a move that came as a surprise to White House officials. Musk also publicly stated that he had rejected a request from Ukraine in 2022 to activate his satellite network in occupied Sevastopol.
In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals.
Reuters reported that SpaceX did not respond to its requests for comment, although Musk noted in a social media post earlier this week that “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).”
The publication emphasizes that the Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to “an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy.”
Earlier on Saturday, sources within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense told Interfax-Ukraine that the Ukrainian Defense Forces and the Ministry had observed the restoration of Starlink—as well as its military version, Starshield—at speeds exceeding 161 km/h, following an outage that had lasted several days. Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara later reported that the terminals were observed functioning at speeds of over 400 km/h. "The connection is stable. This is yet another example of how direct dialogue and the persistent stance taken by the President of Ukraine at the highest level yield results. And this outcome is, above all, vital for our front line, for our military personnel, for the operation of drones, and for logistics and communications," he said.

These tiny snakes roll four times faster than they slither
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:12:03 UTC
21:12:03 KST

These tiny snakes roll four times faster than they slither
Acrobatic body movements allow dwarf reedsnakes to keep their heads stable while much of the body rotates rapidly.
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- Toho University
- Summary:
- Tiny snakes in Southeast Asia have mastered an extraordinary escape technique: rolling across the ground at speeds up to four times faster than ordinary slithering. Scientists discovered that dwarf reedsnakes accomplish this feat through precisely coordinated body movements that allow their bodies to rotate while their heads remain remarkably stable.
- Share:
Tiny snakes found in Southeast Asia have developed an extraordinary way to escape danger. Instead of relying on the familiar side-to-side motion of slithering, dwarf reedsnakes can rapidly roll across the ground, reaching speeds about four times faster than their usual movement.
Scientists have now uncovered how these small reptiles accomplish such an unusual feat. By studying video recordings captured from multiple angles, researchers discovered that the snakes coordinate their movements with remarkable precision. While the rear portions of their bodies rotate rapidly, their heads remain relatively steady, facing forward and staying at a nearly constant height.
[See link to video after the end of the article.]
The findings reveal how an animal can achieve an unexpected form of movement through specialized behavior and body control, even without the physical structures normally needed for rolling.
Why Rolling Is So Difficult for Animals
Rolling might seem like an effective way to travel quickly, but it presents a major challenge for living creatures.
A wheel can spin continuously around a fixed axle, allowing it to rotate without disturbing whatever it supports. Animals, however, have no comparable mechanism separating their rotating bodies from their heads.
If an animal's entire body spins together, its head and sensory organs must also rotate. This can make it difficult to maintain balance, adjust body position, and steer in the intended direction. As rolling speed increases, these problems become even harder to manage.
Yet dwarf reedsnakes belonging to the genus Pseudorabdion have found a way around these limitations.
These small Southeast Asian snakes are among the few animals known to deliberately roll as a means of escaping potential predators. Their unusual behavior has appeared in field guides and was previously documented during a field observation, but scientists had not fully understood the movements that made it possible.
Tiny Snakes Roll Four Times Faster Than They Slither
To investigate this remarkable escape strategy, researchers filmed dwarf reedsnakes from several angles and carefully examined how different parts of their bodies moved during rolling.
The results revealed impressive speeds. While rolling, the snakes reached peak forward velocities ranging from 1.72 to 3.69 meters per second, approximately four times their maximum speed when moving through lateral undulation, the familiar side-to-side motion used by most snakes.
Despite traveling so quickly, the snakes were able to follow a narrow racetrack measuring just 20 centimeters across, demonstrating that their rolling movements are not simply uncontrolled tumbling.
Closer examination of the recordings revealed a surprisingly intricate sequence of movements.
Rather than spinning their entire bodies together, the snakes alternate between rolling on one side and swinging a curved section of their bodies downward beside their heads. The researchers called this downward sweeping movement a "stroke."
During each successive cycle, the side touching the ground switches, and the stroke changes direction from left to right or right to left. By repeating this carefully timed pattern, the snakes generate continuous forward rolling motion.
The Remarkable Secret Behind Their High-Speed Escape
One of the most surprising discoveries involved what happens to the snakes' heads during these rapid movements.
Although the rear portions of their bodies undergo substantial rotation, the snakes keep their heads pointed in the direction they are traveling. Rather than spinning along with the rest of the body, the head remains comparatively stable.
The researchers also found that the snakes maintain a relatively consistent head height above the ground. This stabilization becomes especially noticeable at higher speeds, when the snakes tend to hold their heads elevated and minimize upward and downward movements.
Keeping the head steady while the rest of the body rotates may help the animals maintain control and navigate effectively during their rapid escapes.
This ability is particularly remarkable because the snakes accomplish it without a mechanical separation between the rotating and stabilized portions of their bodies.
What Rolling Snakes Reveal About Evolution
The discovery demonstrates how sophisticated coordination can allow animals to overcome physical limitations that might otherwise make certain types of movement impractical.
Although dwarf reedsnakes lack anything resembling a wheel's axle, they effectively divide their bodies into regions with different functions. Much of the body performs the powerful rotational movements needed for propulsion, while the head remains stabilized to support controlled travel.
This unusual strategy allows the snakes to combine speed, directional control, and rapid body rotation in a way that would be difficult to predict from their anatomy alone.
More broadly, the findings highlight an important principle of animal evolution: physical structure does not necessarily determine the full range of movements an animal can perform. Innovative behaviors and precise muscular coordination can open up entirely new possibilities, allowing creatures to accomplish feats that their body shapes might initially suggest are impossible.

- Kadena Air Base will bar all BYD vehicles from Oct. 26, including private cars, taxis and delivery vans, Yonhap reported.
- The U.S. Air Force’s 18th Security Forces Squadron will turn back BYD vehicles at every gate with no exceptions.
Kadena Air Base in Okinawa will bar all vehicles made by Chinese electric carmaker BYD from entering the installation starting Oct. 26 over concerns that the cars could expose sensitive military information, Kangnam Times reported.
The ban covers privately owned cars as well as contractor vehicles, taxis, delivery vans and other commercial vehicles. The 18th Security Forces Squadron, which guards the base’s key facilities, will stop BYD vehicles at every gate and direct them to turn around, and the base does not plan to grant exceptions, according to the report.
Kadena is one of the U.S. Air Force’s largest bases in the Indo-Pacific and home to the 18th Wing, part of Fifth Air Force, which operates fighters, aerial refueling and surveillance aircraft from the island.
The concern centers on how modern electric vehicles work. Many use cameras and sensors to map their surroundings and rely on software and network connections that can send data to outside servers or allow remote access. Information gathered by a car driving through a base could reveal the layout of facilities and patterns of military activity.
A similar problem surfaced last month in Norway, where rental cars used by the Norwegian Armed Forces during Exercise Hovedstad near Oslo Airport from Sept. 14 to 18 recorded soldiers, their movements and the access codes they typed at military gates. At least two of the vehicles were Deepal models built by Chinese state-owned automaker Changan and supplied by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by China’s Geely group, Norwegian business daily Dagens Næringsliv reported.
Other militaries have already restricted Chinese-made cars. Poland has barred Chinese-made vehicles from certain military facilities, citing the risk that onboard sensors and cameras could collect sensitive data, and the Israel Defense Forces has banned Chinese vehicles from its bases.
The U.S. military has tightened rules on Chinese technology at its installations for years. In 2018, the Pentagon ordered base exchanges worldwide to stop selling smartphones made by Huawei and ZTE over security concerns. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of War reportedly added BYD to its list of Chinese military companies operating in the United States, a list that does not by itself ban the use of a company’s products.
BYD has been expanding in Japan, launching models tailored to the Japanese market and opening more dealerships, particularly in regional areas where public transportation is limited.
