Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaska Senate race
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had instructed his administration to file a lawsuit to block the certification of the US Senate race in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that voters would be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have similar names. The legal battle is ramping up questions over whether Trump will accept a potential midterms defeat.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Trump administration has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent candidate loses narrowly, saying voters could be confused because two Republicans on the ballot have almost identical names.
The Department of Justice's lawsuit, filed in federal court in Anchorage on Thursday, signals the willingness of President Donald Trump's administration to contest the results of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress, where his fellow Republicans narrowly control both chambers.
Read moreOssoff and El-Sayed: Two Senate races and what they say about the Democratic Party
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
Control of the Senate could come down to Alaska, where incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan is running a close race against Democrat Mary Peltola.
The suit, which names the state and local election officials as defendants, takes issue with the presence of another contender in the race, another Republican named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, alleging he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him".
The DOJ asks a judge to block the certification of an outcome "that may be impacted by voter confusion", so that there can be "an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan".
Read moreGeorgia on Democrats’ minds: Powering up the Black vote to counter Trump's meddling
Trump told reporters on Friday that he supported the lawsuit, saying "I'm the one that said do it." A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that the agency is taking "necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters".
Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are preparing for potential federal interference in the elections, including legal challenges and disputes over voting that could disrupt certification of the results.
Trump has a long history of challenging election outcomes and encouraging supporters to contest results he views as unfavorable.
Alaska's other US senator, Senator Lisa Murkowski from Trump's Republican Party, said on Friday the Justice Department "should never have filed this lawsuit".
Election law experts said the lawsuit has no merit and seeks relief not allowed under federal law.
"In short, like many Department letters over the last few years, it is designed to win the press release rather than the litigation," wrote Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller in a blog post, adding that "the legal argument is one of the worst ones I’ve ever seen".
Trump's administration "has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election", said David Becker of the Center for Election
Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that advises election officials, adding that "this issue has already been fully litigated by Alaska's courts".
Read more'Thanks a lot, Trump': Wyoming conservatives divided ahead of US midterms
The unelected Sullivan, a former US Forest Service worker and elementary school teacher, filed to run as a candidate on May 29, seeking to unseat Dan S. Sullivan and "put Alaska first," according to his campaign website, which advertised "Dan Sullivan Challenges Dan Sullivan for US Senate Seat". Dan J. Sullivan has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.
The Alaska Supreme Court in June permitted the challenger Sullivan to appear on the ballot. He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent.
Peltola, the Democratic candidate, told MS NOW on Friday that because of how the candidates are displayed on the ballot "there just isn't much room for confusion". The lawsuit is "sending a message that Dan Sullivan does not believe that Alaskans are sophisticated enough to know exactly who they're voting for", she added.
Trump's approval rating has fallen to a record low, hit by rising diesel and gasoline prices during the Iran war, which has proven deeply unpopular with voters.
Public opinion polls suggest Republicans may lose control of one or both chambers of Congress, which would likely limit Trump's ability to enact some of his policy agenda in the final two years of his presidency.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Ukraine says it regained full use of Starlink, after more than a week of disruption
Ukraine's military has regained full use of Starlink satellite links for its drones and other fast-moving equipment, the defense minister said Saturday, ending speed restrictions that Ukrainian officials said had disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.
The Defense Ministry's monitoring systems in Ukraine reported stable connections on objects traveling faster than 250 mph, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told reporters.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that checks were conducted and it was determined Starlink and Starshield were running at the correct speed.
"Now the speed is what we need," Zelenskyy said. "The restoration began last night, and in the morning there were already speeds sufficient to use this connection. This is very important."
"This is significant for our front-line logistics, for protecting Ukraine from reactive 'Shaheds,'" he continued, referring to the Iranian-made drones regularly launched by Russia.
The limitations placed on Starshield — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication — last week alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
The restoration comes as U.S. envoys launched a new push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.
The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."
Zelenskyy on Saturday thanked Americans and "all our partners, who took all this seriously and are really helping us."
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Elon Musk-made satellite internet system that Ukraine has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.
Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. On Tuesday, CBS News reported that Musk was behind the disruption.

Chinese navy flotilla returns after record 378 days at sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:36:07 UTC
20:36:07 KST

- China’s 48th naval escort task force returned to Qingdao on Oct. 23 after a record 378-day mission in the Gulf of Aden.
- The destroyer Tangshan, frigate Daqing and supply ship Taihu sailed more than 150,000 nautical miles and escorted 423 vessels.
China’s 48th naval escort task force returned to a military port in Qingdao on Oct. 23 after 378 days away, the longest deployment in the history of the Chinese navy’s anti-piracy missions in the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia, China’s Ministry of National Defense said.
The task force, made up of the guided-missile destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122), the guided-missile frigate Daqing (Hull 576) and the supply ship Taihu (Hull 889), sailed more than 150,000 nautical miles (about 278,000 km) during the mission and escorted 423 Chinese and foreign vessels, according to the ministry.
The three ships left Qingdao on Oct. 11, 2025, to take over from the 47th task force, carrying two helicopters and dozens of special operations personnel, Xinhua reported at the time. Before departure, the crews trained on weapons use, convoy escort procedures and replenishment at sea.
The deployment extends a run of successively longer missions. The 46th escort task force spent 339 days on deployment and the 47th spent 368, China Defense Blog noted, putting the 48th task force’s 378 days at the top of a steady climb in time on station across three consecutive rotations.
“Incremental progress, repeated often enough that one day it no longer looks incremental at all,” China Defense Blog wrote.
Beyond escort duty, the task force took part in the “Will for Peace 2026” joint maritime exercise in South Africa and the China-Pakistan “Sea Guardian IV” naval exercise in Pakistan. It joined a parade marking the 50th anniversary of Seychelles’ independence, paid visits to Bangladesh, Myanmar and Malaysia, and made technical stops in Oman, Kenya, Singapore and other countries, the ministry said.
China began sending warships to the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia in December 2008, after a surge in piracy attacks on commercial shipping in one of the world’s busiest sea lanes, which links the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Each task force typically pairs combat ships with a supply vessel and an embarked special operations team, and hands over the mission to the next rotation on station.

Will Guinea-Bissau remain trapped in political chaos?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:36:00 UTC
20:36:00 KST

Will Guinea-Bissau remain trapped in political chaos?
October 24, 2026
The parliamentary and presidential elections scheduled for December 6, 2026, in Guinea-Bissau will not take place as planned. Aly Silva, spokesperson for transitional Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te, confirmed to DW that the vote had been postponed until further notice. No new date has been set. The government first intends to discuss the matter in cabinet before publicly announcing when the elections will be held. It remains unclear whether they will take place in 2027 or not until 2028.
The country's political crisis dates back to November 26, 2025. Three days earlier, voters in Guinea-Bissau had elected a new parliament and president. Before the official results could be announced, the military seized power and halted the electoral process. Both then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and his challenger, Fernando Dias da Costa, had claimed victory. The military leadership promised a return to constitutional order.
For lawyer and political analyst Cabi Sanha, the postponement comes as no surprise. Since the coup, little has been done to create the conditions for credible elections, he says.
"The postponement was foreseeable," Sanha told DW. December 6 had indeed been set as the new election date. "But nothing was done to ensure that these elections could actually take place."
Political freedoms under pressure
The transitional government has justified the postponement by citing the lack of organizational and political conditions necessary for elections. The deadline for submitting candidacies had already passed on October 6. Political parties and potential candidates had not submitted their applications. According to the prime minister, the parties had also failed to hold congresses to select their candidates.
Sanha sees this as more than an organizational problem. He points to restrictions on political activities and the lack of dialogue with key actors in the electoral process. Political parties and civil society have not been sufficiently involved, he says. Mediation efforts by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and Senegal have so far failed to produce a solution.
"Free, transparent and inclusive elections are only possible if the necessary conditions are established beforehand," the lawyer says.
He therefore also views the parties' failure to nominate candidates as a consequence of the political environment. "How are parties supposed to nominate candidates when political activities are restricted in the country? They cannot hold party congresses or organize rallies."
Leading opposition figures are also staying abroad. Domingos Simoes Pereira, head of the main opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), was allowed to travel to Portugal in July 2026 for medical treatment after being released from detention. He had previously been held in pretrial detention in connection with an investigation into an alleged coup attempt. His defense team denies the allegations and has criticized the proceedings as politically motivated.
The absence of key opposition figures and restrictions on political organizing are making it harder to conduct an electoral process intended to pave the way for a return to civilian government.
An election date without a timetable
What happens next remains unclear. Government spokesperson Aly Silva says the transitional government will first discuss the matter in cabinet. Only afterward will a new election date be announced publicly. So far, there is no concrete timetable.
It is therefore also unclear when political parties will be able to complete their internal selection procedures, nominate candidates and begin campaigning. For Sanha, this is another indication that there is still insufficient evidence of the political will needed to restore constitutional order.
"I do not believe that logistical problems are the main issue. Rather, there appears to be a lack of political will to move the electoral process forward," he says.
Dispute over the constitution
The political crisis has been compounded by a controversial constitutional reform. In a referendum on August 30, 2026, voters approved constitutional amendments that expand the president's powers and reduce the size of parliament from 102 to 65 seats. Critics question the legitimacy of the process because the reform was prepared under military rule and without a regularly elected parliament. The opposition had called for a boycott of the vote.
Fernando Vaz, spokesperson for the National Transitional Council, defends the changes. He says the process was not a comprehensive rewriting of the constitution but a targeted revision. The reform is intended to help overcome the country's political instability, he argues.
"The constitution must be one of the instruments that lead our country toward greater stability," Vaz told DW. The transitional period had provided an opportunity to amend provisions that, in the military leadership's view, were obstructing the country's political development.
Vaz also rejects criticism that the reform gives the president additional powers at the expense of the prime minister. "The president of the republic is the head of state, while the prime minister is the head of government," he emphasizes.
Critics see it differently. The new constitutional framework strengthens the presidency: the president is to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and the government and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. At the same time, the number of parliamentary seats is being reduced. It remains disputed whether the reform will genuinely contribute to stability or instead concentrate more power in the presidency.
Local elections are not enough
The transitional government has announced plans to hold local elections in 2027. Sanha broadly welcomes the proposal: Guinea-Bissau has never held such elections since independence. Nevertheless, he stresses that they must not replace the outstanding national elections.
"First, parliamentary and presidential elections must take place so that the country can return to constitutional order. Local elections can follow afterward," he says.
Local elections cannot compensate for the lack of democratic legitimacy at the national level. Political freedoms must also be restored so that parties can select their candidates and voters can genuinely choose between political alternatives.
A transition with no clear end
Guinea-Bissau has endured decades of political instability, marked by military coups, institutional crises and repeated interruptions of democratic processes. The latest coup continues this pattern.
The renewed postponement of the elections shows how far the country remains from a return to constitutional order. Setting a new election date alone will not be enough. Political activities must be permitted again, parties must be included in the process, and reliable conditions for elections must be established, lawyer Cabi Sanha told DW.

WFP showcases refugee children’s art to support humanitarian work in Iran
TEHRAN – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has held an art exhibition featuring paintings by refugee children living in 20 settlements across Iran to raise support for its humanitarian operations in the country. The exhibition concluded on Friday.
The initiative brought the creativity, resilience and hopes of refugee children to the public through an art exhibition hosted at two well-known venues in Tehran, offering visitors a glimpse into their dreams, perspectives and experiences. Each artwork told a unique story, highlighting the creativity and determination of children who continue to pursue their aspirations despite the challenges they face, the UN website announced in a press release on October 21.
The artworks were displayed at Haman Store, a prominent concept store located in central Tehran, and Prague Pastry Boutique, an established Tehran brand with four branches across the city and a newly introduced concept store. Both venues were recognized for their distinctive approach to art, design, and community engagement, providing opportunities to introduce the children’s artwork to a wider audience.
Beyond celebrating artistic expression, the initiative also aimed to mobilize support for WFP’s humanitarian operations in Iran. Visitors had the opportunity to purchase the paintings, with proceeds contributing to WFP programs supporting vulnerable communities, including refugee children and conflict-impacted members of the host community.
These programs include school-based assistance, cash transfers and food support, helping families meet their essential needs while promoting children’s well-being and access to education.
WFP currently provides humanitarian assistance to approximately 60,000 people across Iran, including refugees and vulnerable members of host communities affected by the recent escalation.
Through this initiative, WFP seeks to connect the public with the stories of refugee children, celebrate their artistic talents and demonstrate how creativity and community engagement can contribute to humanitarian action.
WFP services
As part of the response to the recent escalation, WFP started to provide cash transfers to affected Iranian households, with the first round completed, reaching 340 households, of which 327 were male-headed households.
Assistance was provided according to household size: IRR 210 million (USD 139.1) for households of one to three members; IRR 350 million (USD 231.9) for households of four to five members; IRR 420 million (USD 278.3) for households of six or more members.
In 2025, WFP sustained food assistance to some 33,300 vulnerable refugees living in 20 settlements across 13 provinces, including 404 refugees with disabilities (40 percent women) who received monthly cash top-ups. About 183 women and 190 men received WFP livelihood support.
WFP doubled cash transfer values since January 2025, safeguarding access to food amid price volatility and protecting the most vulnerable households.
Assistance remained uninterrupted, with targeted adjustments: wheat flour entitlements reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg (Nov-Dec) and school snacks paused (Oct-Dec) to stretch limited resources.
To promote girls’ education and reduce barriers to attendance, approximately 2,629 girl students received cash incentives as part of WFP’s commitment to empowering young women. Some 9,261 boys and girls and their teachers benefitted from WFP school snacks.
For more than four decades, the Islamic Republic of Iran has hosted Afghans fleeing conflict and hardship. In 2025, WFP remained essential to protecting the food security of vulnerable refugees residing in 20 settlements, where households rely on shelter, education and primary health care by the Government and other humanitarian actors, complemented by WFP’s monthly food assistance (through cash and in-kind modalities).
The program’s focus is on maintaining a dignified minimum basic needs while prioritizing those with the highest vulnerability, including households headed by women and persons with disabilities.
Operations are implemented in close collaboration and coordination with the Center for Alien and Foreign Immigrant Affairs (CAFIA), WFP’s primary governmental counterpart, and with International Non-Governmental Organizations (INGO) and UN agencies, mainly the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), to ensure coherent refugee support and referral pathways.
Despite a complex year, marked by economic volatility and temporary operational risks, WFP sustained core assistance to settlement refugees. To safeguard purchasing power, WFP increased cash-based transfer values by 100 percent in January 2025 following the recommendation of a settlement-specific Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) assessment; this was complemented by a one-time cash top-up to cushion households during market instability and reduced income after the Iran-Israel 12-day conflict.
Targeted adjustments preserved program continuity: wheat flour entitlements were reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg per person for November-December, and the school snacks program was suspended for October to December.
These measures limit service disruptions while protecting life-saving transfers for the most vulnerable. Livelihood activities were scaled down given funding shortfalls and corporate efficiency measures, with WFP continuing to explore cost-effective, resilience-building options that can be re-activated as resources allow.
By December 2025, Iran continued to be one of the world’s largest refugee-hosting countries, sheltering approximately 2.5 million Afghans, including 773,000 individuals with official refugee status. Among them, around 35,000 critically vulnerable refugees reside in 20 settlements across 13 provinces.

Meet the original 'Ghost Busters'—the 17th century scientists who investigated hauntings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:34:52 UTC
20:34:52 KST

About 1671, parson Symonds, who officiated at Garsdon church in north Wiltshire in south west England, was riding home late one night when a specter leapt up behind him. The specter rode parallel to him until they came to the parsonage, where it jumped off. The apparition then turned to face Symonds, and “gap’d at him”. Symonds identified the ghost as that of John Estcourt, a gentleman who had died about two years earlier.
Halloween is all about witches and ghosts. In English scientific circles in the second half of the 17th century, there was a discussion about whether such things existed and how their existence could be proved.
The Royal Society, founded in 1660, was the country’s principal scientific institution. Joseph Glanvill, a Royal Society fellow, investigated spirits and witches. His Saducismus Triumphatus(1681) aimed to prove their existence by cataloguing cases in detail. He argued that denying them was to deny God’s existence.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Symonds’ haunting was recorded by that of another of the society’s fellows, John Aubrey, in a survey of Wiltshire’s natural world. Aubrey agreed with Glanvill that the supernatural deserved serious study and directed his readers to Saducismus, but he thought Glanvill somewhat gullible.
Aubrey was born in 1626 at Easton Piercy, a few miles from Garsdon. I have edited John Aubrey’s Natural History to mark his 400th anniversary.
This natural history of Wiltshire was begun in 1656 and was the first English county survey of nature to be attempted – although by the time he finished it, decades later, other surveys had already been published. It was an important scientific work, and in 1691, acknowledging that, the Royal Society had the Natural History copied and added to its library.
Its subject matter is highly idiosyncratic, and Aubrey sometimes goes off on tangents. He covers swan-sized dragons in north Africa in a chapter on birds and the existence of giants in a section called “Men and Women”. Almost at the end of the text is a chapter titled “Accidents” that records extraordinary events, including supernatural ones, like the haunting of Symonds.
Aubrey has long been seen as naive, partly because of Miscellanies (1696), the only book he published, which recorded tales of the unexplained. In the Natural History, he was clear:
Though I myselfe never saw any such things, yet I will not conclude that there is no truth at all in these reports. I believe that extraordinarily there have been such apparitions: but where one is true, a hundred are figments.
He also documented exposed frauds, such as Katherine Waldron, who pretended to be bewitched and endured pins being driven into her flesh to prove it. As the objective of natural history at this time was to gather evidence from which new scientific theories could be developed, Aubrey’s method in chronicling cases was entirely in keeping with the aims of scientific enterprise.
So, Aubrey was neither uncritical nor dismissive about Symonds’ story. Symonds was “a lusty strong fellow”, presumably not someone nervous or hysterical and prone to flights of imagination. His position as a churchman also gave authority to his testimony. Yet Aubrey noted a French saying that drunk men saw devils, a skeptical observation that cast doubt on the account. But he concluded with a strange detail: it was corroborated by the parson’s horse, “that trembled and sweat, when he came home and continued to do so the next day, and would not eat his oates”. The horse could not lie or get drunk; its fear, manifest in the trembling and sweat, was genuine.
Aubrey recorded another anecdote about a night ride. It concerned Sir Ralph Bankes’ valet:“a briske young fellow”, who, riding late over Badbury Warren, Dorset, discerned something that looked black, which, as he approached, became bigger.
Feare came upon him, and he protested his haire stood on end: but thought he, I have but a life to lose and I will see it, be it spirit or not.
The valet spurred his horse and came to the place, only to find the apparition was “a heap of horse dung”.
In Symonds’ haunting, the truth of the specter could not be tested; but witnesses were recorded, and their testimony weighed. In the valet’s case, the witness tested the truth of the ghost himself and found it was a pile of dung.
Aubrey applied the same empirical method throughout his Natural History to both natural and supernatural phenomena. He assembled evidence with care, tested it if he could and resisted easy conclusions. It’s an approach worth remembering this Halloween when fantastical tales hit your social media feed. A phantom may prove to be a load of poo.

National poison prevention week: recognize danger, take timely action
TEHRAN – The national poison prevention week began on Friday and will run through October 29, focusing on raising public awareness of poisoning risks and promoting preventive measures.
This year’s observance is being held under the theme “From Recognizing Danger to Taking Timely Action to Prevent Poisoning,” with the aim of highlighting poisoning hazards, improving public awareness, and encouraging timely action to prevent poisoning incidents.
Each day of the week highlights a specific point:
 
Friday, October 23rd, ‘preventing drug poisoning’
 
Saturday, October 24th, ‘preventing poisoning in children’
 
Sunday, October 25th, ‘preventing carbon monoxide poisoning’
 
Monday, October 26th, ‘preventing food, plant, and mushroom poisoning’
 
Tuesday, October 27th, ‘preventing chemical and pest poisoning’
 
Wednesday, October 28th, ‘preventing poisoning by venomous animals’
 
Thursday, October 29th, ‘preventing drug and alcohol poisoning’
According to the head of the Food and Drug Administration, Mehdi Pirsalehi, protecting human health and lives against poisonings requires identifying risk factors, strengthening a culture of prevention, and being prepared to take appropriate and timely action in emergencies, ILNA reported.
Poisoning can occur at homes, workplaces, in nature, and during the course of daily activities. The effects of poisoning range from mild to severe, with some cases being fatal. Therefore, identifying sources of danger and being aware of prevention strategies constitute an important part of public health protection programs, he added.
The majority of poisoning cases can be prevented through storing medications and chemicals safely, using toxic ingredients properly, adhering to safety warnings, avoiding the consumption of unidentified substances, and educating children and families, Pirsalehi noted.
In case of poisoning, or if poisoning is suspected, avoid self-medication; instead, seek immediate medical treatment, he said.
Referring to this year’s theme, he said raising awareness of poisoning symptoms and taking timely action will help prevent potential health complications. The national drug and poison information center affiliated with the Food and Drug Administration strives to enhance public awareness, develop effective practices in prevention, and facilitate access to information and specialized advice.
However, reducing cases of poisoning requires the coordinated participation of the healthcare system, educational institutions, the media, families, and other relevant sectors, Pirsalehi further noted.

- The Turkish Naval Forces used HAVELSAN’s Barkan unmanned ground vehicle in amphibious raid and urban warfare training during TURNAs-2026.
- The vehicle also evacuated simulated wounded during the exercise, held in the Gulf of Antalya and eastern Mediterranean from Oct. 19 to 27.
The Turkish Naval Forces used HAVELSAN’s Barkan unmanned ground vehicle to support amphibious raid and urban warfare training and then to evacuate simulated wounded personnel during TURNAs-2026, the service’s unmanned maritime systems exercise under way in the Gulf of Antalya and the eastern Mediterranean from Oct. 19 to 27, the Naval Forces Command said.
The exercise brings unmanned air, surface, underwater and amphibious platforms into the same scenarios as crewed forces, and the Barkan’s role covered both ends of a landing operation: moving with troops during the raid and urban combat phases, and carrying casualties back once the fighting was over.
TURNAs-2026 involves 18 ships, 11 aircraft, nine unmanned aerial vehicles, seven unmanned underwater vehicles and nine unmanned surface vessels, along with 41 systems from 17 Turkish defense companies, Anadolu Agency reported, citing Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defense. Participating Turkish Naval Forces units include a multipurpose amphibious ship, frigates, corvettes, fast attack craft, a submarine, a mine hunter, amphibious landing ships and SH-70 helicopters, as well as unmanned and one-way attack surface vessels and Coast Guard boats.
Built by Ankara-based HAVELSAN, the Barkan is a medium-class unmanned ground vehicle developed under the company’s “digital unit” concept, in which unmanned ground, air and naval systems operate together and share tasks. The Barkan family entered the Turkish Armed Forces inventory in 2023 and moved into mass production in 2025 following a decision by Türkiye’s Presidency of Defense Industries.
The vehicle is designed for a range of missions, including assault, casualty transfer, bomb disposal, surveillance and reconnaissance, and battle damage assessment. Its modular design lets operators fit different payloads, and HAVELSAN has armed versions of the Barkan with remote weapon stations, a laser-guided missile and loitering munitions in earlier tests.
The company unveiled the Barkan 3 at SAHA Expo in Istanbul in May 2026, where HAVELSAN and the Presidency of Defense Industries signed a contract amendment covering the new configuration. HAVELSAN has said the Barkan 3 is intended to operate in swarms alongside unmanned aerial vehicles and unmanned surface vessels.
Ukraine became the first country to carry out such unmanned landing and supply operations in actual combat during its war with Russia. On July 13, the 123rd Separate Territorial Defense Brigade used an unmanned surface vessel to land an armed ground robot on the Russian-occupied Kinburn Spit, in what the brigade called the first known combat mission of its kind. Ukrainian forces later used a heavy hexacopter to deliver an ARK-1 ground robot armed with anti-tank mines deep into Russian rear areas, the first known combat operation in which an aerial drone carried a ground robot into battle.
In late September, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said the Alter Ego unit of the 93rd Separate Mechanized Brigade had completed the country’s first frontline supply mission with Triton, a domestically built amphibious unmanned ground vehicle that switches from driving to swimming within seconds. The vehicle covered more than 40 km (25 miles) of land and water to deliver supplies to troops on a section of the front cut by rivers and marshland.

New mRNA Vaccine Reduces Risk of Melanoma Recurrence by Over 40 Percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

An experimental vaccine offers new hope to patients with melanoma, one of the most aggressive forms of skin cancer. The pharmaceutical companies Merck and Moderna released the results of a Phase 3 clinical trial that evaluated the efficacy of a personalized mRNA-based vaccine that, when combined with immunotherapy, reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 42 percent compared to treatment with the immunotherapy drug alone.
Georgina Long, medical director of the Australian Melanoma Institute and the study’s principal investigator, said in a statement that these results are “transformative” and “have the potential to make a foundational shift in how we treat patients with earlier-stage melanoma.”
The trial, known as INTerpath-001, included 1,137 people with high-risk melanoma who had undergone surgery to completely remove their tumors. The participants were divided into two groups. Those in the first group received only Pembrolizumab, a drug that helps the immune system detect and fight cancer cells, while those in the second group were treated with the same drug in combination with the mRNA vaccine, called Intismeran Autogene.
After monitoring the participants for an average of 24.6 months, the researchers determined that addition of the vaccine reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death by 42 percent compared to Pembrolizumab alone.
The results also showed that the experimental treatment reduced the risk of the disease spreading to other parts of the body by 38 percent. At the end of the follow-up period, 82.2 percent of patients who received both treatments remained recurrence-free, compared with 70 percent of those who received Pembrolizumab alone.
“The results of the INTerpath-001 study represent a major breakthrough in the treatment of melanoma and, in particular, in the development of personalized medicine,” Eva Muñoz Couselo—who leads a melanoma research group at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology, in Barcelona and who was not involved in the study—told SMC Spain. “For the first time, a Phase III trial has demonstrated that an individualized therapeutic vaccine, designed on the basis of the molecular characteristics of each patient’s tumor, can significantly improve the outcomes of conventional immunotherapy.”
The laboratories explained that the vaccine was developed from a tumor sample taken from each patient, which was used to identify specific mutations that would create distinct proteins the immune system could learn to recognize in order to attack cancer cells. The scientists selected up to three of these molecular signatures per patient.
During the trial, some participants experienced mild side effects such as fever, fatigue, and pain at the injection site. These side effects were seen in earlier trials as well, and the Phase 3 findings demonstrate similar safety when the vaccine is used in the combination with Pembrolizumab.
“These results reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer,” Stéphane Bancel, CEO of Moderna, said in a statement.
The pharmaceutical companies emphasized that the vaccine is not designed to prevent melanoma but rather to reduce the risk of recurrence and death following prior medical treatment. They also noted that the therapy remains under investigation to validate its efficacy and obtain approval from health authorities before widespread use.
Most people diagnosed with melanoma have a high chance of survival, especially if detected early, but as one of the most common cancers, melanoma kills over 50,000 people globally each year. In theory, similar vaccines could be developed for other kinds of tumors in the future. Earlier this year, another trial demonstrated that personalized mRNA vaccines can greatly improve survival among patients with pancreatic cancer, one of the deadliest kinds of tumor.
“This is the major breakthrough, because conceptually it would make it possible to treat not only melanoma but also other tumors in which the immune system can be reactivated,” Marisol Soengas—a leading melanoma researcher at Spain’s National Cancer Research Center also not involved in the trial—told SMC Spain.
That doesn’t mean a cure for cancer is right around the corner. “The challenge is to ensure that this personalization can be scaled up to a large number of patients and that the cost is affordable for health care systems,” Soengas said. “It is logistically complex. It is literally a bespoke vaccine.”

Pakistan can mediate between Washington and Tehran, but it cannot manufacture trust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:27:36 UTC
20:27:36 KST

When Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, met Iranian leaders in Tehran last Tuesday, he heard a familiar message in a harder form. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Washington must lift sanctions and pressure before talks resume. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei said no enriched material would leave Iran. After Munir left, a Qatari delegation arrived, a reminder that Islamabad no longer carries this file alone.
The real test is not whether Pakistan can soften Tehran’s opening position. It is whether it can help two adversaries negotiate commitments neither believes the other will honour.
The Islamabad Memorandum, signed on 17 June, extended the ceasefire for 60 days and promised to reopen Hormuz and lift the US blockade. It also pledged oil-export waivers. By 8 July it had collapsed after Iranian strikes on commercial vessels and a US response, and Washington reinstated the blockade six days later. The lesson is not merely that signatures are cheap. The text allowed each side to claim a different meaning. Iran read a “best efforts” clause on passage as giving it some authority over the strait, while the two sides disagreed over the strait provisions from the start. No neutral body existed to say who was right.
Pakistan deserves credit for building a channel between enemies. Few governments can speak to Iran, keep close ties with Washington and engage the Gulf capitals. But access is not leverage.
Islamabad cannot lift American sanctions, settle the enrichment dispute or guarantee that armed actors across the region will respect a ceasefire.
Nor is Pakistan an uninvolved broker. It shares a border with Iran, depends on Gulf energy and is a party to the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, under which it has pledged to defend Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks hit Saudi infrastructure. A mediator that has promised to defend one side’s partner cannot claim neutrality. It can claim something narrower and more useful: both sides have reason to keep its channel open.
That is why Pakistan should narrow its ambitions. It should not chase a grand reconciliation. It should help build a process in which limited cooperation does not require either capital to trust the other’s intentions.
The core problem is credible commitment. Tehran sees sanctions, blockades and strikes as proof that American assurances are unreliable. Washington sees enrichment and regional military activity as proof that Iranian promises are. Each wants the other to move first. Reuters has reported Iranian officials saying Tehran is deliberately slowing talks to weaken President Trump before the November midterms. If so, deadlock is a strategy for some, not just a failure.
The strongest objection to mediation is therefore serious: Islamabad cannot change either side’s strategic calculation, and its ties to Washington and Riyadh complicate any claim to impartiality. Iran’s decision-making is also fragmented. Munir’s August visit followed a change in Iran’s military hierarchy, so an understanding with civilian officials could fail elsewhere.
Even so, neutrality is not the only measure of a useful intermediary. What matters is whether messages are conveyed faithfully, whether the channel is trusted and whether steps can be independently checked.
A modest agenda would start at sea. Agreed procedures for reporting attacks on shipping, exchanging operational notices and investigating alleged violations would not need a nuclear settlement. But Iran’s claim to administer the strait is a sovereignty question, not an incident-management one. The June memorandum left the strait’s future administration to Iran in consultation with Oman and other Gulf states. That question must be put on the table, with partners such as Oman, which has facilitated US-Iran channels before, rather than papered over with vague wording.
The second track should pair reciprocal, time-limited steps. The June memorandum already linked the strait to sanctions waivers, so the difference this time must be design: smaller steps, explicit sequencing, reversibility and no side surrendering its main leverage on a promise.
The nuclear file needs different machinery. Iran’s refusal to export its stockpile and Washington’s demand for limits are substantive disagreements, not misunderstandings. The IAEA can verify agreed limits, but it cannot invent the bargain or inspect without a legal basis and access. Reports of a Qatari–Pakistani proposal linking inspections to interest on frozen funds rest on anonymous sources, and an Iranian parliamentary spokesman described Munir’s trip as bilateral only. Still, they point in the right direction: link access to relief.
READ: After Mecca, why Badr? Because this pact builds, not binds
Any new arrangement should specify who verifies compliance, how disputed incidents are judged and what happens after a breach. A joint implementation group with independent technical expertise could set deadlines, document performance and resolve accusations before they trigger retaliation.
Pakistan should also resist competing for credit. Qatar is already a co-mediator, and Oman has long experience with Gulf security channels. The goal is an effective process, not Pakistani ownership of it.
None of this guarantees peace. If either government believes time or escalation favours it, the best verification system will sit unused. Regional actors can also wreck understandings reached in negotiating rooms.
For the world, the stakes are tangible. Threats to Gulf shipping unsettle energy markets and raise costs for households and importers everywhere. For Pakistan, the danger is closer still.
Islamabad has shown it can bring adversaries toward an agreement. The harder, less theatrical task is helping them build one that survives the next crisis. Pakistan can open the door to diplomacy. It cannot supply the trust Washington and Tehran lack. What it can help supply is a system that makes cooperation possible without it.

DOE, IUCN discuss joint programs to protect endangered species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:26:12 UTC
20:26:12 KST

DOE, IUCN discuss joint programs to protect endangered species
TEHRAN – Hamid Zohrabi, deputy head of the Department of Environment (DOE), and Vivek Menon, chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Species Survival Commission (SSC), have discussed ways to strengthen cooperation in developing management and conservation programs for endangered species.
The officials met on the sidelines of the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the Convention on Biological Diversity being held from October 19 to 30 in Armenia, IRNA reported.
The head of IUCN Eastern Europe and Central Asia Regional Office attended the meeting as well.
The talks particularly focused on conservation and restoration programs for the Asiatic cheetah, the great bustard, and the Persian zebra, onager, their respective habitats, as well as the reintroduction of the Persian fallow deer into its natural habitats.
Both parties also discussed enhancing technical and scientific cooperation and providing funding under sanctions.
Menon expressed hope that ongoing collaboration between IUCN officials and Iranian experts would guarantee the survival of endangered species, such as the Asiatic cheetah, in Iran.
COP17 is being held under the framework of the Convention on Biological Diversity, alongside the Twelfth meeting of the Parties to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (CP-MOP-12) and the Sixth meeting of the Parties to the Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from Their Utilization (NP-MOP-6).
The two-week negotiations are being held in two stages: technical-level discussions followed by the ministerial segment.
The leaders’ summit took place on October 16, featuring an address by President Masoud Pezeshkian. It marked the first time a president of the Islamic Republic of Iran had attended a Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.
Addressing the summit, Pezeshkian called for “peace diplomacy” to protect biodiversity, condemning the devastating environmental impact of wars of aggression as ecocide and urging the international community to establish effective, transparent and enforceable mechanisms to safeguard natural heritage during wartime.
According to the latest report by the IUCN Red List, about 154 vertebrate animal species and around 25 percent of plant species in the country are at risk of extinction, with 117 species being classified as critically endangered in the national list. Persian zebra, Asiatic cheetah, black bear, great bustard, and yellow deer are among animals that are in danger of extinction.
Among extinct animals, the Hyrcanian tiger and Persian lion are the two feline species that have disappeared forever in the country. Fortunately, the Persian zebra and the Persian yellow deer are examples of successful conservation efforts where scientific measures and local community participation have resulted in the species’ recovery.
Genetic map for endangered species being developed
The DOE is developing a genetic map of endangered wildlife species to increase their chance of survival, create a breeding plan, manage their population, and address the risks facing them in their natural habitats.
Effective conservation of endangered species is almost unattainable without a precise understanding of population genetics. To this end, genetic and molecular studies of key wildlife species in the country have been put on the agenda, ensuring that management decisions are based on accurate scientific data, IRNA quoted the head of the National Museum of Natural History and Genetic Resources, Leila Ezzeddinlou, as saying.
Preserving genetic diversity within and between populations, preventing declines in effective population size, avoiding inbreeding and genetic erosion, conserving genes adapted to diverse environmental conditions, and providing genetic resources for species restoration, propagation, and introduction or reintroduction programs are among primary objectives of these studies, she added.
Referring to three research agreements signed between the DOE, the College of Agricultural and Natural Resources of the University of Tehran, and Gorgan University, the official said that as part of the cooperation, a project is underway to investigate the genomic diversity and phylogeny of Levant viper and Latifi’s viper populations, employing conservation and therapeutic approaches based on genomic markers.
Moreover, the development of genetic profiles and maps for the Asiatic cheetahs, black bear, and Persian yellow deer, as keystone and threatened species, has kicked off.
The other part of the agreements focuses on the assessment of genetic variation, inbreeding, and kinship relationships within the Persian zebra population, which is being conducted in collaboration with Yazd’s provincial DOE department. The initiative plays a key role in managing small populations and preventing the loss of genetic biodiversity, she highlighted.

Students join Albania’s ‘Flamingo Revolution’ as unrest spreads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:24:35 UTC
20:24:35 KST

Anti-government protesters gathered in Albania’s capital on Saturday as months of demonstrations over corruption, economic hardship and environmental concerns escalated into violent clashes, posing the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government in more than a decade.
The latest demonstrations in Tirana followed a week of confrontations involving students, riot police and protesters who set fires, damaged public buildings and clashed with security forces.
What began in May as a campaign against a controversial coastal tourism development has grown into a broader movement demanding political accountability and better living conditions.
The protests, known as the “Flamingo Revolution,” initially focused on a luxury tourism project linked to Affinity Partners, an investment firm associated with Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump. The proposed development on Albania’s southern Adriatic coast has drawn environmental objections over its potential impact on protected wetlands and habitats supporting flamingos and other wildlife.
Demonstrators argued that the project threatened ecologically sensitive areas around Sazan Island and the Vjosa-Narta region. Peaceful gatherings in central Tirana continued for more than 130 days, with protesters using flamingo imagery as a symbol of their opposition.
Over time, the movement expanded beyond environmental concerns, incorporating allegations of corruption, dissatisfaction with public services, economic grievances and calls for Rama to resign.
The unrest intensified in mid-October when high school and university students joined the demonstrations in large numbers. They cited rising education costs, inadequate university facilities and dormitories, limited financial assistance and poor employment prospects after graduation, alongside the broader cost-of-living crisis.
Marches initially focused on the Education Ministry but soon turned violent. Protesters smashed windows, burned trash bins and kiosks, and damaged bank branches and government buildings. Among the targeted sites was a Raiffeisen bank branch.
Some demonstrators threw rocks, fireworks and flares at police, while others used Molotov cocktails. Riot police responded with tear gas, water cannons and baton charges. By around Oct. 17, security forces also appeared to be using rubber bullets, according to reports from the demonstrations.
The confrontations continued for several days, spreading beyond the capital to cities including Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë, Vlora, Elbasan, Korçë and Gjirokastër.
In Tirana, protesters targeted the Education Ministry, Interior Ministry, Supreme Court and headquarters of the governing Socialist Party. Clashes also erupted near a police station and areas surrounding the prime minister’s office.
Smoke, broken glass, debris and burned barricades littered parts of the capital as security forces struggled to contain the unrest.
Official figures reported during the peak of the clashes indicated hundreds of injuries, including a substantial number of police officers. One tally put the number of injured at about 295, including approximately 186 officers, although subsequent reports cited additional casualties.
Authorities also carried out mass arrests, with reports at the height of the unrest indicating more than 1,000 detentions and nearly 400 criminal prosecutions. Many detainees were subsequently released. Some police officers were suspended amid allegations of excessive force.
Rama, whose Socialist Party has governed Albania since 2013, has rejected demands to step down. He won a fourth term in the 2025 parliamentary elections and has argued that governments must change through democratic elections rather than street violence.
He has portrayed the unrest as a threat to Albania’s democratic stability and its ambition to join the European Union, with membership targeted for the end of the decade.
Rama has also accused unidentified “dark forces,” foreign actors and elements associated with the opposition of exploiting or radicalizing the demonstrations. He has raised concerns about disinformation and possible foreign interference, including alleged involvement by Russia, Iran or other actors. Independent evidence supporting those allegations remains limited.
While condemning arson and attacks on public property, Rama has offered dialogue on students’ concerns, including education costs. He has also defended the police response and announced support for officers, including bonuses and prospective pay increases.
The unrest has disrupted parliamentary proceedings, with sessions canceled or affected by the security situation around government institutions.
Despite the growing violence, many protesters have expressed distrust of the entire political establishment, not only Rama’s government. Demonstrators, many of them young and organizing through loosely coordinated networks rather than a single leadership structure, have rejected both the ruling Socialists and the opposition Democratic Party led by Sali Berisha.
Chants demanding Rama’s resignation have accompanied calls for broader political change, with some protesters invoking revolution and rejecting the country’s two dominant political camps.
The movement’s decentralized character has made it difficult for political leaders to claim control over the demonstrations or present themselves as representatives of the protesters’ demands.
University professors and civil society figures have also criticized aspects of the police response. Some have called for a caretaker government, reflecting concerns that the crisis extends beyond individual policy disputes to wider questions about political accountability and institutional trust.
Albania’s longstanding problems with corruption, employment opportunities and living standards have helped fuel public dissatisfaction. The latest unrest has brought those concerns together with anger over education and environmental protection, turning a campaign against one development project into a wider confrontation over the country’s political direction.
Saturday’s planned gatherings included an opposition rally in central Tirana around midday, student demonstrations and solidarity actions near the Education Ministry, and activities involving university lecturers, including those associated with the Polytechnic University.
The events followed days of tension after the initial wave of violent confrontations. Authorities also reportedly increased border checks in some areas as the situation remained unsettled.
The protests present a significant test for Rama as Albania pursues EU membership and seeks to maintain political stability. Although the government has insisted that the unrest will not determine its future, the scale of the demonstrations and the breadth of the grievances have underscored the depth of public discontent.

Arrest made after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:23:59 BST
20:23:59 KST

Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
- Published
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.
Police said they apprehended the suspect riding a motorcycle near the scene and possible motives were still being examined, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.
There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.
Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.
Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website, external.
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

IMPASCO to offer 2 mineral exploration investment packages in South Khorasan

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

IMPASCO to offer 2 mineral exploration investment packages in South Khorasan
TEHRAN — Iran will launch an auction next week for two mineral exploration investment packages in South Khorasan province, comprising a total of 10 exploration licenses, an official at the state-owned Iran Minerals Production and Supply Company (IMPASCO) said.
Shima Moafi, acting deputy head of development and planning at IMPASCO, said the initiative was designed to encourage private-sector participation and create new investment opportunities in the mining sector.
The first phase will offer two exploration investment packages in South Khorasan through a competitive bidding process, with each package covering five exploration licenses, Moafi said, according to IRIB.
Further investment packages covering the provinces of Ilam, Qom and Isfahan are expected to be offered after the initial phase, she added.
Back in June, the head of the executive board of the Iranian Mines and Mining Industries Development and Renovation Organization (IMIDRO) emphasized the need to transform the country's mineral exploration policies, saying that developing national exploration standards, expanding private sector participation, attracting foreign investors, and training specialized human resources will be the main pillars of Iran's mineral exploration development program.
Speaking at a meeting on Tuesday to review the exploration activities and plans of the organization's major subsidiaries and affiliated companies, Mohammad Masoud Samiei-Nejad described the expansion of mineral exploration as one of the mining sector's highest priorities this year.
He said IMIDRO's policy is focused on implementing development programs in the exploration sector, with a target of completing one million meters of drilling by its subsidiary companies.
Referring to the need for a unified approach to exploration procedures, Samiei-Nejad stated that standardized and integrated policies should be developed for mineral exploration and the issuance of discovery certificates based on the type of mineral, the scale of exploration operations, and the conditions of drilling sites. Once finalized, these standards will be communicated to companies and provincial authorities across the country to ensure that all stakeholders operate within a common regulatory framework.
The IMIDRO chief also stressed the importance of establishing a dedicated exploration working group. Given the prominent role of exploration development in Iran's Seventh National Development Plan, he said, the necessary executive guidelines should be prepared, and—with the participation of the private sector—exploration challenges and obstacles in different provinces should be examined and addressed through specialized reviews.
Samiei-Nejad noted that investment models in the exploration sector require revision, explaining that the current investment structures within IMIDRO's subsidiaries are relatively closed and should be reformed to facilitate the entry of new investors, particularly from the private sector. Accordingly, he said, all subsidiary companies are required to submit operational plans within the next six months outlining how they intend to increase private sector participation in mining activities, especially exploration projects.
He also emphasized the importance of utilizing foreign investment in major mining projects, saying that planning should be undertaken to attract foreign investors—particularly for large-scale mines. At the same time, he called for a thorough study of the experiences of Eurasian countries in advancing mineral exploration, especially in the copper and gold sectors, over the past decade.
Concluding his remarks, the IMIDRO head announced the launch of a specialized workforce training program for drilling operations. He said that expanding mineral exploration would not be possible without skilled personnel. Therefore, through specialized training courses and the participation of leading domestic and international experts, IMIDRO will begin training drilling technicians, with the initial goal of preparing 100 specialized drilling technicians.

IOFS, Iran sign cooperation deal to advance joint agricultural projects
TEHRAN — Iran and the Islamic Organization for Food Security (IOFS) have signed a cooperation agreement to expand agricultural and technological collaboration, with a three-month action plan to be drawn up to translate the commitments into practical projects, Iran’s agricultural research chief said.
Gholamreza Golmohammadi, head of Iran’s Agricultural Research, Education and Extension Organization, signed the memorandum during a visit to Kazakhstan and held talks with IOFS Secretary-General Berik Aryn on cooperation in vaccine and seed production, agricultural biotechnology, water and soil management, and joint research projects, Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB reported.

On the sidelines of the visit, the Iranian delegation also held talks on transferring technical expertise and developing joint production of vaccines against foot-and-mouth disease, as well as expanding scientific and technological cooperation with Islamic countries.
The discussions took place during the delegation’s participation in an international agricultural exhibition in Kazakhstan.

The meeting also discussed proposals to address obstacles facing Iranian exporters of goods to neighboring countries, including Iraq, Pakistan and Afghanistan. The proposals could be pursued through negotiations with foreign counterparts, he said.
Ghanbari added that Iran’s embassies and consulates would be instructed to follow up on the proposals.
He expressed hope that, despite what he described as difficulties caused by Iran’s adversaries, the efforts would help preserve existing exports and make future shipments more targeted while improving overall export performance.

Jordan tightens security after deadly church attack kills eight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:22:20 UTC
20:22:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Jordan tightens security after deadly church attack kills nine
Security was stepped up at malls, foreign embassies and other locations across Jordan, the US embassy in Amman said on Saturday, as authorities searched for gunmen who killed nine people and wounded 40 in a church attack.
The assailants fired for several minutes in broad daylight during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate on Friday, in what Jordanian authorities described as an act of extremist terrorism. No one immediately claimed responsibility.
Two people wounded in Friday's attack died of their injuries, bringing the number of people killed to nine, health minister Ibrahim al-Bdour told AFP on Saturday.
"The number of victims who died in the terrorist attack on the church in the village of Al-Hamoud in Karak has risen to nine following the death on Saturday of a second casualty who had been in a critical condition," the minister said.
Another 25 people remain hospitalised, he added.
Such attacks are rare in Jordan, although authorities in the US-allied kingdom say they have repeatedly foiled plots by militants in recent years.
Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a long list of officials condemning what he called a "wicked" attack.
"God willing, this country will remain secure," he said.
Authorities said they were still searching for the attackers, adding it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.
"A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word," said Tarek Ammarin at a hospital where the wounded were being treated. A relative of Ammarin's was injured in the attack.
Reuters video footage showed police patrolling outside the Hamoud church on Saturday, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.
"This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism and we will not allow society to go down this path," Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said in a post on X.
Jordan's King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist".
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
Jordan has been among the US allies in the Middle East to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

Iran has sufficient forex reserves to fund imports through end of Trump term, CBI chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:21:14 UTC

Iran has sufficient forex reserves to fund imports through end of Trump term, CBI chief says
TEHRAN — Iran has sufficient foreign exchange reserves to cover the country’s imports through the end of U.S. President Donald Trump’s term and beyond, Central Bank of Iran (CBI) Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said in an interview with Bloomberg.
In a post on his Telegram channel, Hemmati said he gave a televised interview to Bloomberg on the sidelines of last week’s annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
Hemmati said inflation, which accelerated sharply following a 40-day war, had eased in the three months leading up to the end of Shahrivar, the sixth month of the Iranian calendar which ended on September 22, 2026.
He attributed the earlier surge in inflation to two main factors: supply-side shocks caused by damage to infrastructure and industrial facilities, some of which have since resumed production, and inflationary expectations on the demand side, which the central bank had partly contained through monetary policy tools.
Hemmati said the United States had sought to isolate Iran economically and intensify pressure on the country, predicting that its economy would collapse within two weeks. Despite heavy economic pressure on the Iranian people, Washington had failed to achieve its main objective, he said, describing the prediction as an illusion.
He said he had also raised the issue in an address to central bank governors from the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia.
Addressing the decline in oil revenues, Hemmati said oil income accounted for a limited share of the government budget. He said the government intended to cover its budget deficit through other sources of domestic-currency revenue, including asset sales, reforms in the energy sector and exports of petroleum products.
On foreign currency revenues, he said Iran was still receiving proceeds from oil exports and had made arrangements to maintain supplies in the future.
Asked about the central bank’s foreign exchange reserves, Hemmati said they were in a good position and would be sufficient to finance imports through the end of Trump’s presidential term and beyond.
Hemmati also discussed measures to offset the loss of purchasing power among households, highlighting the distribution of electronic or commodity vouchers and gradual increases in their rial value for low-income families.

Iran needs predictable rules, less red tape to strengthen foreign trade, industry group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:21:01 UTC
20:21:01 KST

Iran needs predictable rules, less red tape to strengthen foreign trade, industry group says
TEHRAN — Iran needs predictable economic policies, less bureaucracy, greater private-sector participation and the smarter use of technology to strengthen its foreign trade, the head of the Iranian Association of Digital Technology and Smart Systems Employers said.
Seifollah Niknami made the remarks at a strategic meeting on Iran’s foreign trade, emphasizing the need to coordinate national capabilities in technology, industry, energy, logistics and the private sector to improve production and trade.
“Technology must serve to solve real economic problems,” Niknami said, adding that the country’s domestic capabilities could become competitive advantages only if they were connected to one another and to global markets.
Producers cannot be expected to plan for the long term when the rules governing their activities may change abruptly through new directives, he said. Maintaining exporters’ credibility in international markets also requires reducing cumbersome procedures, improving coordination among digital systems and avoiding unpredictable policy decisions.
Sanctions and external restrictions pose serious challenges, Niknami said, but regulatory instability and unnecessary procedures should not impose additional risks on producers and exporters.
Regulatory stability is an intangible asset for production and exports, he said, noting that a shipment held up while awaiting an official inquiry or approval could affect not only delivery schedules but also a company’s working capital, contractual commitments and opportunities in target markets.
Niknami outlined four priorities for improving the business environment and strengthening the resilience of Iran’s foreign trade: stable and predictable regulations; eliminating unnecessary procedures and improving coordination among government agencies; risk-based, intelligent oversight; and effective participation by professional and employers’ associations in policymaking.
He said the impact of decisions affecting production and exports should be assessed before they are introduced, with businesses given a reasonable period to adapt where necessary.
Information required by authorized agencies should also be exchanged in a coordinated manner, subject to confidentiality requirements and legal limits on access, so that businesses do not bear the cost of inconsistencies among digital platforms and government bodies, he added.
Niknami said durable policies could not be developed without listening to producers, exporters and specialized industry associations. Such organizations should be involved from the earliest stages of consultation rather than informed only after decisions have been made.
Private-sector participation does not replace the government’s responsibilities, he said, but provides an expert basis for more accurate, realistic and effective policymaking.
Digital transformation must begin with process reform
Niknami said reforming existing procedures was a necessary prerequisite for digital transformation.
Smart systems do not begin with purchasing technology, but with identifying problems and improving processes, he said. Digitizing an inefficient or unnecessary procedure does not necessarily constitute progress, as it may simply transfer an existing obstacle to a computer screen.
Technology, data and innovation should instead help strengthen different parts of foreign trade by lowering costs, speeding up procedures, increasing transparency and improving decision-making, he added.
Five priorities for trade resilience
Niknami said the meeting had been organized around five specialist panels addressing the resilience of Iran’s foreign-trade logistics; resilient trade governance and diversification of markets and value chains; expanding trade through the Eurasian region; energy, infrastructure and technical and engineering services; and the use of technology, data and innovation to make foreign trade smarter.
The meeting should produce more than a discussion of existing problems, he said, adding that the specialist sessions were expected to identify priority obstacles, practical solutions, actionable proposals and measurable indicators of progress.
If international conditions have made trade more difficult, Iran should not further complicate production and exports through unstable decisions and cumbersome procedures, Niknami said.
Responding to difficult conditions requires sound policymaking, coordination and joint action, he added.
Niknami expressed hope that the meeting would help connect the country’s fragmented capabilities, simplify procedures, strengthen business confidence and increase private-sector participation in policymaking.
These efforts, he said, could improve Iran’s economic competitiveness, advance smart trade, support production and employment, and strengthen the reputation of Iranian brands in global markets.

Iran’s largest oil processing plant reaches 320,000 bpd capacity at South Azadegan field

Iran’s largest oil processing plant reaches 320,000 bpd capacity at South Azadegan field
TEHRAN (IRNA) — Iran’s South Azadegan oil processing center has reached its nominal capacity of 320,000 barrels per day following the completion and commissioning of all four processing trains, state-owned Petropars Group said.
Hamidreza Saghafi, head of Petropars Group, an implementing arm of the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC), said the facility was Iran’s largest oil processing center, with four trains designed to handle a combined 320,000 barrels per day.
The third processing train was commissioned on March 19, 2025, and reached stable production on May 14, 2025, Saghafi said. The fourth train was commissioned on Dec. 21, 2025, and reached stable production on Dec. 25, he added.
Construction of the first and second trains began moving towards completion in February 2026 and continued despite wartime conditions. Pre-commissioning and commissioning activities also began, enabling the trains to receive crude oil for processing, Saghafi said.
Following authorization for a four-day production shutdown, the control and safety systems of the first two trains were integrated with those of the third and fourth trains. After approval was granted to introduce crude oil into the first two trains, the facility achieved its 320,000-bpd processing capacity on Oct. 11, 2026, he said.
Saghafi said the center was a key infrastructure project for the development of West Karoun, an oil-producing region in southwestern Iran. The facility is expected to play an important role in transporting, processing and stabilizing crude oil from the area and could help support higher output from other fields in West Karoun.
Overall project progress has exceeded 80%, he said.
On associated gas, Saghafi said completion of the relevant units would enable the facility to send 200 million standard cubic feet of gas per day to the NGL 3200 gas processing plant.
He credited the achievement to the efforts of project specialists and workers, as well as cooperation between the project owner and contractors.
