U.S. Army fields AZAK robotic wheel system in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:20:28 UTC
20:20:28 KST

- U.S. Army soldiers from the 2nd Cavalry Regiment used an AZAK S26 unmanned ground vehicle to evacuate a casualty during training at Grafenwoehr, Germany, on Oct. 21.
- The regiment received the first three of 26 AZAK vehicles through the U.S. Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate.
U.S. Army soldiers in Germany are training with AZAK’s S26 unmanned ground vehicle. On Oct. 21, troops from 2nd Squadron, 2nd Cavalry Regiment used the robot to evacuate a casualty during a platoon situational training exercise at Grafenwoehr Training Area, the first field use of the system by the Vilseck-based regiment since it began receiving the vehicles.
The regiment took delivery of the first three of 26 AZAK vehicles last week through the U.S. Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, a hub set up to get new technology to soldiers quickly, AZAK CEO Ben Meager told Stars and Stripes. The deal follows the Other Transaction Agreement that AZAK signed with the directorate after soldiers tested the system, and the company says the 2nd Cavalry Regiment is the first unit in the U.S. military to receive a wide-scale rollout of the vehicle.
During the exercise, soldiers from Eagle Troop’s 1st Platoon fought an entrenched opposition force atop a hill, cleared an enemy trench using paint rounds and evacuated a simulated casualty minutes before a counterattack. A medic prepared the soldier in the trench, the platoon strapped him onto the vehicle’s flat board, and Sgt. Egan McDermott walked behind the robot with a handheld controller as it carried him to the rear.
“It feels like a ‘Call of Duty’ game, like a future warfare type thing, but it’s happening right now in real life,” said Sgt. Justin Whitlock, Eagle Troop’s senior medic.
Whitlock said platforms like the S26 ease the strain on soldiers by sparing them from carrying stretchers or boxes of ammunition over rough terrain. McDermott, a mortarman from 2nd Squadron, had used the same vehicle the night before to haul a 60 mm mortar system, a Bangalore torpedo and other heavy weapons, covering 8 km (5 miles) of rough ground with a full combat load in just over an hour while wearing night vision.
The Denver-based company builds its vehicles around the S26 wheel, which it first showed publicly at DSEI 2025. Each wheel contains the full drive system of an electric vehicle, including the motor, motor controller, brakes and battery, so the company can scale a vehicle’s power by adding wheels instead of redesigning a drivetrain. In the configuration the 2nd Cavalry Regiment is using, known as the Stoat, four wheels lock onto a small frame topped with a board that can hold a stretcher, ammunition or a mortar tube. The wheels can be swapped out by unlatching two buckles and keep the vehicle moving even if two of them are badly damaged or punctured, McDermott said.
Meager said the Stoat can carry well over 230 kg (500 pounds) over a range of 32 to 97 km (20 to 60 miles), depending on load and terrain, and can be driven remotely or run autonomously. The same wheels can be fitted to other equipment, from weapons to communications systems, and the vehicle can also carry and launch drones, he said. Earlier this year, the company showed a 227 kg (500-pound) version of the robot towing a 24,040 kg (53,000-pound) Palletized Load System truck.
“It’s really kind of cool to see how much Army tech can develop and evolve,” said McDermott.
The U.S. Army evaluated the platform through 2025 at events including the xTechOverwatch competition and a rotation at the National Training Center, where soldiers put the wheel-centric design over rough terrain, and AZAK brought a second-generation version to the AUSA Global Force Symposium in Huntsville, Alabama, in March.
Ground robots have become a regular part of casualty evacuation in Ukraine, where troops increasingly use them to pull wounded soldiers off the front line, and this week the Ukrainian military said it had evacuated a wounded soldier by aerial drone for the first time.
With three vehicles delivered, the 2nd Cavalry Regiment has 23 more S26 Stoats to receive.

Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:16:08 UTC
20:16:08 KST

Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- Weizmann Institute of Science
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that switching off a protein called Mitch makes human cells burn more fat and prevents new fat cells from developing. The breakthrough builds on experiments in mice that showed remarkable resistance to obesity and improved muscular endurance, raising hopes for a new approach to weight-loss treatment.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a remarkable protein switch that influences whether cells burn fat or store it. Disabling this protein increases fat consumption and interferes with the formation of new fat cells, raising the possibility of a different approach to treating obesity. Subsequent research has strengthened the discovery, revealing that the same protein helps regulate how much energy the body burns.
What if one of the keys to fighting obesity lies not in suppressing appetite, but in changing how the body's cells use energy?
Researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science have identified a protein called MTCH2, nicknamed "Mitch," that plays an important role in controlling metabolism. When scientists disabled this protein in laboratory experiments, cells began consuming more fuel, including fats and carbohydrates. They also found that removing Mitch could interfere with the process through which immature cells develop into fat cells.
The discovery builds on earlier experiments in mice, in which switching off Mitch in muscle tissue increased energy expenditure, improved endurance, and protected the animals from diet-related obesity.
The findings, published in The EMBO Journal in January 2025, suggest that manipulating this protein could eventually offer a way to influence both fat burning and fat accumulation. Additional research published later that year has provided further evidence of its importance in regulating body fat and metabolism.
Why Scientists Are Searching for Better Obesity Treatments
Over the past decade, medications designed to promote weight loss have transformed obesity treatment. Drugs such as semaglutide and tirzepatide have helped many patients achieve substantial reductions in body weight, largely by influencing appetite and the body's responses to food.
But losing weight does not necessarily mean losing only fat.
Weight reduction can also involve a decline in lean body mass, which includes muscle and other tissues. Preserving muscle is especially important because it supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.
A 2026 analysis of 20 clinical trials involving 15,782 participants found that lean mass accounted for approximately 25% to 39% of the weight lost with several widely used weight-loss medications. Importantly, the researchers found that comparable proportional losses also occurred with lifestyle interventions, while adding resistance training helped preserve more lean tissue.
These concerns have encouraged scientists to investigate ways to reduce body fat while protecting the muscles needed for long-term health.
Professor Atan Gross and his colleagues at the Weizmann Institute arrived at a possible avenue through an unexpected discovery involving Mitch.
Switching Off One Protein Protected Mice From Obesity
In earlier experiments, Gross's team reduced the activity of MTCH2 in the muscles of mice. The effects were striking.
The genetically modified animals showed increased metabolic activity and were resistant to obesity caused by their diet. Their muscles also developed more fibers with a high capacity for using oxygen, helping improve physical endurance.
The mice performed better in exercise and stress tests and showed improvements in heart function. In addition to resisting excess fat accumulation, they experienced favorable changes in their overall body composition.
The results suggested that Mitch was doing much more than controlling a single metabolic reaction. Somehow, this protein appeared to influence the body's ability to use energy, store fat, and sustain physical activity.
That raised an intriguing question: How could disabling one protein produce such widespread effects?
To investigate, the researchers turned their attention to mitochondria, the microscopic structures responsible for supplying much of the energy that cells need to function.
The Mitochondria Connection Behind Fat Burning
Mitochondria are frequently described as the powerhouses of cells because they convert energy from food into a usable form called ATP, or adenosine triphosphate.
ATP acts as a cellular energy currency. Muscles use it to contract, cells need it to grow and repair themselves, and countless biological processes depend on a steady supply.
However, mitochondria are not static structures. They constantly change shape, joining together into larger networks or separating into smaller units.
When mitochondria fuse, they can form interconnected systems that help coordinate energy production. When they divide, the resulting structures may operate differently, altering how efficiently cells produce and consume energy.
Gross's team had previously established that Mitch plays a major role in mitochondrial fusion, the process that allows separate mitochondria to merge.
Without this protein, the mitochondrial network becomes fragmented. Although the cells can still generate energy, they experience changes in energy efficiency and demand that can force them to consume more fuel.
This offered a possible explanation for the unusual metabolism observed in the mice. Instead of conserving energy efficiently, their cells appeared to be operating in a more energy-intensive state.
But would disabling Mitch have a similar effect in human cells?
Human Cells Begin Burning More Fat Without Mitch
To answer that question, researchers led by doctoral student Sabita Chourasia used genetic engineering to remove MTCH2 from human cells grown in the laboratory.
The change disrupted the normal structure of their mitochondrial networks. Individual mitochondria became more separated, and the balance between energy production and energy demand shifted.
The cells developed a persistent shortage of readily available energy relative to their needs, even as their mitochondria increased their oxygen-consuming activity.
To compensate, they began consuming more nutrients.
"After deleting Mitch, we examined, every few hours, the effect that had on more than 100 substances taking part in metabolism in human cells," Chourasia explains. "We saw an increase in cellular respiration, the process in which the cell produces energy from nutrients, such as carbohydrates and fats, using oxygen. This explains the increase in muscular endurance in previous experiments using mice."
Cellular respiration is the series of chemical reactions that allows cells to extract usable energy from nutrients. Increasing this activity generally requires a greater supply of fuel.
The researchers found that cells lacking Mitch consumed more fats, carbohydrates, and amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.
Fat metabolism was particularly revealing.
Rather than relying on their usual mix of energy sources, the altered cells increased their use of fatty acids for fuel. This indicated that MTCH2 influences not only how much energy cells consume, but also which nutrients they use to meet that demand.
"We discovered that deleting Mitch led to a major drop in fats in membranes," Gross explains. "At the same time, we saw an increase in fatty substances used to produce energy, and we realized that the fat was being broken down from the membrane to be used as fuel. In other words, we showed that Mitch determines the fate of fat in human cells."
Cell membranes are thin, flexible barriers made largely from fatty molecules called lipids. They protect cells and organize many of their essential functions.
The findings suggested that cells deprived of Mitch were changing how they distributed and used these lipids, drawing on some of their available fatty resources to support increased energy consumption.
Detailed analysis also revealed changes in stored lipids, demonstrating that the effect was more complex than simply eliminating cellular fat. Overall, the results showed that MTCH2 is a powerful regulator of how cells allocate nutrients between energy production and other biological needs.
Blocking the Formation of New Fat Cells
The researchers then investigated whether Mitch also influences how fat cells develop.
This question was particularly interesting because previous studies had found elevated MTCH2 levels in fat tissue from women with obesity.
Fat cells, also known as adipocytes, do not appear fully formed. They develop from immature precursor cells through a process called adipogenesis, or fat cell differentiation.
As these precursor cells mature, they must build new cellular structures, produce fats, and activate genes that allow them to specialize in storing energy.
All of this requires considerable energy and raw materials.
Gross's team suspected that removing Mitch might disrupt the process by creating an environment in which cells were too busy consuming fuel to build the components needed for fat storage.
Experiments using mouse precursor fat cells supported this idea. When the researchers deleted MTCH2, far fewer cells successfully developed into mature fat cells.
In the published experiments, approximately 80% to 90% of normal precursor cells differentiated within six days, compared with only 5% to 10% of cells lacking MTCH2. The altered cells also accumulated substantially fewer lipid droplets, the structures used to store fat.
"When we deleted Mitch from the progenitor cells, we discovered that the environment created in these cells was not conducive to the synthesis of new fats," Gross explains. "Reducing the ability to synthesize membranes prevents the cells from growing, developing and reaching the point where differentiation is possible. The process of fat accumulation requires a large amount of available energy, but in cells without Mitch, there is a shortage of energy. In addition, the expression of genes necessary for differentiation is suppressed, and there is a shortage of the substances vital for this process to occur. As a result, differentiation of new fat cells is reduced, along with fat accumulation."
In other words, disabling Mitch appeared to affect fat metabolism in two distinct ways. It increased the consumption of energy-rich nutrients and interfered with the cellular machinery needed to develop new fat-storing cells.
Importantly, the fat cell differentiation experiments used a mouse-derived cell line, while the detailed analysis of nutrient consumption was conducted in human cells. The combined results suggest a broader role for the protein, but they do not establish that blocking MTCH2 would prevent new fat cells from forming in people.
Follow-Up Research Reveals Another Fat-Burning Mechanism
The importance of MTCH2 became even clearer in research published on October 3, 2025, in Nature Communications.
An international research team, which included Gross and Chourasia, investigated how MTCH2 influences metabolism in fat tissue. By analyzing human and mouse fat samples, studying cultured fat cells, and conducting experiments in genetically modified mice, the scientists identified another mechanism linking this protein to energy expenditure.
They found that MTCH2 helps regulate the movement of fatty acids into mitochondria, where these molecules can be broken down to produce energy.
The process involves an enzyme called carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1, or CPT1. This enzyme acts as an important checkpoint, helping determine how much fat can enter mitochondria for use as fuel.
Normally, CPT1 activity is regulated by a molecule called malonyl-CoA, which signals when cells should limit fatty acid consumption.
The researchers discovered that MTCH2 physically interacts with CPT1 and influences how strongly this regulatory signal affects the enzyme.
Removing MTCH2 altered that control system, allowing mitochondria to increase fatty acid utilization and energy expenditure.
This provided a more detailed molecular explanation for why disabling the protein could encourage cells to burn additional fat.
Mice Burned More Energy Without Eating Less
The follow-up study also produced an especially promising result.
When researchers removed MTCH2 specifically from the fat cells of mice, the animals burned more energy without increasing their physical activity or changing how much food they consumed.
Under a regular diet, the genetically modified mice gained weight at a rate similar to that of normal mice.
However, when the animals were fed a high-fat diet, a difference emerged.
Mice lacking MTCH2 in their fat tissue gained less weight and accumulated less body fat than untreated mice, despite consuming similar amounts of food.
Their lean body mass remained comparable to that of the control animals.
The genetically modified mice also demonstrated improved glucose tolerance, indicating that their bodies were better able to manage blood sugar after receiving glucose. In addition, their cholesterol levels were lower.
These findings strengthened the evidence that MTCH2 influences whole-body metabolism, rather than simply changing the behavior of isolated cells.
The scientists also found that its metabolic effects could occur independently of UCP1, a protein commonly associated with heat production in brown fat. Brown fat is a specialized form of body fat that helps generate heat by burning energy, whereas white fat primarily stores excess energy.
Discovering an additional pathway for increasing energy expenditure could be important because it offers researchers another potential target for treating obesity and related metabolic disorders.
Could This Protein Lead to Better Weight-Loss Treatments?
Together, the findings suggest that MTCH2 may be an important molecular switch linking fat storage, energy consumption, and the development of fat cells.
The original experiments showed that removing the protein could increase nutrient consumption in human cells and interfere with fat cell formation in mouse cells. The later research demonstrated that selectively removing MTCH2 from fat tissue could increase energy expenditure and protect mice against excessive weight gain on a high-fat diet.
That combination raises the possibility of developing treatments that change how the body handles energy, potentially complementing medications that primarily work by reducing appetite.
However, several major questions remain unanswered.
Scientists have not yet demonstrated that inhibiting MTCH2 produces safe, sustained weight loss in humans. The protein also participates in other important biological activities, including mitochondrial regulation and pathways involved in cell survival. Blocking it throughout the body could therefore produce unwanted consequences.
Preventing fat cells from forming is not necessarily beneficial in every situation, either. Healthy fat tissue plays an essential role in storing excess energy, maintaining blood sugar balance, and producing hormones. Disrupting its function could potentially redirect fats into organs where they may cause harm.
Researchers will need to determine whether MTCH2 can be targeted safely, which tissues would benefit most, and whether reducing its activity would preserve muscle health while promoting fat loss.
For now, established strategies such as resistance exercise and adequate protein intake remain important for protecting muscle during weight reduction. A 2026 review of clinical trials found that combining lifestyle changes with resistance training produced a more favorable pattern of lean mass preservation than weight-loss interventions without such exercise.
The research nevertheless points toward a compelling possibility: Rather than focusing exclusively on how much food the body takes in, future obesity treatments might also influence how cells decide whether to burn energy or store it.
And one protein, Mitch, appears to be deeply involved in that decision.
Research Team and Publication Details
The original study, titled "MTCH2 controls energy demand and expenditure to fuel anabolism during adipogenesis," was published in The EMBO Journal on January 3, 2025.
The research was led by Sabita Chourasia and Professor Atan Gross at the Weizmann Institute of Science.
Additional contributors included Dr. Christopher Petucci, Clarissa Shoffler, and Dina Abbasian from the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia; Hu Wang and Professor Xianlin Han from the University of Texas at San Antonio; Dr. Ehud Sivan, Dr. Alexander Brandis, Tevie Mehlman, Dr. Sergey Malitsky, Dr. Maxim Itkin, Dr. Ayala Sharp, Dr. Ron Rotkopf, and Dr. Bareket Dassa from Weizmann's Life Sciences Core Facilities Department; and Dr. Limor Regev and Dr. Yehudit Zaltsman from Weizmann's Immunology and Regenerative Biology Department.
The follow-up study, "MTCH2 modulates CPT1 activity to regulate lipid metabolism of adipocytes," was published in Nature Communications on October 3, 2025. It involved an international collaboration, including researchers affiliated with ETH Zurich, Weizmann Institute of Science, and other institutions.

Turkish long-endurance drone tests anti-submarine task at sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:11:21 UTC
20:11:21 KST

- Turkish Aerospace’s Aksungur drone completed its mission with Aselsan’s aselBUOY 100P sonobuoy system during the Turkish Naval Forces’ TURNAs-2026 exercise.
- The exercise in the Gulf of Antalya and eastern Mediterranean involves 18 ships, 11 aircraft and 25 unmanned air, surface and underwater vehicles.
Turkish Aerospace’s Aksungur long-endurance drone has completed its mission with Aselsan’s aselBUOY 100P underwater acoustic listening system during the Turkish Naval Forces’ TURNAs-2026 unmanned maritime systems exercise, the company announced on X on Oct. 24, adding a new capability to the drone’s set of maritime missions.
“With this integration, which offers an important capability for collecting underwater acoustic data and supporting anti-submarine warfare missions, AKSUNGUR takes its multi-role mission capabilities in naval operations one step further,” Turkish Aerospace said.
Sonobuoys are small expendable listening devices that are dropped into the sea, pick up underwater sounds such as a submarine’s engine or propeller noise, and radio that data back to an aircraft or ship, a job long handled by crewed maritime patrol aircraft. Pairing them with a drone that can stay airborne for days lets a navy keep watch over wide areas of sea with an unmanned platform.
TURNAs-2026 began this week in the Gulf of Antalya and the eastern Mediterranean, Anadolu Agency reported, citing Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defense. The drill brings together 18 ships, 11 aircraft, nine unmanned aerial vehicles, seven unmanned underwater vehicles and nine unmanned surface vessels, along with 41 systems from 17 Turkish defense companies, and involves frigates, corvettes, a submarine, a mine hunter, a maritime patrol aircraft and SH-70 helicopters.
The aselBUOY 100P is a NATO A-size passive directional sonobuoy that weighs 10 kg (22 pounds), listens at depths of either 30 m (98 feet) or 150 m (492 feet), and can transmit data over a range of up to 20 km (12 miles) before scuttling itself at the end of its programmed operating time of up to eight hours. Aselsan began developing the sonobuoy as a self-financed project in late 2015 and conducted its first air-launch tests from a Cessna turboprop in 2018.
Aselsan CEO Ahmet Akyol told Naval News at the World Defense Show in Riyadh in February that the system had entered serial production after the company signed its first production contract with the Turkish Naval Forces Command, and that Aselsan would integrate its own launching pods on Turkish drones to deploy the sonobuoys. Akyol also said Aselsan was setting up an artificial intelligence center with the Turkish Naval Forces to train detection models on underwater acoustic data.
The Aksungur, built by Turkish Aerospace, also known by its Turkish acronym TUSAŞ, is a twin-engine medium-altitude, long-endurance drone with a 24 m (79-foot) wingspan, a payload capacity of more than 750 kg (1,650 pounds) and a ceiling of 40,000 feet (12,200 m). The company says it can stay airborne for more than 50 hours and is working toward roughly 60 hours of endurance and a 1,250 kg payload.
The Turkish Naval Forces received their first Aksungur in October 2021, and Turkish Aerospace has displayed the drone fitted with sonobuoy pods at defense shows since then. At NAVDEX 2023 in Abu Dhabi, company officials outlined a three-phase plan in which the drone would relay sonobuoy data to a ground station, process that data on board, and launch its own sonobuoys while sharing the results with other naval units, alongside work to arm the drone with a torpedo.
“With our national technologies, we are adding strength to our power at sea as well,” Turkish Aerospace said.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned Saturday that Russia was seeking to destabilize Germany through cyberattacks, sabotage and other threats, urging his struggling coalition to unite behind economic reforms and defend the country's security.
Speaking at a convention of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU), in Munich, Merz described the security situation in Europe as increasingly dangerous and called for a stronger response to threats from abroad and political extremism at home.
"We are facing a massive threat in the east of our continent. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has profoundly shaken the European peace order," Merz said.
"And we also see that Russia seeks to destabilize Germany, day in and day out," he added.
Merz said the threat extended beyond the war in Ukraine, pointing to cyberattacks, sabotage and attempted attacks against critical infrastructure across Europe. He cited an attempted drone attack involving a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport on Aug. 4 as an example of the risks facing Germany.
"This threat is no longer limited to Ukraine," Merz said, warning that such operations also sought to undermine democratic institutions and weaken public confidence.
"All of this threatens our freedom, and that is why we are investing in preserving our freedom," he added.
Russia has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is conducting a campaign of hybrid warfare against Germany and other European countries. Relations between Berlin and Moscow have deteriorated sharply since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Merz's warning followed remarks by Germany's foreign intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, who told parliament's intelligence committee on Oct. 5 that the confrontation with Russia had entered a more dangerous phase.
"Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia. The attempted attack in Leipzig is only one example of that," Jaeger said.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany," he added.
Merz's security warning came as his government faced mounting political pressure following poor regional election results and declining public approval.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) finished first in two eastern German states, while the far-left Left Party topped the vote in Berlin, highlighting the growing challenge facing the country's mainstream political parties.
Merz's approval ratings have fallen to record lows, while disagreements have intensified within the governing coalition and between the CDU and CSU. Although the two conservative parties have a long history of internal disputes, they have generally managed to maintain their alliance.
At the Munich convention, Merz praised CSU ministers serving in his government and paid tribute to CSU leader Markus Soeder in an effort to reinforce ties between the conservative partners.
He also reiterated his opposition to cooperating with the AfD, which leads national opinion polls. Some conservatives have called for a reassessment of the party's political isolation, but Merz insisted that working with the far right was incompatible with membership in the conservative alliance.
"Any politician who votes with the AfD has no place in our Union," he said.
Merz also urged the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens not to form a coalition with the Left Party in Berlin, accusing the party of tolerating antisemitism within its ranks. The Left Party denies that antisemitism is systemic within the organization.
The conference also exposed lingering disagreements over the succession to German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose term is due to end next year.
Delegates applauded when Merz mentioned Ilse Aigner, a CSU politician proposed by the Bavarian party as its candidate for the largely ceremonial presidency. The CDU has not endorsed Aigner, and party sources say it has not ruled out putting forward its own candidate.
Beyond security concerns, Merz urged his coalition partners to move quickly on reforms to Germany's pension, tax and welfare systems, arguing that economic recovery was essential to restoring confidence in public institutions.
He said the conservative parties had a responsibility to strengthen Germany's social stability by addressing structural economic problems and implementing reforms that could revive growth.
The government has faced growing criticism over its economic performance, adding to the political challenges confronting Merz as his coalition struggles to maintain public support.
His appeal for unity reflected the pressure on the chancellor to demonstrate that his government can respond to security threats while tackling domestic economic concerns and preventing further gains by extremist parties.

====================================================================================================

The Fight Over Who Counts in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

In A Fine Balance, one of the finest novels about modern India set in the 1960s and 1970s, Rohinton Mistry powerfully conveys a sense of the social meaning of the vote for the Indians at the bottom of the ladder. Narayan, a Dalit tailor, insists on marking his own ballot in an upcoming election instead of allowing an upper-caste landlord’s men to vote on his behalf.
Dukhi, his father, warns him against it. “It is still my right,” Narayan replies. “And I will exercise it in the next election, I promise you.”
Dukhi urges him not to risk his life.
“Life without dignity is worthless,” Narayan replies.
I have been rereading Mistry’s novel over the past few weeks as a series of protests has turned October into a month of fierce battles over the integrity of India’s elections, the accountability of its institutions, the right to protest, and the soul of its democracy.
A nascent Gen-Z movement, Cockroach Janta Party, which organized protests over education and unemployment in Delhi in June and July and forced the resignation of India’s higher education minister, gave the call for the October protests. Young protestors answered with an insurrectionary energy in the summer and soon found support from a broader coalition comprised of opposition parties, social movements and other pillars of Indian civil society.
These assorted protesters see the stakes of the current moment as existential: the sanctity of the vote in India, the essential ingredient, in other words, of democracy. Throughout October thousands joined the cause in Delhi and other Indian cities, their marches spurred by anger directed against an ongoing national exercise to overhaul the country’s electoral register.
Known as the Special Intensive Revision, the exercise has, according to the protestors, resulted in more than 130 million voters being removed from electoral lists. Although electoral rolls have been revised periodically, this is the first time such an exercise has placed the burden on citizens to establish their eligibility, raising fears that millions of legitimate voters, particularly the poor and marginalized, could be disenfranchised.
Seeking accountability, they have been calling for the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the country’s chief election commissioner, who oversees the Election Commission of India, the body charged with conducting and safeguarding the sanctity of elections across the nation. The protestors accuse Kumar of abandoning his constitutional obligation to act impartially. In their telling, the mandarin has set the table in a way to favor the interests of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party, a charge denied by those in power.
Already shaken by the summer protests over education, this time the Indian government responded with coercive force, effectively turning central Delhi, the political and administrative heart of the capital, and the place where India goes to protest, into a garrison. On Oct. 10, it deployed tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel, restricted internet access, detained thousands of protesters, and sought to deny the protesters access to public spaces across the capital.
The crackdown was intense. On the night of Oct. 16, there was a palpable sense of panic on social media in India as an urgent question was asked repeatedly: Where is Neha Bora? A 29-year-old doctoral student and left-wing activist, Bora has emerged as one of the most articulate and formidable leaders of these protests, which have rattled Modi’s government and—despite valiant attempts to construct a counter narrative by BJP leaders and other party apparatchiks—become a significant challenge to his popularity and legitimacy.
Bora was detained by the police on their way to join the thousands of protesters who had converged on Connaught Place, a prominent commercial district in the capital, waving the national flag and reiterating demands to protect the right to vote and the sanctity of electoral democracy in India. For several hours after sunset, there was no news of the whereabouts of Bora, who uses they/them pronouns. Their lawyers spoke about the police refusing to reveal their location. Eventually, around midnight, their lawyers located them at a police station.
When Bora was released on Saturday morning, they tweeted, “Fighting for democracy and the Constitution cannot be criminalized.” It was a neat summation of the sentiment moving so many Indians to take to the streets, namely a sense of being robbed of something of existential proportions. “Now if they take away our right to vote,” a protester told a reporter, “what is left with us?”
The power of the vote
The emotional charge behind the protests has its roots in the birth of the modern Indian nation-state itself. India always took great pride in adopting universal franchise rights as the Constitution of India came into effect on Jan. 26, 1950. In its historic first general elections in 1952, every Indian above the age of 21, irrespective of caste, religion, gender, race or wealth, had their constitutionally guaranteed right to vote. It was, as many legal and constitutional scholars have since remarked, a colossal feat, and one that became a touchstone for the modern idea of India.
Hence the current upheaval in the country. The Modi government may be reversing decades of democratic gains by recasting the act of voting as a privilege, conferred at the discretion of bureaucrats or as a favor from the ruling party, rather than a right guaranteed by the constitutional order. Now, every prospective voter must first complete an enumeration form, and many may subsequently be required to produce onerous documentary evidence, such as birth certificates and educational records to establish their eligibility to vote. Tens of millions of Indians from marginalized communities either lack documentary records or possess documents that are riddled with mistakes such as spelling errors, making it harder for them to navigate any process of bureaucratic verification.
The fear is that India is—to put it bluntly—being yanked back to a darker time, one from which it emerged in no small part because of the work done over decades to firmly establish the credibility and broaden the depth of its democratic franchise. In the 1950s, India was an overwhelmingly rural country, with around 83% of its population living in the villages and only about 17% in urban areas. Its nascent democratic system confronted entrenched social hierarchies of caste and power. Early accounts of grassroots democracy in India describe how higher-caste landowners controlled the votes of their lower-caste dependents, sometimes even marking ballots that the voters had to authenticate with their thumbprints.
The pioneering Indian sociologist M.N. Srinivas showed how politicians campaigning for votes treated villagers not as individual voters with agency but as members of “vote banks.” Politicians approached landlords or community leaders to deliver these blocs of votes in return for favors from the government, from “licenses for buses and rice-mills to seats in medical and technological colleges for their kinsfolk.”
And well into the 1960s, millions of Indians were still unable to exercise their constitutional right to vote. In the eastern Indian state of Bihar, landlords used club-wielding enforcers known as lathaits to keep Dalits, members of the most oppressed caste, out of polling booths. “I remember watching members of my caste being dragged out of a polling booth,” an elderly Dalit man in Bihar’s Siwan district recalled in an interview with The Print, an Indian news site.
During the state elections in 1967, Jagdish Master, a teacher turned activist, challenged the veto of the landlords over Dalit suffrage by escorting a group of Dalits to a polling booth in Ekwari, a village in Bihar’s Bhojpur district. The landlords’ henchmen brutally beat him and drove him out. He returned to the village as an armed guerrilla, recruiting Dalit laborers and other poor peasants in a Maoist-style rural insurgency that would flare across the region for decades.
The power of the vote in Indian consciousness transformed radically after the “Emergency,” the period between June 1975 and March 1977 when Prime Minister Indira Gandhi suspended constitutional rights, assumed untrammeled powers, imprisoned opposition leaders and silenced the press. Much of India’s elite—bureaucrats, businessmen, newspaper editors and movie stars—bent the knee and welcomed Mrs. Gandhi’s promise of “order” and “discipline.” Wealth and connections offered protection from the state. India’s poor, stripped of their electoral power, suffered terrible abuses of an unaccountable bureaucracy and police from slum demolitions to forced sterilization of men.
In the general elections held in March 1977 after the end of the Emergency, Mrs. Gandhi’s Congress Party was decisively defeated by the people and tossed out of power for the first time since Indian independence in 1947. The principal victims of abuses of the Emergency—Dalits, Muslims, and the poor of the populous northern Indian states—voted against the Congress party for the first time and contributed significantly to its removal from power
The power of the vote has gradually forced India’s high-handed bureaucracy to recognize the human dignity and political citizenship of ordinary people. The electorate delivered its verdict on Mrs. Gandhi’s breach of the sacred covenant between the Indian state and its people: the people confer legitimacy on the state in exchange for their rights, including its protection of the sanctity of the vote. Having asserted their power, voters proved difficult to subdue again. As the political theorist Partha Chatterjee put it, it was the 1977 defeat of Mrs. Gandhi and the Congress party that established the “capacity of the vote.”
A silent revolution
India’s poor and marginalized took proper control of their voting choices three decades after independence. In the years after the Emergency, they leveraged the vote as a means to a secure livelihood or as a tool for ensuring justice. Politicians could no longer rely on local patrons to intimidate people into voting for them and had to compete on representing their interests. A new competitive politics emerged in the 1980s and led to an upsurge, as Chatterjee wrote, “of popular demands of a kind that had never before been allowed to disturb the order and tranquility of the proverbial corridors of power.”
By the 1990s, political leaders from socially disenfranchised castes and Dalit communities were taking power in the populous, northern Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot memorably described it as “the silent revolution.” This revolution, ushered in by the votes of the historically oppressed communities, did not quite transform the economic and social structures of the region. But it changed the everyday relations of power. Indrajit Roy, a scholar of development studies, recalled a refrain he heard frequently during his fieldwork among Dalits in Bihar in the late 2000s: “There has been development, change has come. Today, we can look the landlord in the eye and speak as equals.”
Vote banks had thus turned into vehicles of collective political assertion. Marginalized communities had become adept at pooling their votes to secure political favors and advance their shared interests. They chose their own patrons, preferring their own caste leaders to represent their interests and negotiate with the state on their behalf.
Over time, the clientelist politics of vote banks became associated with an entrenched culture of corruption. This helped pave the way for Modi’s successful national campaign in 2014, in which he cast himself as a populist strongman who embodied the aspirations for “development” of all Indians while portraying the Congress and regional parties as beholden to their respective vote banks. Modi’s attacks on vote bank politics also carried a more sinister charge: that successive governments had appeased India’s Muslims minority, which accounts for around 14% of the population, for their votes at the expense of the national interest.
Bangladesh borders the Indian state of West Bengal and Modi reserved his sharpest, xenophobic barbs for Bengal’s Muslims, whom he tarred during his 2014 campaign as “Bangladeshi” and “illegal immigrants,” establishing a template for their vilification that persists to this day. In an inflammatory campaign speech, Modi issued an ominous warning: “After May 16 [the day of the results of the 2014 elections], these Bangladeshis better be prepared with their bags packed.”
A dangerous exclusion
The Modi government invoked that very specter of the “illegal, Bangladeshi Muslim” to push through revisions to electoral rolls across most Indian states. India’s home minister, Amit Shah, who had earlier likened Bangladeshi immigrants to “termites,” responded to the ongoing protests by calling them an “action plan to protect infiltrators.”
There are no reliable estimates of how many Bangladeshi immigrants live in India. In 2016, a minister of the Modi government told the parliament, without citing a source, that the country was home to some 20 million “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh.” The government later acknowledged that it had no accurate data on the number of illegal immigrants in India.
Yet the Indian government has used unfounded speculation about “illegal” Bangladeshis to overturn the fundamental logic of the country’s electoral registration system, shifting the burden of ensuring registration from the Election Commission to the voter herself. The commission was responsible for ensuring that every citizen made it onto the electoral rolls.
The exercise has already disproportionately disenfranchised the poor, migrants, religious minorities, women—and is bound to continue doing so. “The majority of voters in Bihar who were excluded from the list were in rural areas,” said retired Maj. Gen. Anil Verma, who heads the Association for Democratic Reforms, a nonprofit group that challenged the electoral rolls revisions in the Supreme Court. “Those worst affected were the poor and the marginalized—they had no documents.”
Opposition parties have also alleged that the electoral roll revisions tilted the electoral field in the BJP’s favor in the West Bengal election held earlier this year, helping the party win power in the state for the first time. An analysis by the SABAR Institute, a public policy research institute, lent some credence to that charge: a disproportionate share of the 9.08 million voters removed from West Bengal’s electoral rolls came from constituencies held by the then-ruling Trinamool Congress or those with large Muslim populations.
The Election Commission has denied the charge that the deletions were politically motivated, arguing that it applied uniform criteria to remove entries for voters who had died, were registered more than once or had permanently relocated. But that claim is difficult to reconcile with the disproportionate representation of certain groups among those deleted from supplementary lists issued for some constituencies after an adjudication process. For instance, although Muslims make up around 23% of the population of Nandigram, a constituency in West Bengal, the SABAR Institute study found that they accounted for 95.5% of the deletions across seven supplementary lists released by the Election Commission for the constituency.
Voting carries an almost existential significance for Indians whose equal citizenship has not been fully recognized by the institutions of the state. Indians see the vote as an affirmation of their existence. If the vote is no longer a gift freely given or withdrawn by the people but a resource controlled by the state, it reduces ordinary voters once again to supplicants dependent on the favor of political elites.
The electoral revisions and mass deletion of voters have provoked such widespread revulsion because many Indians see it as an assault on their identity as citizens and a threat to the social recognition they have won through a long, arduous struggle. Many Indians might have forgiven Modi for his numerous missteps but they are determined not to let him devalue their voting power.
We that are young
The young protesters moving through Delhi’s barricaded streets carry a palpable sense that they are living through a historical moment. References to the Quit India movement against the country’s erstwhile British colonizers and the protests around the Emergency have become commonplace. Memories of seminal events of the past offer a lens through which to consider the present. The future seems open to change through collective action. This sense of a turning point imbues individual actions with a larger purpose and drives protesters to confront a police force intent on clearing the streets by whatever means necessary.
On Oct. 9, a day before Delhi was placed under a lockdown, Bora invoked India’s struggle against British imperialism to denounce the pre-emptive detention of protest organizers. “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop,” Bora said. “This is nothing but a state of open emergency in the country.”
The convergence of young people’s anger over education and employment, fears of authoritarianism, and concern for the sanctity of the vote poses a serious challenge to the Modi government. It could forge a broad popular coalition of unemployed young people, urban poor, Dalits and religious minorities, united in challenging the legitimacy of the government. Unless the government retreats on electoral roll revisions, sustained protests could drain its political capital.
One of Indian democracy’s great achievements is that even its poorest citizens have proved adept at recognizing when the power of their vote is being wrested away, gauging the consequences and organizing to resist. A government in India can retain its legitimacy despite failing to provide functioning schools or decent employment. It cannot do so if it also violates the sanctity of the vote.

Engine faults leave some of Poland’s K2 tanks in repair

11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

- About 30 of Poland’s more than 200 delivered K2 tanks are in military workshops with various faults, some of them engine-related, Radio ZET reported.
- Poland’s defense ministry said the K2’s failure rate is within normal standards and that the manufacturer handles repairs on tanks still under warranty.
About 30 of Poland’s South Korean-built K2 tanks are sitting in military workshops with various faults, most of them at the army base in Braniewo in the country’s northeast, Radio ZET reported, and some of the damage involves the engines of a fleet that has grown to more than 200 tanks delivered so far.
The figure came from the broadcaster’s investigative podcast “W związku ze śledztwem” and journalist Mariusz Gierszewski. When Radio ZET asked the Polish Ministry of National Defense whether roughly one in ten delivered tanks was under repair and how many engine seizures had been recorded, the ministry neither confirmed nor disputed the numbers and instead defended the tank’s overall reliability.
“The failure rate of the K2 tanks does not deviate from the standards adopted for this type of vehicle,” the ministry said.
Braniewo, near the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region, is home to the 9th Armored Cavalry Brigade, one of three Polish Land Forces combat units equipped with the K2GF, the version Poland bought off the shelf from South Korea. Concerns about the engines surfaced publicly earlier this year, when Polish military analyst Jarosław Wolski wrote on X that the tanks were suffering from overheating and engine failures.
“The Korean engines are falling apart like a Christmas tree on Epiphany. (…) What is especially worrying is the overheating of the engines and cases of complete seizure of the power units,” wrote Wolski.
The K2, built by Hyundai Rotem, is powered by a 1,500-horsepower HD Hyundai Infracore engine paired with a Renk HSWL 295 TM transmission. The tank weighs about 55 tonnes (61 short tons), carries a three-person crew and is armed with a 120 mm smoothbore gun fed by an autoloader.
Radio ZET also reported that only Korean technicians can work on the tanks, a claim the ministry’s answer narrowed. Tanks still under warranty, or covered by service campaigns, are repaired by the supplier, while Polish Armed Forces maintenance units take over routine repairs and scheduled servicing once the warranty ends, work that temporarily takes vehicles out of use.
“Temporary withdrawals from operation are a standard phenomenon affecting every type of platform,” the ministry said.
Poland’s Armament Agency, the military’s procurement body, gave a similar response to Polish outlet Defence24, saying the faults are being fixed together with the manufacturer under warranty and do not significantly limit the units that operate the tank.
“The K2GF tanks have the same level of faults, adequate to any other equipment being introduced into service with the Armed Forces,” said Col. Grzegorz Polak, spokesman for the Armament Agency. “The technical faults that occur are being fixed in cooperation with the contractor, as part of warranty repairs. Their frequency does not significantly affect the ability of the units equipped with K2GF tanks to carry out their tasks.”
Poland ordered the K2 under two executive contracts covering 360 tanks in total, plus more than 80 support vehicles. The first, signed in 2022 for 180 K2GF tanks and completed in 2025, equipped the 20th Mechanized Brigade in Bartoszyce, which received the first tanks in 2022, along with the 15th Mechanized Brigade in Giżycko and one of the Braniewo brigade’s tank battalions, which received about 58 tanks.
The second contract also requires production and maintenance capacity, including final assembly of the K2PL, to be set up at Zakłady Mechaniczne Bumar-Łabędy in Gliwice, and the ministry said it plans to hand selected repair work to other Polish defense companies. That transfer is still in progress, with the companies involved negotiating sublicense agreements with the Armament Agency and cooperation agreements with Hyundai Rotem while they begin adapting their plants and training staff.
Poland’s other main tank, the U.S.-built Abrams, has run into its own engine maintenance gap. The country ordered 366 Abrams tanks, whose AGT1500 gas turbine engines require depot-level work at certified aerospace facilities, a capability Poland did not have when the tanks arrived. Military Aviation Works No. 1 (WZL-1) in Dęblin signed an agreement with engine maker Honeywell in May to set up an authorized service center, which is scheduled to come online by 2028, and U.S. technical personnel in Poland support the fleet in the meantime.

The human voice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Our voices have superpowers. From a coach firing up a soccer team before a big game to a mother soothing a cranky baby in the middle of the night, the human voice is key to expressing feelings and forging connections. The tone of a person’s voice might even communicate feelings to loved ones better than facial expressions. So what happens to a person when their voice disappears?
People who have lost the ability to speak due to neurodegenerative disease or brain injury are talking again thanks to groundbreaking technologies that can decode the instructions the brain sends to speech muscles. For this issue’s cover story, senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders interviewed Casey Harrell, a man who regained his voice — lost to ALS — through a brain-computer interface.
You can listen to Harrell in his own words in Season Two of The Deep End, our award-winning podcast. Harrell told Sanders: “It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”
In the podcast, Sanders digs into other innovations, including AI voice cloning, as well as the sinister potential of such technology to hijack people’s voices. “It might be used in a way people don’t want to have happen,” she says. Hear more wherever you get your podcasts.
In this issue, we also report on the progress in developing an effective treatment for stiff person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disorder that makes the body’s muscles freeze without warning. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration hasn’t yet approved any treatments for the disorder, which occurs in roughly 2 in 100,000 people. But that could some day change. Researchers are testing new CAR T cell therapies, senior writer Meghan Rosen reports. The process involves modifying a patient’s white blood cells so they wipe out harmful immune cells. Scientists hope a single treatment could cure the disease.
And there’s more controversy about using AI in mathematics, senior physics writer Emily Conover reports. OpenAI made waves when the company announced that it had solved one of the most famous puzzles in math — a day after mathematicians reported advances on a similar problem. The development is among a flood of AI-fueled achievements this year and raises big questions about who gets credit when the algorithms are doing the work.

Russia secretly financed Alaska gas project

Russia secretly financed Alaska gas project
Almost the entire management team of the US$25 billion US gas project Polar Train LNG has left the company following allegations of undisclosed financing and control by Russia's Novatek.
Source: Financial Times
Details: The Financial Times reported that the company's former chief executive, Joel Riddle, raised concerns about potential violations of US sanctions.
Polar Train LNG is developing a gas export terminal in northern Alaska. The project was launched in March with a plan to use a partially constructed Novatek terminal and relocate it to Alaska. The company applied to the US Treasury Department for permission to negotiate with the Russian group but has yet to receive approval.
Riddle said he discovered that Novatek was already financing the project and directing its operations before the necessary approvals had been obtained. He resigned in September, after which chief financial officer Dan Chandra and other executives also left the company.
"I resigned as chief executive of Polar LNG because I felt uncomfortable that the Russian company Novatek was financing and ultimately controlling the strategic direction of the company," said Riddle.
He initially believed that the funding was being provided by Gentry Beach, an investor with ties to Donald Trump's family, and Abu Dhabi-based company Tech Wave. Riddle said he later discovered that Beach had not invested in the project and was neither a shareholder nor an executive.
The FT also reviewed WhatsApp messages in which Novatek board member Denis Solovyov discussed financing the project and sought to expedite the transfer of funds to Polar Train LNG.
Polar LNG said Riddle had been dismissed, described him as a "disgruntled employee" and stressed that it was developing the project in compliance with US law.
Novatek said it had agreed to grant Tech Wave the right to use its technology in Alaska and had signed a memorandum with Polar Train in April, when Riddle was still running the company.
According to people who spoke to the FT, the project had featured in talks between Washington and Moscow over business deals that could help bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. The discussions included a potential exchange under which Novatek would provide its expertise for the construction of the Alaska terminal in return for sanctions being lifted on Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project.
Background:
- In February 2026, Ekonomichna Pravda reported, citing The New York Times, that Gentry Beach, a university friend of Donald Trump Jr, had announced an agreement with Novatek on a gas project in Alaska.
- On 9 October, it was reported that Russia was demanding sanctions relief as part of negotiations over a possible "energy ceasefire" with Ukraine.

Azmi Bishara: Trump has backed Netanyahu as his Iran war partner
Unknown

2026-10-24

Breadcrumb
Azmi Bishara: Trump has backed Netanyahu as his Iran war partner
Dr. Azmi Bishara has said US President Donald Trump is backing Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel's election because the two are partners in the war with Iran and share a wider regional agenda.
Speaking to Al-Araby TV ahead of Israel's 27 October vote, the Arab thinker said Trump wanted Netanyahu to remain in power in order to "complete the mission" they had begun together.
He argued that there was little fundamental difference between Israel's main governing and opposition blocs on Palestinian statehood or the country's broader regional posture.
Bishara said much of the campaign instead revolved around security, the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 attacks, military conscription and who could project greater military strength.
Israel's election is currently too close to produce an obvious governing majority, with recent polling placing Netanyahu's bloc and Gadi Eisenkot's opposition coalition roughly level.
Arab turnout 'critical'
Bishara said Palestinian citizens of Israel nevertheless had a major stake in the election.
He argued that growing efforts to delegitimise Arab political participation made turnout particularly important and described the vote as a decisive moment for Palestinian citizens.
Bishara said higher participation could help block another government led by Netanyahu alongside far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
He suggested Eisenkot's Yashar party could finish first but still struggle to form a government without support from Arab parties.
That possibility has become central to the campaign, with Palestinian parties potentially holding the balance of power if neither bloc reaches the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority.
Bishara also said Washington favoured the idea of a unity government bringing Netanyahu and Eisenkot together, although he believed such an arrangement would be difficult to achieve.
Iran: settlement or renewed war
Turning to Iran, Bishara said the region was approaching a decisive point.
He argued that the present stand-off between Washington and Tehran could not continue indefinitely and would ultimately end either in a settlement or renewed war.
Bishara said Iran wanted tangible confidence-building measures, including access to frozen funds or sanctions relief, while Washington wanted concessions it could present domestically as a clear victory.
Qatar remains involved in mediation between the two sides, with Qatari and Pakistani mediators submitting a new proposal this week aimed at preventing renewed conflict.
Bishara said mistrust remained deep and warned that a failure by either side to make a meaningful move could push the region back towards conflict after the US midterms.
Yemen and US politics
On Yemen, Bishara said the Houthis could not govern the country alone, but equally could not be excluded from any future political settlement.
He said the best basis for resolving the conflict remained the outcomes of Yemen's national dialogue process.
The assessment comes as fighting has again intensified in Yemen between the Houthis and forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.
Bishara also turned to the US midterm elections on 3 November, saying he expected Republicans to lose their majority in the House of Representatives while the Senate remained less predictable.
Recent reporting has likewise found that Democrats are in a stronger position to retake the House, while control of the Senate remains more contested.
Bishara said a younger generation of progressive Democrats represented a deeper shift inside the party, highlighting New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
The midterms are also exposing growing divisions over Israel and the Iran war, with several closely watched Senate races turning on foreign policy as well as domestic economic concerns.
Bishara argued that the elections would test both Trump's domestic political strength and divisions within the American right over foreign policy, Israel and the Iran war.

19:51:09 KST

PARIS, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- International credit rating agency Moody's on Friday affirmed France's sovereign credit rating at Aa3 with a negative outlook.
Moody's said the Aa3 rating assumes France will adopt a 2027 budget aimed at reducing its fiscal deficit, with borrowing costs and social tensions easing somewhat in the coming months.
The decision came as markets had widely anticipated a downgrade that would have brought France's rating in line with the A+ ratings assigned by Fitch and S&P.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu welcomed the decision, saying the government aims to pass the 2027 budget by the end of this year and reduce the fiscal deficit to 5 percent of GDP.
France has faced mounting fiscal pressure in recent years. The government expects its fiscal deficit to reach 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026. Meanwhile, its public debt has also continued to rise. According to the national statistics institute INSEE, public debt stood at 119 percent of GDP at the end of the second quarter of 2026.
Moody's warned that substantial and sustained fiscal efforts would still be needed after the 2027 presidential election to improve public finances and stabilize debt.
Recently, large-scale protests over education, rising living costs and deteriorating public services erupted across the country.
With the 2027 presidential election approaching, political divisions and social tensions are posing further challenges to the government's efforts to bring public finances under control. ■

Roundup: Ebola's cross-border spread tests Africa's defenses as vaccine trial begins
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:51:09 CST
19:51:09 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Africa's fight against Ebola faces mounting challenges as the virus spreads across national borders, with the second death in Kenya and uncertainties over the source of Nigeria's first infection complicating containment efforts, even as a major vaccine trial launched Friday in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) offers fresh hope.
The latest developments in the disease's spread have heightened concerns over gaps in cross-border surveillance and regional preparedness, with Uganda tightening transit restrictions amid fears of further spread. Scientists, meanwhile, are racing to develop vaccines against the Bundibugyo virus as the DRC battles its deadliest Ebola outbreak on record.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the outbreak has now affected five countries, including four in Africa. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has previously described it as the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak ever recorded on the continent.
In the DRC, the outbreak has claimed 4,687 lives among 9,704 confirmed cases as of Oct. 20, spreading to eight of the country's 26 provinces.
KENYA REPORTS SECOND DEATH
Kenya's Ministry of Health announced late Friday that a 65-year-old woman receiving Ebola treatment had died, bringing the country's death toll to two among nine confirmed cases.
The woman, a close family member of the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, had been placed under quarantine before developing symptoms on Oct. 13. She was admitted to a treatment facility the same day but died Friday evening.
The first patient, who had traveled from the DRC through Uganda, died in Nairobi on Oct. 5.
All eight subsequent infections have been linked to the initial case, including four family members and four healthcare workers. The seven surviving patients remain under treatment at two isolation facilities.
Kenyan authorities said there was "no evidence of community transmission" beyond the identified cluster, while the WHO reported Friday that all 135 contacts of the initial patient had been traced and quarantined.
NIGERIA CASE RAISES QUESTIONS OVER INFECTION SOURCE
In Nigeria, new genomic findings have suggested a close link between the viruses detected in the country's first Ebola patient and Kenya's initial case, as conflicting accounts of the patient's travel history complicate efforts to trace the source of infection.
Nigerian Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Muhammad Ali Pate said Friday that genomic sequencing showed the virus detected in the country's only confirmed Ebola case was "highly similar" to that found in Kenya's first imported case, "differing by just one mutation."
The Nigeria case was confirmed in Abuja, the capital, on Oct. 20. According to the WHO, the patient arrived in Nigeria on Oct. 3, developed symptoms four days later and tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus on Oct. 20.
According to Swiss media reports citing Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, the patient is a Swiss national married to a staff member of the Swiss Embassy in Abuja. Official sources said neither the woman nor her husband, who is in isolation, had traveled to the DRC, contradicting an earlier account by Ugandan authorities.
The Ugandan Health Ministry said Friday the patient had shown no symptoms when departing from the country, adding that investigations were continuing to establish when her symptoms began and where she might have been exposed.
According to the WHO, Nigeria had identified 44 contacts as of Oct. 20 and intensified surveillance and infection prevention measures. Nigeria's health authorities said the patient was showing signs of recovery, with no evidence of community transmission.
UGANDA TIGHTENS TRAVEL RESTRICTIONS
On Friday, Uganda announced additional precautionary measures, including restrictions on travelers with a history of travel to the DRC.
In a statement, the Ugandan Health Ministry said such travelers would no longer be permitted to transit through the country.
Authorities also reinstated traveler locator forms for all passengers, reinforced infection prevention measures at entry and exit points and health facilities, and strengthened nationwide surveillance.
The ministry stressed that Uganda remains free of Ebola.
Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths, before the end of the outbreak was officially recognized by the WHO and Africa CDC on Aug. 27, after 42 consecutive days without a new confirmed case.
The WHO, meanwhile, reiterated Friday that it does not recommend travel or trade restrictions on affected countries, calling instead for stronger surveillance, timely case detection and coordinated cross-border preparedness.
VACCINE TRIAL OFFERS HOPE
As countries stepped up efforts to prevent further spread, a major clinical trial evaluating vaccines against the Bundibugyo virus began Friday in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's hardest-hit Ituri province.
The Phase 2/3 trial was launched with the vaccination of its first participant.
Despite the scale of the ongoing epidemic, no vaccine has been approved specifically against the Bundibugyo virus.
The trial will assess the safety, immune responses and effectiveness of several vaccine candidates, using an adaptive platform design that allows multiple vaccines to be evaluated within a single study.
The WHO said the trial is a critical step toward establishing whether candidate vaccines could effectively protect people against the virus.
The agency has warned that Ebola infections in the DRC had rebounded after a brief decline, with the latest seven-day moving average suggesting "renewed intensification of transmission."
It said that escalating insecurity, population displacement and restricted humanitarian access were further complicating response operations and increasing the risk of undetected transmission. ■

9 Unique Apps to Try on the iPhone Duo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Despite seven years of Android folding phones, Apple's iPhone Duo launch has spurred developers to create quirky, weird, and fun apps that experiment with the folding design (leaving Android owners feeling like second-class citizens yet again).
I've reviewed almost every folding phone in the past decade, and my inbox has never seen this many app pitches from indie developers wanting to show off their app for Apple's first foldable.
Some of these apps aren't necessarily new but use the phone's hinge to offer fresh experiences. You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store. From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset.
Battlefleet Duo
Board games will have a field day on the iPhone Duo, and Battlefleet Duo is the best example. On the larger 7.6-inch screen, you get a sprawling canvas, but in tabletop mode, you can view your ships on the bottom screen and the enemy's fleet above. That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships. You can play two free battles every day, or unlock unlimited battles with a one-time $5 purchase—no ads or subscription.
Flipcorder: Retro Camcorder
Reminiscing about the long-lost days of the pre-smartphone era? Flipcorder offers simple pleasure, turning your iPhone Duo into a camcorder, so you can make new memories that feel like the old days. Open the app, and the outer display will show a “closed lens”—open the Duo to “take the cap off,” then start recording. The user interface is retro, and video clips have a filter to emulate VHS (it has a MiniDV filter too). I really like that you can view your “tapes” and everything is cataloged by day, so you can see 30 minutes of footage in one stitched-together clip.
As you’re recording, the person on the other end can see a preview of the video on the outer display—that kind of dual-display experience is only available to camera apps, so if you were hoping to read a book and have the outer display appear as the book cover, that's sadly not possible at the moment.
RectoVerso: Flashcards
Flashcard apps are a dime a dozen, but nothing quite captures the physical experience of flipping around a flashcard like RectoVerso. This $13 app lets you import your own text—your classroom notes or even a PDF—and uses Apple Intelligence to automatically create flashcards on the subject matter. Alternatively, you can import decks from Anki, another popular flashcard app, or write your own. The magic is when you're actually studying. Don't know the answer? Slightly open the iPhone Duo, and the answer will gradually appear—fully open, and you get the full answer. That way you can bang your hand on the desk and say, “Ah, I totally knew that.”
PianoFold
Who doesn't love a rhythm game? Pop your iPhone Duo into a 90-degree angle and let the blocks in PianoFold reach the middle crease—that's when you tap the corresponding column. You need to time your taps perfectly, unless you enjoy listening to Bach get butchered in real time. There are 40 levels across eight chapters, and the game rates your performance (out of three stars) at the end of each song. You can retry as many times as you'd like. The first two chapters are free, though you can also play one song for free every day. For full access, you'll have to pony up $5. There are no ads and no subscription.
Toastie
When I showed my wife Toastie, she remarked that it might be the first time she ever wanted an iPhone (she uses a Pixel). That's high praise! This delightful $3 app asks you to construct a sandwich on the iPhone Duo's inner screen. Each recipe has specific instructions you have to follow, and when you're done, you'll need to close the iPhone for a few seconds—however many the recipe says—to “grill” your sandwich. Open the phone back up, and it's ready to serve! That is, if you haven't burned it. There are only 10 recipes, so you'll probably get through this quickly. But hey, at least you can say you've used the world's most expensive toaster.
Portal
Want to focus? Or relax? Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. It's very relaxing and an excellent companion for travelers who rely on a sound machine to fall asleep. You can also follow calming breath exercises, or set focus timers to get stuff done. The app boasts more than 100 vistas, from Iceland's black beaches to enchanting UK woodlands. The app is free, though you can only access three portals refreshed monthly. Full access costs $3 a month, $30 per year, or $100 for a lifetime membership.
If you like the idea of Portal, you might want to check out Fold Focus, though it's designed to help you get work done rather than relax. Close the Duo to focus on a task, and the pixel animation on the outer display will start building a city. Open your phone before the timer ends and everything will come crashing down.
FirstSeed Planner
Want to try a new calendar app? Maybe your current one isn't optimized for the Duo (ahem, Google Calendar). Try FirstSeed Planner. The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other. It supports drag-and-drop actions between the two halves of the screen, and I also love the space at the bottom for writing notes for the day. And when Apple enables stylus support on the Duo later this year, you can handwrite in FirstSeed, making your Duo feel more like a paper planner. It's free, but the Pro version costs $3.49 per month, $30 per year, or $90 for lifetime access. The paid versions unlock features like automatic backups and weather forecasts.
Delta Emulator
If you’re big on retro gaming, you’ve probably heard of Delta. The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo. Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it. Just remember: It’s strictly an emulator, so you’ll still need to source your own ROMs responsibly.
Tiny Computers
Bring your favorite PCs and Macs back to life with Tiny Computers. This $4 app houses a library of 10 computers, from the Commodore 64 to the iMac G3. Fold the Duo into tabletop mode to bring the museum of machines to life—a vintage screen up top and a functional, clickable keyboard below. The operating systems are interactive, so you can run retro paint apps, secret terminal commands, or kill time with classic desktop games like Solitaire.
