El-Fasher becomes ‘ghost town’ as RSF crimes continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:09 UTC
19:00:09 KST

Breadcrumb
El-Fasher becomes ‘ghost town’ as RSF crimes continue on anniversary of takeover
One year on from the Rapid Support Forces' (RSF) takeover of North Darfur's capital, El Fasher, Amnesty International is warning that the situation remains dire, with unlawful killings, arbitrary detentions, and torture rife, while the population has dropped significantly.
In a report released on Friday, Amnesty said fewer than 70,000 people remain in the city that once had 1 million inhabitants, with humanitarian access remaining limited, and the risk of arrest for returnees high, despite claims by the paramilitary group that people are free to return.
"What we found is that El Fasher is still very much a ghost town," Laura Mills, the author of the report, told The New Arab.
Amnesty's report is based on the testimonies of 25 civilians, including six humanitarian workers, with 15 having fled the city between July and August 2026, and one who remained in the city.
Mills said part of the reason for the desertion of the city was the high risks of being there, which many of the testimonies confirmed.
"We found that many people were detained, including those who tried to return to the city. Often, men were held in prisons and detention centres where they faced torture and truly horrific conditions.
"Women and children were typically held in schools that had been converted into de facto detention centres," she said, with the report noting high levels of malnutrition in said centres.
"Moving around the city, people didn't feel safe; they felt surveilled," Mills added.
Seventeen of the 19 residents Amnesty spoke to had been arbitrarily detained, with the ethnic minority Zaghawa and Masalit people more likely to be detained. Both groups have been targeted by the RSF since the beginning of the war.
RSF killings during the fall of the city have been described as a massacre, with the UN saying that there were "hallmarks of genocide".
Mills said that ethnic minorities are automatically suspected by the RSF of being close to the country's military, which the group is fighting against in the civil war.
Amnesty spoke to those who were detained and put in prison, with many of them stating that RSF soldiers tortured and committed unlawful killings. Mamoun, a 33-year-old Zaghawa man held in Shala prison, said that the group arbitrarily shot prisoners.
Those detained are often released because families pay ransoms to the RSF, which Mills said reach up to $10,000.
She noted that these abuses by the paramilitary group are widespread across RSF-controlled Darfur, though El Fasher's years-long siege fending off the RSF has contributed to widespread suspicion of the city's residents by the group.
Humanitarian workers still operate in the city, though closely monitored by the group, which restricts their movements and prevents aid workers from speaking with residents.
Despite this, humanitarian assessments place the city, alongside much of North Darfur province, in danger of reaching IPC Level 5 famine, the highest threshold possible, in the coming months.
Mills told The New Arab that the international community had all the tools it needed to safeguard El-Fasher's residents and alleviate suffering in the country, but that it was unwilling to use them.
This includes pushing for a ceasefire and talks between the RSF and the military, which was rejected earlier in October by military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, as well as an arms embargo on the country.
"It just really feels like we have all the tools at our disposal, but the world is just sort of looking on as this horrific disaster continues to unfold, and what happened in El Fasher can easily happen somewhere else," Mills said.

Cloud House by Peter Morris brings "fairytale flamboyance" to London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Cloud House by Peter Morris brings “fairytale flamboyance” to London
Marshmallow-pink walls, sweeping arches and turquoise detailing influenced by a trip to Miami animate architect Peter Morris‘s self-designed home in Gospel Oak, London.
Named Cloud House, the eccentric project combines two offset residences, one for Morris and his partner, producer Emily Kennedy, and a second for a neighbour who shares their love of colour.
According to the architect, the goal of the project was to bring joy to passersby, while giving his “love of postmodernism a chance to reveal itself fully”.
“The key goal was to make a beautiful building which I hoped might create a little moment of joy for anyone walking past it on the street,” Morris told Dezeen.
“It’s easy to dismiss colour and pattern in architecture as frivolous, but there’s something about this visual language that triggers an emotional response that’s different from what you’ll get with elegant modernism,” continued Morris.
“For me, that alone tells us we should push for more variety in the built environment and be open – as Camden Council have been with this project – to the idea of more fairytale flamboyance on our streets,” he continued.
Cloud House occupies the site of a now-demolished Victorian home, adjacent to a distinctive church and school, where the couple have lived since 2016.
Its bold colour palette and cloud-like forms were inspired by the couple’s honeymoon in Miami and the city’s vast collection of art deco architecture.
“Emily and I honeymooned in Miami, where we loved the art deco curves of the buildings, and the pink and turquoise colours everywhere,” Morris explained. “In a way this building is an architectural love letter to my wife, so it felt appropriate to have some of that honeymoon spirit in the mix.”
According to Morris, the project also draws on the curved forms of the neighbouring Grade II-listed school and Grade I-listed St Martin’s Church, which Morris said are “fabulously eccentric buildings”.
“The school, which sits in St Martin’s Hall, has a frontage that looks like a Medieval castle,” he said.
“And the church – described by the historian Nikolaus Pevsner as ‘the craziest of London’s Victorian churches’ – has a knock-out interior, with a brightly coloured chancel ceiling and a nave with dramatic wooden arches.”
Cloud House’s main structure is composed of structural steel and blockwork.
This is clad in decorative arches made of polystyrene, sprayed with a waterproof layer and a textured top coat to match the bright pink render on the elevations, and positioned in place by the architect himself.
Morris’s home is the smaller of the pair, located on the right side of the plot. It measures 133 square metres.
The home is accessed from an entrance on its front elevation. It has a large, open-plan ground floor, comprising a lounge, kitchen and the architect’s studio.
Its two upper floors are each fitted with a bedroom and bathroom, while a roof terrace crowns the home, complete with an outdoor bathtub.
Next door, the adjoining 165-square-metre home is accessed by a side entrance and has an upside-down arrangement.
Its ground floor contains a home office with a kitchenette, and a guest ensuite bedroom at the rear. Above is the main bedroom.
The main bedroom has a dressing room and ensuite, and sits alongside another smaller ensuite bedroom.
Meanwhile, the social space with seating, dining and cooking spaces is on the top floor, with an adjoining terrace. A second larger terrace tops the home.
While the interiors of Morris’s house boldly match its vibrant exterior, the interiors for the neighbour’s home were left blank and ready for them to customise.
Interior highlights of the architect’s home include turquoise epoxy floors, colour-drenched bathrooms and an emerald-green striped kitchen.
Cloud House was featured on the TV show Grand Designs in September and has been shared widely on social media. Morris said the response to the project is sharply divided.
“I know that not everyone will love the Cloud House as much as we do – the reactions to it on social media have been either overwhelmingly positive or overwhelmingly negative, with nothing in between,” he reflected.
“My final goal, and hope, is that some of the people that do love it might one day be keen to commission me to create something colourful and joyful for them too.”
Other pink dwellings featured on Dezeen include a concrete “fun house” on the English coast by RX Architects and a guesthouse in the Azores contained within a converted stable.

"A butter knife against a nuclear arsenal:" Tech billionaires vastly outspend wealth tax supporters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

“A butter knife against a nuclear arsenal:” Tech billionaires vastly outspend wealth tax supporters
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
More than $351 million in political donations has been poured into a high-stakes contest about a proposed wealth tax on the November ballot, making it one of the most costly campaigns in California history.
About 90% of the money is being spent to defeat a statewide initiative to impose a new tax on the assets of billionaires, a multifaceted opposition effort bankrolled primarily by ultra-rich Californians being targeted by a measure that supporters call an economic reckoning.
The billionaire tax, Proposition 40, would levy a one-time, 5% tax on many assets of California billionaires who lived in the state as of Jan. 1.
Millions of dollars continue to flow into the campaigns of three intertwined ballot initiatives at the center of the debate: Proposition 40, and Propositions 41 and Proposition 42, which would neuter the Proposition 40 through strategic, esoteric tax law changes.
“The pro-40 campaign picked a fight and then came to that fight with a butter knife against a nuclear arsenal,” said GOP strategist Rob Stutzman, who is not involved in any of the wealth-tax-related ballot measures. “Because they’re so well funded, in today’s multifaceted media world, they are able to show up everywhere from network TV to inside video games. That is a very, very large advantage few campaigns ever get to have.”
But, Stutzman warned, money does not guarantee a win.
In the most expensive ballot measure fights in California history, $463 million was spent on two gambling proposals 2022. The initiatives pitted some of California’s most successful Native American tribes with gaming interests against gambling corporations, including online sports gaming companies DraftKings and FanDuel. Both side’s measure failed.
The tax measure was crafted by Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West in response to federal healthcare funding cuts signed by President Trump last year that are expected to reduce California’s healthcare budget by $100 billion, burdening the state’s most vulnerable residents.
“Trump’s ‘Big Beautiful Bill’ slashes healthcare funding, with major coverage cuts scheduled to hit after the midterms,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the union’s chief of staff. “More than 3 million Californians could lose their health insurance. Hospitals and emergency rooms face closure. Patients will die unnecessarily when the care they need is no longer there. Proposition 40 is an emergency response to that looming disaster.”
The proposition’s supporters raised $34.3 million, nearly all of it from Jimenez’s union.
The two other measures, Propositions 41 and 42, would nullify the billionaire tax if either receives more votes.
Proposition 41 supporters say the measure aims to cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits for new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that exempt their revenue from a state spending limit. Backers of Proposition 42 argue it would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other forms of personal savings.
Advocates for the billionaire tax say both are well-financed smokescreens to undercut Proposition 40.
Opposition campaigns to the wealth tax as well as the two countermeasures have received enormous donations from several of the state’s billionaires. But Building a Better California, the main funder of efforts to defeat the wealth tax, noted that its allies included Democratic and Republican politicians, prominent labor groups and business leaders.
“It’s rare for such a broad coalition to unite around any single cause in California, but it reflects the potentially devastating impact of this measure on healthcare, education, and our state’s economy,” the group said in a statement.
Among the largest donors opposing the wealth tax are billionaires Sergey Brin, a co-founder of Google who has donated more than $100 million to anti-wealth-tax efforts, and former Google leader Eric Schmidt and venture capitalist L. John Doerr, who each kicked in $40 million.
Brin, Schmidt and Doerr did not respond to requests for comment.
The spending disparity also reflects a divide among Democrats and their allies, many of whom support wealth taxes, but argue that the way Proposition 40 was written is disastrous to California’s volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s wealthiest residents.
Jodi Hicks, chief executive and president of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, said that while her organization would support a nationwide or a California wealth tax, their primary concerns are about 40’s impacts on the state budget and healthcare in the state.
“We are opposed to this particular proposal because we think it does more harm than good,” she said, adding that after what her organization “faced last year having to scramble for dollars because of [federal funding cuts] we are committed to work with the stakeholders facing cuts and not harming the budget and finding revenue in a smart way.”
The cash imbalance between supporters and opponents of the billionaire tax is vast. Those opposed to the measure raised $316.7 million, while proponents raised nearly $34.3 million.
The supporters of the wealth tax spent nearly all of their money gathering signatures to place the measure on the ballot. They had $1.6 million on hand as of Oct. 17.
Now, as voters cast ballots, their campaign appears reliant on public events and media coverage, such as of Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-Vt.) recent rally in support of Proposition 40 in downtown Los Angeles.
“What you are showing people from coast to coast and all over is that, yes, we can take on the greed of the oligarchs,” he said, calling it the most important ballot measure in the country. “Yes, we can create an economy and a government that works for all of us, not just the 1 percent.”
Labor leaders argue that the billionaires tax includes a loophole that would allow state lawmakers to tax the savings and retirement accounts and home equity of all Californians.
Facebook creator and Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg was among the California billionaires Sanders name-checked in his remarks. After Zuckerberg told company leaders that he planned to leave the state to avoid his control over the company substantially reduced by being forced to sell enough of his stock in the social media giant to pay the proposed levy, the company on Wednesday announced the creation of a new, non-voting type of stock that would allow Zuckerberg to sell enough shares to pay the proposed tax while retaining his voting power in exchange for him agreeing to remain in the state for eight years.
The pro-wealth-tax campaign is sending voters emails and texts and has an online presence.
“Remember: it’s not enough to vote YES on 40. You also need to vote NO on 41 + 42,” read an email sent to voters on Tuesday. “Don’t be fooled: Props 41 and 42 are billionaire-funded initiatives designed specifically to undermine Prop 40, the California Billionaire Tax.”
Meanwhile, the anti-40 and pro-42 campaigns are inundating voters on television, streaming services, in mailboxes, through online influencers and even in digital video games such as Sim City.
Jimenez said voters will see through the blizzard of campaign messaging.
“The billionaires think voters are stupid. They think they can bury the facts under millions of dollars in advertising and disguise Prop. 42 ... as protection for ordinary taxpayers,” she said. “Their spending also makes our case for us. When billionaires can afford to spend millions a day protecting their fortunes, voters can see that billionaires have plenty of money to spare.”
Sheri Sadler, a veteran Democratic media buyer, questioned how much voters were hearing about the rationale for the proposed billionaire tax.
“The yes side is severely lacking in getting their message through while the no side is dipping into different kinds of pockets,” she said.
Jessica Levinson, an election law professor at Loyola Law School, said that beyond voter confusion about the competing ballot measures, it is certain to face legal challenges, notably about the retroactive nature of the tax, which would apply to any billionaire who lived in California as of Jan. 1. She described that as “the biggest legal pressure point.”
“It’s kind of a mess,” she said.
Times staff writer Gabrielle LaMarr LeMee contributed to this report.

The Qubitunes Soundstage Toy Is a Great Gift for Kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Most parents worry about exposing their kids to too much screen time, but it can be tough to find alternatives that children find entertaining and that might be beneficial. Enter Qubitunes, a screen-free play stage and speaker for kids. Content comes in wooden cartridges that you slot in the top, and kids can place wooden character pieces on the circular soundstage, divided into four sections, to change the audio it plays.
This seemingly simple design allows for interactive stories that change based on the characters and spots your kids choose, music that can be layered up with different instruments, and themed games and quizzes. I’m a huge fan of Qubitunes, and it has a deserving place in my guides to the best STEM toys and speakers for kids. As Black Friday and gifting season approaches, the Qubitunes starter kit is one toy to keep an eye on for discounts.
I played with Qubitunes for hours when it arrived and really enjoyed it. The stereo speakers are decent, there's a headphone port, and it can be recharged via USB-C for up to six hours of play. It has since gone into my wife’s classroom, and it’s usually the first thing picked when kids have finished their work and it’s choosing time. It’s very popular with 7- and 8-year-olds, but kids aged 3 years and up (all the way up to adults) will potentially get a kick out of this.
There is a caveat: the need to purchase content separately. These add-ons cost between $10 and $20 each. Stories, games, and other options come in wooden blocks that slot into the device so you can download the content. You need a Wi-Fi connection for the initial content download and firmware updates, but then you can play offline. They usually come with three or four character blocks and a labelled bag to keep them in.
My top pick is the Little Maestro set ($20) featuring players in an orchestra covering Mozart, Vivaldi, Beethoven, and Bach. There are also stories about quirky characters, such as The Groblies ($20), a fun cooking game called Bernard’s Kitchen ($20) with different ingredients, and various themed soundscapes and quizzes. I prefer activities where there’s some creativity or a learning game involved, but the stories and soundscapes are good for very young kids. The interactive nature of these sets elevates the experience beyond passive listening and provides replay value, as kids experiment to discover what happens when they move and replace pieces on the stage.
Qubs has also recently released a Maestro expansion ($10) with four new composers, a Jurassic Sounds Dinosaur Game ($20) with facts and T-Rex roars, and versions of Little Red Riding Hood and Hansel & Gretel, among many others. If you like the idea of sustainable, screen-free toys, the maker Qubs also made a clever wooden car STEM toy called Cody Block ($70) that introduces kids to basic coding concepts, and it’s on sale right now, down from $100.

Our Brains Weren’t Built for This Much Comparison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

More than 20? Or less than 75? As I scan my feedback on a recent social media post, my brain just can’t seem to help registering the number of “likes.” I’m not alone.
Under a recent settlement that Meta recently reached with states, Facebook and Instagram are about to look different for minors Among the new protections, one seemingly modest change caught my eye. By default, users under 18 will no longer be able to see likes and other reactions in response to their posts or those of others. The reforms are designed for children and teenagers, but touch on a psychological phenomenon just as relevant to adults. As a psychiatrist, I found myself wondering: Why does that little number beneath your post matter so much?
The answer has less to do with social media and more to do with an ancient human tendency: social comparison. Social comparison is the psychological process by which people assess themselves, including their own abilities, opinions, and achievements, in relation to those of others. Likes can both reward us and rank us. They show us that people are validating our posts and also quantify that validation.
We know how much approval we receive relative to what we might have expected, what we got the last time we posted, and what others receive. Feedback is scored. Likes are just one example. Follower counts, views, and shares are other metrics that make social information measurable. When social approval is numerically valued, comparison becomes harder to avoid.
From an evolutionary perspective, social comparison may have served an adaptive purpose. Humans evolved in social groups. Knowing where you stood relative to others might have helped you identify what behaviors were approved, whether you belonged, and how to navigate hierarchy. But moving beyond prehistoric time to the last century, comparison still had constraints. Your 25-year high school reunion? It happened once in your lifetime, maybe in a city far away from you, with only your fellow classmates in attendance. Now, the high school reunion lives in the device in our hands, capable of giving anyone quantitative signals from a vast reference group at any moment on our personalized scoreboards of social approval. If the subjective question is whether we belong, what can feel like an objective answer is the 100 likes our post gets from 2,500 followers. The scale, frequency, quantification, and accessibility of social comparison have all changed.
Our brains weren’t built for this much comparison. Neuroimaging studies show that our brains allocate value to how we believe we stack up next to others. Downward social comparison, in which we learn someone performs worse than us, can engage neural circuits associated with reward and valuation. Upward comparison, in which we learn someone performs better than us, can engage neural circuits associated with processing unpleasant emotions. These are ways in which our brains process social outcomes much like other kinds of gains or losses.
But our brains don’t just register numbers; we also tend to evaluate their meaning. In one study, likes functioned as a type of currency that adult users compared themselves on, shaping how they felt in that moment. In another set of studies, adults who made more frequent and extreme upward comparisons reported an immediate decline in self-evaluation and cumulative declines in self-esteem and life satisfaction over a browsing session. Research has also found that across generational groups, greater user tendency to engage in social comparison, together with greater maladaptive ways of coping with emotions, is associated with more symptoms of anger, anxiety, and depression.
Social comparison isn’t inherently harmful. But as repeated opportunities to compare mount, the mental health effects can add up.
While hiding likes may not eliminate social comparison, it does remove a metric from the scoreboard. The instinct to compare or desire to belong won’t just vanish. But even if we might wonder where we stand next to who’s performing better, there’s a difference between wondering and a number answering that question for us.
Social media didn’t invent our instinct to compare ourselves to others. We’ve had that for millennia. What it did was shift the environment surrounding our instincts, encoding one form of social feedback into numbers we can monitor.
That's why changing our relationship with social comparison will mean more than adapting digital platforms. What do we value? What gives us purpose? What makes our lives matter?
The cultural shift that lies ahead is to ask the questions about our social worth that don’t need a scoreboard to answer.

Saved wounded soldiers since 2015: Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:00:00 EEST
19:00:00 KST

Saved wounded soldiers since 2015: Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies
Olena "Jane" Sharhovska, a veteran of the Hospitallers medical battalion who worked as a translator and journalist in civilian life, has died. Olena had been saving wounded soldiers since 2015.
Source: Yana Zinkevych, commander of the Hospitallers medical battalion; Sharhovska's former colleagues at Novynarnia
Details: Olena had extensive experience in the media, working as a journalist, translator, editor and social media specialist. Over the course of her career, she worked in television and print media, as well as on projects for Ukraїner and Osvitoria.
From 2015 onwards, she dedicated herself to saving others. Jane volunteered on the front line with the First Volunteer Mobile Hospital named after Mykola Pyrohov. She later joined the Hospitallers.
"Having mastered tactical medicine, Jane went to evacuate the wounded from the hottest sections of the front line, snatching the lives of our soldiers from the jaws of death on the way to stabilisation points," Zinkevych said.
In addition to helping the wounded, the paramedic and her fellow servicewomen campaigned for women's right to serve in the Armed Forces of Ukraine on an equal footing with men.
In particular, she became a co-organiser of the Invisible Battalion March, an event held in Kyiv in 2016. Participants called on the authorities to allow women to hold military positions that had previously been open only to men.
Jane was in Portugal when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. An injury prevented her from returning to Ukraine immediately, but she supported the country as a volunteer.
On 10 September 2022, her birthday, Olena joined the military. Serving with the International Legion of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, she was deployed in Bakhmut, Toretsk and Kharkiv Oblast.
In addition to carrying out medical evacuations, Jane provided tactical medicine training to other service members and, as a member of the Women's Veteran Movement, campaigned for female defenders to receive proper equipment.
She was discharged from military service in August 2024 due to health reasons.
"Olena was a person of words and travel, with a deep interest in the world and in people [...] Despite all the difficulties and trials, she retained her love of words and people, continued helping her brothers- and sisters-in-arms with fundraising, and bought vehicles for the front.
"Her motto in life was: 'Do what you believe needs to be done, and then come what may,'" Novynarnia said.
Bohdan Lohvynenko, a serviceman, journalist, writer and founder of Ukraїner, also shared his memories of Olena.
"We lived in neighbouring buildings in Vynohradar and often sat in one of our kitchens discussing editorial matters. You were an enormous source of support and a driving force behind many processes, while at the same time remaining quite harsh towards the unknown. I would always remind you of what you had once said about those whose ranks you later joined. And we often laughed about it," her former colleague wrote.
Background: Earlier, Yaryna Nishtuk, a defender from Lviv who served as a platoon commander of strike unmanned aerial systems, was killed in action.

The Israeli army continued its siege of Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank for a second consecutive day on Saturday, forcing dozens of Palestinians from their homes, according to Palestinian media.
Israeli forces raided the al-Jilda and Deir Bahha areas in central Hebron and placed them under a complete siege, the official Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
The army also forced dozens of residents to leave their homes and stand outdoors in the early morning hours, according to the news agency.
The incursion involved the deployment of additional military vehicles and bulldozers, the closure of main entrances and roads leading to Hebron, and the isolation of the city from surrounding areas, Wafa said.
It said Israeli forces also raided and searched homes, detained dozens of residents and subjected them to field interrogations before releasing them on Saturday morning.
Separately, Israeli forces detained 19 Palestinians in raids across the occupied West Bank.
The arrests included two Palestinians from the Hindaza area and al-Azza refugee camp in Bethlehem governorate, 16 from Nablus governorate and a young man from Aqabat Jabr refugee camp in Jericho.
The occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, has seen an escalation in Israeli military attacks and violence by occupiers since Israel launched its war on Gaza in October 2023.
The attacks have included killings and arrests of Palestinians, demolitions of homes and other structures, the burning of mosques and vehicles, and the levelling of agricultural land.
They have also involved restrictions on farmers' access to their fields, the displacement of Palestinian communities and the expansion of settlements.
On Friday, the Israeli army claimed that two Palestinians were killed in a shootout with Israeli forces.
The army alleged that the Palestinians had opened fire at illegal Israeli settlers in Hebron, wounding five people.
Following the reported shooting, the Israeli army announced on Friday a complete closure of Hebron and several surrounding towns.

Ashoke Sen: Indian Physicist honoured with 2026 Oskar Klein Medal for string theory work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:50:04 UTC
18:50:04 KST

Ashoke Sen, a distinguished physicist from ICTS, is honored with the prestigious 2026 Oskar Klein Medal.
Physicist Ashoke Sen has been awarded the 2026 Oskar Klein Medal, becoming the first physicist from India to receive this honour.Sen, who holds the ICTS-infosys Madhava chair professorship at the International centre for theoretical sciences (ICTS), tata institute of fundamental research (TIFR), Bengaluru, is widely recognised for his pioneering contributions to modern string theory.String theory proposes that the fundamental building blocks of matter are tiny, one-dimensional strings rather than point-like particles. The theory seeks to provide a unified framework for understanding matter and the forces governing interactions between its constituents.Established in 1988, the Oskar Klein Medal is named after Swedish theoretical physicist Oskar Klein. It is awarded annually by stockholm university and the nobel committee for physics of the royal swedish academy of sciences.As part of the oskar klein memorial lectures, a distinguished researcher is invited each year to deliver a lecture in klein's memory and receive the medal.Sen delivered his memorial lecture, titled ‘gravity from strings and strings from gravity’, on October 22 at the AlbaNova university centre in Stockholm.His presentation explored how string theory can provide a consistent quantum description of gravity and help address unresolved questions surrounding the quantum physics of black holes.
Contributions to modern string theory
A recipient of the Padma Shri in 2001 and the Padma Bhushan in 2013, Sen has made several influential theoretical contributions that have helped shape the field of string theory.His work was recognised with the breakthrough prize in fundamental physics in 2012. The research helped establish the idea that different string theories could be understood as distinct limits of a single underlying theory.
Congratulating Sen on the achievement, ICTS director Rajesh Gopakumar said, “On behalf of all of us, very warm congratulations to Ashoke. It has been no less than wonderful having Ashoke with us and setting the tone for excellence here at ICTS.”In a statement, ICTS highlighted Sen's internationally recognised contributions to S-duality, the precise counting of black-hole entropy and string field theory, describing them as key areas of work that have helped shape modern string theory.
Previous recipients of the Oskar Klein Medal
The medal has previously been awarded to several prominent scientists, including Kip Thorne in 2016, Peter Higgs in 2009 and Stephen Hawking in 2003.Other recipients include nobel laureates Hans E. Bethe, who received the medal in 1990; Steven Weinberg, honoured in 1989; and Chen Ning Yang, who was the recipient in 1988.

France mounts huge security operation as protesters prepare to march
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:42:10 UTC
18:42:10 KST

France protests begin under heavy security as police seek to prevent fresh unrest; 135 arrested
- France saw protests under heavy security, with 70,000 police deployed and 135 arrests made as officials tried to stop fresh unrest after last weekend’s riots.
- Shops, museums and metro stations shut in Paris, while police used tear gas in Lyon and moved the main march away from the city centre after a legal fight.
- Protesters said the government was over-reacting, while tensions rose after a deadly shooting near Paris and as the far-right National Rally held a congress in Orleans.
AI generated
PARIS – Demonstrators took to the streets of France on Oct 24 under the watch of 70,000 police officers, with unrest appearing markedly less severe than a week earlier despite scattered confrontations in several cities.
Tens of thousands of people marched peacefully through the French capital, according to police numbers, denouncing the high cost of living and accusing President Emmanuel Macron of cutting public services while failing to tackle rising inequality.
“Down with the state, the police and the fascists,” some of the flag-waving crowds chanted.
Elsewhere, police fired tear gas at people in Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice, where a water cannon was deployed after protesters refused orders to pull back.
In France’s second and third cities, Marseille and Lyon, clashes broke out between hooded youths and police.
The government has deployed 10,000 more police and gendarmes than on Oct 17, when nationwide protests descended into some of the worst unrest France has seen in years.
“We have to be ultra, ultra responsive,” said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who has accused far-left groups and criminal gangs of fomenting violence.
Nunez told reporters that police had arrested 135 people nationwide by early afternoon, many following pre-emptive searches that he said had uncovered fireworks, ball bearings and other items that could be used as weapons.
Shops, museums shut
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
“There are hardly any customers, so it’s not really worth staying open,” said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital’s best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d’Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
“Everything’s boarded up and we’re not quite sure where we should be,” said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
The route for Paris’ main demonstration was settled only after a legal battle triggered by a last-minute police order moving organisers away from the city centre towards the south-eastern fringes of the capital.
Police argued that the original route passed through areas with a high concentration of businesses similar to those targeted last weekend. Leftist leaders said the late change was aimed at causing confusion and keeping people away.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a “magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint”.
He said the protests would continue unless Macron addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world’s richest nations but with a growing debt that has alarmed investors.
“Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door,” Melenchon told reporters.
Far-right party holds congress
Many demonstrators accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.
“We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round,” said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
“My friend and I almost didn’t come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it’s important not to let repression win,” she added.
The first authorised march on Oct 24 passed off peacefully in Orleans, around 120km south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.
A shooting west of Paris on Oct 23 heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
“We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party. REUTERS

Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:39:23 UTC
18:39:23 KST

Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Kiev has moved to block a planned tribute to Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich, who was involved in the killing of an estimated 100,000 Poles during World War II ethnic purges, officials in Warsaw have claimed.
The reported retreat comes amid a series of disputes between the two countries in recent months over Kiev’s veneration of Nazi-linked figures that have eroded Polish support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.
The controversy erupted on Tuesday when the Lviv Regional Council in western Ukraine voted to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and to celebrate the 120th anniversary of its commander Roman Shukhevich while deciding to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national patriotic rallies on the occasion.
The move triggered a fierce response in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and Shukhevich as a key “architect” of the massacres. Before becoming a UPA leader, Shukhevich served in Nazi Germany’s Nachtigall Battalion and the German-controlled 201st Schutzmannschaft Battalion, which operated in occupied Belarus.
On Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk condemned the resolution as “unwise” and “suicidal tactics,” saying it “harms Ukraine,” while Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called the move “unacceptable,” warning that it would deepen divisions between the neighboring countries. Meanwhile, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski called for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremeta, to be put on a list of individuals deemed undesirable in Poland.
Following the backlash, Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said on Wednesday that officials of Vladimir Zelensky’s office had assured Warsaw that the controversial resolutions would not come into force. On Friday, Tusk echoed the claim, saying that Zelensky had personally signaled he would not endorse the resolution, adding that the Ukrainian leader was “unhappy” with the situation.
This also came after the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry called the Shukhevich tribute in Lviv “counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations.” The ministry stressed that the local authorities had sought no advice from government bodies to assess the consequences of their actions.
An unnamed source in Zelensky’s office cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda went so far as to describe the decision as a “catastrophe.” “Ukraine looks erratic. We have just resolved the previous crisis – and now this,” the source said, accusing regional officials of pursuing “cheap one-day hype” despite knowing all too well what the resolution would lead to.
While senior Ukrainian officials apparently distanced themselves from the controversy, the Lviv council’s original announcement remains accessible as of Saturday. Sheremet also previously defended the resolution, saying “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honor their memory.”
The dispute is the latest in a series of heated clashes between Kiev and Warsaw over Ukraine’s continued veneration of nationalist figures that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II.
In May, Zelensky awarded an elite Ukrainian special operations unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA,” prompting another diplomatic uproar, with Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripping the Ukrainian leader of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration.

How much must the world cut emissions to return to 1.5°C?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:37:45 UTC
18:37:45 KST

How much must the world cut emissions to return to 1.5°C?
The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, published on October 21, outlines a scenario in which global temperatures peak at 1.7°C to 1.8°C above preindustrial levels around midcentury before returning to 1.5°C or below by 2100. The scenario has about a 50% chance of success.
The required cuts are measured against 2025 emissions levels. Emissions would also need to fall 69% by 2040, the report says.
Current national climate pledges fall far short. Even if countries fully implement their existing commitments, emissions would decline by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said the world could still limit the scale and duration of warming above 1.5°C.
Under current policies, global warming could reach 2.8°C this century and continue rising afterward, the report warns.
If countries meet their existing climate pledges and maintain similar efforts, warming could reach 2.6°C. Even if they fulfill their pledges and achieve additional net zero targets, temperatures would still rise by about 2.1°C.
Every 5 years of continued CO2 emissions at current levels could add about 0.1°C to peak warming, the report estimates.
Returning to 1.5°C would also require removing and permanently storing around 320 billion tons of CO2 from the atmosphere over the course of this century. That is equivalent to roughly 8 years of global CO2 emissions at 2024 levels. The report cautions that technological and economic challenges make achieving this uncertain.
Renewable energy
Despite the gap between current efforts and the required cuts, UNEP points to progress since the adoption of the Paris Agreement.
Renewable energy has expanded rapidly, coal and oil supplies have grown more slowly than previously projected, and climate policies have reduced emissions in several countries and sectors.
An assessment of more than 220 policy evaluations found that electricity sector policies reduced emissions by an average of 9%. Economic measures, including carbon taxes and emissions trading systems, cut emissions by 5% to 13% across the sectors studied.
However, these gains remain concentrated in particular countries, sectors and periods. Governments need to expand and sustain successful measures to achieve the necessary global reductions, the report says.
New targets for 2035 and 2040
To align with the lowest possible 1.5°C overshoot scenario, global renewable electricity capacity would need to reach at least three times its 2025 level by 2035 and 4.5 times that level by 2040.
Over the same period, the energy intensity of global economic output would need to fall by at least 30% by 2035 and 40% by 2040, relative to 2025.
The report also calls for major cuts in fossil fuel use. By 2035, the shares of coal, oil and gas in total global energy supply would need to fall by at least 55%, 15% and 5%, respectively, compared with 2025. By 2040, the required reductions would reach 75%, 30% and 35%.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that more than half of the estimated heat-related deaths in 854 European cities between 2000 and 2025 were attributable to human-induced climate change.

5th Asian Para Games: Kazakhstan finishes 9th with 50 Medals
Kazakhstan finished ninth overall at the 5th Asian Para Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Japan, capturing 50 medals — 12 gold, 16 silver, and 22 bronze, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Kazakh Sports Committee.
150 athletes from Kazakhstan competed across 12 sports: Para athletics, Para swimming, Para judo, Para taekwondo, Para powerlifting, Para table tennis, Para shooting, Para archery, Para cycling, sitting volleyball, boccia, and wheelchair tennis.
The national team achieved its strongest results in Para judo, securing 13 medals—five gold, one silver, and seven bronze. Moreover, it topped the sport's team standings.
Para judo gold medalists included Ibragim Nurmakhanuly (J2, -70 kg), Bexultan Kulmurza (J2, -81 kg), Zhurkamyrza Shukurbekov (J2, over 95 kg), Aktolkyn Seilbekova (J1, over 70 kg), and Zarina Raifova (J2, over 70 kg).
Zhanbota Amanzhol earned silver in the men's J2 -95 kg division.
Galymzhan Smagululy, Yermek Nurkabayev, Baglanbek Onalbek, Yerlan Otepov, Alfiya Tlekkabyl, Dayana Fedossova, and Ayala Mereke each claimed bronze medals.
In Para swimming, Kazakhstan collected 10 medals (one gold, five silver, four bronze).
Dias Kenzhebek claimed gold in the men's 100-meter backstroke S10 event, while adding silver medals in the 100-meter freestyle and 200-meter individual medley, alongside a bronze in the 100-meter butterfly.
Ali Turganbekov earned a silver medal in the men's 100-meter breaststroke SB4. He captured another silver medal as part of Team Kazakhstan in the mixed 4×50-meter medley relay, competing alongside Natalya Zvyagintseva, Zulfiya Gabidullina, Aisultan Kulkeyev, and Siyazbek Daliyev.
Team Kazakhstan claimed an additional silver medal in the mixed 4×50-meter freestyle relay, featuring a team of Natalya Zvyagintseva, Aisultan Kulkeyev, Siyazbek Daliyev, and Zulfiya Gabidullina.
In addition, Roman Potapov, Viktor Volkov, and Alina Sinelnikova secured bronze medals in their respective disciplines, adding to the national team's medal count.
In Para cycling, the national team captured nine medals: four gold, four silver, and one bronze.
Nail Yermukhambet became a two-time Asian Para Games champion in the men's B class, winning gold in both the road race and individual road time trial.
Anastassiya Kalaus also secured two gold medals in the equivalent women's events. Furthermore, she earned a silver medal in the 4,000-meter individual track pursuit.
Kirill Ilyukevich claimed two silver medals in the road race and individual road time trial, as well as a bronze medal in the 4,000-meter individual track pursuit. Zhuldyz Kainarova won a silver medal in the women's road race.
In Para powerlifting, Team Kazakhstan pocketed six medals: one gold, two silver, and three bronze.
David Degtyarev became the Asian Para Games champion in the men's -54 kg division, lifting 192 kg to set a new Asian Para Games record. Tursynay Kabyl won a silver medal in the women's -41 kg category, while Alina Solodukhina earned silver in the -45 kg class.
Stanislav Shakiyev and Aizhan Berimkulova took bronze medals in their individual events. Additionally, the Kazakh men's team, comprising Yerbolat Karibay, David Degtyarev, and Stanislav Shakiyev, won a bronze medal in the team competition.
In Para athletics, Kazakhstan captured four medals — two silver and two bronze.
Islam Salimov earned silver in the men's long jump T13, while Dastan Mukashbekov secured silver in the men's shot put F36. Bronze medals in the shot put were claimed by Ivan Zaleznyak (F36) and Makhambet Serikkaliyev (F53).
Additionally, Aisulu Suleimenova set a new Asian record in the women's 100 meters T62, clocking a time of 16.18 seconds.
In Para table tennis, Kazakh athletes took four bronze medals, marking the national team's first-ever podium finishes in the sport in Asian Para Games history.
In Para archery, Team Kazakhstan won two medals — one silver and one bronze.
In the men's doubles W1 class, Nurshat Toleukassym and Temirlan Seitkamal took silver, marking Kazakhstan's first-ever Para archery medal at the Asian Para Games.
Nurshat Toleukassym also earned a bronze medal in the men's individual W1 event.
In Para shooting, Yerkin Gabbasov became the Asian Para Games champion in the men's R1 10m air rifle standing SH1 event.
In sitting volleyball, the Kazakh men's national team clinched the silver medal. Kazakhstan defeated Iraq 3–2 in the semifinals before falling 3–0 to Iran in the gold medal match to complete the tournament as runners-up.
Thus, Kazakhstan concluded its campaign at the 5th Asian Para Games with 50 medals, including 12 gold, 16 silver, and 22 bronze, and finished ninth overall in the final standings.
The 5th Asian Para Games took place from October 18 to 24, 2026, in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, Japan.

British ships defy Chinese warnings in South China Sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:27:12 BST
18:27:12 KST

Two Royal Navy patrol ships have finished a ten day exercise in the South China Sea alongside Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, working with fifth generation fighters, a Singaporean submarine and New Zealand boarding teams, according to the Royal Navy.
HMS Spey and HMS Tamar led the British contribution to Bersama Lima 2026, the annual exercise of the Five Power Defence Arrangements, whose name means Together Five in Malay. The participating navies brought corvettes, frigates, patrol ships and a submarine, and the exercise built from familiarisation scenarios to a two day war game.
Before sailing, the crews spent a week learning each other’s vessels, systems, procedures and the language they would use at sea so that they could work together once the pace picked up. The maritime phase covered boarding and searching suspect vessels, naval gunfire directed onto targets ashore by soldiers embarked in the ships, a submarine hunt and an air defence exercise supported by aircraft.
Commander Tom Lindsey, the commanding officer of HMS Tamar, said: “Bersama Lima was an excellent opportunity to put my ship’s company through their paces and refresh their war-fighting skills with our Five Power allies.
“There was a great breadth to this iteration of Bersama Lima: fifth-generation fighter jets, international boarding teams and Singapore’s newest submarine which, combined with the level of competence and professionalism showed, levelled up the experience gained.
“These war-fighting serials demonstrated that we can put a task group together in short order and successfully operate together to achieve a spectrum of scenarios.”
Tamar hosted a Royal New Zealand Navy Deployable Boarding Team which was put through repeated serials investigating suspected illegal fishing and narcotics smuggling, work the team and the ship will be doing for real on their next mission.
Able Seaman Mansfield, one of Tamar’s seaman specialists, said: “Driving a Kiwi boarding team up to a suspect vessel with a second sea boat, armed to the teeth, was a surreal experience which really brought the exercise to life.
“We also got the opportunity to replenish underway at sea where we exchanged some goods from home with HMAS Stalwart, who sent Tim Tams [Australia’s favourite biscuit] in return!”
A sailor from HMS Spey said: “It was a privilege to attend Bersama Lima 26 alongside our FPDA partners, an exercise which demonstrates over five decades of commitment to training and working together.
“Throughout the harbour phase, HMS Spey’s sailors took the opportunity to learn from each of the Five Power nations and share their skills to enhance interoperability and build stronger friendships in the region.”
Each British operation in the region since has drawn the same response as Beijing previously accused Britain of flexing its naval muscles over the 2021 carrier deployment. After HMS Spey passed through the Taiwan Strait in June 2025, Senior Captain Liu Runke, spokesman for the navy of the People’s Liberation Army Eastern Theatre Command, said British remarks about the transit had distorted legal principles, and that troops remained on high alert and would resolutely counter all threats and provocations.
When Spey exercised navigation rights and freedoms around the Spratly Islands in May this year, China’s ambassador to the United Kingdom said the 2016 arbitration award was illegal, null and void and that the British position would not shake China’s resolve, as this publication reported at the time. In July the Chinese Embassy in London told Britain to stop stirring up trouble after it backed a statement on the same award, and the embassy’s position was set out again as the two ships entered the sea at the start of this month.
Spey and Tamar are Batch 2 River class offshore patrol vessels, each crewed by around sixty sailors. They have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021 under Operation Highwall. The Five Power Defence Arrangements date from 1971 and remain the only standing multilateral defence arrangement in the region involving Britain.
Spey is now heading to south-east Asia for several weeks of patrols and diplomatic engagement, while Tamar is making for Australia and New Zealand by way of Pacific island chains, where she will carry out maritime security patrols and counter illegal fishing.

Owners of mobile phones that are not set to update their time automatically, or users who prefer not to rely on automatic updates, can adjust their devices manually. They can also restore automatic date and time synchronization at any point.
Android
Android menus vary across models, but time settings are generally found in the device's main Settings menu or under the clock settings.
In Settings, select "Date & Time" and disable the "Automatic date and time" option. Then select the appropriate time zone – Jerusalem – and set the time and date manually.
iPhone
In Settings, select "General," then "Date & Time." Turn off "Set Automatically," select the appropriate time zone and adjust the clock manually.

Starlink in Ukraine back to normal after week of throttling
KYIV, Oct 24 - Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.
Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometres per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
"The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app.
According to Zelenskiy, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph.
Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains vital for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
LIMITATIONS ORDER
The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, US administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.
On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out". REUTERS

Ray-Ban Meta Audio Review: The Best Smart Glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.
“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”
The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.
This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.
It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.
It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)
It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)

Trump’s Iran pause is for November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:12:09 UTC
18:12:09 KST

President Trump’s pre-midterm pause on strikes against Iran landed as a claim of diplomatic momentum, not a concession of failure. The pause was framed as proof that negotiations are working. Look closer, and a different mechanism appears. The war meant to project strength has become an electoral liability, and the president’s response is to bury its most visible costs until voters have finished deciding. Then the option can reopen.
The White House insists Washington is negotiating from strength. Military options remain on the table. The blockade stays in force. The administration has not ended the war, only hidden its sharpest edges from the campaign season. That sequence matters. It allows Republican candidates to campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or another energy-price spike, while preserving the argument that renewed action may be warranted later. Nothing has been settled. Everything has been postponed.
Trump’s political identity rested on rejecting costly, open-ended foreign interventions. His appeal to swaths of the MAGA movement included the claim that American leaders had squandered resources and neglected domestic problems chasing overseas conflicts. “America First” was a promise about priorities as much as power.
The Iran war has strained that promise to its breaking point.
Back in February 2026, it looked like a pressure campaign: force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms. Months later, it’s a drawn-out confrontation with no clear settlement. Rising fuel prices, stubborn inflation, and the uncertainty over how long the war will last have turned it into a domestic political problem.
Consumer sentiment has fallen close to a record low, dragged down by rising living costs linked to the conflict.
This creates a tension the Republican coalition cannot easily absorb. Some supporters prioritize nationalist strength and a confrontational stance toward Iran. Others were drawn by pledges to avoid costly wars and focus on economic grievances at home. An extended conflict makes satisfying both impossible. Pausing attacks before the midterms offers a way to postpone the reckoning.
The question is whether this pause is a genuine step toward peace or simply an attempt to protect Republicans from the political costs of an unpopular war. The attacks may have stopped, but the naval blockade remains in place, economic pressure on Iran continues, and neither side appears any closer to a lasting agreement. Trump has ruled out further strikes before 3rd November. What he has not ruled out is a return to military action once the election is over. This sequence allows the administration to present the pause as controlled progress, lets Republican candidates campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or energy-price spikes, and preserves the option of arguing later that renewed action may be warranted.
The reports tell a different story than the public messaging. The Pentagon has been instructed to prepare for a potential resumption of large-scale operations. Discussions involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have touched on a major new operation before elections in both countries. The White House calls such reports false. But the military remains on alert, and preparations are being finalised.
For many MAGA voters who supported Trump in part because he promised to reject endless wars, a purely electoral pause represents a significant contradiction.
An unpopular foreign war won’t turn MAGA loyalists into Democrats. The real hazard for the GOP is exhaustion: an endless conflict paired with painful pump prices gives frustrated voters every reason to leave their ballots on the kitchen table.
By removing the immediate threat of renewed attacks, Trump can try to prevent the war from becoming the dominant symbol of Republican failure and shift attention toward negotiations. If the conflict remains relatively quiet until November 3, Republican prospects improve. If Democrats gain control of one or both chambers, congressional scrutiny of military spending and presidential war powers would intensify.
This is where the powerless ballot enters the picture. Elections are meant to give citizens influence over decisions made in their name. That relationship weakens when a president can temporarily reduce the visibility of a policy’s costs until after ballots are cast, then resume the same course. Trump’s approach could turn the midterms into a debate over whether he appears willing to pull back from the war, rather than whether his Iran policy has actually changed. Americans are already feeling the strain of higher living costs, and consumer confidence has fallen sharply. A brief pause in the fighting will do little to ease that burden, much less resolve the underlying conflict. What is needed is a lasting diplomatic settlement, not a temporary break that leaves the same problems unresolved.
Neither a Republican nor a Democratic outcome automatically resolves the strategic problem. Iran has its own calculations.
Iranian officials continue to demand sanctions relief and an end to the blockade while Washington insists on further concessions. A pause that leaves these disagreements unresolved may simply delay the next confrontation.
The bigger question is not whether Trump keeps his promise before the election, but what he plans to do once the votes are counted and the political pressure has eased. If the coming weeks bring a verifiable agreement backed by credible safeguards, the pause could be a genuine first step toward ending the war. If instead November 3 is treated as the moment political restraints disappear, then the restraint will have functioned primarily as an electoral maneuver.
In that case the danger is clear. Voters are being asked to endorse the appearance of an ending while the means to continue the conflict remain intact. The ballot becomes a ratification of a decision already made elsewhere.
If the fighting resumes after the votes are counted, the question will no longer be whether Trump delivered peace, but whether his supporters were ever given a genuine choice between peace and a war that had only been postponed.

Expert warns of complex ecological fallout from Mongolia grassland fire linked to Japanese company
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:06:24 CST
18:06:24 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A large grassland fire in Mongolia reportedly linked to activities by a Japanese company's subsidiary may have caused extensive ecological damage, with its broader environmental impact requiring comprehensive assessment, an expert said.
The fire broke out on Oct. 8 in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Mongolia's eastern province of Dornod. The flames were extinguished on Oct. 16, according to Mongolian media reports. Japanese telecommunications operator KDDI said on Oct. 20 that the fire was linked to activities by its Mongolian subsidiary Mobicom.
The fire may have affected not only grasslands but also riverbanks, wetlands and other ecosystems, said Wang Qinxue, a researcher at Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies who has long studied the region's ecological environment.
A comprehensive assessment is needed to determine whether soil conditions can recover alongside vegetation, whether wildlife can safely survive the winter and whether the fire has caused any transboundary environmental pollution, Wang said.
Preliminary data released by Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change showed that the fire had burned about 530,000 hectares of land, including approximately 470,000 hectares within the Numrug Strictly Protected Area, accounting for 79.8 percent of the reserve's total area.
Located in eastern Mongolia near the Chinese border, the reserve features a mix of grasslands, forests, rivers and wetlands. It provides habitats for a variety of wildlife and plays an important role in conserving local biodiversity, Wang said.
Even if vegetation regrows the following year, plant species composition and soil conditions may not recover at the same pace, he said.
Assessing damage to forest ecosystems is particularly complex, requiring an examination of tree survival rates, the availability of seed sources and the growth of new seedlings to determine the extent of damage and the potential for recovery, Wang added.
The fire's potential transboundary ecological effects also warrant further investigation. It remains necessary to determine whether ash and sediment could be carried into rivers and wetlands by surface runoff and whether smoke from the fire had crossed national borders through the atmosphere, Wang said.
Citing research on Mongolia's Dornod Province, Wang said fire occurrence from autumn through the following spring was associated with the number of dust storm days in spring.
Reduced vegetation cover after a fire leaves soil more vulnerable to wind erosion and makes surface materials easier to transport by wind, he said.
Wang called for systematic surveys of the burned areas, categorized by ecosystem type, to scientifically assess the actual damage and determine the scope for ecological recovery. ■

The following are some highlights of his remarks.
Sept. 13, 2026
At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Xi said all countries, regardless of their size, strength or wealth, are equal members of the international community.
"Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the United Nations, support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, and ensure the equal participation of all countries in international affairs," he said.
July 17, 2026
At the opening ceremony of the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance held in Shanghai, Xi said that AI is an invaluable asset that encapsulates humanity's collective wisdom.
"We should practice true multilateralism and recognize the important role of the United Nations," he said. "We should enhance alignment and coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards, so as to form a consensus-based global governance framework at an early date to make this frontier technology better benefit humanity."
Sept. 1, 2025
At the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting in north China's port city of Tianjin, Xi said the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations must be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"We should firmly safeguard the status and authority of the United Nations, and ensure its irreplaceable, key role in global governance," he said.
Aug. 30, 2025
When meeting with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the SCO Summit 2025, Xi said that China will always be a trustworthy partner of the United Nations.
China is willing to deepen cooperation with the United Nations, support the United Nations in playing a central role in international affairs, and jointly shoulder the responsibility of safeguarding world peace and promoting development and prosperity, Xi told Guterres.
June. 28, 2024
At the conference marking the 70th anniversary of the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence held in Beijing, Xi said that in the face of new developments and challenges, "the authority and central role of the United Nations can only be strengthened rather than weakened."
"The purposes and principles of the UN Charter are never outdated, and they are getting ever more important," he said. "China advocates the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit, and China believes in true multilateralism." ■

Thirty-three British warships left service since 2010

Thirty-three Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service since 2010, of which eight have been sold, fifteen recycled and ten are still waiting to be disposed of, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, had asked how many warships had been taken out of service, sold or scrapped in each year since 2010.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Since 2010, 33 Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service. Of these, 8 have been sold, 15 have been recycled and 10 are pending disposal.
“As vessels may be withdrawn from service in one year and sold or scrapped in a later year, these categories are not mutually exclusive, and the figures should not be aggregated.
“As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, this Government is investing in new frigates, amphibious ships, new submarines and new standardised vessels alongside a new Hybrid Navy of uncrewed and autonomous systems to increase our Navy’s lethality and deterrence.”
Thirteen new frigates are being built across two classes, eight Type 26 anti-submarine ships on the Clyde and five Type 31 general purpose ships at Rosyth, and Norway has since selected the Type 26 design for its own fleet. Three Fleet Solid Support ships are under construction to resupply the carrier groups, new transport ships are planned to take over from the amphibious and Bay class vessels. The submarine service is completing the Astute class before moving to the four Dreadnought ballistic missile boats and then to SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, which ministers have said will be delivered at a rate of one every eighteen months from the mid-2030s.
The period covered includes the retirement of the Type 42 destroyers, the progressive withdrawal of the Type 23 frigates, and the decision to dispose of the amphibious assault ships Albion and Bulwark, the latter of which is being sold to Brazil.
