L3Harris to develop long-range drone killer for U.S. Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:37:45 UTC
16:37:45 KST

- L3Harris received a three-year contract worth up to $60 million to develop a long-range ramjet-powered drone interceptor for the U.S. Army.
- The company advanced to the Xtended Range Counter-sUAS Missile program’s second phase, which covers flight performance testing of a fully integrated interceptor.
L3Harris Technologies has received a three-year contract worth up to $60 million to develop a long-range, maneuverable missile for the U.S. Army that is designed to shoot down small and medium drones at greater distances than today’s interceptors.
The company announced the award on Oct. 23, 2026, under the Xtended Range Counter-sUAS Missile program run by the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation & Missile Center at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama. L3Harris said it has advanced to the program’s second phase, which involves flight performance testing of a fully integrated interceptor that offers greater range, speed and operational flexibility than current systems, and the missile is meant to engage traditional short-range air defense threats such as aircraft and helicopters as well as drones.
“We are leveraging L3Harris’ deep technical expertise across propulsion, guidance and advanced manufacturing to deliver a next-generation interceptor that meets the Army’s evolving mission requirements,” said Scott Alexander, president of Propulsion Systems at L3Harris Missile Solutions. “This design combines innovative propulsion with advanced seeker technologies to provide a highly capable, modular and cost-effective solution deployable from existing launch platforms.”
The key to the design is an air-breathing ramjet engine. Unlike a conventional rocket motor, which has to carry both fuel and the oxidizer needed to burn it, a ramjet takes oxygen from the air it flies through, freeing space inside the missile for more fuel. L3Harris said its approach improves fuel efficiency and extends engagement range, and the company is also adapting the interceptor to work with existing U.S. military platforms so it can be integrated quickly into current air defense networks.
The Army launched the program, also known as XRC, to find a missile that can be fired from the Stinger Vehicle Universal Launcher with more range than the current Stinger for the counter-drone mission. The service has said it wants the new weapon to reach farther, react faster, hit harder and reload more quickly, with a focus on larger drones that fly higher and from greater standoff distances, while still protecting maneuvering forces carried by systems such as the Maneuver Short Range Air Defense, or M-SHORAD, vehicle.
L3Harris is one of several companies working on the effort. Northrop Grumman received an $18.8 million agreement from the same Army center earlier this fall to develop and integrate solid fuel ramjet propulsion for XRC missile prototypes, with ground and flight testing planned through December 2029 at its Allegany Ballistics Laboratory in West Virginia.
The L3Harris contract runs for three years, and the full $60 million value depends on continued funding as the company moves its interceptor through the second-phase flight tests.

Paris museums close, shops build barricades ahead of more protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:33:31 UTC
16:33:31 KST

Clashes break out between police and protesters in France after largely peaceful demonstrations
Clashes broke out in Paris late Saturday after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful.
The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in protests around the country. Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000. An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Saturday that 135 people have been arrested and a variety of weapons have been seized. The items confiscated include metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said. Nuñez added that, so far, "there has been no major incident" in the country.
Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week. About 3,000 shops were looted or damaged last weekend, CBS News previously reported.
Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march
Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm."
Thousands gathered at the Port d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change.
The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000.
As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Police used batons and tear gas, and officials said a water cannon was also used. Some protesters threw projectiles at police.
The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said.
Protesters march against far-right gathering
In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen.
"Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.
Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes, a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident.
French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday.
Protesters and police clash in smaller cities
Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city.
A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile."
In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.
Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, police said. Water cannons were used in Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned.
Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint.
Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations
One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron.
Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms."
The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.
More protests spread across Europe
Other protests are expected across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.
Italy deployed soldiers to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, as the city braced for fresh demonstrations one week after looting and police clashes. Many stores were boarded up with wooden planks on Saturday. Premier Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters.
In Rome, authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up patrols around key sites. Several hundred students demonstrated peacefully in the historic city. Organizers of peaceful events sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and their hands visible.
In Albania's capital of Tirana, riot police used water cannons to subdue large groups of protesters. Some of the demonstrators threw projectiles at police, the AP reported. A separate protest organized by the opposition outside the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama turned violent earlier Saturday, with some activists lighting fires on the street. The demonstrators are mainly high school and university students, demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. A broader anti-government movement is calling for Rama's resignation.
In Spain, thousands of retirees and others marched through central Madrid to demand that public pensions aren't meddled with.
Protesters in Lisbon, Portugal, are expected to march across the city Saturday to demand affordable housing.

U.S. Air Force details $20.7B AMRAAM missile contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:33:18 UTC
16:33:18 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded Raytheon a $20.7 billion sole-source contract for AMRAAM Production Lots 41 through 47, with work in Tucson through June 2033.
- A 2017 justification document found no other company interested in becoming a second source for AMRAAM production.
The U.S. Air Force has published new details of its $20.7 billion contract with Raytheon for AIM-120 AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, confirming that the sole-source deal covers seven production lots and will keep the Tucson, Arizona, production line busy until mid-2033.
An award notice posted on the federal contracting site on Oct. 23, 2026, shows the fixed-price incentive contract was signed on Sept. 25 for AMRAAM Production Lots 41 through 47. It covers AMRAAM missiles, AMRAAM telemetry sets used in testing, initial and field spares and other production components, with all work in Tucson and an expected completion date of June 30, 2033. The notice gives a base and all options value of $20,699,334,581 but does not list how many missiles the contract buys.
RTX announced the deal on Sept. 28 as a multiyear contract worth up to $20.7 billion over five years, with two option years, for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and international customers buying through Foreign Military Sales. The award is more than five times the size of the previous record AMRAAM contract, a $3.5 billion award in July 2025 for Lots 39 and 40, which itself surpassed a $1.19 billion contract for Lot 38 in September 2024.
The AMRAAM is the primary beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile of the United States and many allies, guided by an active radar seeker with mid-course GPS guidance and a two-way datalink. Raytheon says it is fielded by 44 countries on 14 platforms, from fighters such as the F-15, F-16, F/A-18, F-22 and F-35 to the ground-based NASAMS air defense system widely used in Ukraine and across Europe. Recent lots have included the AIM-120D-3 for U.S. services and the AIM-120C-8 for export customers.
The Air Force awarded the contract without competition under federal acquisition rules that allow a sole-source buy when only one responsible source can meet the requirement. A justification notice tied to the award was published the same day, and an earlier class justification signed in 2018 for Lots 34 through 43 lays out the reasoning the service has used for years.
That document traces Raytheon’s position to 1997, when Raytheon and Hughes Missile Systems Company, which the government had funded as competing AMRAAM producers, merged into Raytheon Missile Systems and left a single contractor able to develop, produce and sustain the missile. The program office concluded that qualifying a second source would require buying the technical data package, replicating the factory and requalifying suppliers, at a cost that competition would not recover, and that suppliers below Raytheon would remain sole sources regardless.
“No company has expressed any desire to be a second source for AMRAAM production/sustainment,” the 2017 justification states.
A 2017 market survey drew only limited interest, all of it in managing obsolete parts rather than building missiles, and the interested parties either withdrew or said their services were better suited to a subcontracting role.
The new contract comes as the Department of War pushes to rebuild missile stocks. Under a February 2026 framework agreement, RTX committed to producing at least 1,900 AMRAAMs a year, and the company says it nearly doubled output in 2025 compared with 2024. Work on Lots 41 through 47 is scheduled to run through June 30, 2033.

Labs that design U.S. Navy reactors get $2.4B more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:21:50 UTC
16:21:50 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Fluor Marine Propulsion a $2.4 billion modification for naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory.
- The laboratory designs and supports reactors for U.S. Navy submarines and aircraft carriers, with work in Pennsylvania, New York and Idaho.
The U.S. Navy has added $2.4 billion to Fluor Marine Propulsion’s contract to run naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory, the network of government labs that designs and supports the reactors powering every U.S. Navy submarine and aircraft carrier.
Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the $2,409,077,590 cost-plus-fixed-fee modification on Sept. 24, 2026, according to a Department of War contract announcement. Work will be split among the laboratory’s main sites near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (47%), Schenectady, New York (45%), and Idaho Falls, Idaho (8%). The announcement lists $582,062 in fiscal 2026 Navy operations and maintenance funds and $15,838 in fiscal 2026 shipbuilding funds obligated at the time of award, with the shipbuilding portion expiring at the end of the fiscal year.
The Naval Nuclear Laboratory is owned by the Department of Energy and overseen by Naval Reactors, a joint Energy Department and Navy program. It includes the Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory in West Mifflin, Pennsylvania, outside Pittsburgh, the Knolls Atomic Power Laboratory in Niskayuna, New York, near Schenectady, the Kenneth A. Kesselring Site in West Milton, New York, where sailors train to operate naval reactors, and the Naval Reactors Facility at the Idaho National Laboratory.
The labs develop new nuclear propulsion systems, provide technical support to keep the fleet’s reactors safe and reliable, and train the sailors who run them at sea. Knolls is the lead design laboratory for the Virginia-class attack submarines and is leading reactor design work for the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines, while Bettis supports the Nimitz-class aircraft carriers and Seawolf-class submarines. The laboratory employs more than 7,500 engineers, scientists, technicians and support staff.
Fluor Marine Propulsion, a wholly owned subsidiary of Fluor Corporation, took over management of the laboratory from Bechtel Marine Propulsion Corporation on Oct. 1, 2018. The Navy-funded portion of its contract started with a cost-plus-fixed-fee base of about $1.2 billion and options that could bring its total to about $13 billion, alongside a separate Energy Department contract for the same laboratory. Earlier modifications have included a $1.78 billion award in March 2020 and a $1 billion option in 2021.
The new modification covers continued naval nuclear propulsion work across all three regions, and the Department of War contract announcement did not list a completion date for the effort.

Interview: China's clean energy achievements accelerate global energy transition, says IEA chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:21:06 CST
16:21:06 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's achievements in clean energy technologies are impressive and have accelerated the global energy transition, Fatih Birol, executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), told Xinhua in a recent interview.
The global energy crisis is reshaping energy markets, prompting the adoption of renewable energy and electric vehicles (EVs) as countries seek to reduce their dependence on traditional energy sources, said Birol on the sidelines of the just-concluded Berlin Global Dialogue.
Birol highlighted China's important role in addressing current energy challenges and promoting international energy cooperation, recalling that at the 16th APEC Energy Ministers' Meeting, held in Beijing in September, representatives discussed the current energy crisis and ways for Asia-Pacific economies to work together to address it.
He said that since March this year, the world has faced an unprecedented energy security challenge following disruptions to the two major arteries that had long underpinned global energy flows: energy supplies from western Siberia, Russia, to Europe, and shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to Asia and beyond.
To mitigate disruptions in global oil markets, the IEA announced on March 11 that it would coordinate the release of 400 million barrels of oil reserves by its member countries. The move helped calm market concerns after oil prices initially surged, Birol said. However, he stressed that strategic stock releases could only cushion the impact of supply disruptions, rather than provide a lasting solution.
Beyond their impact on oil and gas prices, supply disruptions are also reshaping global energy trade relations, with some longstanding partnerships giving way to new ones, Birol observed.
He identified key trends emerging in the global energy sector since the outbreak of the war in the Middle East: rapid growth in renewable energy, rising EV sales, a modest increase in coal use, and renewed momentum behind nuclear power.
He said that solar power is the leading source of growth, followed by wind, and that biofuel use was also rising strongly, partly due to higher diesel and gasoline prices.
Birol pointed out that the rapid expansion of renewable energy was driven not only by climate and environmental concerns but also by energy security considerations and countries' efforts to increase domestic energy production.
Noting that EVs are growing rapidly in many markets around the world, Birol said reducing dependence on oil is an important factor driving this trend, which is evident not only in Europe but also in Brazil, Australia and Southeast Asia.
Highlighting China's role in the global energy transition, Birol said that China's electric vehicle market is developing rapidly, with EVs now accounting for about 60 percent of new car sales in the country.
The widespread adoption of EVs is not only fueling a transformation in the automotive industry but also changing the global energy consumption structure and will have a profound impact on the future energy market, he added. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has endorsed Gianni Infantino for re-election as FIFA president, marking a turnaround from two months ago when it criticized him over a controversial World Cup investment plan.
AFC President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa voiced his support at the confederation's extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, embracing Infantino and pledging the region's backing for his bid for a fourth and final term.
"We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president," Sheikh Salman said.
In August, the AFC joined UEFA and CONCACAF in accusing Infantino of a "fundamental breach of trust" over his plan to open FIFA's premium competitions, including the World Cup, to private investors. The plan was subsequently scrapped, prompting several European football associations, including the English Football Association, to withdraw their support for Infantino's re-election.
"Gianni, yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past. But let's not relate the two things together," Sheikh Salman said. "We need to move forward ... football is strongest when we work together."
He acknowledged that not all AFC member associations might follow his lead but expressed confidence that most would support Infantino.
"My feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," he said.
Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is seeking a fourth and final term in the election scheduled for March 2027 in Morocco. The deadline for candidates to register is November 18 this year, and no challenger has announced a bid so far.
Addressing AFC delegates, Infantino acknowledged his mistakes and stressed the importance of learning from them.
"When you do many things, you do -- hopefully, as we did, many good things -- you do some mistakes as well," Infantino said. "The important thing, however, is, as you said, to learn always from the experience, from the mistakes, to apologize, to move ahead, to come together, to unite, to build for our future, for your future."
Infantino has also received backing from the Confederation of African Football, while South America's governing body CONMEBOL is largely supportive.
The AFC has 47 member associations, 46 of which are FIFA members eligible to vote in the presidential election. While the endorsement does not guarantee unanimous support from its members, it significantly boosts Infantino's re-election bid.
FIFA's president is elected by its 211 member associations. ■

Feature: Global BASE jumpers meet at the world's highest bridge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:20:26 CST
16:20:26 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Hundreds of meters above a canyon in southwest China, the appeal of BASE jumping from a bridge is obvious: breathtaking height, open air and a few precious seconds of free fall.
But for many international jumpers, the experience extends well beyond the leap itself, encompassing spectacular scenery, cultural encounters and friendships forged through a shared passion.
At the edge of the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in Guizhou Province, German BASE jumper Hannes Grossmann launched into the air, performing a 360-degree forward somersault, a side flip and another rotation before deploying his parachute and landing smoothly in the designated area.
"The coolest thing about this bridge is that it is super high," Grossmann said. Its open surroundings also give experienced jumpers more room to maneuver.
This is Grossmann's third trip to China for BASE jumping, but his first time leaping from the Huajiang Bridge.
From Oct. 20 to 23, more than 30 BASE jumpers from 19 countries and regions gathered at the bridge for the 2026 International High-bridge Skydiving Invitational, following an earlier competition at Guizhou's Baling River Bridge.
BASE jumping involves parachuting from fixed objects or natural formations rather than aircraft, often leaving participants with only seconds of free fall before they must deploy their parachutes.
Certified by Guinness World Records in April as the world's highest bridge, the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge rises 626.01 meters above the water. The structure has cut travel across the canyon from around two hours to about two minutes. For BASE jumpers, however, its remarkable height offers an entirely different kind of advantage.
Grossmann began BASE jumping in 2019 and has completed more than 2,000 jumps worldwide. His previous trips to China took him to several other jumping sites, including the Nizhuhe Grand Canyon in Yunnan Province.
What distinguishes Huajiang, he said, is the combination of height and open space. With no cliff face immediately beside the exit, jumpers have greater freedom to experiment with different maneuvers.
Grossmann completed three jumps at Huajiang on Wednesday, trying backflips, front flips and other rotations. He gave the site a nine out of 10 for its suitability for practicing new tricks.
For Turkish jumper Ogulcan Geldikaya, who was making his second BASE jumping trip to Guizhou, the extra height offers another benefit: more time to enjoy the free fall.
The additional seconds allow jumpers to perform more maneuvers or attempt two- and three-person jumps with friends. On Friday morning, Geldikaya teamed up with an Australian jumper for a synchronized leap. Wearing their parachutes, the two stood side by side, clasped hands and jumped together. After several seconds in free fall, they let go, deployed their parachutes and landed safely in the designated area.
"The height of the bridge means more time for maneuvers and more fun. But safety is the priority," Geldikaya said.
That priority sometimes means staying on the ground. He had planned to celebrate his birthday on Thursday with another jump from the world's highest bridge, calling it "the perfect gift for myself." Strong winds, however, forced him to postpone the leap.
For Geldikaya, knowing when to wait is just as important as knowing how to jump.
The bridge events have also become a gathering point for athletes from around the world, giving them an opportunity to experience China beyond the competition.
Dutch jumper JP De Kam, who helps bring international athletes to the event, said the bridge initially draws people in, but the local culture is what makes them want to return.
During his visits, he has explored local streets, admired traditional Chinese architecture and taken in Guizhou's mountainous scenery. Just as important, he said, is the chance to see how local people live and discover how their daily lives differ from his own.
On Tuesday evening, the athletes visited Zhenfeng ancient town, where they joined local residents in traditional dances.
"We've been dancing together, doing the Chinese dances," De Kam said. "That's a very big attractive point."
For Portuguese referee Nuno Cunha, the event marked his first visit to China. One aspect of daily life in Guizhou particularly impressed him: the widespread use of digital payments.
"Everywhere I visited, people were prepared to accept digital payments," Cunha said. Even in villages, he saw elderly residents selling local produce to tourists and receiving payments through QR codes.
The event has also helped build friendships among athletes from different countries.
Geldikaya said he had made new friends from around the world during the gathering. He welcomed them to visit Türkiye and jump with him, assuring them, "My house is your house."
Some of these connections have continued long after the competition ended. Athletes who first met at events in Guizhou have since reunited in Türkiye, Japan and Europe, turning a few seconds of free fall into friendships that endure across borders.
De Kam hopes to bring even more athletes to Guizhou in the years ahead. "I would love to be back here for more than 10 years," he said. He wants more jumpers to experience "the culture, the food, the bridge, everything." ■

US President Trump’s defeat turns into a domestic challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

07:17:54 UTC

Nowadays, there is a growing public dissatisfaction with the United States regarding the US war waged against Iran and this issue has been turned into a challenge, a challenge that, in addition to increasing economic pressure on American citizens, could also impact the political standing of the Republicans ahead of the congressional midterm elections. Recent polls indicate that a majority of Americans are unhappy with how the US President has handled this crisis, and skepticism has grown regarding Washington’s ability to achieve its stated objectives.
Within this framework, a Democratic Senator from Connecticut and member of the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations Chris Murphy has criticized the Trump administration’s policies toward Iran, emphasizing that American people have no desire for this conflict to continue and that the costs to the nation are far from negligible. Murphy, a staunch critic of the Trump administration’s military policies, highlighted the financial burdens, the risks faced by American forces, and the security implications of these policies. Furthermore, he has called for an end to the conflict, asserting that Congress must take responsibility regarding the continuation of this course of action.
Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump's performance
Data from recent polls indicate that opposition to the handling of the conflict with Iran has spread to a significant segment of American society. According to a Pew Research Center poll, the results of which were released on October 8, 2026, 65 percent of Americans are dissatisfied with how Donald Trump has managed US military action against Iran, while only 33 percent approve of his performance. The survey, which included 5,062 American adults, was conducted between September 28 and October 4. The significance of these figures becomes even more apparent when compared to the results of a poll from March; at that time, 61 percent of respondents were dissatisfied with Trump’s handling of the situation, while 37 percent approved of his performance. Consequently, over the course of a few months, the level of dissatisfaction has risen, while support for the President’s performance has declined.
In general, US President Donald Trump's approval rating has tremendously been plummeted which is unique of its kind as compared with the previous presidents of the United States.
Furthermore, only 34 percent of Americans believe that the initial decision to use military force against Iran was the right one—a figure that represents a four-percentage-point decrease compared to March.
These findings suggest that the issue is not limited merely to disagreements over how government policies are implemented; rather, a segment of American society has also developed a more negative assessment of the very decision to employ military force.
Skepticism regarding realization of Washington’s goals
Another sign of public dissatisfaction is the growing skepticism regarding the Trump administration's ability to achieve its stated objectives. According to the same Pew Research Center poll, 52 percent of Americans have little or no confidence that the Trump administration will achieve its goals in the confrontation with Iran. In contrast, 24 percent stated that they have a great deal or a fair amount of confidence that these objectives will be realized.
On the other hand, a large segment of American society does not expect this crisis to end in the short term. According to the survey results, 47 percent of participants predict that U.S. military action against Iran will continue for more than another year, while 30 percent expect the situation to last between six months and a year. Consequently, approximately 77 percent of respondents anticipate that the conflict will persist for at least another six months.
These concerns arise against a backdrop where a prolonged conflict could impose greater financial and military costs on the U.S. government, further straining the nation’s resources. Consequently, the gap between the administration’s promises regarding the achievement of its objectives and public anxiety over the protracted crisis has become a focal point for criticism of the Trump administration’s policies.
Economic costs and concerns regarding American forces
Concerns regarding the economic consequences of a conflict also play a significant role in shaping public opposition. A survey by the Pew Research Center indicates that 73 percent of Americans are very or somewhat concerned about rising gasoline and fuel prices resulting from a conflict with Iran. Furthermore, 71 percent of respondents expressed concern about the injury or death of American troops. Additionally, 58 percent of participants stated that they are very or somewhat concerned about the deployment of U.S. ground forces to Iran.
These statistics indicate that the consequences of the crisis, as perceived by the American public, are not limited solely to military developments. Rising energy costs, the potential for the conflict to spread, and the risk of casualties among U.S. forces all factor into citizens' assessments of the administration's policy.
Under such circumstances, the continuation of the conflict could become a significant factor in U.S. domestic debates—especially if citizens feel that the costs incurred are disproportionate to the outcomes announced by the government.
Murphy’s warning regarding costs of continuing the conflict
Chris Murphy has also highlighted this same set of concerns in his criticisms. In a speech on the floor of the US Senate on September 24, he criticized Republicans for opposing a resolution to end the conflict, noting that public support for this policy has become very limited.
In this speech, Murphy stated that, according to the data he cited, only 18 percent of the American public supports this conflict; he urged Congress to heed the citizens' call to bring it to an end. He also warned of the security and economic repercussions of the crisis, as well as the risks facing American troops. Murphy argues that, in evaluating the outcomes of this policy, the U.S. government must consider not only the stated military objectives but also the costs imposed on American citizens, military personnel, and the nation's security interests.
Political consequences for Trump and the Republicans
Growing public dissatisfaction regarding a conflict with Iran could have significant political consequences for the Trump administration—especially with congressional midterm elections on the horizon, where the administration’s foreign policy performance could emerge as a key point of contention between Republicans and Democrats.
A decline in public support for government policies could pave the way for intensified criticism from opponents and the raising of more serious questions regarding the costs and outcomes of this conflict.
Notably, this erosion of support is not confined solely to Trump’s political adversaries. According to a Pew poll, his approval rating among Republicans and those who lean toward the party has fallen from 69 percent in March to 63 percent in October. While a majority within this group continues to support his performance, a six-percentage-point drop may signal growing reservations among a segment of his political base. Conversely, the negative view Democrats hold of Trump’s performance has remained virtually unchanged—a fact indicating that opposition to his policies remains widespread among his political opponents.
Generally speaking, polling data and criticisms from figures such as Chris Murphy indicate that the conflict with Iran has evolved into an issue that transcends mere US foreign policy. Economic costs, concerns regarding the safety of American troops, skepticism about the realization of stated objectives, and growing public opposition have intensified domestic pressure on the Trump administration.
In this regard, what Trump’s critics characterize as a failure to achieve stated goals could develop into a significant challenge within the realm of US domestic politics. Nevertheless, the extent to which this issue influences the outcome of the midterm elections will depend on future developments, the state of the economy, and how the administration manages the situation in the coming months.

Canada gets its first two CF-35A stealth fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:13:47 UTC
16:13:47 KST

- The Royal Canadian Air Force received its first two CF-35A fighters at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona for pilot training.
- Canada has committed funding for 16 F-35s so far, while a government review of the full 88-jet purchase continues.
The Royal Canadian Air Force has taken delivery of its first two CF-35A stealth fighters, the Canadian version of the Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II, at Luke Air Force Base in Arizona, the service announced.
The jets will stay at Luke, a major U.S. Air Force training base for F-35 pilots from the United States and partner nations, where the RCAF has set up its first CF-35A training squadron. Canada plans to base its first eight F-35s there during 2026 and 2027 to train Canadian pilots, before the first aircraft arrive at 4 Wing Cold Lake in Alberta in 2028, with initial operational capability planned for 2029.
“The future of air and space power is built on more than equipment alone. We are developing the skilled people, integrated capabilities, and modern tools we need to meet future challenges at home and abroad,” the Royal Canadian Air Force wrote.
The deliveries come one month after Canada’s first CF-35A made its maiden flight on Sept. 23, 2026, at Lockheed Martin’s plant in Fort Worth, Texas. That aircraft, production number AR-1, already wore full RCAF markings, including bilingual RCAF-ARC lettering on its air intakes and a roundel matching the one carried by the CF-18 Hornet it will replace. The CF-35A designation is the first two-digit designation for a Canadian military aircraft since the current naming format was introduced in the 1960s.
The F-35 will replace the RCAF’s CF-18s, which Canada has flown since the 1980s and plans to keep in service until the early 2030s while the new fleet builds up. Canada agreed in January 2023 to buy 88 F-35As for about $19 billion, part of a Future Fighter Capability Project valued at C$27.7 billion including training, equipment, sustainment and infrastructure.
How many of those jets Canada will ultimately buy is still undecided. Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review of the purchase in March 2025, and Ottawa has so far made a legal funding commitment for the first 16 aircraft, with long-lead payments for 14 more confirmed in February 2026. Defense Minister David McGuinty has said the review is ongoing without setting a timeline, and options under discussion include a mixed fleet that would add Saab Gripen E fighters, which Saab has offered to assemble in Canada.
Preparations for the F-35 have continued in the meantime. On Oct. 7, 2026, McGuinty announced nearly C$4 billion for fighter infrastructure at Cold Lake, the first Canadian base that will fly the jet, while 3 Wing Bagotville in Quebec is the planned second operating base.
With two CF-35As now in Canadian hands at Luke, the RCAF expects to receive the rest of its first eight training aircraft there through 2027.

Lockheed gets $115M to update F-35 navigation gear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:07:26 UTC
16:07:26 KST

- Lockheed Martin received a $114.6 million order to redesign the F-35’s GPS electronic unit and NAV100 inertial navigation system with replacement components.
- The work replaces obsolete electronic parts to prevent production disruptions and is expected to be completed in January 2030.
Lockheed Martin has received a $114.6 million order to redesign two key navigation systems on the F-35 Lightning II, the GPS electronic unit and the NAV100 inertial navigation system, replacing electronic parts that are going out of production so the stealth fighter can keep rolling off the line.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee order, announced on Oct. 23, 2026, covers nonrecurring engineering, redesign, integration, qualification and testing of both systems. The new designs will swap in replacements for obsolete components while keeping the same performance and compatibility with the electronics already flying on the jet, so the updated units can be fitted without changes elsewhere on the aircraft. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, issued the order without competition under an existing basic ordering agreement.
The two systems work together to tell the F-35 where it is. The GPS electronic unit processes signals from navigation satellites, while the inertial navigation system tracks the aircraft’s position, speed and heading using onboard motion sensors and keeps working when satellite signals are jammed or unavailable. Both feed the targeting, flight and mission systems that the pilot and the jet’s weapons rely on.
The problem the order addresses is a common one in long-running aircraft programs, known as diminishing manufacturing sources: suppliers stop making specific chips and electronic parts years before the aircraft that use them are retired. The Department of War said the redesigns are intended to prevent production disruptions and support continued production and sustainment of F-35s for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, U.S. Marine Corps and the program’s international partners.
Most of the work, 70.1%, will take place in El Segundo, California, with 27.5% in Fort Worth, Texas, where Lockheed Martin builds the F-35, and 2.4% in Clearwater, Florida. The effort is expected to be completed in January 2030.
The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy are each contributing about $46.4 million from fiscal 2026 aircraft procurement funds, and F-35 cooperative program partners are providing about $21.8 million.
The navigation work comes days after the Department of War and Lockheed Martin unveiled a framework for a 10-year F-35 production and sustainment deal covering 850 aircraft for the United States at a rate of 156 jets a year across all customers. Keeping parts like these available is a precondition for holding that production rate, and the redesigned GPS and inertial navigation units are scheduled to complete testing and qualification by early 2030.

Investment plan not investable as it stands, MPs told
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:00:41 BST
16:00:41 KST

The Defence Investment Plan is not investable as it stands, because it sets out themes without the contracts, programmes and procurement detail industry needs before it will build factories, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Stephen Phipson, chief executive of MakeUK, was giving evidence alongside Kevin Craven of ADS, Julian David of techUK and Arnab Dutt of the Federation of Small Businesses.
Phipson said: “I have been doing this for a long time, to say the least, and, as Kevin said, there is not sufficient detail. It is nothing like an equipment plan. This is not investable as it stands at the moment. It gives you a thematic direction of travel in many areas, a lot of which is welcome and is great news, and attracts a lot of new companies into the market, but the questions are then around where the contracts, the programme and the procurement are. We do not have that yet, and that is the problem.”
Craven said the plan concentrates on the first four years to 2029, where the old defence equipment plan set out a granular acquisition pipeline over ten years. He said: “We can see that the rough shape of the DIP is around 50% to 55% of the total spend over the 10-year period, so some spend has been brought forward to improve the readiness of what we are doing, but there is not enough granularity to provide certainty to industry. Intent is not the same as a commitment that is suitable for investors in defence.”
Asked whether the plan leaves more questions than answers, Craven said there is a clear shift in strategic direction but that “the lack of certainty over that 10-year period is a real problem. Headlines do not make for good investment.”
Ian Roome, the Liberal Democrat member for North Devon, asked how damaging it would be if the next spending review failed to provide a funded pathway towards three per cent of national income, and whether industry would still invest on the strength of the current plan.
Phipson said: “The answer is that it will not. It is only going to invest when there is certainty on what the programme looks like, and we have seen this for decades in defence. It has to be around a certain programme. The thematics that we have are all good and welcome.”
He added: “To your earlier point, industry welcomes the new technologies and innovation, but, until we see certainty, no one is going to invest a penny. We need to see where those contracts are going to come from. We will play with all the innovation that is happening with the MOD, which is good, but we need to start building factories and capability.”
On the backloading of the funding profile, Craven said: “You cannot switch on industrial capacity and production lines overnight. You need a strong demand signal over a long number of years to be able to do so, so a ramp-up towards the back end of a period is not helpful. It creates a future bottleneck where firms will compete for the necessary skills, monies and other industrial requirements at the same time, so it is not a helpful profile in any way.”
He told the committee that building a new production line from scratch takes between two and four years depending on what is involved.
David said the delay itself carries a cost, telling MPs: “this costs the country money, because delay in an inflationary context and, particularly in tech, an availability crisis of certain components means that what you are going to do costs more when you get around to doing it.”

One arrested after fire at Hitler's Eagle Nest mountain retreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:46:59 UTC
15:46:59 KST

Suspect arrested after fire "completely engulfed" Hitler's Eagle's Nest mountain retreat in Germany
A suspect has been arrested in Germany following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as Eagle's Nest, German police said.
Authorities were alerted to a fire at the Nazi leader's mountain residence on the peak of Obersalzberg at approximately 9:15 p.m. local time on Friday, Upper Bavaria South police said in a statement.
The building, also known as Kehlsteinhaus, was "completely engulfed in flames" when firefighters arrived, police said, but no one was found inside and no injuries were reported.
Fire trucks had some difficulty accessing the site "due to the local conditions," authorities added.
"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came into the focus of investigators," the statement said, adding that the cause of the fire is now under criminal investigation and one person was taken into custody.
The 33-year-old suspect, a German citizen who has ties to the Berchtesgaden area but doesn't currently live there, prosecutors said, has been questioned, The Associated Press reported. They said he showed signs of mental illness and he was being sent to a psychiatric facility, but they also would look into the possibility of a political motive in view of the building's history.
There were no current indications that anyone else was involved, police said.
At an elevation of 6,017 feet, Hitler's Eagle's Nest was completed in 1938 and occasionally used by the Nazi leader as a temporary seat of government. The site was spared from Allied bombing during World War II, largely preserving its original state.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist attraction, which also operates as a restaurant and beer garden. According to its website, the Eagle's Nest is "one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era" and it "stands for the insanity of the regime."
Bavaria's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, indicated to reporters in Berchtesgaden that the Eagle's Nest would be restored. But what the site will look like in the future will be a matter for discussions with local officials, historians, preservationists and others.
"We're not going to leave a ruin there," Herrmann said, according to the AP, adding, "I think we will be able to find a sensible solution."
The minister stressed "it is important that we continue to do the work of remembrance."

Türkiye’s energy ambitions, Eurasian financial links dominate Verona Economic Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:45:50 UTC
15:45:50 KST

Energy security, investment, and the financial infrastructure needed to support greater economic connectivity across Eurasia took centre stage on Friday, the second and final day of the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul.
Speaking at the forum, Turkish Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said a world facing geopolitical tensions, supply disruptions, and rising energy demand needs greater diversification, investment, and international cooperation.
Bayraktar said Türkiye imports almost 70 percent of its energy needs, making reducing external dependence a strategic economic and national security priority.
Renewable sources account for more than 62 percent of Türkiye's installed electricity generation capacity, while combined wind and solar capacity has exceeded 43 gigawatts, he said.
Türkiye eyes major energy investments
Bayraktar said Türkiye will need significant investment in its electricity networks in the coming years as it seeks to integrate more renewable capacity, improve grid resilience, and expand cross-border electricity trade.
Türkiye is also preparing to hold its first offshore wind tenders in the first half of 2027, while its Renewable Energy Resource Area program aims to allocate 2 GW of new capacity annually.
On nuclear energy, Bayraktar said it is continuing work with Russia's Rosatom to commission the first reactor at the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant in the coming months. Once all four reactors are operational, the 4.8-GW plant is expected to meet around 10 percent of Türkiye's electricity demand.
The country aims to reach 20 GW of nuclear capacity by 2050, including conventional reactors and small modular reactors.
Bayraktar also pointed to Türkiye's position between energy-producing and consuming regions, saying Ankara wants to strengthen its role as a reliable partner connecting regional energy markets.
COP31 presidency to focus on implementation
With Türkiye set to host next month’s COP31 UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Bayraktar said the Turkish presidency will put implementation at the center of the climate agenda, focusing on turning commitments into investment, technology deployment, and concrete results.
He stressed that countries have different energy systems and development needs, arguing against a one-size-fits-all approach to the energy transition.
Bayraktar said Türkiye would also advance a voluntary "35 by 35" global electrification pledge to boost electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.
Mobilising private capital, international financial institutions, and technology partnerships would be critical to delivering the investments required for the transition, he added.
Eurasia looks to deepen financial links
The broader question of strengthening financial connectivity was also taken up in the "Financial markets in the heart of Eurasia: Resilience, Infrastructure, Undervalued Opportunities" panel, where officials and financial executives discussed how regional capital markets could become more connected.
Russian Deputy Finance Minister Ivan Chebeskov said deeper and more liquid capital markets would become more attractive and efficient, arguing that Eurasian economies still have considerable room for financial integration.
He said the Eurasian Economic Union has already begun introducing mechanisms to facilitate cross-border market access for investors and issuers, while a mechanism to provide access for professional market participants is nearing completion.
Chebeskov said another priority is integrating market infrastructure, including exchanges and depositories. Within the BRICS group – also including Brazil, India, China, and several other nations – he said pilots involving the Moscow Exchange and Russia's National Settlement Depository are testing links between the capital markets of interested member countries.
He also pointed to national currencies as an area likely to play a growing role in financial markets.
Russian capital markets shift toward domestic financing
Moscow Exchange Chairman Viktor Zhidkov said activity in Russian equities is now concentrated in the domestic market, with stock and bond placements taking place locally and domestic demand sufficient to absorb them.
He said retail investors' stock market assets had nearly doubled over five years to 16 trillion rubles ($199 billion), while private investors had put more than 4 trillion rubles ($50 billion) into corporate bonds on the Moscow Exchange since 2022.
Corporate bond placements reached 7.2 trillion rubles ($89.6 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, up 20 percent from the same period last year, according to Zhidkov.
Gazprom's First Deputy Head of Department Ignat Dirks described a similar shift at the corporate level, saying the share of foreign markets in the company's financing portfolio had fallen from 77 percent in 2022 to 13 percent by mid-2026.
Dirks said Gazprom had raised more than $14 billion on the domestic market in the last four years for refinancing and around $20 billion to finance new projects. He said the restructuring of the company's financing portfolio had been made possible by the growing maturity of Russia's domestic financial market.
Common standards seen as key to integration
Gazprombank Deputy Chairperson Elena Borisenko highlighted the importance of greater complementarity and specialisation among financial centres.
She said common standards, compliance rules, and approaches would help build greater financial compatibility, while the quality of settlement systems, capital flows, trade finance, and investment products would determine the resilience and effectiveness of Eurasia's financial architecture.
The 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum, held at Istanbul's Ciragan Palace on Thursday and Friday, was organised by Italy's Associazione Conoscere Eurasia with the support of Türkiye's MUSIAD and Ibn Haldun University, bringing together political, diplomatic, academic and business representatives from more than 30 countries.

Moonshot tweaks the hack out of latest AI model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:43:15 UTC
15:43:15 KST

Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous artificial intelligence could turbocharge hacking.
Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable three-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model's weights –  files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems – by November 4.
Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model while retaining general coding skills.
"We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability," the company said.
Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.
China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. 
The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.
Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.
Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.
K3.1 Pro scored 81 percent on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5 percent for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. 
Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model's offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.
K3.1 Pro has a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model. (Reuters)

Typhoon Champi left over 146,000 households without power in Taiwan: Report

15:39:29 KST

More than 146,000 households across Taiwan experienced power outages as Typhoon Champi brought strong winds and heavy rain, local media reported on Saturday.
Electricity was restored to over 122,000 households by Friday night, while repair crews began work early on Saturday in parts of New Taipei and northern Keelung, which experienced strong gusts overnight, Focus Taiwan reported.
Authorities also dispatched 15 work teams from five regional offices in central and southern Taiwan to support restoration efforts in the north.
At least one person was killed and dozens of others were injured Friday as the typhoon disrupted air traffic.
Authorities ordered schools and offices to close across Taiwan, except in Taitung County and on the outlying islands of Penghu and Matsu, due to the typhoon.
Taiwan's Central Weather Administration said Champi was over waters east of Yilan and was expected to weaken into a mild typhoon Saturday afternoon.
The weather agency also expected to lift land and sea typhoon warnings by Saturday evening.
Rainfall shifted westward Saturday after affecting northern and eastern Taiwan the previous day.
Heavy rain fell in mountainous areas south of Hsinchu early Saturday, with localised torrential rain reported in mountainous areas of Miaoli.
Rainfall is expected to ease gradually in the afternoon, although localised heavy rain remained possible north of Taichung.
The weather agency warned that seas around Taiwan remained rough despite Champi's weakening, with waves reaching 2 to 3 metres (6.6 to 9.8 feet).
Waves exceeding 6 metres (19.7 feet) could still occur in northern and northeastern waters on Saturday.

491 days in the grey zone: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:34:00 EEST
15:34:00 KST

491 days in the grey zone and losing both feet: exclusive details of the first-ever aerial evacuation aboard a Heavy Shot drone
In October, Ukraine's defence forces carried out the first-ever medical evacuation of a wounded soldier using a heavy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The soldier, a member of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade who goes by the alias Magura, was airlifted from the grey zone aboard a Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 drone. No evacuation vehicle had been able to get to the area for over a year.
The roads are heavily mined, and FPV drones prowl the skies, destroying anything that moves within tens of kilometres. The brigade spent over six months preparing the daring rescue operation, which brought together heavy and light quadcopters, ground robots, electronic warfare units and even artillery.
"I realised there was a person down there: I wanted to get him to safety as quickly and safely as possible," a drone pilot recalls.
Ukrainska Pravda has interviewed the soldiers behind the operation, the drone's developers and the wounded serviceman. Find out how troops from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, named after Kostiantyn Ostrozkyi, teamed up with neighbouring units to pull off the evacuation and make history.
The operation was made possible by the coordinated efforts of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, the 14th and 30th Separate Mechanised Brigades, and the 10th Army Corps.
491 days
Sadly, this story began quite some time ago. On 2 June 2025, Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, an infantryman with the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, set off from the rear with a fellow soldier for their positions on the Kupiansk front, which were on the left bank of the Oskil River. In the grey zone, Magura initially took shelter in one spot. But when it flooded, he had to move into an abandoned building.
His brother-in-arms was killed while making his way to a fallback position. Then, on 14 February 2026, a Russian drone dropped a munition that wounded Magura in both legs. Faced with a fight for survival and having lost one of his feet, he amputated the other foot himself, leaving him unable to get out of his position on his own.
There was no way to drag him out overland: the Oskil River, dense minefields and relentless Russian drone patrols made the approaches impassable. The battalion tried to use a ground robotic system to evacuate him, but Russian forces spotted and destroyed it while it was still on its way. Infantry groups also failed to reach him. Russian drones filled the skies, and Russian infantry had infiltrated the area around his position, effectively sealing it off.
All this is further evidence that the "golden hour" – the crucial first 60 minutes after an injury, when prompt medical treatment can mean the difference between life and death – is becoming increasingly difficult to meet on the modern battlefield. Evacuating wounded soldiers is a dangerous mission in its own right, and one that becomes harder with every passing year.
Every four to five days, drones brought Kostiantyn food, cigarettes and sweets. He kept in touch with his brothers-in-arms by walkie-talkie. He held out in his position until his evacuation on 4 October.
It was Alex, the reconnaissance chief overseeing UAV operations for the 2nd Mechanised Battalion, who came up with the idea of evacuating the soldier by air. It took around six months to move from the initial concept to the flight itself. The military had conventional Heavy Shot bomber drones, but these were not up to the task. The soldiers instead turned to the newly developed Heavy Shot Ayudag-6, a heavy-lift drone that can carry up to 130 kg and is equipped with a cargo winch.
"We'd been using Heavy Shot bomber drones for a long time and had an established line of communication with Gurzuf Defence," Alex said. "When I found out they were testing the new Ayudag-6 heavy-lift drone, I went to them immediately with this unconventional task. The drone was still a work in progress, but the developers were immediately fired up by the idea."
Gurzuf Defence designed the drone primarily for frontline logistics, as a heavy-lift modular platform. However, the engineers ensured from the very beginning that it had enough thrust to lift a person. The drone underwent two years of testing, during which the company's chief developer, Oleh Hynda, became the first person to fly aboard the test model.
"We never intended this drone to be just for evacuations – it's a heavy-duty logistics platform," Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence, told Ukrainska Pravda. "But we always knew it might have to be used for a rescue mission in certain circumstances. To prepare for this operation, we brought in units with experience of evacuating people using ground robotic systems. It was their experts who configured the winch and the mounting systems."
The company spent several months fine-tuning the platform at the unit's request. Experts from the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade's unmanned ground systems company then fitted the aircraft with additional equipment, and the 2nd Battalion's headquarters spent two months planning the operation. Around 15 military personnel were involved in preparing and planning the mission.
Pre-flight preparations took seven days. The military personnel worked out the flight routes, planned cover corridors and identified alternative emergency landing sites in case of a technical failure.
The evacuation drone was operated by Chornyi ("Black"), a squad leader in a mortar battery at the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade. "I first got to know the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 a week before the mission, when I took part in special training exercises. Until then, I'd only worked with standard Heavy Shot drones," he says.
The most dangerous part was hoisting the soldier, who had to attach himself to the cable on his own. The day before the flight, the drone delivered off-the-shelf mountaineering equipment and a phone loaded with a video explaining how to put on and secure the harness.
According to the plan, the soldier had to attach himself to the drone's winch with carabiners, sitting in a semi-reclined position. Any mistake when securing himself, or losing consciousness during the flight, could have sent him falling to the ground.
16 kilometres
Russian FPV anti-aircraft drones meant the cargo drone could not fly alone. Slow and bulky, with a payload suspended beneath it, it would be immediately spotted by Russian reconnaissance. The headquarters planned a diversionary manoeuvre to draw attention away from it.
Several formations helped provide cover for the operation. Alongside the 2nd Battalion of the 30th Mechanised Brigade, units from the 14th and 43rd Separate Mechanised Brigades took part, as did personnel and equipment from the 10th Army Corps. The day before the flight, the neighbouring units involved suggested putting it off because there was no fog. But the forecast showed no fog was expected any time soon, so the command decided to go ahead.
"We studied enemy drone activity to find the time when it was at its lowest. We decided to fly at first light, as night gave way to day," explains Alex, the battalion's reconnaissance chief.
The main diversion was carried out by Vampire heavy bomber drones, which flew into neighbouring sectors simultaneously to draw the attention of Russian anti-aircraft drone operators. The Russians shot down one Vampire, but the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 carrying out the evacuation went unnoticed.
Alex spent 48 hours studying data on Russian assets around the planned mission area. Experts from the 3rd Army Corps also helped prepare the Ayudag's electronic warfare system for the flight.
An Autel quadcopter operated by the battalion provided visual cover for the Ayudag-6, giving the crew a pair of eyes in the sky. However, it struggled to keep pace with the faster evacuation drone. A Ukrainian Lucky Strike drone waited nearby, ready to ram any Russian reconnaissance or strike UAVs that appeared. As the aircraft carrying Magura returned, artillery from the 10th Army Corps delivered concentrated suppressive fire against the identified launch points used by Russian drone operators.
Headquarters had a backup plan in case the drone malfunctioned or was shot down over the left bank of the Oskil River. Reconnaissance teams and ground robot crews were standing by near the designated emergency landing sites, ready to respond.
The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 relied on Starlink for communications, which kept Russian electronic warfare systems from jamming it. No interference was detected on the control links. The drone's altitude was adjusted to suit the terrain, and it took a different route back to prevent the Russians from identifying its outbound flight path.
The drone was in the air for less than an hour and a half. The operator spoke to the wounded soldier through the drone's onboard camera and microphone.
The drone could not cover the full 16 km on a single charge: carrying a person drained its batteries too quickly. Two ground support teams were deployed along the route in advance to provide the necessary support.
"On command, I flew to a waypoint, where the team changed the batteries. Then I continued to the evacuation point, picked up the wounded soldier and flew him back," says Chornyi, who piloted the evacuation drone.
At the transfer point, the wounded soldier was detached from the winch. The next leg of the evacuation was carried out by a Peacemaker ground robotic system, as using vehicles would have risked exposing the operation to the enemy.
The troops camouflaged the platform and laid mattresses in its cargo compartment. The remotely controlled Peacemaker then covered another 8 km off-road. Once in a safe area, the team transferred Kostiantyn to a vehicle and took him to a frontline stabilisation point for emergency surgery. The Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 returned to base intact after a battery change at a stop along the route.
Kostiantyn told Ukrainska Pravda: "The flight went smoothly. I spent most of the time looking at the terrain below. When I landed, I felt safe and relieved – I'd finally be able to see my family soon. A special thank you to my unit clerk, Livsha, for keeping me well supplied with treats."
Despite the soldier's calm assessment, the actual flight revealed issues that had been difficult to anticipate during training with a dummy load. He had not been given protective goggles, so the powerful airflow beneath the rotors and the headwind caused discomfort. However, this did not detract from the mission's overall success.
Alex also credited Kostiantyn's calmness during boarding with helping make the mission a success. He had to get onto the drone in an open area while its rotors were spinning above him.
"The soldier was exceptionally quick-thinking and determined to survive," he said. "We had already dropped off his equipment and instructions. When the quadcopter approached, he did everything exactly as instructed, as quickly as possible. There was no panic or hesitation – the whole thing took just seconds and went exactly to plan."
The future of aerial evacuation
One successful operation does not make aerial evacuation a regular option, nor can it replace ground-based evacuation. Missions like this require extensive preparation and coordinated support from multiple units. This operation involved reconnaissance, artillery, decoy-drone crews and ground teams. Without them, the aircraft carrying the wounded soldier would have been shot down by the first Russian interceptor drone on its way.
The drone's developers take a similar view. Gurzuf Defence says the risks to a casualty's life during flight are simply too high for aerial medical evacuation to become standard practice.
"We don't see aerial evacuation becoming routine," says Pavlo Feldblium, co-founder of Gurzuf Defence. "When people talk about thousands of such missions or suggest that drones could help meet the 'golden hour', I think of the science fiction of Ray Bradbury or Stanisław Lem. You can't launch an operation like this on the spur of the moment. Every mission is unique and has to be planned around the specific conditions on that section of the front line. It's important to understand that this is always a last resort."
The experience of rescuing Magura, however, has prompted changes to drone development. Gurzuf Defence has decided to equip its mass-produced Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 logistics drones with the technical modifications and mounting kits needed for emergency evacuations, enabling them to be used for rescue missions when necessary.
The company stresses, however, that the evacuation equipment will not necessarily be used on every flight: the drone remains primarily a logistics platform. The developers are also working on entirely new variants of the platform with a substantially higher payload capacity.
The operation has shown that wounded soldiers can be evacuated by air even if they cannot walk and are stranded in remote positions. Other manufacturers are also exploring this capability. SkyFall recently unveiled its StarGate evacuation drone.
This evacuation, carried out by the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade and the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, has proved the viability of the concept and highlighted the urgent need for an evacuation method that can be used when all other options fail. Magura's rescue has set a precedent for saving lives in situations where conventional evacuation is impossible.
Kostiantyn "Magura" Vlasenko, who held a position on the left bank of the Oskil River for 491 days despite losing both feet, has been nominated for the title of Hero of Ukraine.
After Magura was evacuated to the rear, the commander of the 10th Army Corps visited him in hospital and personally presented him with the Order of Bohdan Khmelnytskyi, 3rd Class. The infantryman had been awarded the order in May, while still holding his position. Soldiers from the 2nd Mechanised Battalion of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade, who planned and carried out the aerial evacuation, have also been nominated for state awards.
Representatives of Gurzuf Defence – the manufacturer of the very Ayudag-6 that flew him out of hell – also visited Magura in hospital.
Yurii Denysiuk

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Russia expects that the election of a new UN Secretary-General will rid the organization’s Secretariat of Western dictate and "backroom deals," Kirill Logvinov, Director of the Department for International Organizations at the Russian Foreign Ministry, said on the occasion of United Nations Day.
"Serious problems within the UN’s operations cannot be ignored. Every effort must be made to restore a spirit of collegiality to the organization’s work, ensure strict adherence to the principles of its Charter in their entirety and interconnectedness, adapt UN mechanisms to today’s polycentric realities, abandon backroom deals in favor of honest and mutually respectful dialogue, strengthen the voice of the Global South, and rid the Secretariat of Western dictate. Logvinov emphasized that the UN is currently experiencing a "profound systemic crisis." "There is a growing tendency toward the politicization of the Secretariat’s work, the bureaucratization of decision-making mechanisms, inefficient budget spending, interference in the internal affairs of states, and the promotion of a neoliberal agenda. It is evident that a number of states are driven by an unrestrained desire to use the UN not to seek collective solutions, but solely to push through their own narrow, self-serving interests. As a result, the organization’s prestige and effectiveness are suffering significantly," the diplomat noted.
"We will continue to strive in every possible way for the full restoration of the UN’s authority and standing, so that its constructive potential may be realized to the fullest," he stated.
The term of Antonio Guterres, who has led the UN since 2017, expires on December 31, 2026. Members of the Security Council will select a candidate to recommend for the top UN post, after which the General Assembly will hold a vote to officially elect the new UN Secretary-General. As Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov previously emphasized, Moscow does not express preferences regarding specific candidates, maintaining that the key requirement is for the candidate to meet the criteria of professionalism and impartiality.
