Why Australia's falling birth rate is everyone's problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:33:47 UTC
04:33:47 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
"I had my baby at 38," says Heer Kaur, an Indian migrant living in Beveridge, north of Melbourne, who had always imagined having a big family.
But the reality of building a life in a new country, establishing a career and raising a child without family support meant rethinking that dream.
Kaur eventually decided to have just one child, weighing her desire for a large family against the financial and practical demands of parenthood.
"As migrants, we have to rebuild everything in the new country. I kept postponing marriage or having children for later. I wanted to be settled first. Be a permanent resident, build a career, have some stability," she tells SBS Punjabi.
"I wanted to have at least two kids. I assumed I would be able to have kids whenever I tried. But that was not the case."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
SBS News has withheld her real name for privacy reasons.
Kaur says the lack of family support in Australia also meant spending more on childcare.
More money spent on childcare meant having to work longer to earn more, and then less time with my child. Then I had to settle for a quality life for my son, even though it meant him being an only child.
"The compromise comes with guilt as a parent. We work hard to ensure he learns social skills, how to share, and has a network of his own, beyond us."
She says she hopes the family she built was the result of her own choices, not dictated by social and economic circumstances.
Kaur's experience reflects a wider question facing Australia: what happens when the family people want, and the family they can afford, are not the same?
Kaur is not alone in finding herself at this crossroads.
The Treasury's Intergenerational Report (IGR) 2026 puts Australia's total fertility rate at a historic low of 1.48 births per woman, lower than the total fertility rates projected in previous IGRs.
The replacement-level fertility rate — the rate at which a population replaces itself over time without migration — is about 2.1 births per woman.
The report projects that Australia's fertility rate will decline further to 1.34 births per woman by 2065–66.
It identifies delayed childbearing as a key factor contributing to smaller families and lower fertility rates.
Why are Australians delaying having kids?
The IGR identifies establishing a career as one reason people delay parenthood. It also points to access to childcare, the burden of unpaid care, housing security, and workplace flexibility as factors influencing people's decisions about whether to start a family or have more children.
The trend towards later childbearing is not unique to Australia.
In 2023, more than one in three births worldwide were to women aged 30 and over, compared with about one in four in 1990.
However, experts say delayed parenthood is only part of the picture. Financial pressures, changing social expectations and individual circumstances can also shape decisions about family size. The reasons vary, and lower fertility rates do not necessarily mean that everyone wants more children but is unable to have them.
But as Australia's fertility rate falls and its population ages, the implications extend beyond individual families.
The IGR warns that if birth rates and migration fall below baseline expectations, Australia's population would be 1.9 million smaller and the economy 7.4 per cent smaller by 2065–66.
And with deaths projected to outnumber births by the 2060s, migration is expected to play an increasingly important role in sustaining population growth and meeting workforce needs.
Australia's growing reliance on migration
Migrants already make up a large and growing share of the health care and social assistance workforce.
The IGR notes that migration can help moderate population ageing as new migrants are "typically younger than the existing population".
Demographer Liz Allen says Australia's ageing population and below-replacement fertility rate mean the country will rely more on migration to support its workforce and economy.
"Australia is on the way to what's considered super-aged. It essentially means that, in proportion speaking, we have more people aged over 65 than we have young people," she tells SBS Punjabi.
"Currently, we rely on individual income taxpayers to contribute to the economy; with an ageing population and below-replacement-level fertility, we have a shrinking relative working-age population. That means fewer tax dollars coming from that biggest source of taxpayers, individual workers."
At the moment, migrants present the biggest share of population growth in this country. And that's because the local population isn't growing the way it used to.
Allen says migration also brings social and cultural benefits alongside its economic contribution.
The IGR found new migrants are typically younger than the existing population, with a median age of 26 compared with 38 in 2024-25. As a result, migration helps slow population ageing and increases the share of working-age people beyond what would be achieved through natural increase alone.
Do migrants have more children?
Research by the University of Melbourne's demographer Peter McDonald shows that temporary migrants are predominantly young adults aged 20 to 35, many of whom come to Australia to study or establish their careers. While they are included in the population's childbearing age group, they contribute relatively few births.
Allen says migrants can also adopt the fertility patterns of their new country, which "in some cases, means even have lower fertility rates than the local population".
"Upon arrival in Australia, many migrants prioritise work and education, which delays family formation into their late 30s or beyond. This trend mirrors the broader patterns seen in the Australian population," she says.
For Adelaide-based freelance photographer Naina Redhu, moving to Australia meant meeting her partner, Jamie. While she says she is happy with her partner, neither of them wants to have children.
The 46-year-old says she has always been clear that she doesn't want children. Yet the decision has often prompted questions and unsolicited advice, including suggestions that she freeze her eggs as a precaution.
"My ex-husband and I were clear that we did not want children, but later, he did want to have kids some years down the line," she tells SBS Punjabi.
This is a fundamental choice; it narrates what kind of life you are choosing for yourself.
"I think it is selfish to have kids, and we ended up parting ways."
Redhu says not having a child doesn't mean she takes motherhood lightly.
"I believe parenting is a 24X7 commitment for the rest of your life. For someone like me, it would mean putting everything aside and being completely focused on raising the child, and I am not ready for that commitment yet," she says.
"There are so many things that I have to do and still want to do."
The barriers to having children
Allen says Australia should focus less on achieving an ideal number of children and more on removing hurdles that prevent people from having the families they want.
"We need to reach a point where having a much-wanted child, or a second child, is truly possible and not obstructed by barriers that feel insurmountable. Otherwise, the consequences ripple across society," she says.
She warns that smaller families may also have broader social consequences, including greater pressure on individuals to provide care for ageing relatives or fewer family connections to rely on.
Ultimately, having a child is not just a mother's responsibility; it is a societal concern.
"Until we address major challenges including housing affordability, economic security, climate change, and gender equality, Australians may lack the confidence and hope needed to plan for the future."

Air Force Considering Air-to-Air Role for Bombers amid Fighter Procurement Constraints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:29:17 UTC
04:29:17 KST

The Air Force’s future strategy for fighting wars could include arming bombers with air-to-air strike capabilities, the service said in a new report to Congress.
The report, titled “Long-Term USAF Fighter Force Structure” and submitted to lawmakers Oct. 16, said that “developing air-to-air capabilities on bombers” is being considered as a way to expand the service’s combat capabilities.
In the report, which was briefed to reporters Oct. 20 and obtained by Air & Space Forces Magazine, the Air Force estimates it will need 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035 to meet the demands of the National Defense Strategy at moderate risk, with about 40 percent of its fighter fleet consisting of F-35A Joint Strike Fighters. That’s up from the 1,288 combat-coded fighters the service has today.
The Air Force is working on ways to procure as many Lockheed Martin F-35As, Boeing F-15EX Eagle IIs, and Boeing F-47 sixth-generation fighters as possible, the report said. However, the report acknowledges that hitting its fighter procurement targets may not be achievable due to “fiscal realities and industrial production limitations.”
Other recapitalization options could include acquiring an entirely new fighter, relying more on semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft—and giving air-to-air roles and capabilities to bombers, the report said.
Air Force fighters have long carried out air-to-ground strikes, but bombers have not traditionally performed air-to-air missions.
However, with the Air Force’s fleet constrained by slow procurement of new fighters and the retirement of aging ones, the service has been looking for new ways to accomplish its missions.
Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin signaled an openness to the B-21 Raider stealth bomber carrying out a greater role in the service’s air dominance plans in an October 2024 discussion with reporters in Washington.
At the time, the Air Force had put its F-47 program—then called Next-Generation Air Dominance—on hold amid concerns about its potential costs. The Air Force was reviewing its approach to air superiority to try to figure out ways to get the job done, potentially without the plane that would become the F-47.
When asked if the air superiority review could lead to a more prominent role for the B-21, Allvin said “We have not taken that off the table.”
A year later, in September 2025, sources told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the Air Force was studying whether a large flying wing-type stealth aircraft—potentially based on a B-21—armed with dozens of air-to-air missiles could be an element of its future air superiority force.
In its latest report, the Air Force wrote that it is “committed to the full modernization and recapitalization of its legacy fighter fleet, while placing an enormous effort into our newest fighter, the F-47.”
CCAs are also rapidly advancing and likely to at least meet, if not beat, the program’s schedule, the report said. But the Air Force said CCAs aren’t yet ready to change how the service plans for its future fighter fleet, though that day will come.
“There is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters,” Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, told reporters Oct. 20.
The report also said it will be “essential” to modernize its current cadre of older F-15s and F-16s into a fleet of “advanced fourth-generation capability” jets—planes that do not have stealth capabilities but can still operate in highly contested environments, often with the aid of advanced sensors and electronic warfare weapons.
But it would take more than a decade of investments in the Air Force’s current depot infrastructure to modernize enough jets to increase the Air Force’s aircraft availability, the report said, calling that approach “insufficient, as it perpetuates reliance on a fleet averaging 30+ years in age.”
Aside from upgrading existing fighters, the service could also buy new advanced fourth-gen jets like the F-15EX and, potentially, a new version of Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Fighting Falcon, dubbed the F-16G. Tabor said the service has not yet made any decision on buying new F-16s, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.”
In its report, the Air Force said it has to pursue a two-track strategy of modernizing existing aircraft to meet immediate operational requirements, while recapitalizing its legacy fighters at the same time.

Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:22:42 UTC
04:22:42 KST

Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
Majid Sharifi, an international affairs analyst, told the Iran newspaper that China’s approach toward Iran is not based on identity ties or ideological alignment. As a result, Beijing does not necessarily view stronger relations with Tehran as entering into confrontation with the United States.
 
China defines its ties with Iran within the broader network of its regional relationships and seeks to maintain balance among them. Therefore, the expansion of Tehran-Beijing relations cannot be explained solely by the intentions of the two sides or by existing opportunities for bilateral cooperation. From this perspective, one of the key prerequisites for deeper economic cooperation and stronger political relations is Iran’s achievement of peaceful coexistence and stable ties with neighboring countries. Such a situation could reduce the complexity of China’s strategic calculations and create more favorable conditions for expanding cooperation.
Kayhan: US not seeking negotiations
Kayhan addressed Trump’s unsuccessful effort to force Iran into submission through negotiations. The newspaper wrote that the confrontation between Iran and the United States spans four dimensions: military, economic resilience, diplomacy, and cognitive-psychological warfare. According to the article, the last of these has become the backbone of Washington’s strategy. It argued that the Trump administration, having failed to achieve its goals in reality, has relied heavily on psychological and influence operations. Recent US military movements, while appearing to signal war preparations, were portrayed as part of a broader strategy aimed at creating the illusion of diplomacy and inducing miscalculations among officials and the public. Referring to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and Washington’s repeated violations of its commitments, the paper argued that these experiences demonstrate that the United States is not genuinely interested in real negotiations or meaningful concessions.
Ettelaat: Short but intense
Ettelaat explored the possibility of another military confrontation in the Persian Gulf region. The newspaper argued that the previous round of conflict involving Iran, the United States, and Israel increased energy prices, accelerated global inflation, weakened Middle Eastern security, and placed significant pressure on Pentagon air defense stockpiles. Citing reports from The New York Times, it said that the United States and Israel have prepared plans to resume military operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in early November. According to the article, planning is underway for a short but highly intense operation. Some officials reportedly believe that another large-scale wave of attacks could push Iran’s economy toward crisis and force Tehran to make political concessions. Iranian officials, however, have stated that they are aware of such plans and are developing new targets and tactics in response. Tehran has also warned that any future conflict would not be brief and could extend to infrastructure in the region, including submarine internet cables and major Saudi oil facilities such as Aramco.
Hamshahri: Iran knows how to play the game
Hamshahri argued that the Islamic Republic, through its firm adherence to its principles, has sent a clear message to the White House that it does not trust the United States. According to the article, Trump and Netanyahu openly speak of weakening or destroying Iran, while soaring energy prices have become the main source of pressure on Trump. Rising oil prices have increased diplomatic activity by mediators seeking engagement with Tehran. The paper suggested that Munir’s recent visit was intended to help stabilize oil markets and provide political relief for Trump ahead of elections. Nevertheless, it argued that the united stance of Iran’s political leaders and senior military officials demonstrated that Tehran fully understands regional power politics. As a result, Munir reportedly left without achieving his objectives.
Sazandegi: America’s strategy through psychological warfare
Sazandegi examined remarks attributed to Trump regarding the possibility of Iranian attacks on cities such as Los Angeles and San Diego. The newspaper argued that, if the statements were accurately reported, they could serve several purposes. First, they may be designed to amplify perceptions of an Iranian threat among the American public and justify confrontational policies or potential military action. Second, they could help rally international allies, increase pressure on Iran, and strengthen support for containment policies. Third, the rhetoric may carry domestic electoral benefits, ranging from reducing voter dissatisfaction to boosting Republican candidates. The article also suggested that such statements could indirectly strengthen the political position of Netanyahu and his allies in Israel. According to Sazandegi, the success of this strategy depends on the credibility of the claims, developments on the ground, and public reaction. It concluded that Iran’s most effective response would be fact-based communication, active diplomacy, and efforts to prevent the country from being portrayed internationally as a threat.

Fatherland Is One of the Most Quietly Surprising Films of the Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:09:12 UTC
04:09:12 KST

The title of Pawel Pawlikowski’s extraordinary, compact drama Fatherland has a double meaning. In this somewhat fictionalized story of Thomas Mann’s brief 1949 visit to Germany, the Nobel Prize-winning author, after having lived in exile in California for 16 years, is challenged with finding his mooring in a country he can no longer call home; if it’s his fatherland, it long ago turned its back on him and his ideals. But fatherland can also be a state of mind where fathers live, a state both more specific and more elusive than fatherhood. In Pawlikowski’s telling of this portion of Mann’s story, it’s during this trip that Mann learns of the death of his son, Klaus—also a writer, though not as successful as his father—by suicide. If the elder Mann feels any emotion when he hears this news, it’s frozen inside him, a bubble of feeling isolated on its own ice floe. Fatherland, so secure in its rigid borders, is a cold, cold place.
Mann’s freedom from this interior island prison happens in the film’s last five minutes, a wordless reckoning that’s as quietly moving as anything you’ll see at the movies this year. But that moment wouldn’t hold so much power if Pawlikowski—with the help of his cowriter, Hendrik Handloegten—weren’t so skilled at sketching in the feathery details leading up to it. Pawlikowski is also the director of the 2013 Ida, as well 2018’s Cold War, pictures that, like this one, deftly balance postwar Eastern Bloc realities with the truth that all humans strive for connection and belonging. These aren’t dour movies, but serious, lustrous ones, less “political” pictures than movies about people trying to sort out what living really means.
At the beginning of Fatherland, no one—not even the aged Mann, played here in a quietly extraordinary performance by Hanns Zischler—has figured that out. The movie opens with a long-distance phone call: Mann’s semi-estranged son Klaus (August Diehl), living in Cannes and clearly in emotional distress, has reached out to his sister Erika—we’ll later realize it’s Sandra Hüller’s voice we hear on the other end of the line. Erika, an actress, writer, and onetime race-car driver, has become her father’s assistant, and she now urges Klaus to join her and their father on the trip they’re about to undertake, from California to the “new” barely postwar Germany. In the year of Goethe’s 200th birthday, Mann will be accepting two awards, one in Frankfurt, in the West, the other in the East, in Weimar: his justification is that his literary idol was born in one city and died in the other, though it’s obvious that Goethe couldn’t have imagined that chasm that would open between the two within 200 years' time.
Both cities are in transition, and in crisis, though neither wants to admit as much. In Frankfurt, a gray city crumbling at the corners and still finding its footing after the war, though somehow doing its best to pretend all is well, Mann and Erika are greeted by the mayor and hustled off to a press conference. There, the esteemed man himself answers the respectful but probing questions of journalists. Once they learn that he’ll also be traveling to the East, it’s not lost on them that doing so could make him a target at home in the States, where anti-Communist storm clouds have long been gathering. And there are other, more spiritual questions for him to consider. An American journalist, a woman who, it turns out, is an old friend of Erika’s and possibly a former lover (she’s played by Anna Madeley), asks him where he feels his true home is, now that he’s an American citizen. His answer is courtly but honest. He may live in the United States, he says, “but where my Heimat is, my home, is a much more difficult question.” He’s a man between states, both literally and figuratively.
In Weimar, the chief way to welcome a returning hero is apparently to greet him with a somber folk song sung by a choir dressed in dark clothing; at one point, he’s serenaded by a group of children singing the then-newly pened East German national anthem. Mann accepts it all gracefully, but there’s also something a bit quizzical and lost in his expression. He’s jarred by one alarming moment: a wild-eyed man appears at the hotel suite where he and Erika are staying, begging him to reveal in his speech that the nearby former concentration camp Buchenwald is now being used as a detention center for political prisoners. The man is whisked way by officials before he can finish his spiel, though it’s doubtful any of it has swayed Mann at all. In both the East and West, when it’s time to address the audiences who have eagerly gathered to hear his thoughts, he gives heartfelt speeches, anchored in the legacy of Goethe, about the power of art to transform and sustain not just individuals, but whole nations. He seems to truly believe, as he says at one point, that art doesn’t recognize borders—or at least, he truly wants to believe it.
Through all of this, Hüller’s Erika serves her father dutifully. When necessary, she translates his responses to journalists into fluid French; she attends cocktail parties in his honor, even when it means suffering the indignity of running into an oily, traitorous, Nazi-loving ex-husband she’d rather forget forever; she drives her father through the countryside, and though we can’t see her face as she does so, we wonder if this particular task gives her some joy, given her car-racing past. But through it all, because Hüller is such a subtly expressive actor, almost gossamer in the ways she shifts moods, we see the ways in which her resentments toward her father can’t help simmering to the surface. When she learns of her beloved brother’s death, her composure doesn’t crumple visibly—only somehow we know her emotional reserves are folding in and flattening like a house of cards. And when she sees how little this event seems to trouble her father, she can barely go through the motions of helping him on his mission, which, as he seems to envision it, is to save his homeland with his lofty views on art.
How these two find their way back to one another, and to a place of acknowledged and shared grief, is a kind of unspoken miracle that unfolds in last 15 minutes or so of this elegant, remarkably economical movie. Artistically and emotionally, Fatherland accomplishes more in its 82-minute runtime than any two-hour-plus movie released this year. Cinematographer Lukasz Zal, who also shot Ida and Cold War, renders Fatherland in the same satiny black and white, as well as the same serenely squarish, or Academy, aspect ratio. Every frame is spare, elegant, intimate, and the film moves along so gracefully that you’re barely prepared for how exhilarating, and how quietly devastating, its final moment is. At one point, Hüller’s Erika tells her father that Klaus had once said he felt Bach made him feel life was worth living. Her father shrugs that information off, but the final moments of Fatherland—incorporating a serendipitous conjuring, like a specter, of “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring”—bring it back to him. Can a person have more than one Heimat? Or can that place of spiritual belonging shift over time? Perhaps Bach had the answer. Perhaps he put it in a piece of music, for us to find when we most need it, in a church or even in a movie.

Palestinian fighters kill 2 Israeli soldiers in fierce Al-Khalil confrontation
TEHRAN — Two Palestinian fighters from Al-Khalil (Hebron) held off Israeli troops for more than 20 minutes on Friday morning, killing two occupying soldiers before they were martyred at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint on the city’s northern edge.
The fighters were Hamouda and Firas al-Jaabah, both 27, from the same family, each married with two children. Shortly after 7:30 a.m., they stepped out of their car at the junction Israel calls “Judea Junction” and opened fire on a Home Front Command unit.
The army named its dead as Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem and admitted to three lightly wounded, though early Hebrew-media reports counted six wounded. The Israeli military concedes it had no warning.
Hamas called it a “heroic operation” without claiming it. In its statement, the movement described the attack as the living embodiment of a steadfast people’s will and a message that resistance will only grow stronger until the occupation is driven from the land and the holy sites.
It described the operation as the natural, legitimate answer to the occupation’s crimes in the West Bank and al-Quds (Jerusalem) and its continuing war on Gaza.
Hamas also called for total mobilization in every city, village and camp to ignite the ground beneath settlers and invaders. Every Palestinian who bears arms, it said, should aim them at soldiers and settlers.
The al-Qassam Brigades praised the attack, Islamic Jihad’s al-Quds Brigades urged further confrontation, and the PFLP and DFLP welcomed it. Hezbollah saluted Hamouda and Firas and described the operation as a response to Israeli killing, genocide, destruction and desecration of holy sites.
Netanyahu arrived in Al-Khalil (Hebron) with War Minister Israel Katz and announced what the city would get. “We will act to destroy this place,” he said, promising to evacuate the neighborhood, search house to house, and apply the method used in the northern refugee camps, whose destruction displaced thousands in 2025.
Katz put it in these words: “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron.” By afternoon, bulldozers were working, and a soldier gave one housing complex five minutes to get out.
Residents told Reuters the homes had no connection to the attackers. Hebron and Halhul sit under cordon, the Ibrahimi Mosque has been shut and its staff expelled, according to the Palestinian Awqaf Ministry, and relatives of the martyrs were arrested.
Involved in the campaign while the elections are close, Netanyahu also floated an operation “on a scale unseen since the Six-Day War,” then trimmed his full West Bank closure to a cordon around two cities.
He accused Israel’s enemies of timing attacks to sway the vote. The territory was due to be sealed for Tuesday’s election anyway.
Bezalel Smotrich ordered demolitions, and he and Itamar Ben-Gvir demanded the Palestinian Authority be dismantled.
Hebron has lived under this logic since 1994, when a settler massacred worshippers at the Ibrahimi Mosque and Israel’s answer was to hand settlers half of it and split the city.
Smotrich moved this year to revoke parts of the Hebron agreements. Palestinian monitors logged 647 settler attacks in September alone.

Kushner’s hacked iPhone exposed billions in secret Saudi and Emirati money

Kushner’s hacked iPhone exposed billions in secret Saudi and Emirati money
TEHRAN — Dutch military hackers sat inside Jared Kushner’s iPhone in 2018 and watched him log in to a Dubai bank account that had taken in hundreds of millions of dollars, according to a new book by journalist Matthew Cole.
The account was allegedly one of at least two through which Abu Dhabi and Riyadh gave Donald Trump’s son-in-law access to about $2 billion while he steered Middle East policy from the White House.
Cole’s excerpt, published October 22 in Vanity Fair, starts with a GRU operative who specialized in stolen bank data. The Dutch MIVD learned he was headed for Britain, got London’s permission to seize him on arrival, and gave him a choice between working for The Hague and facing espionage charges.
He chose The Hague. In late 2017, he opened a GRU server in Rostov, where the Dutch found screenshots of Kushner’s iPhone X.
The MIVD reverse-engineered the Russian break-in. By early 2018 its team could watch Kushner’s screen whenever he used the phone.
Dutch press reported they spent years inside the Cozy Bear hacking group and fed the Americans warnings. This time the target worked in the White House.
Alpha, Beta and a defense fund
On that screen, Cole writes, was a First Abu Dhabi Bank account that Kushner signed for but did not own.
It belonged to the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a state-funded Emirati “charity” that Cole says doubled as cover for covert weapons purchases abroad.
Roughly $750 million in cash reportedly entered through Azerbaijan, a channel that Cole says was used to conceal the money’s origins in the Arab monarchies of the Persian Gulf.
The ruling Arab families had initially floated a fund exceeding $10 billion to advance Trump’s foreign policy agenda, before settling on accounts for Kushner. “Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” one source told Cole.
A second account, Beta, allegedly held about $1 billion in Israel’s Central Bank by spring 2018. Netanyahu supposedly demanded notice of any transfer, relayed through Ambassador David Friedman, and much of the money later went to Cyprus.
A third deposit was reportedly earmarked for Israeli assistance to the UAE in countering Iran. Cole says the Dutch probably saw only Alpha.
In return for these financial commitments, Kushner backed Abu Dhabi and Riyadh’s regional demands from inside the White House and helped negotiate a secret defense pact committing Israeli military aid to provide military backing to the UAE.
Four senior Trump officials, among them two national security advisers, a chief of staff and a former CIA director, told Cole they knew of no presidential approval for Kushner to use a foreign government account.
A former Mueller prosecutor told him any promise made in return for the money could break bribery and foreign agent laws. House Oversight Democrats say Kushner must answer before the American people.
A marketplace, and Iran across the table
In 2018, The Intercept reported that Mohammed bin Salman bragged to Mohamed bin Zayed that Kushner was “in his pocket.”
Months after leaving office, Kushner took $2 billion from the Saudi sovereign fund for Affinity Partners, over a screening panel’s finding that its due diligence was “unsatisfactory in all aspects.” Rep. Jamie Raskin has since put Affinity’s assets at $6.16 billion.
Cole’s account paints a stark picture of how Washington, Tel Aviv and the Arab monarchies in the Persian Gulf operate behind closed doors.
Israel wanted “normalization” with the Arab states on its own terms. Mohamed bin Zayed and his Israeli allies wanted the 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA) blown up. Mohammed bin Salman wanted the crown.
Kushner, an unpaid White House adviser with signing rights on an Emirati account, sat at the center of all three demands. Trump pulled out of the Iran deal in May 2018, in the very months the Dutch say they were watching that account.
On the book’s account, the strategy against Iran and the wider Resistance ran on secret slush funds, dark money and a corruption so routine that one source told Cole the Arab rulers in the Persian Gulf spend a billion or two on such arrangements every year.
The reports in Cole’s book date from Trump’s first term. In the second, the money may no longer need hidden accounts, because it moves through deals in plain view.
A $2 billion Emirati investment was tied to the Trump family’s USD1 stablecoin. Steve Witkoff met Tahnoon Bin Zayed on a yacht off Sardinia, and months later the White House moved to ease AI chip exports to Tahnoon’s G42.
David Sacks, the administration’s AI and crypto czar, received an ethics waiver to join those talks despite earlier fund ties to Persian Gulf investors. Tahnoon is the same man who chaired First Abu Dhabi Bank when, Cole says, the Alpha account was filling up.
What has emerged is a marketplace where Saudi and Emirati money, Israeli strategic interests and a president’s son-in-law met behind closed doors and conspired.
That same son-in-law is now a White House envoy deeply involved in Washington’s regional misadventures, including the war on Iran. Tehran has every reason to ask who he really works for.

“Land of Angels” competing in 14th Asian Film Festival Barcelona
TEHRAN – Babak Khajehpasha’s “Land of Angels” has been selected for the official section of the 14th Asian Film Festival Barcelona (AFFBCN), which was launched in Barcelona, Spain, on October 22 and will run until November 1.
The film tells the story of the suffering of children in Gaza and portrays the human consequences of war through the experiences of a woman who struggles to survive while protecting a group of innocent children from the horrors of conflict, ILNA reported.
Amid the bombings and military offensive in Palestine, the story follows the painful and courageous journey of a woman trapped on the front line. As everything collapses around her, the protagonist takes on the dangerous task of surviving the war while trying to protect, feed, and guide a vulnerable group of innocent children, keeping them safe from the horrors of armed conflict. Through her perspective, the feature film becomes a deeply human portrait of the instinct to protect, the loss of childhood innocence, and civilian resilience under extreme conditions.
The film features Arab actors and centers on the lives, dreams, and struggles of children against the backdrop of the war in Palestine. Rather than presenting the conflict solely through political or military events, the film approaches it from the perspective of civilians, particularly children whose lives have been profoundly affected by the violence.
The production was filmed in Tehran over a period of one and a half years. The film’s international screenings began with its participation in the Kazan festival, following its successful national festival run in Iran.
“Land of Angels” received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film at the 22nd Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival.
Prior to its appearance in Kazan, “Land of Angels” was the most decorated film at Iran’s 44th Fajr International Film Festival, where it received five Crystal Simorgh awards and eight honorary diplomas.
Among its Fajr honors, Khajehpasha received the jury’s special prize for directing, while Syrian actress Sulaf Fawakherji was honored for her performance. The film also received awards for set design, visual effects, and other categories.
Babak Khajehpasha is a director and screenwriter. Following a solid career in television, he achieved immediate international critical recognition with his debut feature film, “In the Arms of the Tree” (2023), a drama on family fractures that was officially selected to represent Iran at the Academy Awards.
With “The Land of Angels” (2026), Khajehpasha takes on the roles of screenwriter and director to deliver a humanitarian drama focused on civilian victims of contemporary conflicts in the Middle East. It has also been officially selected as Iran’s submission to the 99th Academy Awards in the best international feature film category.
The Asian Film Festival Barcelona is organized by Casa Asia. True to its commitment to promoting contemporary Asian cinema, the festival presents more than one hundred films representing the latest independent, experimental and auteur cinema from across the continent.
The selection brings together works from 25 countries in the Asia-Pacific region, mostly produced between 2025 and 2026.
This edition pays particular attention to emerging film industries in countries such as Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Mongolia, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Cambodia, as well as established industries with a long history at the festival, including Iran, India, China, South Korea, Japan, and the Philippines.
The program also includes films from Hong Kong, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, as well as productions from Australia and New Zealand.
According to its director, Menene Gras Balaguer, AFFBCN aims to establish itself as a leading international showcase for Asian cinema and to continue attracting new audiences. “We want more and more viewers to discover the vitality and talent of these film industries and to help ensure that their growing recognition translates into a greater presence in cinemas and at festivals. We are committed to cinema that brings us closer to the cultural diversity of Asia and invites us to understand the world from other perspectives.”

IRGC Spokesman: US has suffered strategic defeats in war with Iran
TEHRAN— Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), says the United States has suffered a series of strategic defeats in its war with Iran, including setbacks to its claims of safeguarding regional security and ensuring the uninterrupted flow of energy.
In remarks published on Friday, Mohebbi said the adversary initially sought to change Iran’s political system and break up the country before scaling back its ambitions into 13 more limited objectives, none of which it had achieved.
He said the war had undermined Washington’s longstanding assertion that its military presence in the region was essential to maintaining security. Despite its extensive naval capabilities and network of regional military bases, the United States had faced serious challenges in ensuring security and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, he added.
Mohebbi described the situation as a fundamental contradiction in US military doctrine, arguing that bases established in the name of providing security had instead become sources of insecurity.
He also said the conflict had called into question Washington’s claims of intelligence superiority, exposing vulnerabilities in US intelligence centers and military bases.
The targeting of US fighter jets, the destruction of air defense systems and operations against American naval assets had further undermined Washington’s assertions of technological and military superiority, the IRGC spokesman said.
Mohebbi also pointed to damage to the United States’ international reputation, saying the Jeffrey Epstein case had already tarnished the country’s image and that the targeting of the Minab school and the killing of children had further damaged its standing.
His remarks linked the consequences of the war to broader questions about Washington’s credibility and its international conduct. Turning to the economic fallout, Mohebbi cited rising fuel prices and the United States’ need for raw materials, including aluminum, as signs of mounting economic pressure resulting from the conflict.
He presented these developments as further evidence of the war’s costs for Washington, alongside the military and diplomatic setbacks he outlined.
Concluding his remarks, Mohebbi praised the Iranian people for their resilience throughout the period of resistance, describing their achievements as remarkable and worthy of recognition.
He said the public’s steadfastness had been a significant factor in confronting the challenges posed by the war.

Strange triangular craft reported in new U.S. government UFO release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:03:30 UTC
04:03:30 KST

The Pentagon released yet more documents related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) on Friday.
This is the seventh tranche of records released since May, though, unlike previous releases, there are no videos or images included. Instead the latest trove is an assortment of memos and reports of encounters with possible UAP.
The most in-depth account is a report from this year in which multiple federal law enforcement agents in an undisclosed location witnessed a UAP “presenting as a matte black triangular shape of extremely low aspect ratio.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The object reportedly had a 13- to 15-foot wingspan, measured about six to nine feet in length and had a thickness of one to two feet. According to the agents, the craft was steady as it climbed about 200 or 300 feet into the air above a ridgeline over the course of 10 seconds. At that point, it hovered for another 20 seconds before it flew out of sight at fighter-jet-like speeds into a nearby canyon while hugging the low-lying terrain and executing fluid turns.
The craft didn’t make any of the sounds associated with a fighter jet, however, such as roaring engines or whooshes as it flew through the air. Nor did it display any apparent exhaust plumes or other emissions expected from powered flight. It did show up on an agent’s handheld infrared monocular, however, with a uniform thermal signature across the entire body. According to the report, optical views through binoculars revealed “no propulsive apertures, rotating elements, rivets, panels, windows, canopy, cabin structures, and no protrusions or structural features” on the UAP.
Previous releases have been greeted with skepticism by researchers, who have said that much of what’s been included in those releases was previously seen or had context omitted. But Harvard University professor Avi Loeb, who heads the U.S. government’s UAP Science Advisory Council, said in a blog post that the agents’ newly released story raises questions that could be vital to national defense.
“The fundamental question is whether the triangular object was manufactured in a black project of an adversarial nation or an extraterrestrial project with off-world technology,” he wrote, adding that his current goal for the advisory council is to deploy new sensors in the areas where the UAP were observed.
“As we get higher quality data, we will be able to identify the nature of these mysterious objects,” he wrote. “In collecting better clues, we will either help the Pentagon and the Intelligence Community fulfil their mission of protecting the U.S. from adversaries or discover technology of non-human origin. Investing in the related research is a win-win proposition.”
Friday’s release also included several other witness accounts. Among them was a 1957 Air Force report on an incident involving a B-52 bomber making radar contact with a UAP for five to seven minutes over Saudi Arabia and a 1955 report in which a civilian in California recounted seeing a “very bright and orange” object falling straight down.

The Trump administration is considering a ‘heat ray’ weapon for the border—here’s what to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:03:21 UTC
04:03:21 KST

The Pentagon has granted the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a controversial and little-used “heat ray” weapon at the U.S.-Mexico border, prompting questions over how safe it is and how it works.
The weapon is called the Active Denial System, and it is considered a nonlethal weapon: it causes pain but is not supposed to damage tissue. It works using millimeter waves, which—true to their name—have wavelengths between one and 10 millimeters. Millimeter waves are also used in full-body scanners, such as those in airports—but the military weapon puts out its 95-gigahertz waves at a higher intensity for just a few seconds at a time, says Kenneth Foster, a professor emeritus of bioengineering at the University of Pennsylvania.
This energy penetrates about 0.4 mm, the thickness of about four sheets of standard printer paper, of the skin, where it excites water molecules in cells and heats them up. The feeling is reportedly similar to standing in front of a hot oven. “It causes intense pain, but the exposure is not long enough to do damage,” Foster says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
If the weapon is used at the border, it will mark one of the few uses of this technology ever since its development in the early 2000s, as CNN reported on Wednesday. According to the nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), the system was used briefly in Afghanistan in 2010 but has not been employed in warfare since then. Prison officials in Los Angeles considered testing the device for riot control in 2010, yet pushback from civil rights groups and the Federal Communications Commission led to the program being scrapped.
“The weapon is politically toxic,” Foster says.
The system is bulky and temperamental; it doesn’t work well in rain, fog or mist because the moisture attenuates the heating effect on the targeted person. Foster suspects that the system’s cost, expense and bulk have a lot to do with why it hasn’t been used more; other nonlethal methods such as sound cannons are cheaper and more available, he says.
Persistent concerns about the safety of something that sounds suspiciously like a microwave oven are also a barrier. Microwaves, with their longer wavelengths, penetrate farther into skin and can cause more damage. Military testing suggests that exposure to millimeter-wave nonlethal weapons does not cause skin damage. Tests on volunteers in 2005 and 2006 did lead to a handful of people getting skin blisters and rashes, however. An incident in 2007 in which the weapon was set at the incorrect power and pulse duration led to one airman receiving second-degree blistering burns on 8 percent of his body. So it is possible that improper usage could cause injury.
“There is very, very little published on these weapons,” says Rohini Haar, an emergency physician at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Public Health and a medical adviser at PHR. Without published research, she says, there is little information on their safety in general or on potential differences in safety in real-world usage versus experimental or training exercises.
John Erath, Senior Policy Director for the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation, a nonprofit, points out that testing such weapons in human trials for safety is “an ethical dead-end.”
PHR has also documented numerous cases of crowd-control weapons being used against people with no easy way to escape. Indiscriminate use of the system could cause injury not just from the heat itself but also from the reaction of those targeted, says Michael Crowley. He is a senior researcher at the U.K.-based nonprofit Omega Research Foundation, which tracks the use of military and police weapons and human rights abuses.
“Given its silent and invisible nature, the ‘pain ray’ makes avoidance of the weapon difficult, which could prevent people from dispersing safely, lead to panic-driven stampedes and consequent serious injuries,” Crowley says.
“Furthermore, those subsequently injured or crowd members who have existing mobility difficulties, including the elderly and very young, may not be able to leave the area and then be subject to repeated or prolonged exposure of this weapon, potentially leading to further intolerable pain and serious injuries,” he adds.

Iran calls for end to double standards in IAEA’s implementation of its statute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:58:56 UTC
03:58:56 KST

Iran urges end to double standards in IAEA’s implementation of its statute
TEHRAN — Iran has called on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to end the selective and politically motivated implementation of its founding statute, urging the organization to uphold its legal obligations impartially and ensure equal treatment of all member states.
In a statement issued on Friday, October 23, to mark the 70th anniversary of the adoption of the IAEA Statute, Iran’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations and other international organizations in Vienna stressed that the agency’s founding document must be implemented fully and consistently, without discrimination or political interference.
The mission said the anniversary should serve not merely as an occasion for commemoration but as an opportunity to assess the agency’s adherence to its founding principles, restore institutional accountability and renew its commitment to impartiality.
“The Statute is the Agency’s constitution,” the statement said, emphasizing that it must not be invoked selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful states.
The IAEA’s full mandate
Iran stressed that the agency’s responsibilities extend beyond nuclear safeguards and verification to include promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and advancing international scientific and technical cooperation.
Citing Articles II and III of the Statute, the mission said the IAEA is mandated to expand the contribution of atomic energy to global peace, health and prosperity, support peaceful nuclear research and applications, and ensure that its resources benefit all member states, with particular attention to the needs of developing countries.
The statement warned that an approach focused disproportionately on inspections, at the expense of technical cooperation and peaceful nuclear development, would undermine the agency’s ability to fulfil its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign equality and NPT
The Iranian mission said the principles of sovereign equality and non-discrimination must guide the agency’s dealings with all members, regardless of geopolitical considerations.
It cited Article IV.C, which establishes the sovereign equality of the agency’s members, and Article III.C, which prohibits making assistance conditional on political, economic or military considerations incompatible with the Statute.
As an example of a discriminatory approach, Iran pointed to the scrutiny of its nuclear activities alongside the absence of comprehensive IAEA safeguards covering all nuclear activities of Israel, which is not a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT).
The mission said this disparity raised questions about the consistency and credibility of international nuclear non-proliferation efforts, calling for a comprehensive and non-discriminatory verification framework across the Middle East.
It added that regional security could not be built on selective scrutiny and unequal expectations, stressing that all relevant legal obligations must be applied fairly.
Iran also called for the agency to protect the right of all member states to benefit from peaceful nuclear technology and scientific cooperation.
Independence and institutional credibility
Iran further emphasized the importance of safeguarding the IAEA’s independence, professional integrity and confidentiality.
Referring to Article VII.F of the Statute, the mission said the agency’s director general and staff must remain free from external instructions, while sensitive information obtained in the course of their duties must be protected.
It maintained that the agency’s reports, assessments and decisions should be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal obligations rather than political pressure or selective interpretations. Any misuse of confidential information, it added, could undermine trust and compromise nuclear safety and security.
Reaffirming the importance of credible safeguards and professional verification, Iran said it remained committed to engagement within the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its sovereign rights and interests.
However, the mission stressed that meaningful cooperation required good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the consistent implementation of legal commitments.
It called on the IAEA, particularly its Board of Governors and director general, to end double standards, resist politicization, protect confidential information, condemn attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities and restore the full implementation of its statutory mandate.
The mission also urged the agency to pursue an effective, balanced and non-discriminatory technical cooperation policy, enabling all member states, especially developing countries, to benefit from nuclear science and technology.
Concluding its statement, Iran said the IAEA’s credibility depended not only on its authority to conduct inspections but also on its impartiality, independence, respect for international law and commitment to the legitimate rights of all members.

IRGC Navy chief: US forces have moved 700 kilometers away from Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN— The commander of the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy says US forces have moved 600 to 700 kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz, attributing a retreat from the strategic waterway to the 'sacrifices of Iranian personnel killed in the line of duty.'
Brigadier General Ali Ozmaei made the remarks during visits to the families of Iranian personnel killed in the Ramadan War and in operations related to the Strait of Hormuz. He met the families of martyrs Ghodrat Zarangari, Abbas Eslami, Abdolreza Golzari and Javad Raoufi-Moqaddam at their homes in Bandar Abbas, conveying the message and greetings of Iran’s commander-in-chief.
During the meetings, Ozmaei paid tribute to those killed in the conflict and stressed the importance of continuing their path.
He said the sacrifices of those killed in the Strait of Hormuz had played a decisive role in confronting the United States, describing their actions as a blow to Washington’s regional presence.
‘The US has no place in the Strait of Hormuz’
Referring to the history of foreign powers’ presence in the waterway, Ozmaei said the Strait of Hormuz had once been under the influence of powers including Britain, the United States and Portugal. He argued that the current regional situation was markedly different, asserting that US forces had withdrawn farther from the strait.
“Today, the Americans are not present in the Persian Gulf and have moved 600 to 700 kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that US vessels were no longer visible in the area.
Ozmaei declared that the United States no longer had a place in the strategic waterway, linking Iran’s strengthened position to God's grace and the sacrifices made by those killed in the conflict.
The Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Indian Ocean, is one of the world’s most strategically important maritime passages and a critical route for global energy shipments.
Addressing the families, the IRGC Navy commander expressed respect for their sacrifices and pledged continued support.
He described the families of those killed as a source of pride, saying that serving them would remain a duty for the armed forces.
Ozmaei also reaffirmed his readiness to defend the country, saying he regarded martyrdom in the service of God as his ultimate aspiration.
“If there is a war, we will be there,” he said, asking the families to pray for his martyrdom.
The visits, according to the report, were intended to honor the memory of those killed and reaffirm the IRGC Navy’s commitment to their families and the continuation of their path.

Donc, c'est aussi pour ça qu'on doit tous, d'abord, mettre les bons mots sur ce qui s'est passé. Il faut ensuite élucider la totalité et comprendre, et ça, ça sera dans les mains des magistrats. Mais nous, il faut aussi que derrière ça, il y ait un sursaut. Il y ait un sursaut collectif. Ce sursaut, c'est un sursaut d'unité. Et pour reprendre une formule, il n'est jamais trop tard. Jamais trop tard. Donc, ce à quoi j'appelle chacune et chacun, c'est au respect. C'est à l'unité. C'est aussi que beaucoup de nos compatriotes, je le sais, vont avoir peur demain en se disant, « ça peut m'arriver à moi ». Et ça, c'est non. La police, elle sera là aussi pour les protéger. Je le dis aussi pour beaucoup de jeunes parfois qui pensent que... On a entendu des discours sur la police. C'est aussi pour ça que chacun doit aussi réfléchir après ce qui s'est passé aujourd'hui. C'est nos fonctionnaires de la BAC qui ont arrêté, qui ont protégé, qui ont sauvé des vies. C'est des policières et des policiers municipaux qui, dans les deux communes, sont allés au contact, ont sauvé d'autres vies. C'est ça ce qui s'est passé aussi. C’est ce fil républicain qu'il faut tirer.
Mais ne laissons pas cet attentat terroriste nous diviser. Unité et concorde. Mais aussi, regardons-nous les yeux dans les yeux. Tels que nous sommes tous Français. Compatriotes, concitoyens, enfants de cette République. Et notre responsabilité, c'est de la rendre plus belle, plus grande. Je le disais à cette maman qui pleurait tout à l'heure, qui nous a bouleversés en disant... Moi, chaque jour, on me demande si je suis Française. En raison de ma peau, j'aurais pu mourir parce que ma peau est noire. Ça, ce n'est pas la République et ça, ce n'est pas la France. Parce qu'elle est Française, cette maman. Et qu'elle a sa place ici. Et qu'elle est dans la France, dans la République. Qu'elle n'a pas à se justifier. Mais qu'elle a à pouvoir vivre en paix et élever ses enfants. C'est ça la France et rien d'autre. Je vous remercie.

Iran will not resume talks until its conditions are met: top security official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:48:35 UTC

Iran will not resume talks until its conditions are met: top security official
TEHRAN — Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has stressed that Iran will neither resume negotiations nor reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its seven conditions are met, warning that communications cables, regional data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could be targeted if hostilities resume.
In an interview with Mehr News Agency, Rezaei, who represents the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, addressed recent regional developments and Iran’s position, emphasizing that any action against the country would carry a cost.
“If diplomacy can establish this understanding, we prefer diplomacy,” he said. “But if the war continues, Iran has the necessary capabilities to sustain its response.”
Rezaei noted that Iran had not deployed all its capabilities during previous stages of the conflict. The country had introduced additional capabilities in proportion to the intensity of the fighting, he said, adding that Iran was prepared for the next stage.
Prolonged conflict threatens energy stability
Warning of the broader consequences of continued hostilities, Rezaei said the current situation would have far-reaching strategic implications, including prolonged instability in global energy markets.
“Energy markets will not return to calm for the next three years,” he said.
He also argued that the continuation of the conflict had shifted regional dynamics in Iran’s favor, pointing to a rapid reassessment of relations with Tehran by Persian Gulf states.
According to Rezaei, these countries have come to recognize that the US military is unable to protect even its own bases, despite their expectations that Washington would defend their territories.
US regional assets could be targeted
Rezaei warned that the United States maintains valuable assets across the region that could come under attack if a new war breaks out.
“Cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could also be within range if war resumes,” he said, adding that Iran had a broader plan prepared for a renewed confrontation.
His remarks signaled that a potential escalation could extend beyond conventional military targets to include digital and communications infrastructure.
Strait of Hormuz: Security, not revenue, is the priority
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Rezaei said the strategic waterway was under Iran’s control and that Tehran was managing it.
“Smuggling exists everywhere in the world, but the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he said.
Command (CENTCOM) of leading these operations and said Emirati military forces were also being used.
Rezaei emphasized that Iran’s management of the strait was a strategic national asset and that the issue went well beyond collecting transit fees.
“The main issue is security,” he said, adding that charges could also be levied to cover security, insurance and environmental costs. However, he stressed that the strategic importance of managing the waterway far exceeded any revenue it might generate.
Seven conditions must be met before talks resume
Rezaei said Iran would not return to the previous diplomatic process but would not abandon diplomacy altogether.
According to Rezaei, Iran has conveyed seven new conditions through mediators. He said the country would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to negotiations until those conditions had been implemented.
He outlined a proposed sequence for a new agreement, saying that its structure would itself contain guarantees for compliance.
“First, the commitments must be implemented. Then Iran will decide to reopen the strait, followed by the resumption of maritime traffic under new arrangements agreed upon with Oman,” he said.
Rezaei stressed that Iran was no longer interested in an agreement whose only safeguard was the other side’s political goodwill.
Iran will not relinquish its leverage prematurely
Rezaei said a path remained open to reopening the Strait of Hormuz and continuing diplomacy if Washington honored its commitments.
“Iran will not first give up the leverage that brought the other side to the negotiating table and then wait to see whether its promises are fulfilled,” he said.

UN sounds alarm on besieged Yemen city Taiz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:39:42 UTC
03:39:42 KST

Breadcrumb
UN sounds alarm on besieged Yemen city Taiz
Time is running out to get aid into Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching Yemen's third-largest city, the United Nations said Friday.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognised government.
"Safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access is urgently needed so that essential supplies and life-saving assistance can reach people in need," said the UN humanitarian agency OCHA.
"It's 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off," said OCHA spokesman Jens Laerke.
"We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out," he told a press conference in Geneva.
Laerke said the dwindling water supply was a growing concern, as most residents depended on water brought in by trucks.
"With the roads closed and the diesel to run the trucks very scarce, water production in the city has fallen by about half," he said.
"The cost of the truck water has roughly tripled. You can imagine what that does to these people who are trapped there."
Laerke said that while local humanitarian groups were distributing their remaining supplies, including fuel to keep water pumps and hospitals running, "it comes with a time code: the clock is running out".
"Cooking gas is another item that is largely unavailable, and the shortage is already threatening community kitchens that provide hot meals to families," he added.
Hospitals struggling: WHO
The Houthis, from Yemen's rugged north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, sparking a brutal civil war with a Saudi-led coalition fighting for the government.
The civil war reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.
The World Health Organisation said hospitals in Taiz governorate were struggling to maintain life-saving services, faced with critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and medical supplies.
"With hospital services severely disrupted and stocks running dangerously low, urgent action is needed to sustain life-saving care for thousands of patients," the UN health agency's spokesman Christian Lindmeier said.
"In Taiz city alone, 42 health facilities are reporting acute shortage," he said.
Fuel shortages were threatening oxygen production, emergency transport and vaccine cold chains, he added.
The UN children's agency UNICEF said that in Taiz alone, it had screened more than 168,000 children this year, with over 52,000 found to be acutely malnourished, including more than 11,500 suffering from severe acute malnutrition -- the worst form.
The malnutrition situation "remains extremely concerning", spokesman Ricardo Pires said.

Finding community saved a young Magda Szubanski's life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Magda Szubanski tells how finding community saved her young life
When Magda Szubanski's mother held her newborn daughter for the first time in 1961 she looked at baby Magda, her third child, and announced, "This one's for the world".
Sixty-five years on, after a career in comedy, on Australian TV, stage and movie screens, Mrs Szubanski's prophecy has all but come true with her daughter easily described as a national treasure.
While Szubanski is known for embodying the hilariously accident-prone and eternally optimistic Sharon Strzelecki in Kath & Kim, life hasn't always been a barrel of laughs.
In fact, the opposite was the case when, as a young gay person, she felt the intense isolation of growing up in an era when homosexuality was widely stigmatised.
"Realising I was gay was terrifying," Szubanski told Richard Fidler on ABC Conversations.
"I used to pray that I would not be gay."
With a Polish father and a Scottish mother, Szubanski was raised as a practising Catholic, hearing strict messaging condemning homosexuality.
It was a time when homosexuality was criminalised in many Australian states, and being openly gay could lead to being rejected by your family, friends and community.
Szubanski said the "terror" she felt that her secret would be found out was akin to living under Poland's post-war regime.
"Having been to Warsaw and having seen how circumspect people had to be under communism, that's what it felt like being gay," she said.
"You could not let your face betray anything. It was the most horrible feeling."
As a teenager, while she watched her older sister openly sharing anecdotes about her life with their mother, Szubanski withdrew.
"I wouldn't tell anything because I couldn't let anyone go near it because I knew they might find out," she said.
"I became even more isolated, until I eventually told my sister because I felt suicidal.
"I don't mean I started making plans, but I was just so desperate because I knew more and more that this was my truth and that it was going to, at the very least, have to be suppressed for my whole life, which was a form of misery."
At 17, Szubanski found love and support from opening up to her sister, but, as she has written in her latest memoir, coming out to the rest of her family was too uncertain.
"My parents were born in 1924. How would they react? There was simply no knowing," Szubanski wrote.
"In 1978, reactions to homosexuality were unpredictable like Russian roulette. I simply felt I couldn't risk it."
As an emotional distance from the rest of her family grew, things changed for Szubanski when she started university.
She found refuge and belonging through Melbourne University's Women's Room, and the "terrible shame" she felt about her sexuality subsided.
"When I got into that world, I didn't feel that [shame] so much. In fact, that changed completely," Szubanski told Conversations.
"Melbourne Uni saved me. It really actually saved me … I finally felt safe.
"Losing that intense, terrifying sense of isolation was literally a lifesaver."
Fighting for marriage equality
While Szubanski was openly gay among her comedic peers, it wasn't until Australia's same-sex marriage campaign reignited that she came out publicly.
It was Valentine's Day 2012 when she declared live on Channel 10's The Project that she was "absolutely not straight".
"I wouldn't define myself as bisexual either.
"I would say I am like gay, gay, gay, gay, gay, gay, gay, a little bit not gay, gay, gay, gay, gay."
It was a defining moment in Szubanski's advocacy for marriage equality that made national headlines. Szubanski was met with an outpouring of public support.
"And actually, the number of women who told me they felt incredibly relieved when I said that — because that was their experience — was great," she said.
Five years later, Australians voted in support of same-sex marriage.
Once the vote was passed, Szubanski said she felt "joy" as she celebrated the result.
"It was nothing but relief because we were safe. We were safe with the Australian public behind us," she said.
But for Szubanski, marriage equality is about much more than "love and rainbows".
"It's about helping someone to die. That's the thing that we have never felt safe with," she said.
"If you look at what happened to a lot of gay men during the HIV/AIDS epidemic, the way they were treated when their partner died was horrific, just absolutely discounted.
"It's having the right and the capacity to be able to be there at the worst time … caring for the people that you love."
'I knew something was wrong'
If Szubanski's younger years were marked by keeping a significant part of herself hidden, her experience with cancer was almost the opposite.
"I'd been feeling ill for a really long time," she said. "I knew something was really, really wrong."
After receiving a stage-4 mantle cell lymphoma diagnosis in May last year, a rare and aggressive cancer, Szubanski said she immediately turned to her support network.
"I just got on the phone … texting my friends and calling my friends," she said.
"I was just in complete shock for about two weeks.
"I started realising that it was gonna shorten my life expectancy. We don't know by how much, but at that point, before you've reached remission, it could be pretty drastic."
Her diagnosis was accompanied by something else unexpected.
"I felt — from me — this outpouring of love for my family, my friends and the world," Szubanski said.
"I just felt pure love. And I still feel that a lot of the time."
Loading...
Szubanski says she is now in "deep remission" after completing chemotherapy and won't be doing maintenance therapy.
While her body is weak as she continues recovering, Szubanski says she's feeling like herself again.
"I feel strong in spirit, but physically I'm knackered," she said.
"I had dinner with my friends a few weeks ago, and they went, 'You're back. She's back.'"
With treatment behind her, Szubanski explained how her diagnosis has fundamentally shifted her perspective on life.
"It completely changes everything," she said.
"One is the uncertainty — the fear of relapse — because it's known as an incurable, relapsing cancer.
"And then there's the other thing; of not [having] much time for bullshit. 'Cause cancer is a full-time job."

Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:28:53 UTC
03:28:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say.
Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway.
Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change.
"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States.
She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces.
Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said.
The US-Israeli war against Iran -- launched in late February -- is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote.
"Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it.
"There has to be some kind of a resolution, either through diplomacy or through military action," she said.
Asked about the Iran on Friday, Trump told journalists that "we could end it very quickly," but said the question is "do we want to finish it off, or... do we just want to let it wither?"
Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, meanwhile said Friday that there could "absolutely" be a strike this weekend, ahead of Tuesday's Israeli elections.
'Impossible to predict'
Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen.
He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East -- which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three -- as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region.
Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.
However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table."
Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult.
"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said.
Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population."
But that -- or any type of military action -- is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict.
"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.
Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime."
"They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added.
