Haredi Public's Moti Leitner: Israel’s future is our responsibility, too - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:47:26 UTC
02:47:26 KST

Nearly one in three Jewish children entering first grade in Israel attends a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) school. Some demographic projections suggest that by 2050, almost one in three Jewish Israelis could be haredi.
These figures carry a profound responsibility for our community. The education our children receive, the opportunities available to them, and their contribution to the country will help determine Israel’s future.
We are haredim. Torah learning and religious commitment are central to our lives. We know the challenges facing our community because we live within it. And we believe the responsibility for addressing them belongs to us.
For decades, haredi political leadership has concentrated on protecting Torah learning, religious identity, and communal independence. But the challenges of the coming decades demand a broader understanding of responsibility.
A community must prepare its children for the lives ahead, enable its families to achieve economic independence, and accept its share of responsibility for defending the country.
The future of haredi society and the future of Israel are inseparable. Across haredi society, families are already making choices that reflect this understanding.
Parents are seeking schools that combine serious Torah education with broader learning. Young men outside full-time Torah study are entering employment and military service. Women are seeking a greater voice in decisions affecting their communities and the country.
Nearly 19,000 haredi students were enrolled in higher education in 2024-2025, more than four times the number 15 years earlier. State-haredi schools are providing children with religious education alongside general studies.
These developments are taking place through families, educators, rabbis, and organizations working within haredi society.
The Haredi Public party has emerged from this constituency. Its slogan is simple: “Hapam lokchim achrayut.” This time, we take responsibility.
For us, that begins with education. Children deserve serious Torah learning alongside the knowledge and skills to earn a dignified livelihood, develop their abilities, and contribute to society.
It extends to military service. Those seriously devoting their lives to Torah learning should be able to continue learning. Those who are not seriously learning should share responsibility for defending Israel, within frameworks that respect their religious commitments.
Service is not merely a concession made to secure exemptions for others. The obligation arises because Israel is our country too.
Women already carry enormous responsibilities within haredi society. Their experience and abilities should also find expression in political leadership and in decisions affecting the country.
These commitments describe a haredi life in which religious identity and national responsibility belong together.
A lasting political voice
The Haredi Public is contesting the forthcoming election to give political representation to a constituency already pursuing a broader understanding of responsibility.
Representation in the Knesset would give that constituency a voice in decisions about education, employment, military service, and public policy. It would also give greater political standing to the people and institutions already working for change within haredi society.
The significance extends beyond our community. As the haredi population grows, its education, economic independence, and participation in national defense will increasingly affect Israel as a whole. Government policy matters, but lasting progress also requires people within haredi society who are prepared to take responsibility for these questions themselves.
We believe this undertaking should be understood across Israeli society. The responsibility for leading it belongs within haredi society, while its consequences concern the country we all share.
We have recently been approached about withdrawing from the election. We have no intention of doing so.
Our decision to enter politics reflects a commitment that extends beyond a single campaign. The people whose aspirations we represent are already building their lives around these responsibilities, and their political voice deserves to be heard.
We are here to stay. We are not going anywhere.
The question is no longer whether haredi society will shape Israel’s future. It will. The responsibility we are accepting is to help determine what kind of future that will be.

Israel must stop fighting itself and start winning the information war - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:46:36 UTC
02:46:36 KST

At a time when Israel needs every ounce of creativity, expertise, and influence it can mobilize, the government is wasting energy on internal political attacks instead of building the national effort needed to defend Israel against enemies working daily to delegitimize the world’s only Jewish state.
Israel is fighting on multiple fronts. Some are visible on the battlefield; others unfold on university campuses, in newsrooms, across social media and in foreign governments. Israel’s enemies understand that the battle for international opinion is no sideshow. It shapes Israel’s diplomatic room for manoeuvre, the legitimacy of its military actions and the willingness of allies to stand beside it.
Yet while adversaries invest in coordinated messaging, digital networks and international mobilization, Israel’s response remains fragmented. Talented people work in silos. Initiatives compete rather than cooperate. Resources are dispersed, responsibility is blurred, and too often the response begins only after the damage has been done.
This is more than an organizational failure. Why is so much energy spent defending a political monopoly and conducting smear campaigns when Israel needs a national strategy for the information battlefield?
Why have Israel’s extraordinary ingenuity, technological capability and human talent not been mobilized with equal urgency on the information front? Instead of welcoming expertise, innovation and independent voices, the political establishment appears determined to control who speaks for Israel, treating initiatives outside its orbit as competitors rather than allies.
The treatment of our party, People of Israel, illustrates the concern. When Israel should encourage every serious initiative capable of strengthening its international standing, defending political territory risks taking precedence over national security.
Israel needs credible voices able to reach audiences official representatives cannot; professionals who understand digital communication and media; entrepreneurs developing new tools; and partners in the Jewish world and beyond. Credibility depends on authenticity, which cannot be manufactured through political control.
Information war operates alongside the battlefield
One of the main reasons I joined Ofer Winter and the People of Israel party is that Winter is the only general I have met who understands that the information battlefield operates alongside the kinetic battlefield – and that both are matters of national security.
The answer is not simply to spend more money. Resources distributed across disconnected bodies can generate activity without results. Israel needs a unified national framework that turns existing capabilities into a coordinated strategic force.
The People of Israel party proposes establishing a National Command for Strategic Narrative and Public Diplomacy, led by Yoseph Haddad. It would coordinate government bodies, communications professionals, technology experts, independent organizations, and international partners, while respecting institutional responsibilities and operational security.
Its mission would go beyond responding to controversies. It would monitor emerging narratives, anticipate information crises, develop proactive campaigns, mobilize credible international voices, and assess whether communications influence understanding and behavior.
The Foreign Ministry, Government Press Office and IDF Spokesperson’s Unit would remain essential. But they should form part of a broader national capability, rather than carry the burden alone.
The command must be led by experienced professionals chosen for expertise, judgment and results – not political loyalty. Public diplomacy needs its own generals: people who understand international media, audience psychology, digital platforms and narrative warfare.
International opinion affects Israel’s diplomatic relationships and its leaders’ freedom of action. Hostile narratives can spread faster than official corrections. Jewish communities and Israel’s supporters are left answering allegations without timely information or coordinated support. Meanwhile, internal disputes consume energy that should be directed toward those undermining Israel abroad.
The irony is painful. Israel has world-leading capabilities in intelligence, cybersecurity, technology and crisis response. It knows how to identify threats, assemble expertise and act urgently when the stakes demand it. The challenge is to apply that seriousness to the information battlefield – and recognize that no political office can own all the talent required to succeed.
The government must decide what it wants to protect: its monopoly over the national message, or Israel’s ability to defend itself in the world.
Israel cannot afford to turn the defense of its international standing into another arena for domestic political competition. The country’s resources and ingenuity should be directed outwards: countering hostile propaganda, strengthening alliances and making Israel’s case to the world.
The government’s responsibility is not to monopolize Israel’s voice. It is to ensure Israel has the strongest possible voice. Until that distinction is understood, we will keep fighting over who controls the effort while our adversaries exploit the vacuum.
The information war will not wait for our politics to catch up.
The writer is an Israeli politician, diplomat, and former Jerusalem city council member and deputy mayor (2016–2024). She currently serves as Israel’s special envoy for trade and innovation at the Foreign Ministry. She is also a candidate for the 26th Knesset as part of the People of Israel list.

No Persian Gulf for old carriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:47:11 UTC
02:47:11 KST

No Persian Gulf for old carriers
Top commander says American warships will never return as Strait of Hormuz becomes center of war
TEHRAN – The main confrontation between Iran and the United States in this war has been, and continues to be, in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and senior Iranian commanders now say the era when American aircraft carriers cruised these waters with impunity is over for good.
In his strongest remarks to date on the naval war, Chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces and Commander of the Central Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters, Major General Ali Abdollahi, declared that the U.S. Navy has been rendered ineffective and will never be allowed back into the Persian Gulf.
Abdollahi said: The proud Armed Forces of Islamic Iran, with trust in Almighty God, have managed to render ineffective the U.S. Navy, which Trump and the leaders of that country regard as the pinnacle of American power and with which they threaten the region and the world, in such a way that it is no longer able to approach the seas surrounding the Persian Gulf and Iran’s territorial waters.
“The U.S. president must dream of his military and army once again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave forever,” he added.
“We will under no circumstances and at no time allow American military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf,” he stressed.
From overthrow to reopening the Strait
His remarks, delivered as Washington and Tel Aviv openly speak of “finishing the job” and preparing a renewed offensive, underscore how far the war’s objectives have shifted. What began as an American-Israeli campaign to overthrow the Islamic Republic or force its surrender has now, after more than eight months of war, been reduced in practice to a struggle to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
When the war began in June 2025 with surprise strikes in the middle of negotiations, and escalated again in February 2026 and June this year, U.S. President Donald Trump promised swift collapse in Tehran, destruction of Iran’s nuclear program, and an end to its missile and regional power. None of that happened.
Instead, Iran survived, retaliated with massive missile, drone and naval operations against American bases and Israeli targets, tightened its control over the Strait of Hormuz, and imposed an unprecedented energy and military cost on Washington. Moody’s estimates the war has already cost American consumers $265 billion this year, about $2,000 per household, half of it from higher energy prices.
Today, American officials no longer speak of imminent regime change in Tehran. They speak of restoring freedom of navigation, reopening the Strait, securing detained vessels, and preventing oil prices from climbing beyond $110 per barrel after mine incidents involving tankers. In other words, the superpower that came to bring Iran to its knees is now fighting to bring its own ships back through a waterway guarded by Iran.
Abdollahi directly mocked that reversal: Trump has repeatedly claimed that they have destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities, but at the same time they keep repeating that Iran must not have nuclear weapons, and this blatant contradiction has no end.
“If you have destroyed everything, then what is the meaning of repeating these hallucinations? These remarks are utterly meaningless, contradictory and repetitive, and are consumed to deceive world public opinion and especially the American people,” he said.
“If you are sure that you have destroyed all of Iran’s military facilities and capabilities, then why do your rusted carriers, vessels and cowardly military forces not dare to approach the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s maritime and land borders?” he asked.
Fifth Fleet no longer functional
That question now defines the military map of the region. Iranian officials say U.S. forces, after suffering painful blows from the guardians of the Strait, no longer come forward from the Arabian Sea, and whenever they have taken that risk, they have harmed themselves.
Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyed Mojtaba Khamenei made the same point in his message of September 28, which Abdollahi’s statement echoed: These days [the enemy forces], because of the painful blows they have received from the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, do not come forward from the Arabian Sea, and whenever they have risked this danger, they have inflicted damage upon themselves; and soon the Arabian Sea itself will rid itself of them.
Iranian commanders say this is not rhetoric but the result of sustained, heavy strikes on the very infrastructure that once sustained American dominance in the Persian Gulf.
According to Iranian military assessments, U.S. bases around the Persian Gulf — in Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Iraq — have been repeatedly targeted since the start of the war and have suffered extensive damage. Above all, the U.S. Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, the command center of American naval power in the region for nearly three decades, has been rendered completely destroyed and unusable by Iran’s heavy missile and drone attacks.
For years, the Fifth Fleet, with its destroyers, coastal combat ships, minesweepers and logistics hub at Manama, was presented as the guarantor of American order. Iranian officials now say its piers are empty, its command facilities inoperable, and its remaining vessels forced to operate from far outside the Persian Gulf, beyond the reach of Iranian anti-ship missiles, speedboats, submarines, mines and coastal defense systems.
U.S. carriers that once docked in Bahrain and sailed routinely through Hormuz now remain in the northern Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea. Resupply requires long detours. Insurance rates have soared. Even Washington’s allies on the southern shore of the Persian Gulf, who hosted U.S. forces in hope of protection, have found their ports and airfields turned into targets and have quietly asked Washington to reduce its visible presence.
No return to pre-war order
Abdollahi said Iran’s strategy is to deepen that quagmire: Undoubtedly, with the firm resolve of the brave and wise Leadership, the will of the risen and resistant people, the self-sacrificing Armed Forces and the officials of Islamic Iran, it has been decided to drown you day by day deeper into the quagmire you have built with your own hands — America and its illegitimate offspring, the Zionist regime, and your feeble and aggressive armies.
“With the help of Almighty God and divine victory, the strategy of a strong Iran is that the longer this confrontation lasts, the deeper you will be dragged into the swamp of death and decline, God willing,” he added.
Regional and even Western analysts now concede that the security architecture of the Persian Gulf will not return to what it was before the war. For thirty years, that architecture rested on a simple assumption: unchallenged American naval supremacy, an open strait under American escort, and regional states sheltering under the U.S. umbrella while Iran was contained.
That assumption has collapsed. Iran has demonstrated it can close or control the Strait at will, strike any base in a 2,000-kilometer radius, impose costs on global energy markets, and survive direct American-Israeli bombardment. Host states have learned that hosting U.S. strike assets invites Iranian retaliation. Shipping companies have learned that transit without Iranian consent is a military risk, not a routine insurance matter.
Tehran therefore rejects talk of a return to the status quo ante through a ceasefire that merely reopens the waterway for American warships. Iranian officials insist any durable arrangement must recognize Iran’s legitimate security rights, end aggression and sanctions, and exclude U.S. military vessels from the Persian Gulf altogether.
For Tehran, the message is both military and political: the Persian Gulf is no longer permissive waters for aging carriers, rusted destroyers and expeditionary fantasies. It is, in Iranian doctrine, the front line of national defense and the lever that turned an intended war of overthrow into a war of attrition Washington cannot win.

Nigeria's Tinubu launches re-election campaign as economic pain tests support

Nigeria's Tinubu launches re-election campaign as economic pain tests support
KADUNA, Oct 24 - President Bola Tinubu formally launched his campaign for a second term on Saturday in the northern city of Kaduna, where he sought to convince voters that painful economic reforms are beginning to pay off despite a lingering cost-of-living crisis.
Tinubu, 74, faces a contest ahead of a January 16 election that is likely to be dominated by the economy and security. His main challengers include former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, who finished second and third respectively in 2023.
By midday, thousands of supporters of the president's All Progressives Congress party had filled much of the 10,000-capacity Ranchers Bees stadium, with more arriving as the rally got underway.
"Thank you for this massive showing up. It is a promise. Come 2027, January 16, you must go out massively and elect me again," Tinubu told the crowd.
OPPOSITION CREATED PROBLEMS, SAYS TINUBU
Since taking office in 2023, Tinubu has scrapped fuel subsidies, devalued the naira and introduced other reforms credited with improving public finances, foreign reserves and investor sentiment. But the measures have also fuelled Nigeria's worst cost-of-living crisis in a generation.
Petrol prices rose to about 1,400 naira ($1.05) a litre in Lagos and Abuja in September and as much as 1,500 naira in parts of northern Nigeria, adding to pressure on household budgets.
Tinubu dismissed opposition complaints about hunger and poverty, arguing that his rivals created those problems.
"They created the hunger. They created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it."
Security will provide another test. Nigeria continues to battle armed bandits and kidnappers in the northwest and a 17-year Islamist insurgency in the northeast, where militants have stepped up attacks on military positions.
Tinubu nevertheless enters the race with a formidable political machine. His camp says he has the backing of 32 of Nigeria's 36 state governors, potentially giving him an unprecedented organisational advantage, although past elections have shown governors cannot always deliver their states to presidential candidates.
His toughest electoral test could come in the north, where Atiku, a veteran northern politician with an established support base, will seek to erode the president's vote.
Tinubu has said he will not attend campaign rallies in all 36 states as he needs to remain focused on governing. The party's proposed timetable has him personally attending rallies in 12 states, culminating in a major closing rally in his home state of Lagos on January 9. REUTERS
